The Kaulāvalīnirṇaya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda; the first chapter.
Having bowed to the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Guru, who is eternally served by the Siddhas,
who generates liberation from the bondage of Śākta practitioners, and who is the definitive determination of the Kaula lineage;

I shall describe that which increases the Kula, which is always to be served by the virtuous Kaulikas with captivating dispositions, and which is the sole abode of grace for the lotus-feet [of the Guru]. || 1 ||

Jñānānandagiri—who makes the abode of his sole refuge the gracious lotus feet of Maheśa—spreads the wish-fulfilling tree of desire by means of the meaning derived from following the words of Śiva and Śivā. || 2 ||
I bow to that Great Goddess, Speech, the bestower of the power of eloquence, by whose grace one attains the determination of the true meaning of the scriptures. (3)
For the purpose of compilation, he examined the tantric texts known as the *Yāmalas* of Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu,
as well as the *Śaktiyāmala* and the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*.
The Tantracūḍāmaṇi, as well as the Kulacūḍāmaṇi, the Kulasāra, the Kuloḍḍīśa, the Kulāmṛta, and the Kulārṇava. || 5 ||
The entire essence of the Kālikākula, as well as the true nature of the Kula;
the Kulānanda of the Kālītantra, and likewise the Kulacakra. (6)
The Kālikalpa, the Mahākaula, and the Kumārītantra; the Kālītantra known as Samaya, as well as the Phetkārī and the Pheravī. || 7 ||
The Śrīkrama, the Yoginītantra, the venerable Haṃsaparameśvara, the Svatantra, the king of tantras, and thereafter the Jñānamālā. (8)
The Vāyavī, the Haṃsatantra, the Tārākālpa, the Mālinī, the Mantranirṇayatantra, and likewise the Yoginīhṛdaya; || 9 ||
The Kulārṇava, the Gāndharva, the Uḍḍīyāna, and the Toḍala; the Śivaśāsana-tantra, as well as the Mandara and the Plāvanī. || 10 ||
The Vīrābali, the Vārāhī, the Vīratantra, and the Kubjikā;
the Nīlatantra, the Matsyasūkta, and the Lalitātantra as well. (11)
The Śambhunirṇaya Tantra, the Vāmakeśvara Tantra,
the Vaṭuka Saṃhitā, and after that, the Tārārṇava. (12)
The Guptārṇava, the Caṇḍaroṣa, the Māyā, and likewise the Nīlamaṇi; the one called Samaya, the Tantrasāra, and then the Mantravimarśinī. (13)
The *Jñānasāra*, the *Yogavatī*, and the *Bhairavītantra* itself;
then the great tantra called *Bhairava* and the *Siddhasārasvata*.
The Tripurārṇava Tantra, the Uttara Tantra, the Chinnā Tantra, the Vātula, and the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā; || 15 ||
For, having seen various compendiums that are not superior, and having understood the opinion of the teachers, [he realized] this great [work], which is more essential than the essence itself. (16)
The reasoning for the secrecy of the Tantra scriptures:
It bestows the heart's desires upon those devoid of dualistic knowledge;
therefore, it must always be guarded with extreme care, like one's mother or one's own wife. (17)
It must not be given to just anyone, nor under any circumstances to one who is wicked;
likewise, one should not give it to the disciple of another, nor to a deceiver. (18)
One should protect this [teaching] in every way if one desires one's own welfare;
it is to be given to a worthy disciple who is endowed with natural conduct and devoted to service of the guru. (19)
One should cause it to be given to a disciple who is of noble birth, of great stature, devoted to the Goddess, endowed with devotion, and a spiritual practitioner (sādhaka). || 20 ||
Whoever gives [this] to just anyone, in any manner whatsoever, without having first examined them, shall be devoured by the hosts of Yoginīs; and after death, he shall go to hell. (21)
Therefore, the best of practitioners should protect this [teaching] in every way;
for that fool who has not received it from the mouth of the guru merely by looking at the book does not attain it.
If he should act solely under the influence of greed, he too will certainly perish;
for all his actions indeed lead to hell. (23)
A killer of a Brahmin would become a denizen of hell, even if he were to be eaten by the Yoginīs;
therefore, having learned this from the mouth of the Guru, one should apply effort to the practice. 24.
Śiva is the god whose nature is Brahman; Śiva is partless, having the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
He is omniscient, the creator of all, the Lord of all, and of stainless origin.

He is self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, higher than the highest, devoid of qualities, and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; those who are His portions are known as individual souls (jīvas).
Just as sparks [arise] from fire when it is affected by beginningless ignorance,
so too all [souls], though distinct due to their limiting adjuncts, are differentiated by beginningless karmas.
An exposition on the duties of a human being:
Having assumed thousands of various bodies again and again, a person becomes a human through meritorious deeds; if he is wise, he shall attain liberation. (28)
Among the eighty-four lakhs of bodies belonging to embodied beings, the knowledge of reality cannot be attained anywhere except in a human body. (29)
In that regard, through the accumulation of merit, a living being may by good fortune sometimes obtain even a single human birth among thousands of births. (30)
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and serves as a staircase to liberation, who could be more sinful than he who does not deliver himself? (31)
Furthermore, having obtained an excellent birth and the perfection of the senses, he who does not know what is beneficial for himself would be a destroyer of his own soul. (32)
Without a body, no human goal (puruṣārtha) exists for anyone;
therefore, while protecting the wealth of the body, one should accomplish meritorious deeds. || 33 ||
Action must be performed for the sake of attaining knowledge;
one should continue to perform actions as long as knowledge has not arisen.
This applies to both the knower and the ignorant, so long as there is the preservation of the body. (34)
To that extent, one should practice the conduct of one's own caste for the sake of liberation from karma;
once knowledge has been revealed by action, one shall attain the state of Śiva through that knowledge. || 35 ||
One should investigate the knowledge of reality,
or one should perform either occasional (anitya) or obligatory (nitya) duties;
for it is not possible for one who possesses a body to renounce all actions.
Reflecting that "the instruments (karaṇas) engage in their own respective functions," he who acts while thus casting off the sense of "I" is not defiled. (37)
He who abandons the fruit of action is called a renouncer;
[this applies to] actions being performed immediately after the attainment of knowledge. (38)

Just as water does not touch a lotus leaf, so too actions—whether meritorious or demeritorious—do not affect one who knows reality; for one established in reality, such actions reach their complete exhaustion.
Those established in reality never go to hell at any time;
they are always devoted to the knowledge of reality, which is innate bliss.
Having completely renounced all conceptual constructions, that wise man should abandon ritual action;
whereas those who, being unwise, have abandoned the section on rituals in vain.
Indeed, those heretics who consider themselves wise go to hell.
It is said that for one who has attained knowledge, there is no further qualification for the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa);
just as a tree, having obtained its fruit, becomes free from desire and sheds its flowers. || 42 ||
Having attained that reality, the yogi should likewise abandon the undertaking of ritual action;
even by means of a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred killings of Brahmins, [he is not bound]. (43)
Those in whose hearts Brahman resides are not smeared by merits or sins; nor are they affected by whatever actions exist on earth that arise from the tongue and the organ of generation. (44)
What will one who has renounced the tongue and the genitals accomplish through mere action?
Knowledge is of two kinds: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment; thus they declare knowledge to be twofold. (45)
Some desire the non-dual Supreme Brahman, which consists of the scripture of the Word-Brahman and is born of discernment; others desire duality. (46)
They do not know the supreme reality, which is free from duality and non-duality; there are two states leading to bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine."
A living being is bound by the notion "this is mine," and liberation occurs through the absence of "mine-ness.
This is the defining characteristic of knowledge and ignorance;
from the conjunction of knowledge and ignorance, the two sides [of bondage and liberation] are proclaimed. (48)
That action which leads to bondage is proclaimed as ignorance (avidyā);
that action which does not lead to bondage is proclaimed as knowledge (vidyā). || 49 ||
As long as the activity of conceptual construction exists, so long indeed is there bondage;
when that very [activity] no longer exists at all, then indeed is there liberation. (50)
Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, pilgrimage, the Vedas, the Shastras, the Agamas, and so forth—
all these are indeed of value only so long as one does not find the ultimate reality.
Therefore, if the steadfast one desires liberation for himself, he should with effort remain established in reality at all times and in all circumstances. (52)
I shall explain that cause by which [the goal] is quickly produced:
having received the vidyā and the means of accomplishment from the mouth of the guru according to the prescribed rule. (53)
The daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites depend upon one another in their respective order;
otherwise, one should not perform them, for doing so would result in a succession of calamities.
Having understood this, the one of great wisdom should practice in due order:
having risen in the morning, [he should meditate] upon the thousand-petaled lotus on his head.
The wise one should meditate upon his own guru, who resembles the silver mountain and is joined with a circle of light like the filaments of the rising sun. (56)
The description of the meditation on the Guru:
Seated in the vīrāsana posture, adorned with white ornaments,
wearing white garlands and garments, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Accompanied by the power of the beautiful-thighed one (Vāmoruśakti), he gazes with compassion;
his lovely body is held by the left hand of his beloved.
One should remember him, who is endowed with the bliss of primordial wisdom, preceded by his name, together with her who holds a blue lotus in her left hand and is adorned with red ornaments. (59)
The Description of Guru-Worship:
Having worshipped with mental offerings, the wise one should perform the ritual;
he should offer fragrance whose essence is the earth, and thereafter, the flower of contemplation (bhāvapuṣpa).
Incense, which is of the nature of air, should be offered, as well as a lamp of the nature of fire;
one should offer nectar as the food offering and water, which is of the nature of Varuṇa, as the drink.
Then, having worshipped according to the procedure for each respective mudrā, one should worship the Guru;
after displaying the yonimudrā, one should then recite the mantra of the Guru.
11) Having written the word *hsauḥ* according to the procedure for the guru-mantra, [one writes] the letters *sa-ha-kṣa-ma-la-va-ra-a-n-i-lā*.
Having written them joined with fire (the letter Ra) in three ways, they are endowed with the first [vowels] and the three long [vowels].
One should place [the letters] joined with Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā at the end of Śrīparā,
and then the station of the one to be worshipped (Ārādhya), and after that, the entire station above.
At the end of "Nātha Sarvaguru," one should then add "Guru Svayam";
thereafter, at the end of the word "Śrīgurunātha," one should append the syllables sa-ha-ka-sa-ma-la-va-ra-a-ni-la.

One should write the first [syllable] as a compound consisting of the fire [letter], the long [vowel], and their opposites, joined with the resonance (nāda), the point (bindu), and the digit (kalā); then one should write the fourth [syllable].
The third [line] should be written as before, and the second likewise;
then, after the venerable Śambhu and the Guru, one should again write the first [line].
The first peak-syllable, the fourth, again the first, and the third—this mantra of the Guru is adorned with forty letters of the path. (68)
One should perform recitation according to one's capacity, or otherwise recite the Vāgbhava mantra:
"Ga" (the letter *ga*) joined with the right ear (*ra*), followed by "Gau" (the letter *au*), and adorned with fire (*ra*) and Rudra (*ha*). (69)
The mantra consisting of two syllables bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
the letter *ga* is declared to be the giver of perfection (*siddhi*), and the letter *ra* is the remover of sin. (70)
The syllable *U* is Viṣṇu, the unmanifest, the essence of the triad, the supreme Guru.
Having offered that [mantra] into the left hand of the Guru, one should then recite the hymn of praise. (71)
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. (72)
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
"I am firmly Śambhu, the Supreme Self of all, who has transcended the universe"—by whose command this is so, therefore there is remembrance of his venerable sandals (śrīpādukā). 74.
On a thousand-petalled lotus, he is free from deceit and has transcended other scriptures;
he is eternally worshipped by the gods and is the sole cause for destroying the fear of worldly existence.
With his two hands, he displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, his face radiant with a gentle smile.
I bow to such a form, the form of the supreme guru, endowed with compassion.

I perpetually bow to Śiva— the peaceful one with a white body, three eyes, adorned with a lovely form, who grants both desires and protection, and who is like the sun that illuminates the fierce darkness of ignorance;
likewise, I bow to my Guru, who is like the sun and the helmsman for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
The nectar arising from whose glorious lotus feet is constantly drunk by the perfected ones (siddhas). || 76 ||
I perpetually bow to the lotus feet of the Guru, who always dwells in the center of the lunar mandala;
by whose grace I have obtained the seed for the destruction of knowledge along with its latent impressions (vāsanās). (77)
Even the lords of the hosts of gods, born from the lotus, constantly meditate upon whose stainless lotus-feet;
he is an ocean of compassion and the sole repository of all virtues.
This very Guru is within the center of a white lotus upon the head. || 78 ||
For those who have been cast into the midst of the ocean of worldly existence, submerged by the snares of increasing passion and the flavors consisting of all the illusions of *māyā*,
even a mere fragment of compassion from whose feet acts as a boat removes their bondage.
With joy, he also paid homage to him who was the form of the Guru, full of compassion. || 79 ||
Poetic skill, scholarship, sovereignty over the three worlds, or indeed never at any time the attainment of heaven, nor certainly equality with the best of gods;
we do not desire liberation, nor the station of the Destroyer of Cities, nor even the state of Śiva.
If my mind were to dwell limitlessly upon the lotus feet of the Guru... (80)
Having praised with this hymn, one should then receive the command of the Guru and meditate upon the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti residing in the Mūlādhāra.
The description of Kuṇḍalinī:
She has the form of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), is thinner than a lotus fiber, resembles a sleeping serpent in shape, and is endowed with three and a half coils. || 82 ||
Having raised up the Great Goddess, who is wreathed in self-manifested liṅgas and possesses the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning, the practitioner [should do so] with the *prāṇamantra*.
Having pierced the six cakras and having established [the consciousness] above that in the Lord residing in the thousand-spoked [cakra], one should meditate upon the lineage gurus in succession.
Prahlādānandanātha, Sanakānandanātha, Kumārānandanātha, and Vasiṣṭhānandanātha. || 85 ||
The practitioner, having worshipped Krodhānanda, Sukhānanda, and Jñānānanda, and thereafter Bodhānanda, should proceed in this sequence. (86)
Their hearts were overflowing with the joy of the supreme nectar, their eyes were rolling,
and all darkness was completely shattered and pulverized by the embrace of the Supreme Goddess.

Surrounded by their noble disciples, with their inner hearts uplifted in joy, they were the knowers of the entire reality and meaning of the Kula principles, bestowing the gestures of boons and fearlessness.

Thus, having bowed to the lineage-gurus along with their powers and their families—which have been described as bringing happiness—and having caused a rain of nectar to fall, [he should proceed]. (89)
Having gratified that goddess, one should bring her back again to the root;
one should then contemplate one's own body as pervaded by the masses of her radiance.
"I am the Goddess and none other; I am Brahman alone, not subject to sorrow.
I am of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss"—thus one should contemplate the Self. (91)
When the excellent practitioner has gone outside and sees a family tree,
he should diligently pay homage to the Kula and likewise to the Lord of the Kula.
The names of the family trees are:
Aśoka, Keśara, Karṇikāra, Cūta, Tilaka, as well as Nameru, Piyāla, Sindhuvāraka, and Kadambaka. || 93 ||
The maruvaka, the campaka tree, and twelve family trees; or else, I shall describe the family trees for the sake of perfect accomplishment. (94)
Śleṣmātaka, karañja, nimba, aśvattha, kadambaka, bilva, vaṭa, udumbara, and ciñcā is recorded as the tenth. || 95 ||
The Kula-yoginīs always reside within the Kula-trees;
one should not sleep beneath a Kula-tree, nor should one commit any offense against it. 96.
Having seen it, one should pay homage with devotion and never cut it;
one should write the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), the god of desire (Kāmadeva), and finally the word "janam."
This mantra, which reaches the very core of the heart, is for the purification of the teeth;
having thus purified the teeth and so forth, one should then perform the rites prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
If one worships the Goddess with devotion without having performed the morning rites,
that worship is fruitless, just like a ritual action devoid of purity. (99)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter: An Exposition on the Purification of the Self.
Now, I shall describe the ritual bath for the sake of attaining success by the followers of Śakti.
The procedure for bathing: having obtained water according to the rules, one should [proceed] to the temple of the deity. || 1 ||
Having reflected thus, the wise man should bow to Varuṇa, the deity of the waters;
then, having emerged and risen up, he should hold a bundle of *darbha* grass from his family.
One should wear the *pavitra* and keep the hands from being empty by using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass;
in this matter, those following the Śākta tradition should take [the materials] themselves, for wild *kuśa* grasses are not true *kuśas*.
Gold should be placed on the two ring fingers and silver likewise on the two index fingers;
this indeed is the *darbha*, for the *darbha* is not merely that which grows in the forest.
There is never a worship of the Goddess without *dūrvā* grass;
therefore, *dūrvā* must be taken up, for it consists of all flowers.

Holding a blade of *dūrvā* grass in his hand, he should perform all ritual actions; he should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the mantras beginning with the *ātmatattva* and others, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *svadhā*. (6)
The practitioner of mantra should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, heart, and head in three ways; he should then perform the binding of the ears and eyes with mantras.
Having first faced the east, or even facing the north,
the practitioner [should offer oblations] at the end of the root mantra for the Atmatattva, and thereafter for the Vidyātattva.
Having uttered "to the Śiva-principle," the most excellent practitioner,
being wise, should perform the ceremonial sipping (ācamana) with water ending in "svāhā," facing either the east or the north in due order.
Then, having consecrated a worthy vessel along with dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and water, the lord of heroes should place it in the water while reciting the mantra.

Having invoked the sacred water (tīrtha) from the orb of the sun by means of the goad mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā), and having recited the root mantra ten times, one should sprinkle that water upon one's head.
Reciting the root mantra with the mudrā called Kumbhaka,
the eminent practitioner should block the mouth, ears, nose, and eyes with his fingers.
Recalling the root mantra, one should emerge from the water three times and wipe the limbs;
then, one should apply the *tilaka* and fashion the topknot (*śikhā*) with the root mantra. (13)
Then, having sipped water three times, the practitioner of mantra should perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa).
Taking water in the left hand with the right hand, [he should proceed]. (14)

Then, having covered the sky [with the syllable *haṃ*], one should next cover it with air (*yaṃ*) and fire (*raṃ*), and then consecrate the seed-syllables of earth (*laṃ*) and water (*vaṃ*) three times.
Having recited the root mantra seven times with the mudrā known as Tattva,
one should sprinkle the water upon one's own head and place the remainder in the right hand.
Having meditated upon water consisting of light, one should then draw it up through the left nostril;
having thus lifted the sin residing within the body, one should wash it away with the [water] from the left [nostril].
Having pushed it aside, the wise man should crush it upon a prepared slab of diamond-stone;
then, having washed both hands, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). || 18 ||
Then one should say: "To Mārtaṇḍabhairava, whose mantra consists of *māyā* and *prāṇa*, and who is endowed with the power of illumination (*prakāśaśakti*), [this] *arghya*, svāhā! (19)
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun, the *śakti-sandhyā* is proclaimed;
then, having visualized the *yantra* before him, [he should worship] the Goddess there, accompanied by her attendants.
Then, having taken scented water from the family vessel, the best of practitioners should duly offer libations into the mouths of the deities according to the rite. (21)
Having fully uttered the root mantra, at its end one should place the name of the deity in the accusative case, followed by the words "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) and the word "namas. (22)
At the end of the root mantra, "I satiate" (tarpayāmi) should be added, followed by "svāhā"; such is the libation (tarpaṇa).
[One should likewise offer it] to the Guru along with his retinue, as well as to the weapons and the vehicles.
Having offered libations according to one's capacity, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra according to one's capacity,
while meditating upon the Goddess who dwells within the solar orb together with her retinue.
At the end of the root-mantra, while [the breath] resides in the rising sun, immediately thereafter, one should recollect "to Śiva-consciousness, to her, to me, svāhā" at its conclusion.
Then, having offered the *arghya* to her and brought her forth with the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the practitioner, having established her in his heart by means of the mudrā, rises from the water. (26)
One should wear two garments of the family (kula) cloth with the root mantra;
for one seeking liberation, it should be red cloth, and for one seeking enjoyment, white cloth. (27)
For killing, one should always wear black clothing; for subjugation, red;
for expulsion, a tiger skin; and for auspicious rites, tree bark.
Having put on [the garment], the practitioner, remaining silent, should touch the mantra in his heart; then, having washed his hands and feet, he should enter the place of worship. (29)
Since worship without bathing is fruitless, bathing is prescribed as that which bestows eligibility;
for one who is devoid of bathing and libations (tarpaṇa), there is no eligibility for worship.
Endowed with a spirit of devotion and various ritual services, worship performed without bathing is fruitless and a cause for the loss of spiritual accomplishments. (31)
Therefore, having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminary rites, one should thereafter put on red garments. Then follows the determination of the place of worship:
at a solitary liṅga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, by a river, on a mountain peak, in a thicket, in a deserted place, in an underground chamber, or in a temple; || 33 ||
Or else, near an aśvattha tree, at the root of a vaṭa tree, on a trident-shaped spot, in a marketplace, in one's own house, or in a place free from the sight of cattle. (34)
The worship should always be performed either in a royal pavilion, or in a mountain cave, or in a secure, gapless pavilion. (35)
p. 23) The etymology of Ekaliṅga is the place of worship; it is declared to be the supreme sacred seat (pīṭha) of the Great Goddess.
Within the interior of the five sheaths, where one perceives no other sign.
They call that the Single Linga; therein is unsurpassed accomplishment.
Regarding the definition of a crossroads:
one should recognize a crossroads as that place where the stone of Caṇḍikā resides. (37)
In that regard, those who desire accomplishment should proceed with effort and perform recitation;
having then gone to the gateway, they should worship the deities of the gate.
There, the excellent practitioner should likewise cause musical instruments and the like to be played, along with dance and song,
using white mustard seeds, unbroken rice grains, and dūrvā grass mixed with sesame seeds.
May those beings depart who are stationed upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. (40)
Having uttered the mantra beginning with Vāgbhava and, by means of the Nārāca-mudrā,
the wise practitioner should expel those who have become obstacles to the Kula, and then enter the sacrificial ground.
One should fashion the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) according to the rules prescribed in the tantra;
four lines should be drawn by joining the directions of Indra (east) and Varuṇa (west).
From north to south, let there be nine compartments;
in the directions of Indra (east), Agni (southeast), Yama (south), Nairṛta (southwest), and the West (Paścima), there shall be five groups.

For the sake of attaining success, the practitioner should inscribe four *laks* each of the letters beginning with *ya*, *ra*, and *la* respectively in the directions of Vāyu, Kubera, and Śambhu. (44)
Then, in the central square, one should fashion a nine-square grid as before;
from the east to the northeast, one should inscribe the sixteen vowels.
Following the sequence beginning with the letter 'a', according to the division of each pair of letters,
that place where the syllable of the field (kṣetra) and so forth resides is determined to be its head.
That indeed shall be the place for the lamp; therein lies unsurpassed accomplishment.
[Otherwise], one becomes destitute at the feet, and there is certainly disease in the flanks. (47)
One should always know that there is loss in the tail; one should always take recourse to the location of the lamp.
Indeed, he who performs recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa) without the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) [incurs misfortune]. 48.
One should know that all of that is fruitless and serves only for malevolent magic.
Whatever is performed by one devoid of the five purities is as if it were not performed at all; such is the teaching on the five purities.
As long as one does not perform that [preliminary rite], how can there be worship of the deity? Without the fivefold purity, worship leads to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). (50)
Purity of the ground, purity of oneself, as well as the purification of the ritual substances, purity of the mantra, and purity of the deity—this is declared to be the fivefold purity. (51)
I shall explain the fivefold purification according to the prescribed sequence;
thereafter, the practitioner should prepare the general arghya for the purpose of sprinkling.
Then one should draw a square, a circle, and a triangle to the left;
there, having worshipped the fire-mandala, one should place the support.
Having sprinkled the vessel with the Astra-mantra and placed it there, one should worship it;
having recited the Sūryamaṇḍala-mantra, one should worship it with the Hṛdaya-mantra. || 54 ||
Then, having drawn a mandala in the water as before, one should worship it;
having honored the lunar mandala, one should cast into it perfumes and flowers.
Having invoked the Tīrtha as before, one should then worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions—namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center. (56)
One should recite the root mantra eight times and sprinkle [the area] with that water;
having uttered the root mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should [protect] oneself on the sacrificial grounds.
Then, having offered arghya to the Earth in the southwest, the best of practitioners should utter the Praṇava, followed by "Bhagavati," and then "Dharani" with the suffix "Ṅi. (58)
Having offered the *arghya* with "Svāhā to Dharaṇīvedhas," and having worshipped Brahmā and the personage known as Vāstu; || 59 ||
By means of sweeping, smearing with unguents, and so forth, it should possess a luster like the surface of a mirror;
it should be adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, and flower garlands.

The purification of the ground is said to consist of a mandala painted with powders of five colors; having drawn the mandala on the ground as before, the foremost of practitioners [should proceed]. (61)
One should establish the seat there according to the Tantras;
now I shall describe the seat for the sake of the stability of the Śaktas. (62)
Regarding the description of various seats such as the soft one: seated upon a soft *cūḍaka* or on other soft things,
or seated upon a grass mat (*viṣṭara*), one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
The wise say that a fetus which has fallen [prematurely] within six months is "mṛdu" (soft);
they know one who is devoid of the tonsure and initiation ceremonies as "mṛdu," specifically as an "acūḍaka" (one without tonsure).
A boy who has completed the tonsure ceremony but whose initiation (upanayana) has not yet been performed—if he dies in his fifth year, they know him as "Komala. (65)
Regarding the description of various seats:
indeed, he who worships the auspicious Caṇḍikā without a soft seat shall remain a denizen of hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
A seat made of fifty blades of kuśa grass is for Brahmā, while one made of half that number is for Viṣṭara.
Silk is said to bestow enjoyment, and a red woolen blanket is remembered as granting success.
Clothing is known to remove disease; liberation and prosperity are found in a tiger skin;
wool is said to remove suffering; and the accomplishment of knowledge resides in a deer skin. (68)

But for a renunciant (sannyāsī) who is a celibate student (brahmacārī), there is this distinction: he should not sit upon a black antelope skin or a wooden seat, where he might become unfortunate. (69)
One should avoid a seat that is too high, too low, or sunken; a seat that is captivating to the mind, soft, and smooth is highly recommended. (70)
Having obtained one of these for the purification of the seat,
one should thereafter sprinkle it with the water of the general *arghya* by means of the ritual of the cupped hands (*puṭāñjali*).
Merupṛṣṭha is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is said to be the meter (chandas),
and Kūrma is the presiding deity (adhidevatā) for the installation of the seat.
The application (viniyoga) should be fully understood and recited; then one should say:
"O Goddess Earth, you uphold the worlds," and thereafter utter the mantra. (73)
"You were upheld by Viṣṇu; therefore, uphold me as well.
Make [this] seat eternally pure," and one should recite this. (74)
With this [mantra] beginning with the *praṇava*, one should cast three blades of *kuśa* grass there;
having consecrated the *ādhāraśakti*, one should invoke the Lotus-Seated One (*kamalāsana*) joined with the suffix *-ṅe*.
Having recited the mantra ending with the heart [seed-syllable] and preceded by Māyā (Hrīṃ), the practitioner should worship;
thereafter, he should sit upon the seat in the vīrāsana posture.
One should place the right ankle upon the left thigh and the left ankle below it;
with the body and neck held straight, one should maintain the body in a straight posture. (77)
Then, having assumed a straight neck, one should perform the supreme vīrāsana;
facing the direction of Kāmākhyā or facing east, remaining well-composed, one should perform the worship.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial grounds with water from the general *arghya* vessel.
Thus has the procedure for the seat in worship been described to you here. (79)

Having bathed in the pure waters of his family within a flawless dwelling, and having prepared the vessel of offerings (arghyapātra), he who— endowed with devotion and faith— draws the King of Yantras upon the lotus of his own lineage,
worships it with well-born young women adorned with vermilion, and performs the recitation (japa), for him prosperity shines eternally in the lotus of his eyes and eloquence in the moon of his face.
It was gathered on the sacrificial grounds by initiated women of noble birth, who were young, of pure character, and devoted to the deities and their gurus.
Various kinds of flowers and diverse fragrances, scented with camphor, agallochum, incense, and the like, and perfumed with fine cloth. || 82 ||
Betel, a beverage, incense, lamps, and so forth—
adorned with all ornaments and decorations, the supreme practitioner [offers these]. (83)
One should sprinkle the sacrificial materials with water consecrated by reciting the root-vidyā;
having placed everything on one's right, one should set the water-pot (kumbha) on the left.
In the western direction, one should place the ritual substances of the deity's family;
alternatively, the food offering (naivedya) should be placed to the right, the left, or in front, but never behind.
Alternatively, one should offer it from the left, but never from behind;
one should place the lamp on the right or in front, but not on the left.
One should offer incense on the palm of the left hand, either in front [of oneself] or not on the right;
one should present perfumes, flowers, ornaments, and so forth in the space before [the deity].
A wise person should always discard a flower that is dirty, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, hair, or the like, touched by a limb [of the body], or smelled.
One should not offer even a flower bud by splitting it in two;
nor should one offer red arghya, white dūrvā grass, nīlakaṇṭha, or kuruṇṭaka flowers.
One who desires one's own welfare should not give [these] to Mahādevī;
rather, one should worship her with fragrant white and red flowers and with kuśa grass.
One should not worship the Goddess with auspicious leaves such as bilva, maruvaka, and others, provided they are devoid of tulasī; nor should one worship her without bilva leaves. (91)
One should not worship with scentless flowers, but rather with fragrant flowers and all kinds of substances,
such as the *javā*, *bandhūka*, *mandāra*, *sindūra*, and great blue lotuses (*mahotpala*).
And one should worship with fragrant flowers as well as with red sandalwood,
nandyāvarta, tilapatra, and likewise keśarapatra.
With madana, maruvaka, pomegranate, and kunda flowers, and with various charming offerings and oblations consisting of diverse flowers; || 94 ||
The wise one [should worship] her with auspicious Apāmārga leaves, Bhṛṅgas, and Tulasī-free [offerings], as well as with family-specific flowers, incense, and the family-specific lamp. 95.
The wise one should worship Caṇḍikā; otherwise, she creates obstacles to success.
One who worships Tārā and Kālī should not offer jasmine flowers.
The high-souled practitioner must not give that which is stale;
there is no fault in using water-born lotuses, blue lilies, or campaka flowers [even if they have stood overnight]. 97.
One should place the flowers of one's own deity separately in vessels within the waters of the Agastya-vakula, as well as the bilva and the Gaṅgā. || 98 ||
One who desires one's own welfare should not effect a unification [of the deity with oneself]; know for certain that this applies to all offerings, such as the *naivedya* and so forth. (99)
But when the time for worship has arrived, he who remembers Vāsudeva does not obtain the fruit of the worship and instead falls into hell.
Having touched Vaiṣṇava flowers at all times during the period of worship,
one should perform purification by washing the hands and then carry out the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Without the Śakti, worship is fruitless;
therefore, having become pure and attentive, and endowed with devotion and faith, one should establish the Śakti, who is devoted to her Lord, on one's left side. (102)
She is clothed in red garments, initiated, and possesses a beautiful smile;
for without the Śakti, worship is fruitless—of this there is no doubt. (103)
Therefore, the hero should become endowed with power through diligent effort;
that which is power is the Great Goddess, while the practitioner is the form of Hara.
Divinity arises precisely from mutual contemplation;
for without the vital breath (prāṇa), the embodied being is unable to move at all. 105.
In that case, one would have no authority to perform worship even without the *śakti*;
worship must be performed with its proper cause,
for without the consecration of the materials (*dravyādhivāsa*), one should never recite mantras nor ever practice meditation.
Without first tasting it with the causal [mantra], a person would become agitated;
he should perform neither worship nor recitation, neither meditation nor contemplation. (107)
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
one should know this to be the truth, the word spoken by Śaṅkara. 108.

There is no fault of sequential death, nor is there any corruption by a defect in conduct; one need not worry about having eaten or drunk, nor that one might fail to remember or recite [the mantra] at that time.
Those foolish men who remember [other deities] encounter suffering at every step;
for he who worships Caṇḍikā without joy [is likewise lost]. (110)
He too shall become diseased and miserable, and upon death, he shall go to hell;
therefore, at the outset, one must perform the preparation of the *samvit* and *āsava*.
The superiority of consciousness:
between consciousness and liquor, consciousness alone is more weighty.
That man who performs meditation after having taken Vijayā [the goddess of victory]— || 112 ||
Then, his form consisting of meditative absorption becomes manifest to him;
therefore, the best of practitioners employ that consciousness here in worship and other rites. (113)
And a great worship (mahāpūjā) should be performed by those who rejoice in the nature of compassion;
I shall explain its divisions according to their true meaning, following the path of the Tantra. (114)
And she is of four kinds:
the Brāhmaṇī has white flowers, while the Kṣatriyā is known to be red;
the Vaiśyā has yellow blossoms, and the Śūdrā has black flowers. (115)
I shall now state their purification mantras and the purification mantra for these [other goddesses] individually:
"O Samvidā, born of Brahmā, daughter of Brahmā, forever sinless! (116)
"Be forever gracious for the sake of the satisfaction of the Bhairavas.
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmāṇī, svāhā; thus one should purify Brahmāṇī. || 117 ||

O Goddess, you who are the root-activity of accomplishment, who suppresses and overcomes all obstacles; O you who bring kings and subjects under your control, you who wield the trident against the throats of enemies! (118)
Oṃ ai& namaḥ svāhā to Kṣatriyā; this is remembered as the mantra of Kṣatriyā.
O fire kindled by the fuel of ignorance, O fire of knowledge, you whose form is knowledge! || 119 ||
Grant me the oblation of bliss, joy, and perfect knowledge.
Hrīṃ, salutation to the Vaiśya woman, Svāhā! Then one should purify the Śūdra woman. 120.
Oṃ! I pay homage, I pay homage to you, O Mother who reveals the path of yoga;
O Conqueror of the Three Worlds, grant me the fruit of meditative absorption. 121.
*Klīṃ* (*Śrīṃ*) *śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā*—this is declared to be the supreme mantra. Then follows the words: *Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi*. (122)

"Amṛtam ākarṣaya dvandvam, siddhiṃ dehi" (Draw forth the nectar, O couple; grant success), and after that, "trailokyaṃ me" (the three worlds for me), and after that, one should say "vaśam ānaya" (bring under control). 123.
This mantra, ending with two *ṭha*s, is proclaimed for the purification of the four groups;
or else, it is *hasakṣamalavarayūṃ* followed by *hasarauṃ*. (124)
"Ānandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ" is the other mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*.
Then, having purified the Vijayā with either one of these two [mantras], || 125 ||
The procedure for seizing Vijayā is sevenfold; one should recite the root mantra over them and display the Āvāhanī and other mudrās, as well as the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās. || 126 ||
One should perform the binding of the directions with three snaps of the fingers;
one should ward off obstacles with a divine gaze and kicks of the feet. (127)
The excellent practitioner should satisfy the group of gurus seven times upon the head;
and by means of the ritual of the *tattva-mudrā*, he should satisfy the Goddess together with her attendants in the heart.
Having gratified the Great Goddess, he should then offer [the remainder] to the Śaktis;
then, taking it with his left hand, he should recite this mantra.
Having first uttered "aiṃ vadavada padaṃ," then "vāgvādini," one should thereafter write "mama jihvāgre sthirā bhava sarva. (130)
Immediately thereafter, the best of practitioners seeking liberation should accept [the offering] with the mantra "Sattvavaśaṅkari svāhā," while observing with composure. (131)
Regarding the description of the alternative methods for the practice of Vijayā:
it should be consumed sequentially during the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, with milk, ghee, honey, and wine serving as the respective post-medicinal vehicles (anupāna). || 132 ||
She, who bestows accomplishment and is the root of accomplishment, should be worshipped once, twice, thrice, or five times a day, in due order. (133)

One must maintain secrecy regarding the mantra while practicing with Vijayā; likewise, the consumption of the sacramental wine (samvid-āsava) should be performed in such a way that there is no public disclosure at the assembly of initiates (paśu-melaka). 134.
It should always be performed in a secluded place and in the presence of the guru; it should not be done in the presence of one's father, nor likewise in the presence of one's mother. (135)
Or rather, one should not even look at birds or insects;
[one should avoid] family flowers, family substances, family worship, and family recitation. (136)

One should by no means reveal the Guru, the head of the lineage (kulapati), the lineage garland (kulamālā), the lineage and non-lineage (kulākula), the lineage wheel (kulacakra), or the lineage meditation (kuladhyāna). || 137 ||
From manifestation comes the loss of accomplishment; from manifestation comes bondage and the like;
from manifestation comes the destruction of mantras; from manifestation comes the harming of the deity. (138)
If death should occur through exposure, it must never be revealed;
however, when the time for worship has arrived, if anyone should happen to enter here— || 139 ||
One should indeed display the Vaiṣṇava mudrā, as well as the Viṣṇu-nyāsa and the hymn of praise;
if there is concealment due to public exposure, that exposure is not a fault.

(38) If manifestation were to occur through concealment and the like, yet there is never any manifestation, it would be better not to perform worship at all, for there is never any manifestation. || 141 ||
The procedure for worship:
Wearing red garlands and garments, accompanied by a woman, noble-minded, with his mouth filled with betel-leaf, and fragrant with the scent of incense. || 142 ||
Having become a god, one should worship the God; one who is not a god should not worship the God. With hands made fragrant by perfume and flowers, [one should worship] with the Astra-mantra.
The best of practitioners should perform the purification by reciting the root mantra over one another;
having performed the wiping three times with the left hand while using the *astra* mantra. (144)
The mantra-practitioner should cast that flower from afar with the nārāca-mudrā,
having joined the tip of the index finger to the tip of the thumb along a line running downward and upward.
Likewise, the arrow mudrā consists of extending the other fingers upward;
having meditated upon the Guru, one should place him on the left, and likewise Gaṇapati on the right.
Thereafter, the practitioner should [invoke] his own goddess in the center, with slaps from the heels, clapping of the hands, and faces turned upward. (147)
39) In that regard, one should perform the three *tālas* with sound according to the oral tradition. This is the procedure for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
For one who lacks breath control (prāṇāyāma), [the fruits of] recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, [are lost]. || 148 ||
Actions performed with effort do not bear fruit at all;
therefore, before the recitation, those who are composed should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). 149.
Otherwise, all recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, are fruitless;
[the rites should be performed] according to the sequence of six, four, six, six, and three [units]. 150.

Having recited the *praṇava* with its constituent measures (*mātrās*) through the processes of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), [one should do so] through the left, the middle, and likewise the right channels (*nāḍīs*). || 151 ||
The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*. (152)
(Alternatively,) the knower of mantras should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with either the root mantra or the syllable Om;
while uttering the syllable Om, he should do so with only the left nostril. 153.
Having filled the abdomen with air until it remains steady, this indeed becomes prāṇāyāma known as pūraka, which fills the body. (154)
Having covered all the limbs and being devoid of inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled water-pot; that is the *kumbhaka* breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Likewise, the knower of mantras should release the breath with a single exhalation;
joined with the practice of breathing out, he should expel the air through the external [nostril]. (156)
This is indeed declared to be *recaka* breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), without a doubt;
having circumambulated the knees, neither too quickly nor too slowly. (157)
The snapping of the fingers is declared to be one *mātrā*;
then, with twelve *mātrās*, the wise perform the inhalation (*pūraka*). (158)
Therefore, the pure exhalation (recaka) is performed with twice that measure;
likewise, the retention (kumbhaka) is performed with twice that measure. || 159 ||
The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is described as follows: by means of three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should perform for each [element] a triad;
the sign to be produced is the consciousness residing in the heart, the witness of all. (160)
Having drawn it out through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) by means of the syllable Om,
the wise one should enclose it with that very same syllable and place it above the head.
The body, both external and internal, is devoid of consciousness;
it resides in the center of the navel-mandala and within the center of the wind-mandala.
Having meditated upon whichever seed-syllable is grey and scorched, one should purify each respective [impurity] by means of the seed-syllable RAṂ,
which has the form of fire and is situated within a circle of fire.
Then, having burned it away, that heap of ashes would take the form of a body;
one should meditate upon the mandala of Varuṇa situated between the eyebrows or in the heart.
[One should visualize] a white [moon] in the shape of a half-moon, adorned on the right with two lotuses;
one should cause it to overflow by means of the syllable *va* situated therein, which has the form of nectar.
Having placed the living soul (jīva) within the earthly [element], one should contemplate a golden mandala;
having divided it into two by means of the Praṇava, which consists of the nature of consciousness, [one should place the soul] therein.
Having placed it upon the head, one should unite it with consciousness;
thus the body is bathed in nectar, and that mortal is cleansed of all impurities.
Thereafter, one should contemplate oneself in the form of the deity;
then, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is taught, as well as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 168 ||
Alternatively, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is described in another manner:
having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then carry out the purification of the elements.

(42) Without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), worship is fruitless; without the purification of the elements, rituals such as recitation, fire-offerings, and adoration are likewise ineffective.
All that, even if performed with great illumination, is entirely fruitless for that long.

Indeed, for one who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the entire web of placements is in vain, and that worship shall become fruitless. || 171 ||
Therefore, the best of practitioners should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, the Tantrika [should draw] the vital breath from the mūlādhāra through the path of Brahman.
One should unite the *haṃsa* with the *puṣkara*, that is, with the Supreme Self;
by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), one should extract the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
Having performed the drying, burning, and floating [of the elements] by means of the syllables of wind, fire, and water,
the practitioner of mantra should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to this procedure.
The Installation of the Life-force of the Deity in One’s Own Body:
Having visualized himself in the form of the deity, the most excellent practitioner should thereafter install the life-force of the deity within his own body. (175)
The wise one should perform the placement (nyāsa) either with flowers, or with water, or even mentally.
The mantra prescribed for the placement of the vital breath (jīva-nyāsa) should be employed in all instances of jīva-nyāsa.
Having uttered the *mukhavṛtta* of the *jīvanīyasamantra*, the *haṃsa* is reversed;
thus, in sequence, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are here the vital breaths, and likewise the life-force (*jīva*) is established here. (177)
Again, for that [deity], all the sense organs [are worshipped], followed by the word "pada" (foot) for that [deity];
then the words for speech, mind, eye, ear, nose, and breath, each followed by "pada. (178)
Then, having come here, may they remain happily for a long time—this is the pair of *ṭha* syllables.
Alternatively, there is the seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśa*), the syllable of modesty (*lajjā*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*) itself. (179)
Thereafter, one should perform the *prāṇamantra* and the remaining rites as before; this is declared to be the *jīvanyāsa-mantra*, which one should employ in all instances of *jīvanyāsa*. (180)
Then the excellent practitioner should perform the ritual assignments (nyāsa) and so forth as prescribed in his own tantra;
the mudrās, locations, and mantras for the six limbs are now declared. (181)
Following the sequence of three, two, one, ten, three, two, and one nights, [the mantras are applied] to the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, the eyes, and the weapon. (182)
One should apply, in sequence, the utterances *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*;
[the mantra] should be joined with the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the deity, the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the power (*śakti*). (183)
The practitioner should place everything, conjoined with the syllable *ṅe* and fixed with the *kīla*, upon these:
he should place them on the head, face, heart, secret parts, feet, and all the limbs. (184)
Then one should perform the assignment of the six limbs by the very same method previously described;
that which is the specific distinction in the assignment of the fifty syllables is now stated. (185)
One should place the ring finger and the middle finger on the path of the mouth at the forehead;
the index, middle, and ring fingers, along with the thumb and the ring finger, [are placed] on the two eyes.
Placing the thumbs on the ears, the little fingers and thumbs on the nostrils, the three middle fingers on the cheeks, and one should place the middle fingers on the lips. (187)
Placing the ring finger between the two teeth, the middle finger on the head, the ring and middle fingers in the mouth, and [the remaining fingers] on the hands, feet, and sides; 188.
One should place those [fingers]—the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger—on the back;
all of them, including the thumb, one should place on the region of the navel, and [all] on the belly.

First, one should strike the palm on the heart, then on the two shoulders and the region of the hump; first the heart, then the hands and feet, and likewise the palms on the sides and the mouth. (190)
These mudrās of the Mātṛkās have thus been proclaimed in their proper order;
for him who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing them, that placement shall be fruitless.
The placement of the fifty syllables has been revealed in their proper sequence; they may begin with *Oṃ* and end with *Namaḥ*, or include the nasal bindu, or be devoid of the bindu. (192)
The wise say that [the seed-syllables] preceded by the *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, and *bījapūra* should be placed;
or else, they should be placed alone, joined with the *sarga* and the *bindu*, and endowed with the *kalās*. (193)

One should place [the mantra] ending with the third Rudra and Śakti, endowed with Smara and the others as its filaments, preceded by Śakti, joined with Śrī, or having nectar as its face, upon the body.
The Mātṛkā-mantra consists of the Śakti, the Śrī-bīja, and the Kāma-bīja at its end, preceded by the Vedas and the Śakti;
it is the Ajapā, the Supreme Self, and the sacrifice of the dualistic phenomenal world. || 195 ||
She is said to consist of twelve [suns] and to have the nature of the final letter of the Mātṛkā;
in whichever form one’s own inclination lies, one should contemplate her in that very form within one’s own body.
Having performed the placement [of the mantras], the practitioner of mantra, becoming one with them, attains the state of Vāgīśvarī;
the wise one should perform the placement either by touching, or by speech, or even mentally.
One should conclude with the [mantra] pervading from the Ṛṣi up to the end, as prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa).
Through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other such ritual placements (nyāsa), the purification of the self (ātmaśuddhi) arises. || 198 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter: Exposition of the Inner Sacrifice. Having fully explained the purification of the self, the inner sacrifice is now described.
Having performed the rite of the inner sacrifice, one should perform the outer sacrifice.
One who is devoid of internal sacrifice has no authority for external sacrifice;
never, without internal worship, is there any fruit from external sacrifice.
Therefore, the hero should diligently commence the internal sacrifice (antaryāga),
having performed a shower of nectar through the union of Śiva and Śakti, as described in the section on mental worship.
Having gratified the Great Goddess in each and every lotus,
the excellent practitioner should then bring her down to the *mūlādhāra* and contemplate "I am He."
Thus has been declared the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows all accomplishments;
or rather, I shall now describe the internal sacrifice for the complete success of the practitioner.
One should meditate within one's own heart upon an excellent ocean of nectar;
in its center is an island of jewels consisting of golden sand.
The mantra-practitioner should visualize a beautiful *pārijāta* tree all around;
there, he should meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) consisting of fifty syllables.
At its base, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon [the throne] adorned with various jewels,
resembling the rising sun, and pervading the entire sphere of the universe.
A hundred yojanas in extent, it was a supreme palace of light,
provided with four gates and adorned with golden ramparts.
It was adorned with canopies of many yak-tail whisks, bells, and other ornaments;
it was fanned by gentle breezes and embellished with fragrant incense and perfumes.
In the center of that, one should meditate on an altar adorned with various jewels;
one should contemplate an excellent parasol fashioned from golden threads.
One should visualize the great yantra as filled with a flood of nectar;
one should prepare three vessels for water for the feet (pādya) and likewise three vessels for the respectful offering (arghya).
Then, the practitioner [should place] six vessels for sipping water (ācamana), three vessels for the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
and one vessel for enjoyment (bhoga) upon the sixteenth petal.
One should likewise fill the vessels with the nectar from the thousand-petaled lotus;
then one should perform the worship of the pedestal according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual. (14)
Then, having performed the ritual worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā), one should meditate upon [the deity] above all, with a lotus-face turned toward the west,
constantly streaming nectar within the divine-limbed lotus.
Having invoked her own essential nature, who rejoices in the bliss of nectar arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti, together with her retinue of attendants; 16.
Regarding the offerings of mental worship:
through these mental services, the most excellent substance is offered—namely, the seat, the welcome, and thereafter an inquiry after one's welfare. (17)
One should offer water for the feet at the two feet and present the arghya offering upon the crown of the head,
[the latter] having fallen from the stalk of the *lambikā* flower, which is like a thousand-petaled lotus-stand.
Having placed the supreme nectar-water, combined with the flowers of meditative states,
within a golden vessel, one should offer it for sipping (ācamana) into the mouth.
One should offer the madhuparka into the mouth and again offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
The wise practitioner should then offer fragrance with the twenty-four principles (tattvas). (20)
One should offer Svayambhūkusuma, saffron, and red sandalwood;
having worshipped with seven or eight varieties of flowers, one should present incense and a lamp.
One should offer pleasing food-oblations (naivedya) imagined by the mind to the Goddess,
and then satisfy the Goddess three times according to the prescribed ritual.
One should worship the six-limbed [mantra], the lineage of gurus, and the deities of the limbs;
having worshipped them with diligence, one should cause the bathing water to be offered as follows.
Having fashioned a mandala to his left, provided with a jeweled lion-throne, he should bring the Goddess there, accompanied by various fragrances. (24)
Having performed the ritual rubbing with fragrant unguents and the like, and having offered Nārāyaṇa-taila and other oils, one should then diligently cause the goddess to be given her bath.
One should bathe the Supreme Deity with golden jars filled with scented water and with the waters of various sacred fords (tīrthas). 26.
Having wiped the body with fine silk cloths (dukūla), one should cause [the deity] to be clothed in fine silk;
one should indeed wipe the body with that [cloth], for the eyes are the essence of splendor.
The principle of space (ākāśatattva) resides in the ear; with that, one should fashion the garment.
Having performed the salutation according to the rule, one should carry out the grooming of the hair.
The supreme practitioner, using a comb adorned with various jewels,
[should place] a cluster of silk ribbons, strewn with various jewels, upon his mass of hair. (29)
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead and vermilion in the parting of the hair;
one should offer a beautiful conch fashioned from the tusks of a lordly elephant.
One should likewise give armlets for the arms, as well as bracelets and bangles, and a ring for the toe, adorned with various gems. (31)
One should give anklets for the feet and small bells for the waist;
one should also bestow a crest-jewel and a crown fashioned with gems.
She should provide well-adorned earrings and pendants as ear-ornaments, apply collyrium to her eyes, and place an elephant-tusk pearl at the tip of her nose. (33)
A neck-ornament, a throat-decoration adorned with pearls and gems, three joyous necklaces, and a jeweled ring.
One should apply an ointment to all the limbs using perfumes, sandalwood, and sihla;
and one should apply lac-dye to the lips, which are adorned with golden earrings. (35)
Having brought her into the pavilions upon a swing fashioned of jewels, he gave her golden sandals marked with coral teeth.
Having again offered water for the feet and other items, one should worship that Eternal One;
then, having offered perfumes and so forth, one should worship her with flowers of devotion.

The names of the mental flowers are: freedom from deceit, freedom from egoism, freedom from passion, and freedom from pride; likewise, freedom from delusion, freedom from hypocrisy, and freedom from hatred and agitation. || 38 ||
The wise know that non-miserliness and non-greed are two flowers;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower. (39)
With compassion as a flower, forgiveness as a flower, and knowledge as the fifth flower—thus, with these fifteen flowers of disposition, one should worship Śivā. (40)
Karavīra, javā, droṇa, campaka, nāgakeśara, as well as other kadamba, pārijāta, and so forth. || 41 ||
One should diligently offer to the Goddess a garland accompanied by fragrant scents,
as well as a beautiful girdle, a lotus garland, and various kinds of flowers.
The excellent practitioner should offer to the Goddess that which has arisen from the seven continents;
he should also offer incense produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, along with fragrant smoke. (43)
The thousand-petaled lotus is the vessel, and the supreme nectar is the oil;
in the *mūlādhāra*, the fire of consciousness exists in the form of a wick as a lamp. (44)
From the base to the aperture of Brahmā, by means of the breath struck within the Suṣumnā, one should offer this bell consisting of the sound of the unstruck resonance (anāhata). || 45 ||
An offering of food endowed with the six flavors, a garment, and likewise a fly-whisk;
a sun, a mirror, a lunar disc, and an excellent parasol.
An ocean of nectar, mountains of meat, heaps of fish, and fruits;
well-cooked caru-rice, and supreme food (paramānna) smeared with ghee. || 47 ||
One should offer food that is chewed, eaten, sucked, licked, drunk, and masticated;
then, with the remaining water for the *arghya*, one should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Then, one should offer the outer wheel with the wind arising from the mūlādhāra, enriched with the qualities of rajas and sattva and mixed with camphor powder. (49)
Having prepared betel-leaf in a jeweled vessel, one should offer it;
then, having gratified the Goddess once more, one should worship the deities of her limbs.
Having performed the libation for them, one should worship the Goddess again;
having performed the worship according to the rules, one should thereafter offer the libation. 51.
Having recited the inner *mātṛkā* and offered it, one should recite a hymn of praise;
then, one should consecrate the flower-bed there for the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods.
The best of practitioners should satisfy the Goddess with various kinds of songs that arise from the erotic and other sentiments (rasas), accompanied by rhythmic claps for the dancer-like mind. 53.
Therefore, when the Goddess Kāmeśvarī and that Kāmeśvara are pleased, the practitioner shall partake in success after having meditated upon their unity within the mind. (54)
Thus has been described the internal sacrifice, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he who mentally offers thousands of red lotuses [attains this]. (55)
Having remained in the city of the goddess for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, that glorious king shall thereafter be born upon the earth.
Even if a man endowed with devotion merely desires to offer food oblations to Mahādevī even in his mind, he shall become long-lived and happy. (57)
And whoever, even with mere mental devotion, should perform a circumambulation of the Goddess,
he too shall dwell in the abode of the Goddess and shall not behold the hells.
The man who bows with devotion to the Goddess in his mind shall quickly conquer the worlds and be glorified in the realm of Śiva. (59)
Now I shall describe the internal sacrifice, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits;
the wise one should perform the meditation on the Guru as previously instructed. (60)
One should bathe in the pure sacred site (tīrtha) of Puṣkara, which is situated within the heart;
or one should bathe in Bindu-tīrtha, and then rebirth no longer exists.
In this auspicious sacred ford (*śivatīrtha*) of the *iḍā* and *suṣumnā* channels,
which flows through the body filled with the water of knowledge—
he who always bathes therein with the waters of Brahman.
What need has he even for the waters of the Gaṅgā or the Puṣkara lakes?
Thus, bathing has been fully described; now one should perform the *sandhyā*.
[This is] the exposition of *sandhyā*.
At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti proceeds, [that is the moment]. || 63 ||
That twilight is proclaimed by those established in samādhi as the ultimate goal of the Kula;
it is the supreme nectar that has flowed forth from the friction of the moon, the sun, and fire.
With that divine nectar, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
This is declared to be the divine libation (tarpaṇa); now the preparation of the arghya is described.
In the lower portion of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there is an excellent lunar vessel;
having filled it with the essence of the digits (kalāsāra), one should satisfy the Khecarī [with that].
As a secondary topic, the description of the six chakras:

in the *ādhāra*, the *liṅga*, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, and the forehead; [the chakras] have two petals, sixteen spokes, twenty-two and ten petals, twelve and half [six], and four [petals].

At the end of the garments (the shoulders), in the middle of the arms, and at the region of the throat accompanied by the syllables ḍa, pha, ka, ṭha, and sa, let the one of pure intellect place the vowels and the syllables ha and kṣa in the middle of the bow, for the sake of attaining perfection in the ritual placement (nyāsa).
p.
57) Thus one should meditate upon the letters of the internal *mātṛkā* according to the sequence of the throat-cover;
then one should perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by which one becomes identical with the Goddess. 68.
This heart, whose object is being destroyed, should become the heart consisting of consciousness;
thereafter, it is rendered supreme by means of the *hṛnmantra*.

The teachers perform the intake of the sense-objects into the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness and who is exalted by the qualities of all the limbs and so forth, by means of the Śiraḥ-mantra.
The preceptors perform the firm visualization of their own body as the form of Hṛcchiva, the abode of consciousness, using the Śikhā-mantra. (71)
The concealment of that body, which consists of mantra, is performed on all sides by the radiant energy expressed by the mantra and by the syllables of the mantra.
That which bestows supreme knowledge within the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, is the light consisting of the heart and other centers; this is what is designated as the "eye. (73)
That mantra which destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner—born of ignorance—is declared to be the supreme abode. (74)

Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then meditate upon the conscious self (cidātman) situated within three hundred thousand *halas* inside the enclosure of two powers (*śakti*).
One should meditate on that which consists of the essence of light through the union of the Kula and Akula;
it is encased within two Śaktis situated in the center of the Śṛṅgāṭa.
That which is always of equal flavor (samarasa) is the object of meditation for the Kulayogins;
(or rather,) it resides in the rays, it resides at their tip, and it is situated between the moon and the sun. 77.
Having brought about dissolution in the great void, the king of yogins remains full;
that splendor which arises in the supportless, empty state [is the goal]. (78)
One should constantly practice meditation upon that womb, for this is indeed the meditation of yogins.
Now, I shall describe the worship according to the tantras. (79)

By worshipping the procedure for the worship of the Blessed Lady with objects and flowers, one becomes identical with her at that very moment. Nyāsa is the realization of identity with her; one should perform the worship with the sense of "I am He" (so'ham-bhāva).
The excellent practitioner should offer the previously mentioned flowers of inner disposition to the Goddess;
now I shall describe the recitation there, using a rosary of beads situated upon a lotus.
The procedure for recitation is as follows:
the rosary is said to consist of fifty beads; the thread is of the nature of Śakti and Śiva.
Kuṇḍalī-śakti is strung upon it, and at the end of the digits (kalās), the Meru is situated.
Having uttered the phoneme together with the bindu, one should then recollect the root mantra;
one should perform the recitation according to one's capacity, both in direct and reverse order. (83)
Having recited [the mantra], one should subsequently offer everything there with hymns of praise, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual, again and again.
Now, the exposition of the ritual of the fire-oblation (homa):
I shall now describe the procedure for the fire-oblation by which one may attain the state of pure consciousness.
The supreme practitioners must realize the Self as being undivided. (85)
The Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self are proclaimed as the nature of consciousness;
one should meditate upon this form as a square fire-pit (*cit-kuṇḍa*). (86)

Beautiful with the girdle of bliss, endowed with the *bindu* and the three folds (*tribali*), having the form of the source (*yoni*) of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), it shall consist of the bliss of Brahman. (87)
The practitioner, with a steady mind, should offer the oblation into the fire of consciousness, which consists of the supreme deity and is expanded by the lamp of all-knowledge. 88.
The form known as sound, consisting of the *mātṛkā* and adorned with the letters of the alphabet—when the syllables are offered into this [fire], the soundless Brahman arises. (89)

The supreme practitioner should conceive of what is to be done and what is not to be done, of sins and merits, and of conceptual thoughts and mental constructions, as being the sacrificial oblation consisting of both dharma and adharma.
The practitioner of mantra should perform a mental oblation in the fire of consciousness, using the root mantra at the end [of the sequence] in the proper order,
offering with the mind as the ladle into the fire whose nature is the consciousness within the navel-center.
I perpetually offer the functions of the senses into that which is illuminated by wisdom;
one should offer the first oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of fire (svāhā).
In the fire of the Self, kindled by the oblation of dharma and adharma, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses with the ladle of the mind, via the path of the *suṣumṇā*. (93)
One should perform the second oblation with the mantra ending in the wife of fire (svāhā),
supporting [the offering] with the hands of light and space, using the ladle of unmanī.
"I offer dharma and adharma into the fire filled with the oil of the kalās. With this mantra ending in the wife of Fire (svāhā), one should perform the third oblation.
While the fire of consciousness— whose internal bond is uninterrupted, which grows ever stronger, and which is the adversary of the darkness of illusion—
is blazing forth, I offer the entire universe, from the earth down to the very quarters of space, as a sacrifice into that wondrously radiating flame within some ineffable ground.
This supreme nectar of intense heat, filling the vessel,
I offer as a full oblation into the fire that consists of the final oblation.
Having performed the internal sacrifice in this manner, one becomes directly composed of Brahman.
I shall describe the great internal sacrifice, which is the very nature of the Brahma-sacrifice.
The knower of Brahman should always perform the great inner sacrifice, the sacrifice of Brahman, which is the great sacrifice;
having perceived the mind with the mind, like a river flowing into the ocean. (100)
In that same way, the great yogin who performs the sacrifice should apply all bodies to the Great Void; then he should again recite every mantra. (101)
The sacrifice situated within the self is indeed the sacrifice of all, devoid of external sacrifices;
it is the sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of mind, the sacrifice of breath, and the consumer of oblations. (102)
The mantra-sacrifice ends within the *suṣumnā*; one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. (103)
One should attain Brahman alone through concentration on the action of Brahman;
one should perform all actions upon all paths as if they were Brahman. 104.
Now I shall describe the procedure for the outer sacrifice; the procedure for the outer sacrifice follows the path of the Tantra.
Having performed one of these, one should draw the king of diagrams (yantrarāja). 105.
The procedure for engraving the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) [is performed] on gold, silver, copper, stone, or the eight metals;
or else—
Likewise on a stone on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, or on a seat of choice.
On a pedestal made of white sandalwood, or one made of red sandalwood, or likewise on gold, silver, copper, or a mirror; || 107 ||
One should construct the yantra according to the prescribed rite on ground originating from Kashmir, on a delightful plot of land smeared with cow dung. (108)
Either with vermilion powder or with red saffron,
[one should write] on a clean, smooth birch-bark leaf or else on another copper plate. (109)
On dry and level ground, in an underground chamber, on crystal, a gold plate, a gem, or a piece of kula-cloth, the adept should draw the yantra. (110)
One should smear the tower with the single substance to be described:
the flower of the self-arisen [liṅga], that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, yellow orpiment, and agallochum. (111)
Saffron from Kashmir, musk, and sandalwood from the Malaya mountains—this fragrance is proclaimed to be always dear to Caṇḍikā. || 112 ||
With this preparation of fragrances, one should draw the King of Mandalas;
or else, with self-arisen flowers, or again with the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*. 113.
Then all success arises for him; there is no doubt about this.
Or else, [it may be done] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, or even with vermilion powder. (114)
With substances such as musk, saffron, or even with yellow pigment (rocanā) and lac;
or else, with substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola* [types of union], and with the *svayambhū* flower. || 115 ||
With *rocanā*, lac, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood,
using a pen made of gold and jewels, for the sake of accomplishing all tasks and goals. (116)
Alternatively,
the skilled practitioner may draw the king of diagrams with a flower,
or with the rays of the sun and moon, or else with the thorns of the *bilva* tree. (117)
Having obtained any one of these— moonlight, sunlight, the heat of fire, or the flames of a burnt offering— and bilva thorns, one should extract one's own yantra.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by bathing in three and a half million sacred fords (tīrthas),
that same fruit the hero attains by performing the vision of the desired discus (iṣṭacakradarśana).
Without having observed the path of noble birth, without having understood the application of the measuring-line,
and without having recognized the perfect symmetry of the lines, one has not painted a face of exquisite beauty.
The Lord shall take away everything from him who worships within this yantra.
Now I shall describe the supreme general yantra of the Śāktas.
The procedure for constructing a general yantra is as follows:
it should be made where the Aparājitā flower and the Javā flower are present,
or in a Karavīra that is red or white, or in a Droṇa, or in a king of yantras.
The Goddess should always reside there; in that yantra, one should perform the worship of Caṇḍikā.
One should take great care to ensure that no animal is seen there. 123.
If, by some chance, there should be writing on the forehead of the animal, it is here that the evil-minded one inflicts a wound upon the limb of the Goddess. (124)
When one raises the wheel while facing the northern direction, then that northern direction is indeed the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt.
The northeast corner shall be that very same as the southeast; of this there is no doubt.
Facing the western direction, the mantra-practitioner should extract [the syllables] according to the wheel. (126)
