Then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction, without a doubt;
the wind-corner (northwest) becomes the fire-corner (southeast), and the northeast becomes the southwest (rākṣasa). || 127 ||
When the practitioner facing south raises up the wheel,
then that direction is the east, and the southeast corner becomes the southwest.
When one faces the eastern direction and raises up the wheel, then that very direction should be known as the east; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, the southeast is for Āgneya and the northeast is for Īśaka; facing whichever direction the practitioner faces, he should worship the auspicious Caṇḍikā.
That [direction] should be known as the east by the high-souled practitioner;
behind the Goddess it would be the west, while in front of Caṇḍikā it is the east.
Furthermore, the ritual for other deities is also proclaimed here;
the interval between the worshiper and the object of worship is declared to be the eastern quarter. (132)
Having written it, the best of practitioners should place the yantra upon a seat in front of him, either on lead, in a bronze vessel, or in vermilion. (133)
One should never place it on a wooden plank, a cloth, or a wall;
even if it is placed there out of greed, delusion, or ignorance. (134)
One's family, wealth, and offspring will utterly perish in every way;
having cast a flower there, combined with fragrant sandalwood [powder]. (135)
The adept should establish the wheel as non-empty; if it were empty, he would become like an obstacle.
Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual, the excellent practitioner should proceed.
Having conceived of it as non-different from oneself, one should place the flower upon one's own head.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Mantras.
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for mantras, wherein each one's specific application occurs.
Regarding the distinction between deities according to the left-hand and right-hand traditions, the procedure for worship is as follows:
one may worship the goddess Bālā, or Tripurā, or likewise Bhairavī. || 1 ||
One should worship Kāmeśvarī and Kāmākhyā according to one's desire;
whether through right-handed (dākṣiṇya) or left-handed (vāma) practice, one shall attain perfection in every way.
One should worship Mahāmāyā, Śāradā, Śailaputrī, and Ambikā in whatever manner appropriate, on the left and the right sides.
Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālī, and Ugratārā as the fifth;
likewise Ucchiṣṭabhairavī, Tārā, and Tripurasundarī.
Unmukhī, Durgā, Mardinī, and Svapnabodhinī—
these should be worshipped with the left-hand method (vāmamārga), without the right-hand orientation.
Success does not arise from the Dakṣa [path], even if one were to worship for a hundred thousand births;
through the Vāma [path], there shall be all prosperity, and one becomes most dear to the Goddess.
If one receives it from the right side, one incurs a curse; if the teacher dies, one falls into hell.
Even Brahmā becomes the left side, as do Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva.
The leftward form of Viṣṇu is the lineage of Nārasiṃha;
she should be worshipped with effort by means of both the right and the left [hands].
In that very same way, he who was the form of the Supreme Self as a child and cowherd became a glutton for fish,
meat, and liquor, and was always lustful for women.
Gaṇeśa, Vetāla, Vāmanāyaka, Bhairava, Vāma, and other such deities have also been mentioned. || 10 ||
These, however, are especially to be worshipped with the left-hand practice (vāmamārga);
others are remembered as the girl-forms (bālikāmūrti) of the goddess Caṇḍikā.
Lakṣmī and the others are the forms of Vāmikā; Daśabhairavī is red;
and Vāgbhavī Sarasvatī is declared to be the form of Bālikā.
Success may arise through the left-hand path (vāmamārga), but never without the right-hand path (dākṣiṇya). The worshipper should likewise always be on the left-hand path, as should the Guru.
One should worship me especially with meat, fish, sexual union, and so forth,
as well as through the union of passion in the form of Mahābhairava.
The accomplishment of mantras is certainly not attained otherwise;
therefore, I shall now fully explain the determination of the five principles (pañcatattva). 15.
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for the five principles (pañcatattva), the method for the five according to the path of the Tantras;
for the Śāktas, there is nothing superior to these five for the sake of happiness and liberation. (16)
By the fifth alone, the practitioner becomes perfected;
by the first yoga alone, the practitioner becomes Bhairava. (17)
By means of the second reality, the worshipper partakes of the form of Brahmā;
by the third alone, he attains the state of Mahābhairava.
By the fourth reality, however, he becomes a leader of worshippers on earth; by the supreme [reality], that practitioner attains supremacy, becoming equal to Śiva.
By the fifth [tattva], one becomes an enjoyer, intent upon all accomplishments,
provided that the constant arising of the five principles occurs within him. (20)
The hero who abides in the five principles (pañcatattva) is a practitioner worthy of being saluted by Śiva.
Worship devoid of the five principles is fruitless;
yet he who worships the Goddess Pañcamī [must do so] with the fifth.
But that slayer of a Brahmin shall become a denizen of hell, to be devoured by ḍākinīs;
however, this is always the case for other forms of Durgā, with the exception of the fifth.
It is certain that there will be no success from recitation, fire-oblations, or libations for one who is devoid of that [initiation];
likewise, any worship, recitation, or further libation performed by such a person is likewise fruitless.
For that fallen one who worships Caṇḍikā without the five *makāras*, Raurava certainly awaits him with certainty. (24)
Four things of his perish: life, knowledge, fame, and wealth;
yet the five things beginning with *ma* bring delight to the deity. (25)
But by the fifth, O Lord of Heroes, one is liberated from all sins:
liquor, meat, fish, ritual gestures (mudrā), and sexual union.
O Goddess, the fivefold *makāra* bestows delight upon the deity;
for he who performs the worship of the Goddess without the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) [is deficient]. (27)
He shall become food for the yoginīs and will encounter evil at every step; without meat and wine, there is no *nāsana* nor *vilīva-pum*. (28) p. 72)
One does not attain the accomplishment of the mantra; therefore, one should be intent on diligence. If it should be omitted through negligence, one would incur the curse of the deity. || 29 ||
One should always worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite with the five *makāras*,
for the satisfaction of all the gods and for the arising of the knowledge of reality.
I shall describe the definition and the method for those [substances], as well as their purification, in due order;
and I shall describe the characteristics of wine for the benefit of practitioners. (31)

In the Kṛta age, the Goddess was worshipped in due order by the four castes with milk, clarified butter, honey, and flour-cakes; in the Tretā age, she was worshipped with clarified butter by all classes.
In the Dvāpara age, the Goddess was worshipped with honey and all varieties of grain; in the Kali age, she is to be worshipped with those very same fermented liquors alone.
She is always to be worshipped with the fourfold liquors throughout the four ages; those various substances are now described according to the path of the Tantras. (34)
That which is derived from trees, from molasses, from flowers, from honey, or produced from fruits— among these,
that substance which arises from food should be known as the most excellent. (35)
Alternatively,
juice is traditionally said to be of ten kinds, produced from leaves, flowers, sprouts, fruits, roots, bark, grains, trees, creepers, and sugarcane. (36)
The juice of the jackfruit tree, grape wine, honey-wine, date-palm wine, palm-wine, sugarcane wine, that produced from honey, *sīdhu*, *mādhvīka*, *maireya*, and that produced from coconut; || 37 ||
These eleven types of liquor bring about both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
but the twelfth, the spirituous liquor of *surā*, is the most excellent of all. (38)

Liquor produced from the juice of honey-flowers and that produced from rice-grains [grant] all accomplishments; that made from flour (paiṣṭī) brings about all siddhis, while that made from molasses (gauḍī) bestows enjoyment.
The honey-wine (mādhvī) is said to grant liberation; the date-wine (khārjūrī) destroys enemies;
that produced from coconut bestows prosperity; and sugarcane wine increases happiness. (40)
Elsewhere as well,
the Gauḍī liquor produced from flour, that from the tāla tree, the Mādhvī from grapes,
the Khārjūrī from dates, and that from the fresh coconut tree— the Gauḍī— bestows enjoyment.

The *paiṣṭī* [liquor] bestows success and destroys adversaries; the *tālī* and *drākṣī* are auspicious; and whatever other [liquors] are prepared are always auspicious and granters of liberation—these are the seven [kinds]. || 41 ||
(74) With substances both unripe and well-ripened, which are like nectar,
the satiation of the Supreme Goddess bestows the fruit of all desires. 42.

As long as the practitioner of mantra does not perform the fivefold purification— the purification of the self, the place, the materials, the body, and the fifth, [the purification of the mantra]— how can there be worship of the deity? (43)
One who forcibly consumes unprepared substances, engages in sexual intercourse by force, or eats meat killed for one's own pleasure shall go to the Raurava hell. (44)
If a practitioner engages with women or intoxicants without first performing purification,
even if [the rite] has been performed, there will be a loss of accomplishment, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.
Regarding the description of the purification of liquor: therefore, I shall explain the purification according to the Tantras.
On the left side, there is a hexagon, and in its center is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having made a mandala outside of that, one should draw it as a square;
then, one should sprinkle the mandala with the water of the general arghya offering.
Having worshipped the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti), one should spread out the base of the jar;
there, immediately thereafter, one should worship the circle of fire (Vahni-maṇḍala). || 48 ||
Regarding the procedure for the construction of the pitcher:
there, one should place a pitcher made of gold, or likewise silver, copper, or even earthen, provided it is free from iron. (49)
A golden vessel is said to bestow enjoyment, while a silver one brings liberation;
a bell-metal vessel brings peace, and likewise, an earthen one grants nourishment.
The length of the jars shall be fifty finger-breadths, their height sixteen finger-breadths, and their mouth shall be eight finger-breadths. || 51 ||
Then, having washed one of these jars with the Astra-mantra and placed it upon the support, one should worship the solar orb.
Then, reciting the root mantra, the practitioner should fill [the vessel] with divine substances and adorn it with red flowers and a red garland.
Having wrapped it in a red cloth, one should smear it with red sandalwood paste;
then, having worshipped the lunar mandala and contemplated it as nectar. (54)
Then, one should visualize the five mudrās, beginning with the square [mudrā], and the substance in the form of one's chosen deity;
one should prostrate with a spirit of devotion by means of these five named mudrās. (55)
Having placed both palms flat on the ground with their faces downward,
this is the Caturasrikā mudrā, properly formed with all the fingers together.

The two fists joined together with the palms facing downward is proclaimed as the *saṃvṛtta* [mudrā]. One should form the two hands facing each other in the shape of a hollowed bowl (*puṭa*). || 57 ||
The great mudrā called Saṃpuṭa is employed in the act of bowing;
it is formed by placing [the hands] at the base of the little fingers of this very same mudrā. (58)
One should also place the two thumbs there; this is called the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed-hand gesture).
Having made the two middle fingers straight and positioned them above the two index fingers, [this is the next mudrā]. (59)
Likewise, with the ring fingers and little fingers positioned in the middle, all [the fingers] should be joined together and pressed by the thumbs. (60)
This supreme mudrā is proclaimed as the yoni-mudrā.
Regarding the description of the mantras of the five mudrās: "hrāṃ namaḥ" is the square [mudrā], and likewise "hrīṃ namaḥ" is the contracted [mudrā]. (61)
*Klāṃ namaḥ* is known as the *saṃpuṭa*; *bluṃ namaḥ* is the *añjali-saṃpuṭa*.
*Saḥ namo* shall be the *yonimudrā*; these are proclaimed as the five mudrās. || 62 ||
With devotion, one should look at the substance while reciting the root mantra:
the *praṇava*, the syllable of Varuṇa (*va*) with the moon (*i*), and the *vāmadeva* mantra joined with *ṅe*. (63)
Having uttered [the mantra] ending with *vauṣaṭ*, one should worship the supreme yantra;
then [one should utter] *viṣaṃ kūrcam*, and immediately after that, *paśupataye*.
The supreme mantra consists of the seed-syllable for armor (*varmabīja*) followed by *astrāya* and ending with *phaṭ*;
having first worshipped with this, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) for the traveler.
One should draw a triangle, a circle, and a square near the water-pot with vermilion and saffron, [representing] all the deities of the travelers.
Having performed worship there, one should thereafter offer a bali-oblation;
having placed meat along with rice, one should recite the mantra.

Having extracted the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and the *lakṣmī* (the syllable *śrīṃ*), and having uttered the heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*) for all the deities of travelers, the practitioner should release it with this [mantra]. (68)
Having lifted it with the left hand, one should whirl it above the jar;
then, while reciting the root mantra, one should throw it into a place outside.
The extraction of the mantra for removing disorders:
Having first fumigated the substance, one should then destroy the disorders.
[The mantra consists of] Māyā (Hrīṃ), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), the pair of Paśus (Huṃ Phaṭ), followed by the Moon (Oṃ) and endowed with two long vowels (ĀḤ). 70.

One should recite the mantra: "churikā me" (the beautiful knife is mine), followed by the name of the person's transformation, then the name of the object, and the pair of *hari*s (the syllables *hrīṃ hrīṃ*), ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā). (71)
Having recited the *vikārahāriṇī* mantra, one should perform the fourfold purification;
then, one should strike [the object] with the *astra* mantra and sprinkle it with the *varma* mantra.
Having performed the inspection with the root mantra, one should sprinkle [the materials] with the heart mantra;
then, taking the fragrance with the root mantra, one should place it three times into both nostrils.
One should draw the yoni in the midst of the substances and write *hasauḥ* in its center;
one should worship it with the mantra *hsauḥ sahauḥ namaḥ* in the middle of the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Regarding the ritual procedure for the Gāyatrī of Ānandeśvara:
having uttered *vāṅ-māyā-kamalā*, one says: "We know Ānandeśvara;
we meditate upon the goddess Sudhā; may that Ardhanārīśvara [bestow grace] upon us. (75)
The wise one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times with the words "pracodayāt.
This is the extraction of the mantra for liberation from the curse of Brahmā: [the syllable] Māyā (Hrīṃ) joined with Vahni (Ra), followed by Kāma (Klīṃ) endowed with Rati (Ī) and Bindu (M). (76)
The state of the Supreme Mistress is the supreme space and the void;
it flows from the moon at the end, and is also known as the devourer of sun and fire.
One should recite "pātraṃ viśa" at the end of the foot [of the verse], and then "viśa svāhā" thereafter;
one should thus mutter the mantra three times and thereby release it from the curse of Brahmā.

The seed-syllable of Varuṇa, which begins with the Vedas (the letter *va*), modified by the six long vowels, followed at the end of the phrase "brahma-śāpa" by the word "vimocitā" joined with the suffix *ṅe* (dative case). || 79 ||
One should recite the mantra ten times, ending with "namo" for Sudhādevī;
[the seed-syllable] consisting of Māyā (Hrīṃ), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), and Kama (Klīṃ), joined with the Moon (Oṃ), and followed by fire (Raṃ) with the six long vowels.
The extraction of the mantra for liberation from Kṛṣṇa’s curse:
at the end of the form of the nectar-Kṛṣṇa, [place] "liberate me from that curse" (śāpaṃ mocaya tatparam);
then the pair that causes the flow of nectar (amṛtaṃ srāvayat-dvandvam), ending with the dviṭha (svāhā). This is the supreme mantra. (81)

Having recited it ten times for the sake of liberation from Kṛṣṇa’s curse, [one should perform] the extraction of the mantra for release from Śukra’s curse: the syllable *viṣa* (sa) joined with a bindu (*m*), followed by *vānta* (pha), and endowed with the six long vowels. (82)
Having uttered the words of Śukra’s curse, one should release [the mantra] with the addition of the syllable *ṅe* (ṅeḥ),
and then recite the mantra ten times, ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) for the goddess Sudhā.
Alternatively, one may release the curse of Śukra in another manner:
[recite] "Māyā Kāmeśvarī Vāc Amṛte Amṛtodbhave. (84)
Having uttered "Amṛtavarṣiṇi," then the Kāmabīja, and then the two [syllables] causing the flow of nectar, one should extract the Śaktibīja of Bhārgava.
Having spoken thus, one should release the curse and bestow knowledge;
then, having addressed the power of accomplishment, one should utter the two syllables "daha" and the great word [of power].
Having extracted the mudrā from the word *khecarī*, as well as the two [mantras] that reveal it, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā) after *astrāya phaṭ*, one should recite them ten times. || 87 ||
Alternatively, I shall proclaim another [method] for liberation from the threefold curse: formerly, the nectar of the gods was [taken] by the wise Baladeva. (88)
The wine Vāruṇī was diligently brought for the purpose of drinking by the sage Dattātreya and the high-souled Śukra. (89)
Having recited [the mantra] three times, the wise one should then recite whichever other mantra is desired, just as in ancient times Balabhadra drank from the ocean that had risen up.
The speech [Vāṇī] conjoined with Śiva and Śakti, and Varuṇa conjoined with Kṣiti;
these are permeated by the six long vowels and adorned with Nāda and Bindu. (91)
Having uttered the words "O Amṛta! O Source of Nectar!
O Showerer of Nectar!", she then released the two from the curse of the gods' semen.
The mantra "amṛtaṃ srāvaya dvandvaṃ svāhā" is the remover of curses;
having recited it ten times, one should release [the deity] from the threefold curse.
Having recited the mantra that releases one from the three curses, one should then recite the one endowed with light;
then [the seed-syllables] Māyā and Lakṣmī, followed by Vāk: "O Amṛte, O Amṛtodbhave! (94)
Having uttered "Amṛtavarṣiṇī" and also "Mahāprakāśayuktā," one should recite the end with the *dviṭha* (svāhā) and then utter [the name] ending in Kubjikā.

The extraction of the Kubjikā mantra: having uttered the seed-syllable of the Preta (the letter *ha*), one should likewise utter *hasaklīṃ*, *hasarīṃ*, *hasakhphreṃ*, and *hasarīṃ*; then one should say "O Bhagavatī. (96)
Then, after *anugraha*, *hasa*, *prānte*, and *kubjikā*,
one should utter *sahasraphreṃ* twice and then say *sanoreva*.
Ghora-kha-prāñca, Khasa-prīñca, accompanied by two *kila*s;
likewise Vicco, Hasa-khānn, Hasa-khabla, and Hasarī. (98)
At the end of the two syllables Śiva and Śakti, one should then utter Māyā (Hrīṃ).
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should contemplate the Nectar;
then he should meditate upon Tiraskariṇī, the destroyer of the bonds of the bound souls (paśu). || 99 ||
The meditation on the Tiraskariṇī-vidyā:
[one should visualize her] as she proceeds ahead, mounted upon a blue horse, richly adorned with blue garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents,
concealing the worlds with the lids of her eyes as if in sleep.
May the Blessed Lady, armed with a sword, protect her devotees. || 100 ||
Having meditated thus, the best of practitioners should recite the two vidyās;
having extracted Māyā and Lakṣmī, [he should say] "namo bhagavati" and so forth. (101)
At the end of the word *māheśvarī*, one should utter "the deliverer of all bound souls" (*sarvapaśujano-ddhara*),
followed by the pair *manaścakṣustiraskariṇīṃ kuru* and the two *ṭha*s. (102)
The description of the Tiraskariṇī-vidyā: Next, I shall describe another Tiraskariṇī, the Māyā-kāmeśvarī. [The mantra is: Vāṇī, GLĀIṂ, Tiraskariṇi, SAKALAJANETI. (103)
At the end of the word *vāgvādini*, one should utter *sakalapaśu*; then, at the end of *jana*, the words *manas-cakṣuḥ-śrotra-jihvā* follow. (104)

Then, having uttered "ghrāṇa" (the nose), one should utter "tiraskānte" (at the end of the rejection), followed by two "riṇī"s and two "ṭha"s joined with the visarga; this great mantra ends with two "ṭha"s. || 105 ||
Having recited [the mantra] three times, the Lord of Heroes should then contemplate his own Guru, who is of the nature of Śiva, upon the Haṃsapīṭha consisting of the mantra within the triangle.
Having contemplated thus—"The three rows beginning with 'a', adorned in the middle by 'ha' and 'la'"—one should thereafter perform the purification of the ritual substances;
or else, one may perform the purification of the substances in another manner. || 107 ||
The Haṃsavatī Ṛc: Oṃ. The Swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house;
dwelling among men, dwelling in the best, dwelling in the sky, born of the waters, born of the cows, born of Truth, born of the mountains—the Great Truth. 108.

Aiṃ! To the one born from satisfaction, born from the perfected ones, born from the omniscient, born from the progenitor of all; to the Immortal One, to the Lord of the Immortals, to the Vase of the Immortal Lineage—Aiṃ Phreṃ! Move! Move!
Drink, drink, O Kulakuṇḍalinī! O Amṛtakuṇḍalinī, flow, flow with nectar! Flow, flow like a mountain torrent! Aiṃ Hrīṃ, O Kulakuṇḍalinī, make [this] nectar! Svāhā! || 109 ||
First is the Praṇava; immediately after that, "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"; then "sadvasurantarikṣasat"; and then "saddhotā vedisat. (110)
"atithir duroṇasat"—this would be the second half-verse of this *ṛc*.
Having spoken "nṛṣad varasad," [one recites] "sadr̥t" immediately after "atithi. Then:
"sadyomasaḍ abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijā."
And the half-verse beginning with "ṛtaṃ bṛhat" has been cited from this same Ṛgvedic hymn. || 111 ||
One should recite the mantra three times, or otherwise recite whichever one is appropriate;
at the end of the arising of speech, there follows the arising of accomplishment.

Having uttered "Obeisance to the Source of the Omniscient One" at the end of all [mantras], and "Obeisance to the Source of the Progenitor" joined with the dative suffix -ṅe, one should then say "Obeisance to the Nectar of Nectar" for the Lord, word by word. || 113 ||

For the Kulakumbha, one should utter the Vāgbhava (AIM), then the pair of *phreṃ*, followed by the pair of drinking mouths (*pibadvandva*), and having spoken "Kula," one should then say "Kuṇḍalinī. || 114 ||
From the station of nectar is Kuṇḍalinī; "amṛtam" means liquid.
[The seed-syllables] Vāgbhava and Bhuvaneśvarī are the pair of twin waterfalls. (115)

Having uttered the mantra "Kulakuṇḍalinī" followed by the pair of "Amṛta" (amṛtāmṛta) ending with the syllable Dviṭha (svāhā), and having caused Kuṇḍalī to drink [the nectar], [he should worship]. 116.
Having meditated upon the union of Śiva and Śakti,
the practitioner should produce nectar from that and fill the supreme vessel.
By this very procedure, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances; I shall now describe the specific [purification] for Kālikā according to the path of the Tantra. (118)
The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle; by means of that, I destroy for you the sin of Brahmin-slaughter born of a mere flash of thought. 119.
O Goddess, born from the solar disc, arisen from the abode of Varuṇa, composed of the seed-syllable Amā— may [this person] be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
If the *praṇava* is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess, may it remove your sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having thus consecrated the auspicious liquor with these three mantras, one should offer it to Kālikā; thereafter, one may partake of the food offering (naivedya).
Thus, these three purifications should be known as the supreme means for liberation from curses;
having performed any one of these, one should meditate upon Ānandabhairava. 123.
(p. 86) Meditation on Ānandabhairava:
[He is] resplendent like ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.
The god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes. || 124 ||
Seated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, established upon the Brahma-lotus,
mounted upon the bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god bears a skull-topped staff and a khaṭvāṅga, sounds a bell and a ḍamaru drum,
holds a noose and a goad, and carries a mace and a club.
He holds a sword, a shield, a battle-axe, a mallet, a trident, and a staff;
his hands carry a shield and a severed head, and his form displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should place the Lord of the Gods of gods, Lohita, in the midst of the ritual substances;
upon his lap is the goddess Surā, possessing the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
The meditation on Ānandabhairavī:
She is white as snow, jasmine, and the moon; she has five faces and three eyes;
she is endowed with eighteen arms, and all her hands are raised, brandishing various weapons. 129.
One should meditate on the wide-eyed goddess of the gods, smiling and facing the God of Gods;
or else, one may contemplate the goddess of the gods in another manner. (130)
One should meditate upon that supreme deity, who is white like a moonbeam, belonging to Varuṇa, and having the form of Brahman, flowing down from the moon on her head. 131.
Having meditated thus, the hero should then perform worship while reciting the mantra,
[offering it] to the god Ānandabhairava and likewise to Ānandabhairavī.
The first syllable is Śivacandra (Śi); then Kāla (Ka), Bhū (Bha), Varuṇa (Va), and Anala (Ra).
This is conjoined with the sixth vowel (Ū) and the letter Vāyu (Ya), adorned with the Bindu and Nāda. (133)
Then one should utter the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra): "To Ānandabhairava.
Then, as before, having extracted the two syllables with their faces reversed, [one should proceed]. 134.
O best of men, the seed-syllable of Vāyu, followed by the goddess Ānandabhairavī with the letter *ṅe* attached, and then the eye-mantra—this is what has been taught. 135.
Having worshipped Varuṇa in the midst of the ritual substances, one should recite the Vasudhā mantra;
then, having recited the root mantra over them, one should contemplate [the contents] as nectar. || 136 ||
Immediately after that, one should display the mudrās beginning with the āvāhanī;
having displayed the āvāhanī, one should display the sthāpanī immediately thereafter. (137)
Having performed the *sannidhāpana-mudrā*, as well as the *sannirodhanī-mudrā* and the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, the most excellent practitioner [should proceed]. (138)
One should perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) for the six limbs along with their mudrās, preceded by three claps of the hands, followed immediately by snapping the fingers.
Having performed the rite of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), one should practice the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
Having rendered [the substance] immortal by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should perform the purification of the materials.
A substance is purified by exposure to light, by smelling, by meditation, and by bathing;
therefore, one should perform the ritual bath of the substance after placing the small vessel in the right hand. (141)
The practitioner, having placed the vessel containing the substance in his right hand,
should pour it onto the articles of worship by means of the union of the left nostril and the thumb.
Having cast a drop [of water] into one's own mouth, one should wipe both hands;
then, reciting the root mantra, one should wipe the body with both hands. 143.
This is the etymological derivation of "surā": it is a divine cause served by the hosts of gods; for this very reason, its name is "surā" throughout the three worlds. (144)
The fruit of beholding Surā:
by the mere sight of Surā, one is liberated from all sins;
by the mere smelling of its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. || 145 ||
By the mere touch of the liquor, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords;
likewise, by drinking it, one directly attains the fourfold liberation.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in the fragrance of the wine; the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in its flavor;
and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in its taste—this is the means for purifying the mind. (147)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter: Description of the Muscles according to the System of the Tantras.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the muscles according to the system of the Tantras.
Regarding the classification of meat:
meat is said to be of three kinds—aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial. (1)
The eightfold "great meat" (mahāmāṃsa), produced from the elephant, camel, horse, buffalo, boar, goat, and deer, is said to cause delight to the deities.
Alternatively:
"The flesh of the cow, goat, elephant, horse, boar, buffalo, deer, and rhinoceros—this group of eight meats is declared to be that which causes delight to Caṇḍikā. (3)
(Alternatively:
The goat, the horse, the rhinoceros, the buffalo, and likewise the yak;
the boar, the tiger, the bear, the rabbit, the tortoise, and the cock. (4)
The black antelope, the deer, as well as variegated wild animals, the human, the gayal, and especially the porcupine. || 5 ||
Swans, pigeons, and likewise village cocks—
these are prescribed as offerings and declared to be pleasing to Caṇḍikā.
(91) By the gift of their flesh, all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) arise. Having obtained any one of these, one should prepare it for the purpose of satiation. || 7 ||
Even the sight of meat yields a result like the sight of wine;
for in the Vedas, violence is prescribed for sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods.
O beloved, the harming of living beings for one's own sake has never been enjoined;
one should never cut even a blade of grass without a purpose.
There is no fault in killing an animal for the sake of a deity;
having killed a twice-born man or a cow for the sake of a deity, one is not tainted by sins.
Yet, even without meat, if one performs worship [in that manner], there would be sin at every step.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice; otherwise, one would go to hell.
Then, having consecrated the animal with this mantra, one should strike it.
This body has been severed by Śiva; therefore, you have attained the state of Śiva.
Awaken to that, O bound soul (paśu), for you were not Śiva before, yet now you are indeed Śiva.
Brahmā resides in the flesh, Viṣṇu in its fragrance, and Rudra in its taste;
the Supreme Self dwells in its bliss. Therefore, O beloved, this [flesh] should be consumed.
Having thus slain the sacrificial animal, one should subsequently prepare it well-cooked;
however, a practitioner should never offer raw meat during the rites of worship. (14)
But with the exception of the blood from the head, that [flesh] becomes immortal;
one should purify the meats according to the authoritative measures prescribed in the scriptures. (15)
The Procedure for Purifying Meat:
I shall now declare the purification of meat for the sake of the accomplishment of the Śākta practitioners;
having sprinkled it with the root mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the practitioner [should proceed]. (16)
One should perform the fourfold purification by means of the previously mentioned method;
one should dry it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu and burn it with the seed-syllable of Agni.
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti, prepare the nectar with the Vāruṇa mantra;
then, for the purification of the meats, one should mutter the mantra.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then recite "pratad viṣṇuḥ"; having fully proclaimed "stavate mṛgo na bhīmaḥ," he becomes a wanderer in the mountains. (19)
And after that,
he in whose three wide strides it was declared, "He is most heavy," then [the gods] cast down all the worlds in his strides. (20)
The hero should display the previously mentioned mudrās known as Āvāhanī and the others;
thereafter, he should mutter the root mantra seven times.
I shall describe the purification of fish according to the tantras. Regarding the enumeration of the types of fish:
the pāṭhīna, the vodāla, as well as the śakula and the śālaka. (22)
The great *śakula*, the *citrī*, the *khaḍgī*, and the water-scorpion—all these fish have been ordained by him as bestowers of auspiciousness. (23)
One should first perform the purification of the fish meat, sprinkling the fish as previously described;
thereafter, one should recite the mantra for the complete purification of the fish. (24)
Oṃ. We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one who increases prosperity.
Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, but not from immortality. 25.
Having performed the remainder as before, one should purify the mudrā;
it is made of rice, circular in shape like a mandala, auspicious, and resembling the orb of the moon. (26)
Beautiful, ripened, and captivating, filled with sugar and other ingredients—
this is proclaimed as the *mudrā* for the deity at the time of worship. (27)
Whatever chewable food, such as parched grain and the like, she may prepare—its name is known as Mudrā, which increases great joy. (28)

It is called a *mudrā* because it bestows joy (*mudaṃ rāti*); by means of which, through the various types of hand-clasps (*muṣṭi*), one should first consecrate the *mudrā*, and perform the remainder as previously prescribed. || 29 ||
Oṃ. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. 30.
Oṃ! The wise, the eloquent, and the vigilant kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 31.
Having thus recited the mantra, the lord of heroes should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for the nectar arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, which originates from the *kuṇḍa* and brings delight to the deities;
[this is accomplished] even with thousands of jars of wine and hundreds of loads of meat.
The Goddess would find no satisfaction whatsoever without that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*;
the Goddess is of the nature of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and her essence consists of the nectar of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*. (34)
The Goddess has the nature of both semen and menstrual blood;
she is of the form of semen and resides in semen, and she is of the form of menstrual blood and resides in menstrual blood.
She is the form of the bindu, residing in the bindu, and her essential nature is the bindu of rajas.
The Goddess is fond of the bhaga and liṅga; she is fond of the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga.
Therefore, one should worship her with the very nectar of the bhaga and liṅga. || 36 ||
He who worships the Goddess with the drinking of the hero’s substance, with dalliance with another’s wife, and indeed with the nectar of the vulva and the phallus; || 37 ||
No suffering arises for him; that man becomes one whose mantra is perfected by means of the flowers of the noble family, the substances of the noble family, and the nectar of the noble family. (38)
By worshipping her, the practitioner obtains his desires and the eight supernatural powers;
yet he who would worship Caṇḍikā without substances originating from the Kula lineage [is deficient]. (39)
The merit of thousands of other births is destroyed for him.
Having performed the purification of the ritual materials, one should perform the purification of the *śakti*. (40)
The purification of the Śakti:
Having brought the Śakti together with the ritual substance in the proper sequence—the divine woman who has been bathed, endowed with the [proper] cause, and initiated—[one should proceed]. (41)
Whether she be his own wife or another's, devoid of shame and modesty,
adorned with ornaments and well-attired, he should place her upon the couch.

One should perform the network of placements (nyāsajāla) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual (kalpa). Having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās, one should then perform the placement of the Kalās. (43)
One should place the syllable *hrīṃ* on the forehead, likewise the syllable *klīṃ* on the face,
the syllable *aiṃ* on the heart, and the syllable *blūṃ* on the navel.

The wise practitioner should place the syllable *strīṃ* in the secret part and place the five objects of desire there; then, having performed the rites beginning with the seer (*ṛṣi*) as prescribed in his own ritual manual, he should worship [the deity] with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
One should place the Drāviṇī in the yoni, and after that, the Mūlavidyā;
one should then place them in sequence in the ādhāra, the heart, and the middle of the eyebrows.
Furthermore, the eminent practitioner should place the root [mantra] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
thereafter, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) from the head down to the feet.
Speaking of sexual union,
pulling the hair on the head, kissing the eyes, biting the cheeks with the teeth, pressing the lower lip, and gently striking the chest and the navel with the fist;
Nail-marks should be applied to the belly, the throat, the cheeks, the breasts, and the hips; then, scratching with the nails along the parting of the hair, one should firmly grasp the breast.
In the temple of the mind-born god, lovers should incessantly perform mutual striking with the shanks, big toes, feet, thighs, and ankles, like the playful movements of elephants. (49)
The seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa) consists of the left eye (va), joined with Kāma (ka) and Varuṇa (sa),
enriched by the eleventh vowel (au), and endowed with the lunar drop (bindu). || 50 ||
The best of practitioners should install [the mantra]: "Amukīm drāvaya svāhā.
He should recite the two [mantras] beginning with "Vāmā yā capalacitte" and "reto muñca. (51)
The seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm), joined with Varuṇa (Va), Bhū (La), Dakṣa (Ra), and Karṇa (Śa);
conjoined with the consort of Soma (Ū) and endowed with the final vowel (Au), it forms the Moon-mantra (Klūṃ). || 52 ||
The seed-syllable of Drāviṇī has been declared for the benefit of practitioners.
One should place the Vidyā within its womb: *re-t-hu-mā-to-ca-mai-na-ta*. (53)

The practitioner, having uttered the root mantra, should meditate upon the Goddess within himself as the primordial Śakti, whose form is the syllable Niṃ, and who resides in the limbs of the body. 54.
In the fire of the Self, kindled by the oblations of dharma and adharma, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses with the ladle of the mind, through the path of the *suṣumṇā*. 55.
This great mantra, ending with "svāhā," is proclaimed for recitation at the beginning;
thereafter, while approaching a woman, one should drink the nectar from her mouth with the tongue. (56)
Having brought the *kulamadya* and prepared it with *vāruṇa*,
one should add *varuṇa* together with its own essence (*svarasa*), endowed with the five long vowels. (57)
Having purified the water with the syllable *vauṃ* for Varuṇa using the king of mantras (*praṇava*), one should drink it repeatedly, having stirred it with the tongue empowered by the *śakti*. (58)

One should contemplate her as having become the Goddess through union with the Goddess within oneself; one should contemplate her as having become one through union with Śakti within oneself. || 59 ||
One should contemplate the self as a subtle form, the power (śakti) in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, the tongue as consisting of the root, and the womb as having the nature of the Kula.
By means of the distinction between the *kula* and *akula*, the self is led into you; it is purified by mantra and medicine alone, just as [impurities are removed] from semen. 61.
Furthermore, as it is being churned, the supreme reality arises from it.
By abandoning that [lower] reality, the practitioner of steady mind should drink the root [essence] of the sacred seat (pīṭha). || 62 ||
Supporting [the ladle] with the hands of light and space, I offer into the fire—filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit—the sacrificial spoon of *unmanī*. 63.
This great mantra, ending with "svāhā," is proclaimed for the emission of semen;
wherever the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, [this mantra is to be used]. || 64 ||
In each respective case, one should join these two together in due order;
one should diligently take that substance which is known as "born from a pit" (kuṇḍodbhava).
(99) This substance produced from a *kuṇḍa*, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been described.
Now I shall proclaim that produced from a *goḷa* for the sake of the spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the heroes (*vīra*). (66)
One who is of noble birth, initiated, intoxicated, husbandless, discerning, adorned with ornaments, motivated by a specific purpose, childless, and charming. (67)
She was beautiful and radiant, with slender yet full and elevated breasts; her heart yearned for the practitioner, and she was a connoisseur of the arts and sciences. (68)
One should perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and other rites according to the procedure prescribed in one's own tantra;
then, through the application of the sequence mentioned previously, the wise practitioner should generate the Tattva.
The supreme practitioner should diligently take up this essential substance for the purpose of worship;
this material produced from a cow brings satisfaction to the deity. (70)
Having taken the appropriate ritual substance into a copper vessel—
endowed with various fragrances and combined with the three pungents (kaṭutraya)— [he should proceed].
The purification of those born from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* unions and others is now declared.
One who is concentrated in worship should purify the *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, and so forth, leading them [to the state of purity]. (72)
The purification mantras:
Oṃ, may Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;
may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. || 73 ||
"O Sinīvālī, bestow the embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow the embryo.
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place the embryo within you. (74)
Pluṃ jluṃ mluṃ gluṃ tataḥ svāhā; then one should say "amṛta.
Then [one says] "amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇī. (75)
One should also remember to recite "Amṛtaṃ srāvaya svāhā" twice;
then, having performed the remaining rites as before, one should perform either this or another [rite].

Having uttered the *tāra* (om), the *kūrca* (hūm), and the *astra* (phaṭ), joined with the three points (*bindu*) starting from Śiva; then the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā), the *tāra* (om), the *māyā* (hrīṃ), and the *śrībīja* (śrīṃ), O beloved of sexual delight! (77)
Then [one should add] the Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīm), Ramā (Śrīm), and the Astra (Phaṭ), followed by the Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā) in a circle;
then "to the one born from nectar" (Amṛtodbhavāyai), and finally "the showerer of nectar" (Amṛtavarṣiṇī). || 78 ||
O dear goddess, one should release the pair of feet from the curse of Śukra by means of the mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), and thus perform the purification of the substances. 79.
Having undertaken this vigor, one should apply it toward that which is distinguished and worthy;
with that nectar, the best of practitioners should satisfy the Goddess of the Gods.
The presence of the Goddess arises, and one may obtain all desires;
yet that lowest of men, having engaged in sexual union, meets with death before long. (81)
One who is free from doubt should perform the family rites; with a mind free of conceptual construction and well-composed, one should indeed act in this way.
From doubt arises exhaustion, and through doubt one becomes a vessel for suffering. (82)
Through doubt there may be the loss of everything; through doubt there is the loss of wealth;
through doubt there may be the loss of success; therefore, one should abandon doubt.
Now, after explaining the distinctions between the powers of substances, I shall describe what occurs through the specific powers of substances:
with a pure disposition, the practitioner [should seek] one who has slender limbs and long hair. (84)
One should worship the Goddess with flowers and perfumes, using *javā* flowers and fragrances;
by means of her flowers, one may diligently obtain every desire. (85)
Long-limbed, long-eyed, youthful, and always modest,
she is fragrant and made sweet-scented by the bilva leaves used during lovemaking and other rites.
With the flowers of that [tree], one should diligently worship the supreme Goddess—she who has a fair complexion, well-developed calves, full hands, and is intoxicated with passion. (87)
One should worship with Madagandhā, dates, and Palāśa flowers;
she is Puṣpagandhā, the sustainer of the world, who is eternally of the form of Kṛṣṇa. 88.
(102) One who is slender-limbed and slender-waisted should worship the Supreme Goddess after offering honey.
When she is thin-limbed, dark-complexioned, long-haired, and intoxicated with passion— (89)
That which has a pungent scent, is always nourished by mandāra and coconut trees, is short and dark-limbed, shall be the abode of Madana. (90)
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with lotus flowers and honey-scented offerings from the Gauḍī region;
she who is slender-limbed and fair and tall is the Supreme Goddess adorned with a garland of porpoises.
The practitioner should especially worship the Goddess with jasmine flowers—
specifically those that are full, short, white-limbed, and accompanied by the blossoms of the blue water-lily.
This slender, tall, and fair-limbed woman has been emaciated by sexual indulgence combined with the scent of *ketakī*; she is now joined with the fragrance of *mālatī*.
She would be named Aṅkuśā; if she is fair-limbed, with Bandhūka flowers serving as her sexual organs and a beautiful girdle for her loins. 94.
One should worship her with substances such as camphor and turmeric;
having taken these substances, one should perform purification by means of them alone.
Having worshipped with each of those respective flowers, one shall indeed obtain all perfections;
for if one should worship the Goddess without knowing this sequence, [one gains nothing].
Indeed, everything in sacrifices would be fruitless if devoid of clarified butter;
for that which was described as the tenth power exists in a state of mixed conduct. (97)
One should perceive only the fragrance and not differentiate the color;
one is oneself the Creator, oneself Viṣṇu, and oneself the Lord Maheśvara. (98)
With a state of bliss born from practice, one should worship the Goddess according to the Kula tradition with blood as red as that of elephants, horses, bulls, goats, and men. (99)

The praise of the five principles (pañcatattva) is realized by men through the flesh produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, through self-arisen flowers (*svayambhūkusuma*), and through fish, wine, and food offerings at all times. (100)
Furthermore, on that day, one should not observe distinctions of caste;
no unrighteousness whatsoever arises during the accomplishment of the great mantra. (101)
All success is indeed attained through the offering of the five elements;
one should never omit the regular rite due to the absence of pure substances. 102.
(104) If [the practice] should be omitted through negligence, one would go to the Raurava hell;
but by performing the five *makāras*, there is no further rebirth. (103)
Therefore, one of great wisdom should perform worship by means of the five elements;
for by that, the offering and reception of wine must certainly be performed. (104)
Offerings made with food that is spoiled, stale, leftover, foul-smelling, or lacking fragrance, or with substances placed in another's vessel, shall be fruitless. (105)
He whose mouth is devoid of the fragrance of the savory offerings (āmiṣa) and the Soma juice (āsrava) must undergo penance and be shunned; he is indeed nothing but a beast, without a doubt. (106)
As long as there is the scent of impurity (āsava), one is Paśupati himself;
without the scent of wine and meat, one is a mere beast, even if he is Paśupati himself. 107.
One should not satisfy [the ancestors] even with wealth that is devoid of fish and meat;
nor should one offer even a piece of flesh the size of a sesame seed, or even half a sesame seed, as a mere drop.
By merely performing this single satiation, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Having covered [the vessel] with red cloths, one should protect the five principles (pañcatattva). || 109 ||
(p.105) Worship of heroes is forbidden in the presence of bound souls (paśu).
One should not worship the Goddess with the five [syllables] beginning with *ma* in the presence of bound souls.
One should not establish it on the right; thus is the purification of substances declared.
This substance which has been described is the bestower of all accomplishments;
however, it is a secondary alternative for the twice-born, and not a direct option for those who have already attained perfection.
The substitute for family property:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the preparation of substances and so forth.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, should prepare honey-wine in a copper vessel. (112)
Alternatively, one should offer cow's products except for ghee in copper vessels;
likewise, coconut water, jaggery, and ginger should be offered in bronze vessels.
Gauḍī liquor should be given by a Kṣatriya, and Mādhvī indeed by a Vaiśya;
everything may be given by a Śūdra, or whatever he may take pleasure in. || 114 ||

Alternatively, having thoroughly mixed fish, meat, and the like with *vijayā* and the eight fragrant substances (*aṣṭagandha*), the wise one should knead them, form them into pills (*vaṭikā*), and then collect them. (115)
In its absence, however, one should satisfy [the deity] by stirring Vijayā in water;
or one should satisfy [it] with buttermilk mixed with molasses and joined with honey. (116)
Or one may perform this rite with *sauvīra* (sour gruel); one must not omit it.
In the absence of meat, however, one may use garlic, fresh ginger, or *nāgara*.
One may consume śūraṇa, meat-balls, or any one of the roots; these are declared as substitutes for meat. Now, listen to the procedure for fish. || 118 ||
Buffalo milk, gayal milk, and likewise goat’s milk, as well as any fruit or root—once burnt, these become meat. (119)
The ritual procedure for the fish, which is a substitute for the *kuṇḍagola* and others, has been told; now hear the rite arising from the *kuṇḍagola*.
Within the womb of the *aparā* flower lies the beautiful seat of the *kula*. (120)
All that bliss shall be of the nature of the great art of desire;
Sadāśiva himself is eternally present within the Hayāri-flower.
Taking a substance into its mouth, one should place a flower and sandalwood—or the dye of red saffron—within it; this is the differentiated reality whose nature is Śiva. || 122 ||
One should unite [the two], contemplating with the intellect the oneness of Śiva and Śakti;
having reflected for a moment upon that very [union], one should worship the Supreme Goddess there. (123)
Having recited that very mantra, the substance arising from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is known to be supremely difficult to obtain;
this substance is to be understood as even more internal and exceedingly rare.
Whatever substance has been prescribed as an alternative for those who have made such a choice, one should take that and worship the Goddess; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
Having failed to perform worship on the fifth day and having not obtained the approval of the Guru,
one who kills an animal with his own hand shall go to the Raurava hell.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter. Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the *arghya*;
having received the command of the Great Goddess, one should perform the special *arghya*. (1)
Then, between the two goddesses of the self, one should draw a wheel upon the ground:
a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and joined with an enclosure of earth.
Having drawn the Māyā-bīja in the center,
one should thereafter sprinkle it with the root mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) and with the water of the general arghya.
Having worshipped the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), one should worship the deities of the seat:
Pūrṇaśaila, Uḍḍīyāna, and Jālandhara within the square [mandala].
One should worship Kāmarūpa according to the sequence starting from the east;
there, the knower of mantras should worship the six limbs within the six corners.
Having worshipped the root mantra within the triangles,
the best of practitioners should then worship Ādhāraśakti in the center.
Regarding the description of the supporting vessel and so forth:
the practitioner should place the support, which has been washed with the Astra-mantra, there;
for without the support there is a lapse, and the Mothers are not satisfied.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should prepare a support according to the prescribed rule;
the support is said to have three feet, or six feet, or four feet.
Alternatively, one should fashion an excellent circular base;
having established any one of these, one should worship according to the Kula path.
Having constructed the maṇḍala as before and worshipped it by that same path,
one should first [worship] Mahākāla together with the moon, and the fire-maṇḍala joined with the suffix -ṅe.
Having recited the mantra ending with the heart-mantra (hṛt), one should then worship in the foundation (ādhāra);
there, one should worship the ten digits (kalās) of Fire by their respective names.
The ten digits (kalās) of Fire are Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and also Havyavahā and Kavyavahā. 12.
Those beginning with "abja" and ending with "indukṣakāra," joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī* and ending in "namaḥ," are proclaimed as the digits (*kalā*) of fire. (13)
The excellent vessel— whether made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, skull, gourd, or clay— is washed with the root mantra recited without weariness.
One should prepare a beautiful vessel originating from coconut, conch, copper, pearl-oyster shell, or produced from a sacred tree. || 15 ||
Alternatively, this beloved golden vessel—made of gold, silver, glass, copper, or brass; fashioned from pearl or skull; composed of *viśvāmitra* [crystal]; granting all desires—is made of crystal.
The skull-cup vessel originating from the noble coconut produces devotion, joy, and the eight supernatural powers;
the pearl-vessel clearly produces the perfection of mantras and bestows liberation.
Alternatively,
vessels made of gold, silver, and copper bring about all accomplishments;
for pacification, a stone vessel is used, and for immobilization, one made of clay.
A coconut is for all-encompassing subjugation, while a pearl is indeed for liberation;
a skull bestows knowledge, and iron is excellent for killing.
One should fashion a golden vessel, a skull-cup for Viśvāmitra, a conch that bestows knowledge, and a pearl-oyster shell that grants learning. (19)
Bowl-vessels made of skull or gourd bring about the perfection of yoga,
while rosary-beads made from sacred trees remove all sins.
Among these vessels that have been described, one should prepare a single vessel sixteen finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height.
Alternatively, it may be half of that, or even half of that again;
its measurement should indeed be one finger-breadth, one and a half, or six [finger-breadths]. || 22 ||
One should avoid that which is too thin, too thick, or has holes;
one should not employ a broken vessel. One's own span (prādeśa) is recommended.
One should place one of these vessels upon three supports;
having prepared the mandala as before, one should worship it according to the previous procedure.
Having meditated there upon the orb of the sun, one should then worship it;
the solar orb consists of the letter 'A' preceded by a vowel and joined with a bindu, followed by the syllable 'ṅe'. (25)
Having recited the mantra ending with "namaḥ" and having worshipped the vessel for the *arghya* offering,
one should worship there the twelve digits (*kalā*) known by the names of the Sun. (26)
The twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun are:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 27 ||

The seed-syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) in their proper order, are to be known as the *kalās*; they are to be used in the dative case and followed by the word *namaḥ*. (28)
These digits (kalās) should be worshipped well, and then one should worship the vessel with red sandalwood, fragrant flowers, and other very beautiful offerings. (29)
Then, for the purpose of the water-pot (kumbha), one should fill the vessel to three parts while reciting the Varuṇa mantra, the root mantra, and the Mātṛkā in reverse order.
The best of practitioners should fill one part with water,
and therein place it together with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, red flowers, and sandalwood.
Then one should cast into it the previously extracted *kuṇḍagolaka* and *bilva* leaves;
having placed meat and fish therein, one should especially perform the ritual hand-gesture (*mudrā*).
One should scatter various fragrant substances and the nine gems, together with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and nutmeg. (33)
Moon, sandalwood, musk, yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum, saffron, the self-arisen flower, and that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*— these constitute the eight fragrances. (34)

Having cast [the seed-syllable] there, the Lord of Heroes should worship the lunar mandala—the lunar mandala which consists of the letter *ca* with the bindu and the left ear (*va*), joined with *ṅe*. || 35 ||
Having uttered the mantra ending with the heart-mantra, one should worship within the center of the vessel;
there, one should worship the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon.
The sixteen digits of the moon are Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. (37)
The digits born of the vowels—Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and Kāmadāyinī—are joined with the nasal dot (bindu), followed by the dative suffix -ṅe, and end with "namaḥ. || 38 ||
All these digits of the moon should be worshipped with effort;
one should invoke the sacred waters as before and draw the mandala as before. (39)
Having recited the mantra as before, one should worship Ānandabhairava;
there, the preceptor, having fully worshipped the goddess Ānandabhairavī, [should proceed].
Thereafter, he should invoke his own chosen deity there;
then the practitioner should display the mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhanī). || 41 ||
Then, one should display the mudrās according to the ritual procedure prescribed in one's own Kalpa;
having displayed the mudrās, one should thereafter worship the chosen deity.
And as before, one should worship the six limbs within the triangles;
in the center of the three lines beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha', one should draw the Māyā syllable.
Having written the syllable *hasau* in the center and within the four squares starting from the east,
the excellent practitioner should thereafter worship the five jewels.

One should extract the mantra for the ritual of the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna-pūjā) as follows: the five vowels ending with the final one (Ū), joined with the letter KṢI and the right ear (R); then at the end of the sky (Ā), followed by "to the Jewels" (ratnebhyaḥ) and ending with "namas". (45) *pañcaratna-pūjā-vidhānam* *pañca-anta-kam* (the five ending with the last) *kṣiti-yutam* (joined with the earth) *dakṣa-karṇa-samanvitam* (endowed with the right ear) *gagana-ante* (at the end of the sky) *ratnebhyaḥ* (to the Jewels) *namaḥ-antam* (ending with *namas*) *anu* (mantra) *muddharet* (one should extract)
Having uttered "Śītala," "Saṃyukta with Śakra," and adorned with the supreme bindu, one should also recite "Svargapada" and "Namaḥ ratnebhyaḥ. (46)
The fifth [syllable] is "devarājaṃ" endowed with "dakṣaśrotra"; then "pātālapada" followed by "ratnebhyaḥ" and ending with "namaḥ"—this is another mantra. (47)
[One should then extract] Mahākāla joined with Kṣiti and endowed with the right ear (Śa);
thereafter, one should extract "Martyaratnāya namaḥ" here. (48)
Having placed the left foot upon the ground and adorned with the right ear, one should utter "nāgapada" and also "ratnebhyaḥ namaḥ. (49)
Having thus worshipped well in the center, thereafter, upon the three lines,
[one should worship] the Divine Current (divyaugha) at the end of the Vāgbhava syllable, as well as the sandals (pādukā) bearing the name of the Guru.
Thereafter, one should worship this triad in such a manner;
having worshipped the Siddhaugha and the Mānavaugha, one should recite the mantra.
The mantra of Amṛteśvarī:
O You who bestow the bliss of the undivided single essence, O Supreme Self of nectar, O You whose form is Akula, place within me the spontaneous radiance here! 52.
O Supreme One, who abides in the non-clan (akula), whose form is nectar, and who produces the knowledge of purity—
place the state of immortality within this very substance, which has a moist nature.
Having bestowed unity in that very form upon me, who am of this same nature, and having become the embodiment of supreme nectar, cause the flash of consciousness to arise within me. 54.
Having thus consecrated it with these three mantras,
thereafter [one should offer] that which is produced from a fragment of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and arises from the entirety of essences.
"O you who bring forth the nectar-essence, fill the great vessel!
[The mantra consists of] Vāgbhava, the fifth [vowel], and Kṣauṇī, joined with the left ear. (56)
"KṢAUṂ JŪṂ SAṂ! O Amṛte, O Amṛtodbhave, O Amṛteśvari, O Amṛtavarṣiṇi!
Having uttered this, we two cause the nectar to flow forth. (57)
Having uttered [the mantra] ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), one should then extract the other;
then the Vāgbhava [bīja], a pair of words, and thereafter "Vāgvādini."
Having uttered the words *vāṅmanaḥ pada*, one should then say *klinne kledini*; thereafter, one should utter the pair *kledaya* twice and the pair *kuru* twice for the sake of great liberation.
One should utter the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), the seed-syllable of power (ŚAKTI), and the two words for liberation (MOKṢA).
Then, having pronounced the seed-syllable of the preta (PRET), one should say HASAU NAMAS thereafter.
Having consecrated [the substances] by this very procedure thereafter,
one should worship the god Ānandabhairava as well as Ānandabhairavī.
Having satiated [the deity] three times upon the head, one should then display the mudrās;
first those previously mentioned, such as the square (caturasra) and others, and after that, the conch mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā).
Regarding the description of the conch mudrā:
the fingers of the left hand are thus joined together and well extended, while the right thumb is pressed against them;
this mudrā is known by the name of the conch.
(p. 117) Regarding the description of the fish-seal (matsyamudrā):
the right hand is turned downward, and the left hand likewise.
The straight fingers are joined together, one above the other. || 65 ||
One should slightly move the two thumbs; this mudrā is known as the Matsya (Fish).
Having displayed the Matsya mudrā, one should then display the Dhenu (Cow) mudrā.
Then, having veiled [the deity], one should subsequently display the *yonimudrā*;
thereafter, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with three *tāla* claps and snapping of the fingers.
Having recited the root mantra eight times,
the best of practitioners should then meditate, visualizing himself in the form of his chosen deity.
The placement of the *arghya* is declared in all scriptures to bestow success;
likewise, the conduct of those who possess perfected knowledge is now being described. (69)
Then, one should place the conch, the vessel of heroes, in the central part;
thereafter, one should perform the worship according to the procedure prescribed for Śrīvidyā.
A hero who has mastered the conduct of the vidyā should not extract nor move [the drop] until the time of dismissal;
therefore, having cast the bindu into the general arghya vessel thereafter, [he should proceed]. 71.
p.
118) Determining the Number of Vessels: One should place the vessels between the vessel for the Goddess and the *arghya* pitcher as follows.
The vessel for the Guru is at the end of the jar; at the end of that is the vessel for enjoyment.
At its end is the vessel for the Śaktis, and near that is the vessel for the Yoginīs;
at its end is the vessel for the Vīras, and near that is the vessel for the bali offering. || 73 ||
The wise man should arrange the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya), as well as the vessels;
nine vessels are considered best, while seven are middling.
Some experts in mantra say that five vessels are middling;
those vessels are inferior, and one should not employ a single vessel.
One should not use a single bowl, even if it belongs directly to the Lord of the Family;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step. (76)
In this world one suffers poverty, and after death one goes to the state of an animal;
these three are considered the vessel of the Goddess, the vessel of the Guru, and the vessel of enjoyment. (77)
The vessel for worship and the vessel for bali—this is the rule for five vessels. The vessel for śakti and the vessel for the hero—this is the rule for seven vessels. (78)
One should know that [the vessel] is the recipient of worship during the veneration of the Yoginīs;
this is the procedure for the water for the feet and the water for sipping in the nine vessels. (79)
The Procedure for Placing the Vessels:
I shall describe the placement of the vessels according to the rules of the Tantra.
One should construct a triangular circle within a square ground on the south of the pitcher. (80)
Having performed the sprinkling and other rites as before, one should deposit the support;
immediately thereafter, one should worship the fire-mandala therein.
Then, having washed the vessel as before, one should place it upon the support;
having worshipped the mandala there, one should then fill it with [the water] of the Sun.
Having worshipped with the nectar from the jar, one should worship the mandala of Soma;
there, one should cast flowers, incense, and sandalwood into the *kuṇḍagola*.
Having drawn a hexagon filled with circles and squares, one should then worship it;
one should perform the six limbs, the six corners, and the mudrās as previously described. (84)
Then, having performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana) preceded by three claps of the hands (tāla),
and having recited the root mantra eight times, one should then cast the drop (bindu).
The procedure for libation:

the lord of heroes (vīrendra) should thoroughly satisfy the gurus with special arghya offerings, as well as the divine assemblies of Siddhas and Mānavas, each accompanied by their respective names. (86)
Having offered libations, one should always perform the rite known as *tattva* upon one's own head with the *mudrā* formed by the thumb and ring finger of the left hand.
This Tattvamudrā has been described by the wise as being employed for the libation (tarpaṇa) to the Guru, the Paraguru, and likewise the Parāparaguru. || 88 ||
Immediately thereafter, one should satisfy Parameṣṭhiguru;
then, with the nectar of the special arghya offering, one should satisfy one's own deity.
In the lotus of the heart, the practitioner [should contemplate] either fivefold or sevenfold;
having explained the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi), he should prepare the vessel for enjoyment (bhoga-pātra) for the gurus who are skilled in the vessels.
Having established the vessel as before, one should perform the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi);
having wiped both hands with the nectar from the vessel of enjoyment (bhoga-pātra), [one should proceed].
In the right hand, one should draw a circle together with the nine-yoni diagram;
there, one should place the fourfold purification, which resembles a pea.
(p. 121) The Description of the Purification of the Body:
One should hold [the breath] with the union of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger as one.
O best of Brahmins, he should accept it with his left hand by means of this [mantra].

One should [place] the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), the seed-syllable of Kamalā (*śrīṃ*), Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva; then the Self consisting of Vidya and Kalā ending in *ṅ*, together with the nasal bindu and the sixteenth vowel (*auṃ*). || 94 ||

Having uttered the Vāgbhava root-mantra, that which follows by means of the principle of the self (ātmatattva), one then [utters] the word "I purify the gross body" followed by the dual Ṭha (ṢṬHAṂ). 95.
Having accepted the lower pure portion by means of this [mantra], immediately thereafter [he accepts] Māyā and Lakṣmī, and then [the principles] called Māyā, Kalā, and Niyati.
Kalā, Ātman, Śuddhavidyā, and Rāga belong to the Puruṣa principle;
and the group of five beginning with Ka, joined with the Bindu, is the Kāma-bīja. (97)
Then, one should know that with the root mantra and the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), one purifies the subtle body;
thereafter, one should take possession [of it] with "svāhā" and another [mantra]. 98.
Modesty, Fortune, Nature, Ego, Intellect, Mind, Ear, Skin, Eye, then Tongue, Nose, Speech, Hand, and likewise Foot. (99)
The term *pāyūpastha* (anus and genitals), sound, touch, and form, then taste;
smell, space, wind, fire, water, and from the word "sound" [the sequence continues]. (100)

Having uttered the syllable "Bhū" for the self of the earth, followed by the pair of bindus and the initial letter, then the seed-syllable of Śakti, one's own mantra, and thereafter that which is the Śiva-tattva. (101)
"Paraṃ dehaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā" is the third;
having again taken up Māyā, one should utter the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī. (102)
Again, having uttered [the mantra] beginning with Śiva, then that beginning with Māyā, and having pronounced that beginning with Prakṛti, ending finally with the fifty Mātṛkās. || 103 ||

I purify the child, the root-vidyā, and that which is supreme through all the principles (tattvas), as well as the individual soul (jīva) resting upon the three principles; therefore, svāhā! || 104 ||
One should accept this pair by means of this [mantra], following the sequence from right to left.
Oṃ. The moist burns; I am the light.
The light burns; I am Brahman.
I am that; I am Brahman; I am.
I alone am the Self; I offer myself as an oblation, Svāhā! || 106 ||
Oṃ! That very Brahman which is directly perceived, I shall speak;
I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect [me].
May they protect me, the speaker; svāhā! || 107 ||

Oṃ! May the seers of the meters, the cows, and that which is the immortal meter of the earth, along with Indra, protect me with wisdom; may he take up the sacrificial ladle upon the earth with his mind—svāhā! || 108 ||
Having touched both hands with a cloth, one should purify the body;
by rubbing the entire body with both hands, this is the purification. (109)
One should wash both hands, or perform one or another [of these acts]. || 110 ||
The mantras for the extraction of the principles (*tattva-uddhimantra*):
Oṃ, may my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified;
may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā! || 111 ||
Oṃ, may earth, water, fire, air, and ether be purified for me;
may I become light, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā! || 112 ||
Oṃ! May my primordial nature, ego, intellect, mind, and ears be purified.
May I become light, stainless, and free from evil; svāhā! || 113 ||
Oṃ! May my skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and speech be purified.
May I become light, free from passion, and free from evil; svāhā! || 114 ||
Oṃ! May my hands, feet, anus, genitals, and sense of hearing be purified.
May I become light, free from passion, and free from evil; svāhā! || 115 ||
Oṃ! May touch, form, smell, taste, and space be purified for me.
May I become light, free from passion, and free from evil; svāhā! || 116 ||
Oṃ! May my selves consisting of air, fire, water, and earth be purified.
May I become light, free from passion, and free from evil; svāhā! || 117 ||
One should recite this very sevenfold mantra for the purification of reality. || 118 ||
Then, having performed the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi), one should establish the vessel for the Śakti;
after that, having established the vessels for the Yoginīs, one should place the vessel for the Vīra.
Thereafter, one should designate the vessel for the bali offering and the vessel for the water for the feet;
the wise practitioner should place the vessel for the water for sipping (ācamanīya) as before. || 120 ||
One should satisfy the multitude of rays by means of the reality of the Yoginī-vessel;
and one should likewise satisfy Vaṭuka and the others with the nectar from the bali-vessel.
Due to the absence of those [specific offerings], the hero should satisfy [the deities] with the general arghya;
he should cast a drop of the nectar from the Goddess’s vessel upon the sacrificial substances. || 122 ||
Having sprinkled his own body with water, he should contemplate it as being composed of the deity;
immediately thereafter, he should partake of the drop of nectar from the vessel of enjoyment.
The Description of the Five Offerings (Balipañcaka):
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme five offerings;
for as long as one has not offered them to Vaṭuka, to the Yoginīs, and to all the Bhūtas.
Likewise, O Kṣetrapāla and Rājarājeśvara, how indeed can a practitioner perform worship without first offering a bali-oblation? (125)
How can one worship in the fields without first giving to the guardian of the field?
He who worships Caṇḍikā without having given to Vaṭuka and the others [is guilty]. (126)
His worship becomes fruitless and the curse of the Goddess arises;
the offering for Vaṭuka should be given to the south, and the bali-offering for the Yoginīs to the north. (127)
The diligent practitioner should offer an oblation to all beings in the west, and an oblation to Kṣetrapāla in the middle, [and] to Rājarājeśvara.
One should draw a maṇḍala in the four directions, beginning with the south, as before;
having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) as previously described, one should contemplate Vaṭuka there.
The meditation on the Baṭuka [form of Śiva]:
holding a skull-cup in his hand, adorned with earrings, staff in hand,
dark blue like fresh darkness, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of accomplishments upon practitioners, who is the cause for severing obstacles to the sequential worship of the samaya. || 130 ||
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should offer the previously mentioned *bali*;
one should present the *bali* for Baṭuka with the thumb and the ring finger.
(126) Viṣa, Māyā, and the Goddess Ramā; from Devīputra Vaṭukanātha;
from Piṅgalapada; having uttered Jaṭābhāsvara and Piṅgala. (132)
Then, having uttered the mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), one should offer this oblation and worship to the three-eyed, great-souled Vaṭuka. 133.
Having offered this bali-oblation, he should thereafter contemplate the yoginīs.
The description of the meditation on the Yoginīs:

The Yoginīs are of the nature of desire-forms, possessing all virtues, having the character of a radiant lover, and being intoxicated; their breasts are adorned with garlands of skeletons, and they wear red garments as upper cloths.
Bearing the *liṅga*, the noose, the skull, and the trident, they are beautifully smiling and very gracious, well-attired as they bestow the fruits desired by their devotees and practitioners. (135)
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should thereafter offer the bali;
with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, one should present the bali to the Yoginīs.
Having uttered "Tāraṃ, lajjāṃ, ramāṃ, sarvasiddhiṃ ca yoginībhyaḥ,
sarvābhyo mātṛkābhyaśca," one should offer the bali.
p.
127) Then [one should utter] "viṣam," then "māyām," and after that "sarvabhūtebhyaḥ";
having uttered "sarvabhūtapatim," one should pronounce "bhyaḥ" ending with "namaḥ. || 138 ||
Having offered the bali-oblation to all beings, one should present the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla;
thereafter, for the sake of attaining success, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Field.

The meditation on the Protector of the Field is the state of nirvāṇa— non-conceptual, incomparable, complete, and changeless; it is the syllable *kṣa*, the syllable *hūṃ*, the one with adamantine fangs, the fire-mouthed, the fierce, and the one in a state of madness.

I bow to Kṣetrapāla, who utters the sound "phaṭ," whose face is furrowed with a frown, who is terrifying, who holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff, who is as blue as the sky, and who is accompanied by a ḍamaru drum. || 140 ||
Having meditated on the offering of the oblation (bali) to the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) and having worshipped him, one should subsequently present the oblation.
[The mantra consists of] the Viśa, Māyā, and Ramā seeds, followed by the letter Kṣa adorned with a nasal drop (bindu). (141)
Intermingled with the six long vowels, together with the Kṣetrapāla of his own station—this offering (bali) at the end of the word; then the pair "pūjāṃ gṛhṇa. || 142 ||
Having uttered the mantra ending with "svāhā," one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla;
having offered the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla, one should thereafter give [the offering] in the center.
Having thus cast forth the offering, one should present it to the Lord of the Kings of Kings;
and with the nectar from the vessel of the offering, one should satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.
Or one may offer the five-fold oblation (*pañcabali*) in a single location within the pervasive maṇḍala;
by remaining on the left side, one shall become the remover of all obstacles. (145)
One should offer Vaṭuka in the south, the Yoginī-bali in the north,
