the Bhūta-bali in the east, and that of the Kṣetrapāla in the west.
The excellent practitioner should offer the bali-oblation to the Lord of the Kings of Kings in the center.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter:
The Ritual of Worship.
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship, wherein whatever [is required] occurs.
And at the beginning of worship and recitation, and likewise at the end of the recitation. || 1 ||
At the conclusion of the worship and at the conclusion of the fire-ritual, the best of practitioners should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas),
having performed the six-limbed practice of breath-control.
One should perform the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭhapūjā) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual;
having meditated upon the Goddess with a concentrated mind according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
Having brought [the goddess] from the heart-lotus through the path of the nostrils,
the wise one [should contemplate] the Great Goddess, consisting of light, like one lamp from another lamp.
Thereafter, one should bring [the deity] into the midst of the mantra within the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali);
immediately after that, one should display the mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhanī).
Description of the Mudrās, beginning with Āvāhanī:
1. Āvāhanī-mudrā; 2. Sthāpanī-mudrā.
If one lowers the raised añjali [gesture], this becomes the invocation (āvāhanī);
if it is reversed, however, it becomes the installation (sthāpanī).
3. Sannidhāpanī-mudrā 4. Sannirodhanī-mudrā
The two fists joined together constitute the form of *sannidhāpana* (invocation);
with the thumbs placed inside the fists, it constitutes the form of *sannirodhana* (confinement).
5. The Avaguṇṭhanī Mudrā:
If the two index fingers of this very same mudrā are straightened, it becomes the Avaguṇṭhana mudrā when rotated all around. 8.
6. Sakalākṛtimudrā 7. Paramīkaraṇīmudrā 8. Dhenumudrā

The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs upon the limbs of the deity constitutes the act of "making complete" (sakalīkṛti). [This is performed] with the hands joined such that the thumbs are interlaced and the fingers are extended. || 9 ||
The wise have described this as "Mahāmudrā" for the purpose of supreme transformation.
Thereafter, having rotated the hands, one should join the pair of index fingers and middle fingers. (10)
Join the pair of the little finger and the ring finger together;
this is called the *dhenumudrā* by the wise for the purpose of making [substances] nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
Then, one should display the mudrās according to the procedure prescribed for each respective kalpa.
Having displayed the mudrā, one should then perform the three *tāla* claps. (12)
Having performed the binding of the directions with finger-snaps, one should then place the *jīva* [the vital breath];
or, having touched the *yantra* with the *lelihā* mudrā or with the five-fold *kuśa* grass.
For the lelihā-mudrā, having made the index, middle, and ring fingers equal and facing downward,
one should place the thumb upon the ring finger and keep the little finger straight. (14)
She is renowned as Lelihānā and is celebrated in the Jīvanyāsa;
with the root mantra, one whose self is radiant [should perform it] with water from the arghya substances. 15.
The wise one should sprinkle [the deity] three times; this is declared to be the purification of the deity.
Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra). || 16 ||
The worship with sixteen services:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), further sipping, bathing, garments, and ornaments. (17)
Likewise, there are offerings of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food, as well as salutations;
or else, the water for the feet, the respectful offering, water for sipping, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments. (18)
Then [there follow] perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and water for sipping;
thereafter, betel, worship, hymns of praise, and finally the libation.
Having offered the *arghya*, the *pādya*, and likewise the *ācamanīya*,
then the *madhuparka* and another *ācamana*, followed by fragrance and flowers. (20)
Incense, lamps, and food offerings are known as the ten-fold service (daśopacāraka).
Worship beginning with fragrance and ending with food offerings is the five-fold service (pañcopacārikā).
Worship is said by the wise to be of three kinds according to the distinction of superior and so forth: superior, middling, and inferior, respectively.
In the absence [of these], it is performed with flowers and water; and in the absence of those, with leaves.
In its absence, one should use white mustard, especially;
in its absence, with unbroken rice grains (akṣata); and in the absence of that, with dūrvā grass.
Or [one may perform it] with water in the absence [of flowers], and in the absence of that, with mental [offerings].
At the end of the root-mantra, one should utter the name of the deity joined with the suffix -aṅe.
Having recorded the name of the donor's property, one should thereafter offer water for the feet with the heart-mantra and the respectful offering (arghya) with the head-mantra. || 25 ||
The sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed with the Vāruṇa mantra, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with that same mantra;
one should cause the scent and flowers to be offered with the Śikhā mantra, and the eye-ointment with the Netra mantra.
The excellent practitioner should offer everything into the mouth;
having first presented the water for the feet and so forth, he should then present the water for bathing.
p.
133) Then, having placed the two sandals in the bright red bathing chamber, [one should perform] the description of the Goddess's bath.
It was provided with golden lion-thrones adorned with various jewels.
Having brought the Great Goddess there, the practitioner, with a pure disposition, should then perform an anointing with ghee while focusing on her in his mind. (29)
With fragrant divine oils, and with thousands of celestial maidens [offering] thousands of golden jars filled with fragrant water.
One should sprinkle Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, with a spirit of devotion using pure waters from various holy fords and thousands of fragrant substances.

Immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the image] with thousands of Naga maidens, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases, using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, with coconut water, likewise with sugarcane juice,
and with cool water mixed with seven kinds of earth.
One should perform the bathing of the Goddess with cool water, warm water, likewise with water containing jewels, and indeed with well-perfumed water. (34)
Having performed the ritual bathing of the Goddess with the *Sahasraśīrṣā* mantra and likewise with the *Pāvamānī* hymns, using eight jars and golden pitchers; 35.
Then, having performed the ritual services, one should cleanse the body with pure silk garments.
Cotton, bark, tree-bark, or silk cloth is prescribed as clothing. || 36 ||
A garment of red silk is recommended for Mahādevī;
or one of yellow silk may be offered to one's own deity.
One should offer to all the gods a variegated celestial garment;
however, one should avoid at all times any cloth that is blue or red.
One should avoid clothing that is stained with various colors or torn at the edges; one should give such cloth to Mahādevī, but never to anyone else.
Having given red garments, red garlands, and likewise red ornaments,
one should apply an ointment to the body consisting of *kākirya* mixed with fragrant sandalwood and *sihlaka*.
Furthermore, having offered the two beautiful sandals, the excellent practitioner,
being composed, should bring them into the center of the yantra and pay homage.
Again, having offered water for the feet and other items, one should worship according to the prescribed rite;
one should offer whatever fruits, flowers, and leaves are available. (42)
This rule does not apply to the offering of a handful of flowers;
that "one should not offer fruit with its face downward" is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures. (43)
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the knowledge-mudrā (jñānamudrā) and indeed with the mudrā called knowledge;
the knowledge-mudrā is proclaimed to be formed by the thumb and the index finger. (44)
Then, with the tips of the thumbs pressed against the middle and ring fingers, the practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the root mantra as before. (45)
Just as with the incense, so too should the wise preceptor offer the incense smoke using the middle and ring fingers at the middle joint. (46)
Holding the incense with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it,
raising it three times while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra in conjunction with the root mantra.
Joining the ring finger and the thumb, he should offer the food oblation;
all else that hero should present with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā).
The *madhuparka* is proclaimed to consist of curd, honey, and ghee;
one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice mixed with sesame (*kṛśara*), and food for the children combined with honey. (49)
Then one should offer flour-cakes, sweetmeats, milk, curd, as well as fruit, and betel leaf well-scented with camphor and other fragrances. (50)
At various intervals between the ritual services, one should offer water;
furthermore, garlands, perfumes, salutations, and lotuses should be presented.
One should offer a mirror, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, and sandals;
having performed worship according to the rules, one should satisfy [the deity] with the *tattvamudrā*.
The *tattvamudrā* is always formed by the union of the thumb and the ring finger of the left hand;
Bhairava is the deity in the thumb, and Caṇḍikā is always in the ring finger. (53)
The ritual of libation:
one should satisfy the lineage of the Kula by joining the ring finger and the thumb;
for the rite of subjugation, one should satisfy them with the thumb and the middle finger. (54)
Then, for the purpose of paralyzing, one should offer libations using the union of the little finger and the thumb;
for malevolent rites, one should offer libations using the union of the index finger and the thumb.
Having thus gratified the Goddess of the Gods with the substances of the Kula according to the rule,
the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed eight times or even once, as desired. (56)
One should not worship with only one hand, nor should one offer libations with only one hand;
having offered libations to the Great Goddess, one should then perform one's own ritual sequence.
One should always attend upon the deity with prepared flowers;
at the time of worship, one should not wave one's hand over the deity.
Having obtained the permission of the Goddess, the wise practitioner should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās),
while likewise meditating upon the lineage of gurus and the multitude of rays.
The procedure for the worship of the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās): having invoked them into their respective places, one should worship them immediately thereafter.
For he who, without the worship of the Guru, should worship his chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), [is at fault]. (60)
There is no atonement for that very person even within tens of millions of ocean-like hells;
therefore, one should perform the worship of the guru with every effort. (61)
The gurus of the divine lineage, the gurus of the perfected lineage, and likewise the gurus of the human lineage— these should be worshipped with diligent effort, in brief.
Alternatively, in all the scriptures, the gurus have been previously indicated;
and in whichever mantras those various groups of seers (ṛṣis) are remembered, [they are the gurus]. (63)
Each of these is worthy of worship at the beginning of the ritual service; I have described them to you in brief.
Without knowing the names of one's specific gurus, one should worship the triad of gurus.
Or there may be a group of four; no reduction beyond that should be made.
These are the Guru, the Paraguru, and then the Parāparaguru. || 65 ||
The supreme preceptor and others have indeed been described as auspicious gurus;
yet I do not know the name of my own guru, nor his lineage's purity at any time.
"Place the pollen of your lotus feet within my ear; [grant me] the state of servitude.
Having thus praised him with this hymn, if [he places] his own guru upon him... 67.
Whoever worships by means of that [disciple's] name, by him the worship of the Guru is performed;
for if one should perform worship without the worship of the Guru, [it is fruitless]. (68)
And for the pacification of those defects, one should perform the worship of the lineage (kulapūjā);
having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) as before, one should worship the multitude of rays.
Wherever [the deity] resides, if one does not worship it there,
his breaking of the fast occurs with nothing but flesh and blood.
He who performs worship separately on a single seat without [the prescribed] yantra, having abandoned the relationship of limb and possessor of limbs, shall incur the curse of the deity. (71)
(139) Invoking one deity while worshipping another,
the practitioner whose mind is fickle incurs a curse from both. (72)
Therefore, with every effort, having worshipped all the deities in their respective places in due order, one should thereafter perform the libation (tarpaṇa). || 73 ||
Having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmāṇī, he should offer libations;
then he should worship the Goddess again with extensive ritual offerings (upacāras).
First, one should provide a seat made of silver or wood, or a cloth or leather cover; one should place it in a case within the northern part of the pavilion.
Having offered water for the feet to Mahādevī, one should thereafter offer the arghya;
it should consist of śyāmā grass, dūrvā grass, a lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā.
This is declared to be the *arghya* for all the gods: [it consists of] fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* grass. (77)
That sipping of water (ācamana) is desired to be done with pure water alone;
however, if available, it should be perfumed with fragrant substances and the like.
One should offer the eightfold fragrance and the water for honor (arghya) and so forth; indeed, one should present the eightfold fragrance.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, cora, saffron, and gorocana; || 79 ||
They know jaṭāmāṃsī, kapijaṭā, and śakti as the eight fragrant substances;
[as well as] various kinds of flowers, garments, and ornaments.
Then one should offer a garland mixed with fragrant sandalwood to the Goddess;
one should apply an ointment to all her limbs and thereafter offer incense.
Description of the Preparation of Incense:
Uśīra, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, aguru, and likewise guggulu—this incense, combined with honey and clarified butter, is dear to Caṇḍikā. (82)
Alternatively:

O beautiful one, this auspicious incense-stick here has hairs that are like water for diseases—removing disease itself; its leaves are like those of the celestial tree, light and excellent; and it bears the seal of a lotus free from crookedness. 83.
Haritakī, musta, nakhī, māṃsī, jatu, śailaja, devadāru, kuṣṭha, guḍa, and sarjarasa—this ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅgadhūpa) has been proclaimed by the lords of sages. (84)
(Alternatively:
with agallochum, śīra, guggulu, sugar, honey, and sandalwood.
The preceptor should incense the deity with substances mixed with clarified butter, but not from a low position.
One should prescribe either pure guggulu incense or aguru;
having prepared one of these according to the path of the scriptures, one should offer it. 86.
One should not place the incense on the ground, nor on the seat, nor even in the water-pot.
Regarding the ritual for offering the family lamp:
first a lamp of ghee, and after that one produced from sesame oil.

Whether it be mustard oil, resinous extract, or that produced from aquatic plants, one should first recite the *praṇava*, then the words "Victory! (*jaya*), followed by "O Mother" (*mātaḥ*), and finally *svāhā*. (88)
With this [mantra] one should worship the bell, and with this one should ring it.
The lamp-stand should be made of metal or wood, and the lamp-tree likewise. (89)
In this matter, a lamp should never be placed upon the ground;
one should prepare the lamp in such a way that it brings delight to the eyes. (90)
The practitioner of mantras should light a ghee lamp on the right and an oil lamp on his own left;
he should illuminate a row of lamps made of ghee all around.
p.
142) A wick joined with camphor, or saturated with that very [substance], or a camphor-scented wick [anointed] with ghee or sesame oil. 92.
Having placed them, one should display lamps that are intensely fragrant;
then, having offered the lamp-oblation, one should present the family lamp.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with saffron upon a stand made of gold, silver, or bell-metal, the practitioner [should place it] there. (94)
Having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) in the form of the moon using barley, wheat, milk, and other ingredients,
and having placed it upon the eight petals as well as in the center, thereafter—
One should cast the nine-fold offering (navadīpa) there and consecrate it with the root mantra;
having lifted it there seven times, one should then whirl it nine times.
Having emanated the Great Goddess while reciting the root mantra, the best of practitioners should then display the wheel mudrā. || 97 ||
Regarding the characteristics of the wheel mudrā (*cakramudrā*):
having joined the thumb, middle finger, and little finger of the left hand with those of the right, the wise one should place the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*) within the [other] fingers. (98)
When the practitioner places his right thumb upon the left [hand], and through this mutual joining, it is proclaimed as the Cakra-mudrā. || 99 ||
Having offered the lamp of the lineage, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented in metallic vessels, or upon a wooden plank, or on a lotus leaf. (100)
A wise person should prepare the food offering (naivedya) either on a plate made of sacrificial wood, or,
in the absence of all these, on one made of stone if it has been fashioned by his own hand.
One should not give [the offering] in a garment of bark or in a metal vessel; if given in such, one would fall into hell.
Whatever is appropriate, however, one should place it in any worthy vessel and present it.
If it is prepared with food and water other than those contained in the arghya vessel,
the Great Goddess does not accept it, even if it is offered according to hundreds of ritual procedures.
Having diligently offered to the Goddess an oblation consisting of the six flavors, as well as various kinds of fruits and diverse articles, || 104 ||
Having offered wine, meat, fish, and then a mudrā, one should diligently present various kinds of food to the Goddess. (105)
Various kinds of delightful condiments, combined with astringent and bitter flavors, as well as pungent, sour, and sweet, including milk-rice with sugar. 106.
Flour prepared with sugar, milk, pieces of sugar-candy, and so forth, as well as milk, curd, buttermilk, and fresh butter with sugar; (107)
One should offer sugar-candies and other various kinds of sweets;
one should present foods to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, bitten, and eaten.
If one is unable [to offer physically], one should give with the mind; thus, one must not omit this rite.
Then, having offered a handful of water (culuka), one should display the *prāṇa-mudrā*.

Regarding the five mudrās of the vital breaths and so forth: the mudrā of prāṇa is proclaimed [to be formed] by the thumbs and little fingers; the mudrā of apāna is celebrated [as being formed] by the thumbs, middle fingers, and index fingers. (110)
The mudrā of vyāna is shown by joining the thumbs with the middle fingers;
that of udāna is proclaimed to be formed by all the fingers joined together, excluding the little fingers.
The Samāna-mudrā is displayed with all the fingers;
it represents Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna. || 112 ||
The mantra of the Mudrikā consists of the name beginning with the syllable *tārā*, ending in the dative case (*caturthī*) and followed by the wife of Agni (*agnijāyā*).
When this is performed with the left hand, it is proclaimed as the *prāsa-mudrā*, which is like a spear (*prāsa*). || 113 ||

Having again offered water for sipping to the Goddess, the excellent practitioner [offers] self-arisen flowers, those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and agallochum (*aguru*). (114)
One should cause to be offered musk, saffron, and red sandalwood;
likewise, fragrant flowers, garlands, and ornaments such as red blossoms. (115)
One should offer vermilion, collyrium, red lac, a silk cluster,
as well as the flowers of the Droṇa-aparājitā, the Karavīra, and the Javā.
One should offer with great effort that which brings pleasure to Caṇḍikā;
and when a Java flower is offered, one shall obtain the fruit of silk garments.
Furthermore, one can never describe the greatness of Aparā;
thereafter, one should offer betel-leaf well-scented with camphor and other fragrances. || 118 ||
Furthermore, a garland combined with fragrant sandalwood should be offered, as well as a mirror, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a fan, and so forth. (119)
Then one should satisfy Caṇḍikā by offering the sacrifice of a goat and other animals;
however, there is a strict prohibition against cutting the animal with one's own hand— one should present the offering, but one must not kill it oneself.
One should not kill an animal with one's own hands; one must avoid violence committed by oneself.
If one should kill [an animal] through negligence, one will go to the Raurava hell. (121)
Having offered the sacrificial oblation of goats and other animals, one should present incense and lamps;
then, taking the blood arising from one's own heart into a vessel, [one should offer it].
One should offer water mixed with rock salt, along with sugar and honey, to Mahādevī for the sake of attaining all auspicious fortune.
Having sprinkled blood, the wise one should cause it to be offered with the Vāgbhava mantra;
or he may give it with the Śakti-bīja, but neither above nor below the navel.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, he should gratify his own deity;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform the purification of the mantra.
Having taken up the letters of the *mātṛkā* and the syllables of the root mantra, repeating them in successive order twice over is declared to be the purification of the mantra. (126)
Recitation (japa) is of three kinds, distinguished as vocal and so forth;
first, one should perform recitation for the sake of purifying the mantra, and thereafter [the other two].
Recitation is declared to be threefold: vocal (vācika), whispered (upāṃśu), and mental (mānasa). || 127 ||
Know that recitation which arises from the movement of the tongue, lips, and lower lip is vocal (*vācika*); that which involves only the tongue is whispered (*upāṃśu*). (128)
The mental recitation is known as the contemplation of the syllables of the mantra with the mind;
it should be understood that the vocal recitation is one hundred times [more effective], and the whispered recitation is one hundred and one times [more effective].
Therefore, mental recitation is declared to be a hundred times superior;
or rather, the "spoken" (nigada) should be understood as that which is uttered with clear speech. (130)
But the unmanifest (avyakta) is proclaimed as the whispered (upāṃśu), with its face quivering;
and that should be understood as the mental (mānasa), possessing the form of syllables through contemplation. || 131 ||

However, that which is recited a mere hundred thousand times by diligent practitioners through the *nigada* mode of recitation is in every respect equal to silent mental recollection (*upāṃśu*). || 132 ||
Whatever is recited by the practitioner even at a distance of one *pāṃśula-kṣama*, it becomes equal for the practitioner due to its mental utterance. || 133 ||
Having performed the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual beginning with the ṛṣi and so forth;
then, having meditated upon one’s own guru at the crown of the head and the Goddess in the heart. (134)
Meditating upon oneself as the form of Kāmakalā, one should begin the recitation;
at the beginning of the recitation, one should meditate on Śivā, and at the end of the meditation, one should recite again. (135)
The practitioner who is united with recitation and meditation attains success quickly;
having performed meditation, the wise one should recite the mantra according to the sequence taught by the guru. (136)
All mantras shall grant success; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Then, having diligently sprinkled the rosary with water, one should worship it. (137)
Mālā-pūjā: One should worship the rosary with the heart-mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ akṣamālāyai*.
*Oṃ māle māle mahāmāle sarvasiddhisvarūpiṇi* || 138 ||
"The fourfold goals have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me.
Having performed the rite of recitation with the rosary and having worshipped it, one should then take the rosary in the right hand. (139)
Having brought it near the heart, one should not touch it with the left hand;
for without the yantra and the mantra, there is a void of mantra due to the lack of armor (kavaca).
And with the left hand, [he should take] the garland, the characteristics of the signs of death, the prescribed number, the clay, and likewise the unbroken rice grains. (141)

Having placed [the rosary] in the middle part of the middle finger, being composed in meditation, one should not touch the rosary with the index finger, but should move it with the tip of the thumb. (142)
Taking up the dam on both sides, one should perform the rite of recitation;
for without a dam, water flows down into the low ground in an instant. (143)
Likewise, for the twice-born, the Praṇava is declared to be the mantra and the bridge;
for Śūdras, the syllable Au-kāra situated upon the moon-point (bindu) is said to be the bridge.
For Śūdras, there may be one original boundary or two boundaries according to their wish;
however, the twice-born (dvijātis) are declared to have two boundaries in every respect. || 145 ||
Just as the mantra, so too the hymn and the armor; without the bridge (setu), they would be fruitless. Therefore, one should perform the bridge. || 146 ||
Taking each seed-syllable individually from above the limbs, the knower of mantras who, while reciting the preceding seed-syllable, touches the subsequent seed-syllable; || 147 ||
The recitation of one who lacks the thumb is always fruitless;
thus, according to the prescribed rule, one should abandon both slowness and haste. (148)
The best of practitioners, having circumambulated Mount Meru, should perform the recitation;
however, the recitation performed by one who transgresses the rules of counting must be repeated. (149)
Rākṣasas seize [the practitioner] by that means; therefore, the wise one should always count [the beads] according to this method, or likewise using a rosary (karamālā) or the Mātṛkā. 150.
One should perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hands, but never that which is performed for a specific desire (kāmya).
Furthermore, in both the daily recitation and the fire-oblation (homa), no specific number is prescribed.
The number of recitations prescribed therein is said to be one thousand and eight,
or one hundred and eight, or sometimes even thirty. (152)
The practitioner should not perform the daily recitation with fewer than thirty repetitions;
having performed the recitation according to his capacity and having practiced breath control (prāṇāyāma), [he should proceed]. 153.

Having concealed the dedication of the recitation (japa), one should then offer the rosary along with flowers and water for the guest-offering (arghya) into the hand of the Goddess, presenting the fruit of the recitation as consisting of pure light.
Having offered [the deity] with the mantra "guhyātiguhyam" and praising him, one should ring the bell;
one should perform a threefold prostration according to the rules for the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga). || 155 ||
(151) Whether by the chin, the mouth, the nose, or the head, whatever contact with the earth occurs through the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head) or the two ears; || 156 ||
(Alternatively:
Prostration with eight limbs—namely, the chest, head, gaze, knees, mind, feet, speech, and hands—is to be known; thereafter follows the perpetual fire-oblation (nityahoma). 157.
One who knows the mantras should perform the daily and occasional fire-oblations on sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila);
however, one should not perform an optional oblation (kāmyahoma) without a fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
To his right, one should draw a square measuring one cubit, with a height of one finger-breadth, using sand on all sides. || 159 ||
Therein, having drawn a hexagon in the center and sprinkled it with water, one should worship it;
having worshipped the Ādhāraśakti, one should likewise perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) as before.
Then, having kindled the fire,
the practitioner of mantra should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) by means of the weapon-mantra of sound toward the blazing fire in the southwest.
The wise one should establish the fire facing himself;
having kindled the fire with the root mantra, he should display the Jvālinī mudrā. || 162 ||
The *jvālinī* mudrā:
having made the wrists level, the hands are extended with the fingers spread out.
Having joined the two middle fingers together, one should insert the two thumbs into their midst. || 163 ||
This is the Jvālinī mudrā, supreme for the rite of fire-offering (homa);
it is [attained] after worshipping the Fire through the union of Śiva and Śakti. || 164 ||
Having invoked the chosen deity into the midst of the fire with a concentrated mind,
one should display the *āvāhanī* and other mudrās and then provide protection.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then purify the oblation;
having established the sacrificial fire as before, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Having performed the fourfold purification, one should designate the vessel for clarified butter;
having constructed the mandala as before, one should worship it according to the previous procedure.
Having placed the vessel here, one should cause the oblation to be deposited there;
then, having consecrated it ten times with the root mantra, one should offer it into the fire.
The Praṇava, then "bhūḥ svāhā," and "idam agnaye" with the dative suffix; the Tāra, "bhuvaḥ," the wife of Vahni (svāhā), and the word "idam vāyave. || 169 ||
Having uttered "Oṃ svaḥ svāhā, this [is for] Prajādhipati," he then offers three oblations together with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One should contemplate the unity of the oblation, the fire, the Goddess, and the Self;
then, one should offer six oblations with the mantra of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 171 ||
At the end of the root mantra, one should utter the name of the deity joined with the suffix -ṅe;
then, having uttered "svāhā," [one should recite it] one thousand and eight times.
The wise practitioner should offer oblations with clarified butter, sesame seeds, or rice grains, either one hundred and eight times or even half of that. || 173 ||
Alternatively, one may perform eighteen [oblations]; this is the rule for the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma):
with meat, honey, clarified butter, fish, flowers, and likewise sesame seeds. (174)
With barley, grains, mung beans, and likewise with family-flowers and fruits, with apāmārga, bilva leaves, and the beautiful bhṛṅgarāja plants. || 175 ||
The names of flowers are:
karavīras, javā flowers, aparājitās, droṇas, and kiṃśukas;
as well as lotuses, water-lilies, kunda flowers, and blue and red utpalas.
And with *saugandhika* flowers, *bandhūka*, *kesara*, and *campaka*; likewise with *jātī*, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and *kadambaka*.

Having completed the fire-oblation (homa) for the Goddess according to this ritual procedure— with beautiful flowers, fruits, and leaves as prescribed— the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) concludes the rite.
The conclusion of the *homa* consists of five *prāṇāhuti*s with the root mantras and six oblations for the six limbs; thereafter,
having invoked the assembly of gurus and the assembly of rays, one should perform the oblation.
Having offered one oblation at a time in sequence, the excellent practitioner,
having again offered three oblations with effort to the Goddess, [should proceed]. (180)
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamanīya),
one should dissolve [the deity] into the fire with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, [reciting] "Oṃ agnaye" and thereafter [the name of] the Goddess.
One should offer three oblations with the mantra ending in the wife of fire (svāhā);
then, having dismissed both the fire and the goddess, one should sound the conch and the bell.
Having then gratified the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, who resides within the wheel,
and having withdrawn her into the crown of his own body, he should perform the remaining rites.
The description of the fruit of receiving the five principles (pañcatattva) once they have been offered:
thereafter, one should drink the nectar of the Kula (kulāmṛta) together with the Kaulikas.
He who, having given the five principles to the Great Goddess, does not partake of them himself— [is a transgressor]. (184)
Likewise, he who [offers] food offerings and the like to the goddesses shall become subject to their curse;
having become diseased, miserable, and impoverished, he shall attain hell. || 185 ||
Regarding the threefold nature of drinking:
one should not drink alone with Kaulikas through mere illusion.
Drinking is said to be of three kinds, according to the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu). || 186 ||
The divine drink is that which is [offered] before the Goddess; the heroic drink belongs to those who dwell in solitude.
That drink which is devoid of consecration and the like is known as the animal drink. (187)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter:
The Procedure for Worship, Meditation, and so forth of Annapūrṇā.
I shall now proclaim the method that bestows the four aims of human existence.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in the middle of the food, one should indeed [place it] there.
Having placed the full vessel there with the ritual materials,
the practitioner should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the six long vowels.
Then, he should meditate upon Annapūrṇā, the bestower of supreme bliss.
Taking up the visualization of Annapūrṇā, [the practitioner] holds a golden ladle filled with milk-rice in the right hand and a vessel of jewels in the other.
I worship my mother, who is nine years old, golden-hued, adorned with all ornaments, and devoted to the giving of alms-food.

Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess and invoked her there, the excellent practitioner, after displaying the *tattva-mudrā*, should then speak these words regarding the nectar of food: ||| 4 ||
Having uttered the couple [of mantras] ending in *pūrayat*, followed by *namaḥ* and then *svāhā*, one should there satisfy [the deities] with devotion; thereafter, one should worship Annapūrṇā. (5)

One should write the Tāra (Oṃ), Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrībīja (Śrīṃ), and the Kāmabījaka (Klīṃ); at the end of these, one should write "Hṛt" and then the word "Bhagavati," followed by the word "Māheśvari."
Having recited "O Annapūrṇā, O Agnijāyā, O most excellent one who fulfills [the desire for] food" according to his ability, he, being composed, should praise the Goddess.
But those who, having worshipped the Goddess of gods, do not worship the Kaulikas, are the most sinful; they are not recipients of Caṇḍikā’s grace.
The food offering placed before me has been accepted by you through the mere sight of it;
O lotus-eyed one, I shall now eat from the tongue of your virtuous devotee.
The deities, beginning with Śiva and Śakti, reside upon his tongue;
therefore, the best of practitioners should offer oblations into the mouths of the Kaulikas.
Desiring what is dear to Caṇḍikā, one should always worship the devotees of the Goddess. I shall now describe the characteristics of the Kaulas according to the tantras. (11)
The characteristics of a Kaula are as follows:
they are satisfied with the cessation of suffering, and they are free from envy toward the Vidyā and the Āgamas.
Delighting in the knowledge of their lineage, peaceful, devoted to Śiva, and firm in their vows. || 12 ||
Those heroes whose hair stands on end and whose voices become faltering when their lineage is being proclaimed,
and who are filled with tears of joy, are declared to be the lords of the Kaulikas.
"The universal dharma is superior in the world; this is the family dharma (kuladharma) proclaimed by Śiva. Those whose intellects are thus resolved are called the best of the Kaulikas. || 14 ||
Praise of the Worship of the Kula:
He who knows the reality of the Kula and is proficient in the Kula scriptures—he is always superior among men devoted to the worship of the Kula; he is a true Kaulika. 15.

He who is delighted upon seeing those devoted to the lineage, those who follow the lineage conduct, those who possess lineage knowledge, and those who observe the lineage vows— he is a Kaulika and is dear to Śiva.
By accepting the five principles (pañcatattva), one who knows the reality of the meaning of the root mantra and is devoted to the deity and the guru becomes a Kaulika through initiation.
The sight of a Kulācārya is difficult to obtain in all the worlds—he who, having himself summoned the Śaktis as well as those initiated into the Kula, [bestows them]. 18.
Having worshipped with the perception of them as deities using scents, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth,
one should satisfy them with great devotion by means of the five mudrās beginning with *mā*.
When they are satisfied, Śiva and all the other deities are satisfied;
that land where one who possesses knowledge of the Kula dwells is a vessel of merit. (20)
By seeing and worshipping him, one may uplift twenty-one generations of one's family;
this applies upon beholding a knower of the lineage (kulajñānin), whether he is staying in one's own house or in another's.
The Yoginīs arrive there joyfully along with the Yogins;
having entered, the ancestral deities enjoy [the feast] together with the Lord of Kulayogins. (22)
Whatever is performed for those devoted to the Kula is as if performed for the gods;
since all the gods are dear to the Kula, one should therefore worship the Kaulika.
The gods beginning with Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as sages and rākṣasas, are indeed devoted to their family duties; what then need be said of human beings?
Caṇḍikā is not pleased elsewhere even when well-worshipped;
indeed, Caṇḍikā is truly satisfied only when the Lord of the Kaulas is properly worshipped. (25)
The wise person who obtains that fruit from worshipping the lords of the Kaulas could never attain that same fruit through pilgrimages, austerities, vows, or sacrifices. (26)
In censuring him there is fault;
yet from worshipping, reciting, and offering oblations, various merits likewise accrue.
However, for the Kaulika who would show contempt for a Kaulika, all that becomes fruitless. (27)
Know that house to be a cremation ground; it is the abode of the most wicked, the lowest of outcastes, wherein the essence of the family is abandoned and bestowed upon another. (28)
One should know that such a gift is fruitless, and the giver shall also go to hell—[the giver] who is joined with sinful conduct and is excluded from all the worlds. (29)
For the family wealth offered to the Lord of Kula-yogins protects the lineage;
when the Lord of the Kaulas partakes even once, the merit becomes ten millionfold. (30)
What need is there for many meals? That merit cannot even be calculated.
Therefore, with every effort, in all circumstances, and in every way, [one should practice]. (31)
Being devoted to the family dharma, one should worship the knower of the lineage;
then all the ancestors rejoice and the grandfathers sing.
The great-grandfathers dance when a follower of the Kaula tradition enters their home;
for him, there is the fruit of ten million sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya rites. (33)
By the union with the circle of the mere drop (bindu), one gives to the Kaulikas;
this is equal to the gift of the earth filled with gold for ten million kalpas. || 34 ||
That fruit [is attained] through touch and knowledge in the sacrificial hall of the Kaulika;
when the Kaulikas are pleased, Caṇḍikā becomes pleased.
Whether remembered, praised, seen, saluted, or even addressed,
he who is most devoted to his family duties purifies— even if he be a Caṇḍāla— by his very presence.
Whether he be omniscient or a fool, whether he be superior or even inferior—in every respect he is Śiva; therefore, one should worship him with diligent effort.
Truly blessed among all people in the worlds is that man whose impurities are exhausted, to whom the family preceptors and spiritual practitioners draw near. (38)
Then, having summoned the Kaulas and especially the Śaktis—
whether they be his own Śakti, a Vīra-Śakti, or an initiated housewife— (39)
"Having caused [another] to drink, one should drink the substance oneself; such is the determination of the scripture.
But he who, though capable, partakes of the family substance without having first offered it," (40)
His worship is fruitless and the deity is not pleased;
that which is worship without the yantra, and that which is the satiation without meat. (41)
But drinking without the [proper] power (śakti), all of that becomes fruitless;
he who turns away when summoned, and he who enters even when not summoned. (42)
That sinner shall be excluded from all dharmas;
having taken birth in the womb of an animal, he falls into the hells. || 43 ||
In the place of worship, one should diligently provide seats according to the ritual of the wheel (cakravidhi).
Then, all the Kaula women, having washed their hands and feet, [should enter]. 44.
Having prostrated, one should enter the circle with the five types of mudrās;
the place for women is one, and that for men is another, being distinct.
Alternatively, having formed pairs, one should seat them in order,
either in the form of a row or properly in the form of a circle.
But the deluded soul who creates distinctions of caste within the center of the *cakra*—
him the *yoginīs* devour, and Caṇḍikā shall always curse him. (47)
The negation of caste distinctions within the circle:
"In this circle, there is no distinction of caste; all are remembered as equal to Śiva.
In the active wheel of Bhairavī, all castes are considered twice-born. (48)
When the circle of Bhairavī has ceased, all castes become distinct;
indeed, whatever castes there may be, they become devoted to the secret path. 49.
Those various sages are in every way truly true; of this there is no doubt.
For they are indeed like gods in the meritorious worlds such as heaven and the like. 50.
In the very same way, all gods and indeed all humans are within the center of the wheel;
for even in the Veda it is established thus, and [the scripture] declared that "everything is Brahman. (51)
What need is there for much speaking here? Within the circle, the male practitioners are always of the nature of Śiva, and the women are of the nature of the Goddess.
One should worship all [the goddesses] within the circle with the thought that they are Śiva and Śakti;
then, through the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) according to the Jyeṣṭha-krama, one should [worship] on the forehead with sandalwood paste and perfumes.
Having applied the forehead mark (tilaka) along with unbroken grains (akṣata) for both the Śaktis and the practitioners,
the best of practitioners should offer ointment and garlands.
164) Regarding the ritual for drinking wine: having prepared a beautiful vessel that is neither too large nor too small, one should proceed.
And let them be drawn forth by the practitioner with [mantras] numbered as eyes, fires, and arrows. || 55 ||
It is stated in the *Kulasādhana* that the drinking of the causal [substance] should be performed;
however, even this excessive drinking must not be done by practitioners. (56)
Having lifted up the vessel with both hands and [offering] the second in due order,
[he should offer it] then to the feet of the venerable Guru and directly to Paraśiva.
One should offer the meat together with [other substances], perceiving it as the deity, in the proper sequence;
immediately after that, one should give the full nectar-essence to the Guru.
After that, one should give the remainder to women and then to heroes; finally, one should cause it to be given to one who is of noble birth, of noble lineage, and devoted to his family.
One should offer the Guru’s vessel to the gurus, the Śakti’s vessel to the śaktis, and the Vīra’s vessel to the vīras; one should drink the vessel of enjoyment oneself.
If the Guru is not personally present, then one should offer [the vessel] into the water;
thereafter, all [the disciples], perceiving it as nectar, should take up that excellent vessel.
p.
165) One should perform the meditation on the goddess Sudhā according to the authority of the scriptures.
[The Meditation on the Goddess Sudhā]
When the ocean, that best of seas, the milk-ocean, was being churned in its midst.
There, the goddess Sudhā arose, assuming the form of a maiden;
she had the appearance of cow-urine and was born from the foam of nectar.
She is endowed with eighteen arms and has large, lotus-like eyes;
Ānanda and Maheśvara were born upon the peak of bliss. (64)
From the union of those two, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva himself arise;
therefore, being complete, I worship this goddess Surā.
Having meditated thus, one should then recite the root mantra seven times;
thereafter, the hero should display the five mudrās over it.
Thereafter, one should repeatedly show the "cow-source" (dhenu-yoni) mudrā;
by means of three claps of the hands and snapping the fingers, one should perform the binding of the directions.
As before, one should offer libations upon the head to Ānandabhairava, as well as to the goddess Ānandabhairavī and the lineage of gurus with great care. (68)
The chosen deity, the multitude of rays, Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapālaka, Vaṭuka, Bhairava, as well as Yoginī and Ḍākinī; || 69 ||
One should satisfy the great elements and the obstructors in their proper order.
Those who have not received the full initiation have no authority over the drinking [of the sacramental substances].
Without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation of the guru.
Even a hero, having drunk according to the rite of animal-sacrifice liquor, shall go to hell;
likewise, one who fails to satisfy the row of gurus and the multitude of rays [of the deity]. (71)
If a follower of the Kaula path drinks the substance, his drinking is indeed like that of a beast;
so too for one who desires to consume that substance without possessing Kaula knowledge. (72)
He shall become a perpetrator of a great sin (mahāpātakin), excluded from all religious duties;
he shall consume liquor and meat, and being fallen, he becomes a sinner.
For the purpose of recollecting the meaning of the mantra and for the sake of stabilizing the mind, one who is liberated from the bonds of duality should practice the drinking of wine. (74)
He who consumes liquor and other such substances for the sake of pleasure is a sinner;
the practitioner, however, should offer even flesh and other substances to bind [the deity] for the gratification of the God. (75)
One should practice with the five mudrās; otherwise, one becomes a sinner.
Apart from the time of sacrifice, at other times, defilement always arises.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims, attains neither perfection nor the supreme goal in the hereafter. (77)
For one who lives according to his own whims and is devoid of the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā),
there is no auspicious destination whatsoever, neither through austerity nor through meritorious deeds and the like.
For those endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking is absolutely prescribed;
for those devoid of the full consecration, drinking leads to an extremely miserable rebirth. || 79 ||
Those who engage in this wheel without having performed the Kaulika conduct and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru—Bhairavas indeed strike them down. (80)
Those who are uninitiated, who lack proper conduct, and who are devoid of mudrās and mantras must never consume the ritual substances without performing recitation and worship. (81)
By consuming it, one goes to hell and no atonement whatsoever arises; therefore, one whose soul is purified by the consecration of mantras may partake of the drinking of wine (alipāna). 82.
The state of divinity, which liberates one from the bonds of existence, arises;
thereafter, the hero should investigate this especially through sound reasoning. (83)
(p. 168) An investigation into the prohibition of drinking as stated in the Dharmaśāstras:
"The Brahmins eat prepared food and consume powder produced from snails."
Fermented gruel (kāñjika), kāsamarada, and likewise ghee prepared with śivā; || 84 ||
If there were no fault in these cases, then nothing would be subject to fault:
"Having drunk liquor out of delusion, a twice-born man should drink liquor that is the color of fire. (85)
Thus, the prohibition is firmly established in the scriptures of Manu and others;
however, having drunk [the liquor] through delusion or ignorance, an expiation is prescribed. (86)

Whatever fault is declared regarding drinking, the expiation for that indeed occurs at that very time, after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed in the Vedas and Shastras. (87)
From the perspective of gnosis, within the circle of Bhairavī, there is no fault whatsoever for those possessed of knowledge;
remembering the Guru while drinking wine and eating meat, one incurs no sin. (88)
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
just as the drinking of soma is ordained for Brahmins during sacrifices. (89)

The drinking of liquor should likewise be performed at the proper time, as it bestows both enjoyment and liberation; however, for those who seek worldly fruits and possess egoism, it is indeed a source of corruption.

For those who are free from egoism, there is neither prohibition nor injunction. Only for one who would have the delusion that drinking [alcohol] is [merely] blood and semen could there be disgust. (19)

In one who is pure, there arises the delusion of impurity and suspicion of sin regarding sexual intercourse; such a fallen man may worship Caṇḍī, but how could he possibly recite the mantra of the Goddess? (92)
He too shall become diseased and miserable, and he shall go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, the practitioner should worship the fifth [Tattva] with a non-dual state of being. || 93 ||
The wheel-practice (cakrānuṣṭhāna) is the vessel; Brahmā, the gods, Viṣṇu, the taster of nectar (rasāda), and Rudra [are the contents].
Bliss (ānanda) is declared to be the crest-jewel (śekhara), and bliss indeed is Sadāśiva. || 94 ||
The deity Bhairava is wine, and intoxication is said to be his Śakti;
oh, for wine, when consumed, can indeed delude even the gods! (95)
Wine is Śakti and meat is Śiva;
wine is Śakti and meat is Śiva, and he who partakes of them is Bhairava himself.
The bliss arising from the union of these two is called liberation. 96.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established within the body;
wine is its manifestor, and therefore it is drunk by yogis. (97)
Having reflected thus, the wise hero should perform the purification of reality;
according to the previously mentioned rite, he should pay homage to the vessel. 98.
The mantra for the salutation of the first vessel:

This is the ocean of bliss, the great-souled nectar of the three sections (trikhaṇḍāmṛta) in its very essence; it is drenched by the nectar of the moon shining from the crest of the glorious Bhairava, and is frequented by the hosts of Kṣetrapālas, Yoginīs, and Mahāsiddhas.
I bow to the venerable first vessel held in the lotus-hand, which bestows purity. 99.
Then, having paid homage to the vessel, one devoted to devotion should recite:
"O Śivā, whatever is done by me, whether knowingly or unknowingly... (100)
"Considering all this to be your own work, please forgive me.
Having thus praised the Great Goddess, they should perform mutual salutations. (101)
Having obtained permission in their presence, he should say himself, "I shall receive it";
or, being permitted by the Guru or by those of noble family with the words, "Be pleased [to do so]," [he may proceed]. 102.
Having mastered the practice of the wheel (*cakrānuṣṭhāna*), the wise one, having become self-perfected, should assume the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*).
Having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the mudrā with the right, one should [proceed] from the right side.
One should not consume wealth out of a desire for luxury;
one should not lift anything with only one hand, nor drink with only one hand.

Then, one should meditate upon the Goddess, the supreme Prakṛti, who is a single digit (kalā) situated within the triangle that is the root of the self, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. 105.
One should offer the substance accompanied by the mantra into the fire of consciousness, which is the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti;
one should not drink the substance with noise, nor let a drop fall below.
He who makes a sound while performing the libation (tarpaṇa) for the family deity goes to the Raurava hell until the dissolution of all offerings (yāvadāhutasaṃplavam). 107.
Since drinking without that which is to be chewed merely increases the poison, one should therefore chew that which is to be chewed according to the prescribed sequence of ritual. (108)
Those who sit upon a single seat while eating from a single vessel, or drink a substance from a single bowl, indeed go to hell. 109.
One should never touch the ritual substances of the Kula while one is impure from food remnants within the Cakra;
rather, having washed both hands outside, one should cause the Kula substances to be offered. (110)
One should never give [an offering] with only one hand, nor without the ritual mudrās; likewise, one should avoid spitting, discharging excrement, urine, or passing wind.
He who should engage in joking, idle chatter, caviling, or excessive talk within the circle (cakra) shall become a beast for the Yoginīs. (112)
One should avoid indifference, fear, and anger while in the midst of the circle;
one should never touch the vessel with the feet or with any part of the body below the waist.
One should not move the bowl from its place, nor should one cause a mixing of bowls.
One should not lift the bowl with noise, and likewise, one should not fill it [to the brim]. 114.
One should not strike one alms-bowl against another, nor should one bring an alms-bowl down to the ground.
One should not lift an alms-bowl without its supporting stand, nor should one set it down on a surface that lacks a support.
A wise person should not leave an alms-bowl empty, nor should he ever wave it about; he should not step over the bowl, nor should he lift it up and drop it.
Furthermore, one should present the alms-bowl in due order and again pay homage to the bowl; the wise person should then recollect this mantra. || 117 ||
p.
173) The mantra for the second vessel-worship:

Oṃ! This golden [vessel], which brings the essence of fish and was given by my beloved along with drinks and other offerings, has been presented to her by one whose eyes are like trembling red lotuses.
Placing in my left hand that which is sweet and which effects the purification of purity, I now worship my own second vessel, which increases sole bliss. || 118 ||
Having performed the libation as before, one should perform the third [rite];
having held it together with the mudrā, one should salute the supreme vessel. || 119 ||
The mantra for saluting the third vessel:

I now salute the third vessel, which is endowed with the entire collection of the arts of all traditions, which illuminates wonder, and which is served by Candra, Upendra, Mahendra, Śambhu, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and others; it is meditated upon at all times by hosts of gods and groups of sages seeking liberation, and it is capable of awakening one’s own self. (120)
Having performed the libation as before, one should then pay homage to the fourth.
The mantra for the veneration of the fourth vessel:

Oṃ! [This] wine brings forth the essence of fish; it is filled by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others; it is devoted to the ritual acts of mudrā and sexual union; it is the locus of the salty, sour, and bitter [tastes];
it is thoroughly purified by the flesh of the eight Siddhas, Bhairavas, and Kālīs, and by the Ācāryas.
May the fourth vessel, accompanied by the reality of the five aspects, protect [us]; obeisance! || 122 ||
Having performed the libation as before, one should then pay homage to the fifth [deity]. || 123 ||
The mantra for the veneration of the fifth vessel:
Upon the base, which is the circle of the king of serpents, the vessel is the orb of the earth;
the wine is the water of the seven oceans and the flesh; and the eight elephants of the directions [are the offering].
Thus, worshipping Bhairava daily, I am protected by the hosts of stars and by the multitudes of gods and asuras led by Āditya, who act as my obedient servants and attendants. || 124 ||
Then, having worshipped it, the knower of mantras should drink the sixth vessel.
The mantra for the sixth salutation to the vessel:

Oṃ! To Rudra, who has arisen from the supreme bliss of the seat of the auspicious chowrie; to the illuminating Vāmā, who is delightful with sovereignty and brings about auspiciousness, [I offer] the imperial dominion of union (sāyujya).
I worship the sixth vessel: the nectar of Hari, which removes the blind well of existence consisting of various diseases, destroys rebirth, and is the glorious and most beautiful satisfaction.
Having performed the libation as before, one should worship the seventh [deity]. || 127 ||
The mantra for the seventh salutation to the vessel:

Oṃ! [I bow to] that supreme consciousness which [pervades] waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state (turya), which bestows the status of the witness, which resembles lightning and the sun, which possesses brilliance, and which is pervaded by the digits of moonlight;
it is the Kuṇḍalinī, moving upward, situated between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and possessing three coils.
May the vessel, which through its seventh filling surpasses supreme bliss, protect me. || 128 ||
Having bound the vessels with these [mantras], the most excellent practitioner himself shall attain all rites; at the end of the body, he shall become Bhairava. || 129 ||
Having drunk from the seventh vessel, one should then recite the Śāntistotra.
This hymn of peace,
when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, produces here in this world whatever fruit of desire is well-established in the Dharma.
I bow to that wish-fulfilling gem, the lord of the family and the host, whose continuous mental activity fulfills the desires of all practitioners. || 131 ||
Praise of the Baṭuka:
[I bow to] the fierce one, clad in red garments, with a mass of matted hair tawny like fire, and bearing the curved crescent moon upon his forehead.
I bow to Vaṭukanātha, the son of the Goddess, whose complexion is like that of the rising sun, gold, and the golden mountain. || 132 ||
May the Lord of the Kula-gaṇas remove all obstacles without exception;
may the practice of the Kula lead the practitioners to perfection;
and may Vaṭukanātha drink the blood of those who revile us.
May Gaṇeśa grant all the desires of the Kaulikas. || 133 ||
May this Dharma, which brings happiness to the entire world, be victorious;
may all unrighteousness, the root of manifold suffering, perish.
May these words of blessing be like nectar on every side.
May the curses of the Yoginīs fall upon the one who violates the covenant!

Those which dwell in the stages of the sequence of the wheels (*cakra*), those which are situated within the channels (*nāḍī*), those which reside in the pores of the skin that have arisen on the body, those which are established in the elements (*dhātu*),
those which dwell in the waves of the wind of the breath's surges, and those which are the winds of exhalation—
May these goddesses, devoted to devouring the faction of enemies and worshipped by the Kaulas, be satisfied. || 135 ||

All the deities residing within the body— those with elephant faces, the lords of the sacred fields (*kṣetrapāla*), the *bhairavas*, the *yoginīs*, the *vaṭukas*, the *yakṣas*, the *pitṛs*, the *vetālas*, and the *ceṭakas*— [are present].

May other beings—those who move on earth, those who move in the sky, and those who move in the heavens; may the bhūtas, piśācas, and grahas be satisfied as this son of noble family drinks the beverage along with the lamp and the sacrificial oblation (caru). 136.
If the word of the Guru is indeed truth; if the parents, the gods, and the yogis are pleased; if the Supreme Deity truly exists; if the Vedas are indeed authoritative;
if there is the Śākta philosophy; and if there is even the command of the Command (ājñā)—then [so be it].
And may truth and the supreme Kaula dharma be mine; may victory be mine forever. (137)
May the universe—from Śiva down to the earth, including all from Brahmā to a blade of grass, and from the Fire of Time up to Śiva—be satisfied by this sacrifice. (138)
For those who worship, for those who protect, for those of subdued senses and whose wealth is austerity—
for the country, for the kingdom, for the family, and for the king.
May the Blessed Lord Gaṇeśa grant peace. || 139 ||
May there be auspiciousness for the entire world; may the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of others;
may faults come to peace; and may all people be happy. 140.
May the *kulayoginīs* rejoice; may the sons of the family rejoice; and may the *kulācāryas* and all others who protect the family rejoice. (141)
May all practitioners rejoice, and may the detractors be struck with fear;
may we abide in the state of Śambhu, and may the Guru be forever gracious.
Many tens of millions of Kula-yoginīs, stationed within and without the Kaulika-cakra,
[are satisfied] by drinking the supreme nectar (parāmṛta).
May they be pleased, gracious, and granters of boons. || 143 ||
May all those of evil intellect who delight in wickedness, who revile me, whose hearts are ruined by violating the conduct of the gods during worship, and those practitioners who have fallen away;
and those Kaulikas who, having seen the sequence of the ritual, disparage the method of worship—may they all go to destruction here and now by the command of Śrī Bhairava. (144)
May those who hate practitioners and always defile the tradition go forever into the mouths of the ḍākinīs, satiated by their flesh. 145.
Reciting this hymn in this manner, the best of practitioners should perform the drinking. || 146 ||
The mantra for the eighth salutation to the vessel (pātravandana):

Oṃ! [I salute her] whose nature is the fierce fire that burns the forest of the thicket of deluded ignorance, who is supreme, and who fills the darkness of ignorance and all doubts of the mind with a stream of nectar.
I worship the eighth vessel, daily reciting the mantra of the supreme Goddess who blazes upon my head, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and who grants sovereign power. 147.
Having performed the libation as before, one should worship the ninth [deity].
The mantra for the veneration of the ninth vessel:
Oṃ, I consider the Great Brahman to be the essence of all worlds, eternal,
difficult to know for those whose minds are fickle due to the enjoyment of worldly existence, and who meditate upon it as having a gross form.
Having attained this liquid state through compassion, one should quickly drink that very ninth vessel; it is certainly the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (149)
Meditating on the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus and likewise on the Goddess in the heart,
performing the practice of recitation (japa) with the mantra "I am Śiva" upon the tip of the tongue,
and having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oblations into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī.
The mantra for saluting the tenth vessel:
Oṃ, she whose face is like the moon, holds a sweet vessel in her lotus-hand.

Meditation on the venerable Guru at the crown of the head, the mind as the locus for the contemplation of the Goddess, the practice of recitation upon the tongue, and the matured practice of the Kaula lineage—that is the vessel;
one should drink that tenth [nectar], which bestows both supreme worldly enjoyment and liberation. 151.
I am not the doer, nor the one who causes action to be done, nor is there any action;
I am not the enjoyer, nor the one who causes enjoyment, nor is there any object of enjoyment;
I am not the sufferer, nor the one who causes suffering, nor is there any suffering.
Thus, I am that very Self, whose nature is inward-facing consciousness. || 152 ||
Having reflected thus, the lord of heroes should again partake of the drink. || 153 ||
The mantra for the salutation of the eleven vessels:

Oṃ! With the left hand holding nectar and reciting the mantra mentally with the lower lip, the five celestial nymphs sing according to the rules of musical instruments, producing the sounds of lutes and flutes;
they do so out of a playful curiosity for sport, their essence being the graceful charm of Lakṣmī’s beauty.
And at the time full of the playful delight of drinking, the vessel is the eleventh. || 154 ||
One should not offer the substance intended for Bhairava while it remains in one's own vessel;
if it is offered in such a manner, there will be a loss of spiritual power (siddhi) and one shall incur the curse of the deity. || 155 ||
Sometimes, having received [the substance] by chance, or at other times through devotion,
one should take it with one's own vessel and drink the substance while remembering the Guru. (156)
One should eat the remnants (ucchiṣṭa) of the Guru, the Śakti, and the sons; likewise of the elder and younger brothers of the Guru.
One may eat the remnants of women, but one should not offer them one's own remnants.
Otherwise, the practitioner will fall into the midst of the wheel;
he should drink the substance that is the remnant of the Śakti and chew the remnant of the Vīra. (158)
By the grace of Śakti and Vīra, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
One should cause even the remnants [of the offering] to be given to one's younger disciples. (159)
He who gives out of affection to others shall become a vessel for calamities.
As long as the vision does not waver, and as long as the mind does not waver— || 160 ||

One should drink [the nectar] for that long; after this, one should perform the "animal-drinking" (paśupāna) for the sake of the flashing forth of the meaning of the mantra and for the stabilization of the knowledge of Brahman.
One should prepare the drink of honey-wine; a greedy person shall go to hell.
Having drunk again and again, and drinking once more, he falls down upon the surface of the earth. (162)
Having risen and drunk [the nectar] again, rebirth no longer exists. (p.
182) That bliss which arises for men in the union with the woman who is like a bee and a fish—|| 163 ||
That very [state] is liberation for the wise, but for the ignorant it is a sin;
likewise when the jar in the center of the wheel is broken, or when the vessel has fallen. || 164 ||
If a substance falls upon the ground, or if the vessel is likewise broken,
or if the lamp is extinguished, one should perform the cakra ritual again for the sake of pacifying those [obstacles].
Having caused [the deity] to drink as is appropriate, and having drunk himself, the supreme practitioner should offer libations to the Goddess together with her retinue, as before.
Having again offered garlands and other items mixed with fragrant sandalwood,
one should thereafter offer incense, a lamp, a mirror, and likewise a fly-whisk.
The practitioner should offer the food oblation (naivedya) and sound the conch and bell most charmingly;
having performed a hymn of praise according to his ability, he should circumambulate [the deity]. 168.
Having taken the self-offering along with flowers, the water-offering (arghya), and nectar, one should offer oneself as well.
Then one should say: "Oṃ, from this time forward... and thereafter [recite] "life-force, intellect, and body. (169)
By virtue of his duty toward the Dharma, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, [he acts] through deed, mind, speech, with both hands, and likewise with both feet. (170)
Whatever has been done or remembered by means of the belly and the penis,
and whatever has been spoken— having declared all that, one should write it down for me and for my own sake. (171)
Then, at the conclusion of the glorious [mantra], one should offer everything to the deity;
thereafter, one should perform the act of dedication (samarpaṇa) by means of this very [mantra]. || 172 ||
Then, having offered the water for the feet to the Goddess, he should say, "Forgive me. He should then offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) to the Goddess again and again.
Having visualized the offering of the *arghya* and all the coverings as dissolved into the limbs of the Goddess,
the supreme practitioner should thereafter lift up the *arghya* vessel. (174)
Having whirled [the offering] three times above the Goddess, one should thereafter offer it to the Great Goddess, who consists of light, into one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Having brought [the deity] through the path of the nose, one should worship the Goddess who dwells in the floral remains (nirmālya).
Having prostrated before the Guru’s sandals, one should worship the Goddess with the flowers that have been offered.
Upon the completion of the worship,
thereafter, with a state of devotion, the practitioner— having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga)— should then contemplate "I am He" with a steady mind.
One should apply the paste of the yantra at the *brahmarandhra*, the location of the Guru;
one should not bestow it upon atheists, nor upon those who are like cattle (*paśus*), nor upon fools. (178)
It should be given to one of noble birth, or else [thrown] into the midst of water;
the gods always desire the food offering (naivedya) of the goddess Caṇḍikā. (179)
Therefore, flowers should always be offered to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as to me, Śukra, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Yama. (180)
One should offer [the oblation] to Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Dhanada, as well as to Īśāna, Mahādevī, and the Sādhaka. || 181 ||
Alternatively, at the foot of a tree or in a pit in a pure location, the best of practitioners should diligently offer the remains of the flowers (nirmālya). || 182 ||
Having given the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and sandalwood paste to the Śaktis and the practitioners,
and having then given garlands and perfumes, one should thereafter offer up one's own body.
Alternatively, the practitioner of the hero’s rite (vīrasādhaka) should cause [the disciple] to drink with honey;
having first taken hold of the Śrīpātra, he who performs the wheel (cakra). || 184 ||
That practitioner must perform the penance of drinking the urine of a cow;
thereafter, the hero should offer the *arghya* nectar to his fellow initiates (*sāmayika*). (185)
p.
185) The procedure for grasping the remaining principles:
thereafter, the best of practitioners should unite the remainder within himself.
And at the conclusion of the ritual, the most excellent practitioner should take hold of the full vessel. || 186 ||
Having fashioned the body as consisting of mantra and performed prostration before the Guru,
one should purify the Śrīpātra— which is radiant with the Kula-vidyā— into divine nectar;
then, having satiated the four seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) with "Śiva Śive" according to the sequence of attainment (siddhikrama)—
Even now, one should drink the juice beginning with the gift, which brings happiness and uproots suffering. || 187 ||
Whether one is burdened by a great sin or even possessed of many sins, one becomes liberated from that transgression by a mere drop of the *arghya* water. (188)
Having thus partaken of the drink and accepted the full vessel, the wise man should turn it face down upon the ground and scatter flowers there.
Then, having inscribed the seed-syllable of Māyā upon the ground moistened with nectar,
one should likewise apply a tilaka mark with the little finger of the left hand.
With this root mantra, the practitioner, being composed in mind, [should recite]:
"Whomever I touch with my foot, whomever I behold with my eye... (191)
He alone shall become a slave, even if he were equal to Śakra;
thereafter, the lord of heroes, having washed it, should preserve that supreme vessel.
Then, having served the refreshments in their proper order, the wise one should feed [the guests] together with the women and the practitioners. (193)
Having eaten, the excellent practitioner should again offer a garland combined with fragrant sandalwood,
as well as betel, ornaments, and so forth, and likewise a bed.

And when the family-substance (kuladravya) has been consumed by one who perceives the true meaning of the family-reality (kulatattva), the immersion into Bhairava arises, characterized by the vision of equality everywhere. || 195 ||
One should not prevent even a Kaulika from entering the temple;
for if she is prevented, Tripurā becomes enraged, and from that, ruin arises. (196)
A Kaulika who approaches a bound soul (paśu) and forcibly enjoys another's power (paraśakti) must not, with effort, be allowed to touch anyone in the midst of the assembly (goṣṭhī). || 197 ||
Whatever food or drink one might give to a kula-yogin who is intoxicated with honey [madhu], the merit thereof cannot be calculated. 198.
He who gives a family as a refuge is not born again in a womb;
for that Goddess, whose form is the vulva, is always delighted by semen. (199)
The offering of semen to her should always be done together with wines and meats;
having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī power, one should release the semen while experiencing sexual pleasure.
But when a woman who has not been initiated is obtained through force or effort, one should impart the mantra into her ear in the form of one's own body. 201.
Then she becomes the embodiment of Śakti, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and at the time of sexual union as well as during initiation, one should perform the consecration.
During sexual union, one should sprinkle the woman—whether she be a widow or devoid of mantra—with liquor, semen, water, or sandalwood water. (203)
First, having uttered the Bālā mantra, one should utter "to Tripurā";
having uttered the word "namaḥ," one should then say "this initiation. (204)
At the end of the word *pavitrīkuru*, one should utter *mama śaktim* twice and then the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā); this is proclaimed as the purification mantra (*śuddhimantra*). || 205 ||
Women who are always consecrated with this mantra shall be constantly delightful; he shall attain all perfections. || 206 ||
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures in this world, one shall attain liberation. Rambhā, Śacī, Urvaśī, and whatever other women are foremost in heaven or on earth— (207)
And she who resides in Pātāla—her lord is the Kaulika;
and that woman who is to be avoided by him is described according to the path of the Tantras.
Tripura herself is the Guru manifest, and his wife is her very own form;
one should avoid sexual union with her there in thought, deed, or word. (209)
One who is devoted to her feet shall obtain even liberation before long.
The preceptor’s daughter-in-law, his daughter, and his own daughter are like daughters born of mantra. (210)
Even for one who knows Brahman, sexual enjoyment with her must be avoided;
she is indeed the wife of the Kaulika, the manifest Siddhīśvarī Śivā.
By merely enjoying her, a follower of the Kaula path would become a denizen of hell;
likewise, even one's mother should be avoided out of respect, as should any woman devoid of Śiva.
If one deliberates on this in an improper place, the curse of the Goddess arises;
[for she is] the mother of the mantra, the daughter, the sister, and the noble woman of the lineage. (213) p. 189)
A follower of the Kaula path should not take pleasure [in them] constantly; rather, he should worship these women properly.
(Alternatively:
Having set aside the wife of his Guru and the Vīra, he may enjoy all other beautiful women. 214.
There is a prohibition against those of doubtful character who possess dualistic knowledge from accepting the five elements;
these and those who are always doubtful must be avoided with effort.
However, there is no prohibition whatsoever against those who hold the non-dual (Advaita) view. 215.
By means of the seed residing within the mother's womb, he is indeed just an infant; of this there is no doubt.
But at the time of emerging from the womb, the child is indeed naked.
Emerging from the vaginal opening of the mother’s womb, the son attains connection with the mother’s womb through the penis. (217)
When it is reflected upon in this manner, who would not be one who has violated the teacher’s bed?
Because of being free from modification, there is no such thing here; otherwise, it would not be so.
Therefore, when one's latent impression (vāsanā) is contemptible, it leads to fault; otherwise, there is never any defect. || 219 ||
Having become free from conceptual thought, one should worship that which consists of pure consciousness;
for when the heroes have ascended to that state, there exists neither what is to be done nor what is not to be done.
Therefore, one should investigate every source of birth through the form of non-duality;
by perceiving the thousandfold sources, one attains the certainty of liberation. (221)
Improper conduct becomes proper conduct, and a base deed becomes a supreme task;
even that which is impure becomes pure for those who have attained certainty regarding non-duality. 222.

For those who are firmly established in non-duality, even that which is undrinkable becomes drinkable, and even that which is unfit for food becomes fit for food; likewise, even that which is unapproachable becomes approachable. (223)
There is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither merit nor sin; there is neither heaven nor hell—this is the certainty regarding non-duality. (224)
Wherever a prohibition or a prescription is proclaimed, there too it should be understood that what was previously doubtful becomes perfectly certain. (225)
