In no way whatsoever should one practice non-duality in the presence of the Guru;
therefore, the hero should diligently avoid the Guru’s womb.
The great worship has been described according to the distinction between non-duality and duality;
however, he who performs the fifth [rite] without being joined with the five elements [is deficient]. || 227 ||
His worship is lost, and that practitioner must perform penance;
any rite performed devoid of reality, as well as the act of recitation, is fruitless. (228)
Day after day, the sin of killing a Brahmin rages against them who abandon the Cakra and worship the Goddess of the Gods without libations.
Four things of his perish: life, knowledge, fame, and strength;
for whatever is seen in the center of the wheel, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [that comes to pass]. (230)
At dawn, that [practice] must not be disclosed by the high-souled practitioner;
the daily worship has been taught for the successful accomplishment of practitioners.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter: Thus, one who desires the most secret and auspicious path of the Gandharva should worship with the five elements (pañcatattva) through extreme concealment. || 1 ||
Even one of meager fortune attains all accomplishments through worship;
therefore, one who desires success and seeks to gather accomplishments should always perform worship. (2)
The description of the fruit of worship:
through the fruit of worship, one attains the subduing of misfortune, suffering, and poverty;
all [evils] are pacified, and one becomes a lord upon the earth. (3)
Through the momentary destruction of the object of worship, the Yoginī becomes impaired;
one who is devoid of worship is perpetually impure and censured in all ritual actions.
That fool who, having abandoned worship, constantly mutters the mantra, should be known as one whose recitation is fruitless; that practitioner of mantra becomes a sinner.
One who, having received the Vidyā, possesses no faith in its worship,
becomes a perpetrator of great sins and shall attain birth in the womb of a beast. (6)
For one who has performed no worship, the breaking of the fast with meat—and especially with blood—will certainly belong to the Yoginīs and the Bhairavas. (7)
Therefore, one who desires spiritual accomplishment should always perform worship, whether mentally or otherwise;
wherever one worships the Goddess, there indeed is true worship.
Worship is prohibited during the day; it must be performed with extreme secrecy, never by any means during the day.
Indeed, worship performed during the day by the five [classes] causes the ruin of the kingdom.
It certainly bestows great agitation upon the practitioner;
therefore, one should never [partake] of the fivefold [substances] on that day. || 10 ||
Worship is of three kinds according to the distinction of superior and so forth:
the daily worship (nityapūjā) is the superior; the worship on festival days (parvapūjā) is the middling;
and the monthly worship (māsapūjā) is declared to be the inferior. Beyond a month [of neglect], one becomes a beast.
If the victim should again desire entry [into the rite], one should initiate him once more;
one should perform this after a month using the prescribed substances, such as wine and the rest. (12)
The determination of the auspicious times:
the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth, the new moon, and the full moon;
the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti)—these are the five sacred parvan days, as well as other meritorious days.

And one should sacrifice upon attaining prosperity, upon obtaining gains, during penance, initiation, and the celebration of vows, upon approaching a sacred seat (pīṭha), and upon seeing a sacred seat belonging to the assembly of heroes (vīrākulapīṭha). || 14 ||
Upon the arrival of a spiritual guide, at the sight of a holy ford or a deity, and on such occasions as these, as well as on special days. || 15 ||
When the birthday of one's own guru arrives, as well as that of one's guru's guru, and on the birthdays of ordinary people and one's own kinsmen as well; || 16 ||
On the eleventh lunar day and during the Vyatīpāta yoga, one should not allow any omission of ritual acts;
on the eighth and fourteenth days as well, worship must be performed with great care.
One should not skip the eighth [tithi], for by skipping it one becomes a sinner;
thus, having reached the preceding and following [periods], the practitioner [should proceed] with the five elements.
One should perform the worship with diligence; otherwise, one will suffer the loss of accomplishment.
By means of the external ritual of worship, one may even become a Gandharva or a Kinnara. (19)
Neither the king nor the practitioner, nor anyone else on the surface of the earth— whether an ascetic or a monarch— is there anyone else anywhere who is a true worshiper.
The God is not found on mountain peaks, nor in the region of Viṣṇuloka;
the God, who consists of consciousness and bliss, is seen in the heart through devotion.
Wherever and whenever a great soul possesses firm devotion, there and then the Great Goddess follows after that manifestation.
Now I shall describe the sacred fields of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), wherein an abundance of fruit arises from worship:
at Vārāṇasī, great worship bestows the full fruit. (23)

The fruit of worship varies according to the difference in location; it is said to be twofold when performed in the presence of Puruṣottama, and even twice as much again specifically at Dvārakā. || 24 ||
Worship performed at all sacred fields and holy fords is equal to that at Dvārāvatī;
it is said to be a hundredfold greater on the Vindhya mountains, and equal to that on the Gaṅgā.
In Āryāvarta, in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), and likewise in Brahmāvarta,
worship yields fruit just like [worship] at the Vindhyas, at Prayāga, and at the Puṣkaras. (26)
The water of the Karatoyā river is said to yield four times that merit;
and the fruit at Nandikuṇḍa is certainly four times greater than that.
Then, four times that number is declared to be in the presence of Jalpīśa;
thereafter, at the yoni of Siddhīśvarī, it is remembered as being twice even that.
Therefore, it is said that [the merit] is fourfold on the waters of the Lauhitya River;
it is equal to that at Kāmarūpa, and everywhere, both in water and on land.
Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all, and just as Lakṣmī is the most supreme of all,
so too is the worship of the Goddess performed with power at Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods.
O Maheśvarī, in the Kulārṇava, Kāmarūpa is twofold— manifest and hidden—
extending from the Karatoyā river as far as Dikkaravāsinī.
Thirty yojanas in width and one hundred yojanas in length,
triangular and black in color, it is declared to be Kāmarūpa.
The form of desire is twofold;
it should be understood as manifest right there, and also hidden in every house.
The most excellent practitioners obtain great merit from that which is hidden compared to that which is manifest. || 33 ||
One should know that Devīkṣetra is Kāmarūpa; there is nothing else equal to it.
Elsewhere the Goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house.
Then, it is said to be a hundredfold greater on the peak of Nīlakūṭa;
and even twice that much more is said to be present in the Śiva-liṅga on Sumeru.
Twice that [power] is said to reside in the yonis of Śailaputrī;
and a hundred times greater than that is said to be in the circle of the yoni of Kāmākhyā. (36)
And that worship is equal to it within the vulva-mandala of women;
Kāmarūpa, the great family, is the supreme among all sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 37 ||
(198) Thereafter, the maṇḍala of the womb of Kāmākhyā is said to be a hundred times greater; there, Māyā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, dwells together with those who possess ten million-fold [merit]. 38.
That sacred seat (pīṭha) is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness, from which the gods, goddesses, and sages born of his being [originate]. (39)
All [the deities] manifest here; therefore, the great lineage is protected for one who has performed worship even once in the great yoni at Kāmākhyā. || 40 ||
He obtains his desires in this world and shall attain auspiciousness in the hereafter;
for whatever worship is performed here even once by the practitioner, [it yields such results]. (41)
Leaving aside all other seats, Śivā shall dwell within his body.
Now, I shall describe the supreme sequence for the general worship.
The sequence for the general worship:
first, the placement (nyāsa) of the sages and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands;
then the placement of the fingers and the pervasive placement; and also the placement of the heart and other limbs. (43)
The binding of the directions with three claps of the hands, followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation, worship, and recitation—this is the procedure in all tantras. (44)

For the purpose of recitation (*japa*) of all mantras, one should arrange the syllables even without [the physical] script; however, one should know that what is performed [otherwise] is fruitless. Therefore, at the outset, one should arrange the script. (45)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the offering to Śivā;
for one who does not offer the oblation to Śivā cannot attain the state of Śiva. (46)
He is most wicked and lacks the qualification for the worship of the family deity—
he who does not worship the Goddess Śivā in her animal form in a secluded place.
By her howling like a jackal, everything of his—his worship, his recitations, his ritual procedures, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed—is certainly destroyed. (48)
Having received the curse and reached a secluded place, Śivā weeps;
she must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with food and drink. 49.
When Śivā herself is certainly gratified by a single [offering], at that very moment the supreme delight of all the Śaktis is attained, which is otherwise most difficult to obtain. (50)
The power of beasts, the power of humans, and the power of birds—these, when constantly worshipped, transform meritless action into meritorious action, because of this. || 51 ||
With every effort, one should perform this great worship when faced with fear of kings and the like, as well as fear of malevolent planets and the like. (52)
Having reflected upon auspicious and inauspicious actions,
the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation at the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground. (53)
At the time of twilight, one should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat, saying:
"Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate Śivā, you who have the form of the fire of cosmic destruction! (54)
"Tell me clearly the auspicious or inauspicious fruit; accept this offering for you.
Having spoken thus, the offering dear to the family and the people should be given. (55)
There, Umā, in the form of Śivā, should be addressed as "Kālī, Kālī";
she arrives in the form of a beast along with her hosts of attendants.
If, having eaten, she raises her face toward the northeast and cries out with a beautiful voice, then at that very moment there is auspiciousness for the practitioner; it shall not be otherwise.
If it is not consumed there, then no auspiciousness will arise at all;
one should diligently offer the bali-oblation during the daily, occasional, and optional rites.
The ritual for the worship of the family (*kulapūjā*) should be performed with great secrecy; the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) brings about auspiciousness.
I shall proclaim the worship of the Kula according to the prescriptions of the scriptures. || 59 ||
According to the Kula tradition, one should perform the Kula worship on the day of the Kula-week, especially on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
as well as on the Kula-tithi and under the Kula-nakṣatra.
In this [rite], the worship of the Yoginīs is the primary form of Kula-worship;
just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day (Viṣṇutithi), bestows all that is desired.
Likewise, when the lunar day (tithi) corresponds to the family constellation, the Goddess, when worshipped, bestows boons;
as do the daily śrāddha, the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana), and the libation to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa).
In the same way, the Kaulikas have the obligation of constant worship of the Kula;
for if there is no worship of the Kula for one night or two nights, [the rule is violated].
Then, leaving that practitioner behind, Caṇḍikā shall attain dissolution;
there is no other merit equal to the Kula-worship in the three worlds. (64)

Therefore, he who worships with devotion becomes a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation—even if he has not studied, is ignorant of the scriptures, yet is devoted to his guru and firm in his vows. (65)
He who is devoted to honoring his family shall become even dearer to me;
when worshipped, he grants the fruit of the fulfillment of desires, like a virtuous bride.
When the Goddess is not worshipped, she bestows suffering like a wicked wife; indeed, that evil-minded person who creates an obstacle to the worship of the family [deity] [is likewise cursed]. (67)
He goes to a terrible hell along with twenty-one generations of his kin; whatever may be devoid of merit there becomes possessed of merit through the honoring of one's family.
If there were to be a mere inspection of the lineage (or family), whence could there be sprinkling and wiping?
Where would there be bathing, where purification, and where the cleansing through ritual placement (nyāsa)? || 69 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of the Kula;
one obtains all perfections—of this there is no doubt. || 70 ||

The rule regarding the family-day (kula-vāra), lunar day (tithi), asterism (nakṣatra), and so forth is now declared; the determination of the family-day and other factors is for the sake of attaining success.
The second, tenth, and sixth [lunar days] are proclaimed as "family-and-non-family" (kulākula). (71)
All the uneven lunar days (tithis) are akula, while the remaining ones are kula.
The four—Ravi, Soma, Guru, and Śauri—are considered to be akula.
Mars and Venus are called *kula*; Wednesday is *kulākula*.
203) The asterisms Śatabhiṣaj, Ārdrā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be *kulākula*.
Families are presided over [by specific deities], while the remaining ones belong to no family;
those who abide in a non-family (akula) on a particular lunar day, weekday, and asterism are invincible.
Those born under a *kula*-constellation are always victorious, while those born under a *kulākula* constellation experience equanimity;
the performance of rites on lunar days (*tithi*) is prescribed according to the month ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

The Mahāṣṭamī itself should be known as the Kulāṣṭamī, which bestows excellent accomplishment. The determination of the days of the week for the Kula and so forth has been taught for the sake of attaining success.
Having performed the bathing ritual, including the water for the feet and the respectful offering (arghya), according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual,
one should then prepare the "heroic mattress" (vīrastūlikā) with lac juice and the like.
The examination of noble maidens:
an actress, a Kāpālikī, a courtesan, a washerwoman, a barber’s wife, a Brāhmaṇī, a Bhadrakanyā, and likewise a cowherd’s daughter. (78)
The daughter of a garland-maker is proclaimed as the "new maiden" (*navakanyā*);
or else, the *caṇḍālī*, the leather-worker woman (*carmakārī*), the *māgadhī*, and likewise the *pukkasī*. (79)
The Śvapacī, Khaṇḍikā, Kaivarttī, and the women of the Viṭa caste—these are declared to be the eight families; now the eight non-families (Akula) are being described.

Gomukhī, Rajakī, Śilpī, Venakī, and likewise Aṣṭamī as the eighth. || 81 ||
(Alternatively:
A courtesan, a female vintner, a fisherwoman, a washerwoman, a weaver, a leather-worker, a Mātaṅgī, and likewise a Pukkasi. || 82 ||
(Alternatively:
An actress, a Kāpālikī, a courtesan, a Pukkasī, a Yoginī, as well as a washerwoman, a Rajjakī, a servant-woman, and a Vilāsinī. (83)
Khaṭikā, Ghaṭikā, and likewise Gopālakanyakā—all these noble women were endowed with exceptional cleverness. || 84 ||
In the absence of a woman of the aforementioned caste, one should worship Bhairavī as being present within her.
This is the procedure for the worship of Śakti, which is conjoined with mantra and tantra and observes the conduct of the samaya. 85.
They are devoid of heroic vigor yet devoted to their vows, bearing the mudrās of yoga; they are devoted to their gurus and to the gods, while being utterly devoid of compassion and shame. (86)
Young women who are devoted to secrecy generally bestow success;
they may have been initiated by any mantra or even by the root mantra.
205) One should avoid speaking of women; and that woman who is spoken of there according to the path of Tantra should also be avoided.
One who is deformed, a widow, crippled, or an aged ascetic woman—|| 88 ||
One who has missing limbs, wears inferior clothing, is crooked, fond of quarreling, acts in opposition to the world and the Vedas, and likewise speaks harshly; || 89 ||
One should avoid her who is devoted to false speech, who is eager for the intoxication of misconduct, who is possessed of faults such as envy, and who is heedless. || 90 ||
One who has a deformed face, is uninitiated, possesses a conceptualizing mind, is aged, devoted to sin, cruel, and extremely greedy; (91)
The best of practitioners should avoid one who is distressed and whose mind is beyond reasoning;
thereafter, the hero should bring forth a woman born of one of the eight families previously mentioned.
She was free from cruelty, beautiful in form, adorned with ornaments, and well-initiated;
she was devoid of passion and shame, peaceful, and firm in her vows through the words of Śiva.
A young woman who is devoted to the feet of the Guru and the God, who is superior and supreme,
whether she be his own wife or the wife of another, and who is clever and sweetly smiling— (94)
Having offered her water for the feet and other honors, he should place her upon a cushion;
with a steady mind, the practitioner shall accomplish incomparable success. (95)

At the time of worship, the wise declare that auspicious innate powers (śaktis) are present; one should duly perform upon her body the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) as prescribed in her own liturgical manual.
The Goddess Parā, the Blessed One, whose form is the support of the universe, is the womb and the cause of the birth of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. || 97 ||
She is the womb of all beings, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
she is endowed with the three qualities and manifests the threefold speech.
Having assumed the form of the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and attained the shape of a triangle, she resides in the center of the bodies of all beings in the form of the bhaga. 99.
Abiding in the presence of Śiva in the form of a Liṅga for the sake of pleasure, she is indeed the mother of all; for the sake of pleasure, she is the supreme woman.
The womb is the source of man; the womb belongs to women, for she is the giver of fortune and is the very form of fortune.
In her a living being is born, and in her at the end he is dissolved. (101)
The Yoni, accompanied by the three powers and consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, is known as the Goddess Bhagavatī; and Sadāśiva is the Lord (Bhagavān). (102)
The supreme Goddess is indeed one alone, whose nature is the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*;
that Goddess exists in the form of the *bhaga*, as the source (*yoni*) of all things. (103)
Established in the womb, situated in the midst of the womb, and having the very form of the womb;
she is the triangle, she is the triple-guṇa, she consists of the three deities, and she is the supreme. 104.
The proficiency in union is known as the fifth state of perfection;
therefore, one should always worship the Goddess, whose form is bliss, within the womb. 105.
Having washed it with scented water and perfumed it with incense and smoke,
one should draw a wheel upon the vulva using vermilion powder.
One should worship the Goddess there according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual, O Goddess who consists of all women and who bestows all desires and goals. (107)
"O Kāmeśvarī, O you who have become desire, O passionate one, grant your presence! With this [mantra], one should invoke the Goddess and then perform her own ritual sequence.
During the worship on the fifth lunar day, one must avoid the mantra of one's own family;
as long as there is attachment to men here, one should avoid them at will.
If there is cause for suspicion in that regard, then one should dismiss the goddess;
if, through negligence, the evil-minded person follows after her company. (110)
Then he would instantly become a leper and attain a censured accomplishment;
however, he who performs the Kula-worship without liquor and meat [attains success]. || 111 ||

The merit of thousands of other births is destroyed for one who, having performed worship according to the rules, recited [the mantra], offered praise, and prostrated, [does not proceed further]. 112.
Having drawn the yantra upon that [image], one should again present offerings upon it;
one should not dismiss it until she has become overwhelmed. || 113 ||
Having performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), if there is a desire for power, one should indeed receive her command and then [proceed with] the worship of the deities. 114.
Then, while approaching a woman, one should recite [the mantra]; the rest should be performed as before.
Alcohol, meat, and likewise whatever else constitutes the *kula*-practice [should be used]. (115)
Having given that to her, and then having offered the remainder to the guru, and placing his permission upon one's head, one should apply the remainder to oneself. || 116 ||
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Śakti, he, being such as I am, should then reflect upon this;
for this is declared to be the worship of the Kula for the sake of attaining perfection (siddhi). (117)
I shall describe the procedure for the worship of the Goddess as a concise ritual, in accordance with the tantras:
the ritual placement (nyāsa) is said to be an embrace, and the meditative visualization (dhyāna) is said to be a kiss. (118)
The sound "śīt" is declared to be the sacrifice; scratching with the fingernails is the food offering;
the nectar of the tongue is to be known as the drink; and sexual union shall be the recitation of mantras (japa). 119.
Know that the praise is bliss and the emission is the discharge;
relying upon non-dual knowledge, one should always worship the Goddess. 120.
Neither by a hundred horse-sacrifices nor by a hundred killings of Brahmins are those whose hearts abide in Brahman stained by merit or sin. (121)
Whatever actions exist on earth are caused by the tongue and the organ of generation;
one who has renounced the tongue and the organ of generation—what will he do with action? (122)
One should perform ritual actions only so long as knowledge has not arisen;
a hymn of praise is equal to ten million offerings, and recitation is equal to ten million hymns of praise. (123)
Meditation is equal to ten million recitations; dissolution is equal to ten million meditations.
210) There is no mantra higher than meditation, and no deity higher than the Self. 124.
There is no higher worship than the continuous practice [of dharma], nor is there a fruit greater than contentment;
[this is true] even without the twilight prayers with mantras and water, and without recitation, fire-offerings, or austerity.
The yogi should constantly perform worship even without external ritual offerings;
O Goddess, the body is the temple, and the living soul is the deity, Sadāśiva. (126)
One should discard the floral remains of ignorance and worship with the sense of "I am He.
The individual soul is Śiva; Śiva is the individual soul; that soul is indeed Śiva alone. (127)
Bound by fetters, he is a bound soul (paśu); freed from fetters, he is Śiva.
Bound by fetters, O Goddess, he is a bound soul; freed from fetters, he is Sadāśiva.
Just as rice is bound by its husk, yet becomes pure grain when the husk is absent.
Bound by karma, the individual soul (jīva) is always [in bondage]; liberated from karma, it is Sadāśiva.
Even for those who meditate upon the Supreme here with faith for merely a moment, [this result follows]. 129.
The great merit that would accrue from that cannot be reached at its end by anyone who performs self-reflection for even a moment, thinking, "I am Brahman."
It destroys all that sin, just as the rising sun dispels darkness. || 130 ||
p.
211) The characteristic of a lord of yogins is that he has bathed in the waters of all sacred fords and has bestowed the earth upon a brahmin.
Surely by him the ancestors have been fully gratified and the gods have been perfectly honored;
indeed, he has performed the entirety of a thousand sacrifices, he whose mind has attained steadfastness for even a single moment in the contemplation of Brahman. (131)

Whatever fruit is obtained from vows, sacrifices, austerity, visiting sacred fords, giving gifts, worshiping the gods, and so forth— multiplied ten million times, that very fruit the knower of reality attains.
The supreme state is the innate (sahaja), the middling is meditative concentration (dhyāna) and retention (dhāraṇā);
recitation and praise are the inferior, while fire-offerings and ritual worship are the most inferior. 133.
Reflection on reality is the highest; reflection on recitation is middling; reflection on the scriptures is to be known as low; and reflection on worldly affairs is the lowest of the low. (134)
He who is equanimous toward those who revile and those who praise, toward pleasure and pain, and toward enemies and friends—he is indeed a lord of yogis, free from both joy and dejection. (135)
Free from desire, eternally contented, viewing all with equanimity, and having conquered the senses,
that yogi who knows the supreme reality dwells in the body like a traveler in a foreign land. (136)
Free from conceptualization, free from discursive thought, having conquered the latent impressions of limiting adjuncts,
and immersed in his own true nature— that yogi is a knower of the supreme reality.
Just as those who are lame, blind, deaf, impotent, insane, or dull-witted dwell everywhere, so too does that yogi; he is considered supreme. (138)
He who is born from the five mudrās, overflowing with supreme bliss—
he, the lord of yogins, beholds the Self within the self.
With whatever disposition of mind Caṇḍikā becomes pleased, with that very disposition, those whose hearts are satisfied should serve the Goddess; of this there is no doubt. (140)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Jñānānandaparahamsa. 9.
The Tenth Chapter: The Rule for Kaula Conduct.
Now I shall explain the conduct in accordance with the Tantras.
He is intent on the welfare of all beings and devoted to the conduct of his observances. || 1 ||
Regarding the description of the conduct of the observance:
one who has renounced transient ritual acts and is intent upon the performance of the eternal rites, becomes devoted to the state of Śiva through the mere retention of the mantra. (2)
But one who offers all actions to the Supreme Deity, and whose devotion is unwavering toward the Guru, the God, and even toward Manu; || 3 ||
Their success shall be swift; it cannot be otherwise even in ten million eons.
The greatness of the Guru:
the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Guru is Manu, the Guru is Japa, and the Guru alone is the supreme scorcher of foes;
for them, success shall come quickly, but never for one who lacks devotion.
At dawn, the practitioner should meditate upon the Guru in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
having performed worship, he should always carry out all actions according to his command.
If a disciple does not know twenty, or even seven, five, or three generations of his teacher's lineage, he is one whose spiritual succession is lost.
Having meditated upon the dignity of the lineage of gurus, the school of the gurus will not have its path lost;
for those whose path is lost, mantra and vidyā do not come within the range of such accomplishment.
If there is no transmission of the lineage among gurus and their disciples, then the tantras, mantras, and vidyās are fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
The lineage of the Guru, which brings auspiciousness, should be known as superior to one's own lineage;
the father who imparts the mantra is greater than both the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda.
One should always regard him as a teacher even greater than one's father;
likewise, one should consider his going, honoring, sleeping, eating, and sporting [as one's own]. (11)
Having received the command of the guru, one may achieve success even without recitation [of mantras],
provided one does not harbor the notion of a mere human being toward the guru, nor the notion of mere syllables toward the mantra.
One who perceives images as mere stone shall go to hell; a disciple should never regard his guru with the notion that he is a mere human being. (13)
Those who remember and speak of the venerable Guru together with ordinary worldly people will never attain success through mantras or the worship of deities.
For indeed, every good deed of theirs becomes a sin in an instant;
one should strictly avoid fickle behavior and jesting in the direct presence of the Guru. 15.
But the worship and mudrās performed by those of dull intellect are in vain;
while the Śrī Guru is present in person, what is the use of meditation and yoga? (16)
He who worships another deity while the Guru is present goes to a terrible hell; that worship becomes fruitless. (17)
Since the worship of the guru is the most important of all matters concerning mantras, one should never engage in the discussion of mantras and tantras in his presence. (18)
When the feet of the Guru are indeed worshipped, all the gods become happy;
for that Sadāśiva is the father of all mantras and tantras. || 19 ||
Whether it be the worship of another deity or the glorification of another deity,
if done without the Guru-deity and in his presence, one shall go to hell. (20)
For that best of practitioners who performs actions that please the Guru, all accomplishments (siddhis) are always present at the soles of his feet. 21.
Whoever is devoted to the feet of the Guru through body, mind, or speech, for him success shall quickly come to pass, even without ritual worship, fire-offerings, or recitation. 22.
If one is devoid of devotion to the guru, there is loss for him at every step;
whether in the guru's presence or in his absence, one should prostrate to the guru every day.
One should avoid performing separate worship and displaying arrogance in the presence of the Guru.
One should not perform initiation, exposition, or exercise authority in the presence of the Guru. (24)
Having produced satisfaction in every way, one should obtain the favor of the Guru;
likewise, the giving and receiving of debts, as well as the buying and selling of goods. (25)
A disciple should never, under any circumstances, commit these acts together with the guru:
disobeying his command, seizing his wealth, or behaving in a manner displeasing to the guru. (26)
(217) They say this constitutes an offense against the guru; whoever should do so is a sinner.
One should not employ substances for anointing the body without first informing the guru. (27)
But he who performs [the rite] without having offered [the food] would become a slayer of a Brahmin.
One should never utter the name of the Guru except at the time of recitation (japa). (28)

In the course of the practice, one should address the Guru as "Śrīnātha Deva Svāmī"; yet, there may be one who at some time insults him with words, having treated him with contempt or even reviled him with the sound "huṃ. (29)

One should utter the names preceded by "Śrī" for the deity, the guru, those in the position of a guru, the sacred field, the presiding deities of the field, the accomplishment, and those who dwell in accomplishment. (30)
Those who, having conceptualized the Kula scriptures, become Kula-rākṣasas;
and he who would insult the Guru who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable. (31)
Having passed through a hundred births as a dog, one may attain the state of a Caṇḍāla;
one should not perform penance, nor observe fasts, vows, and the like, in the presence of the Guru.
One who undertakes a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) need not perform it for the sake of personal purification;
one should not issue commands to a guru, nor should one contemplate his faults. (33)
One should not experience that substance for which the Guru has a longing;
however, if there is an unavoidable desire, one may experience it with his permission.
He who, out of delusion or greed, lives off even half a sesame seed or half of that half belonging to his guru, shall fall into the twenty-one hells.
For whoever appropriates even a small or large amount of a guru’s property that was not given, having entered the womb of an animal, he is constantly devoured by carnivorous beasts. (36)
For one who covets the property of the guru and is eager to have sexual intercourse with the guru's wife,
there is no atonement even for that fallen person.
One incurs that same sin by speaking untruth in the presence of a guru as one would incur by committing the murder of a cow or a brahmin. || 38 ||
One should not step over the shadow of the *śakti*, the shadow of the guru, or the shadow of the deity.
Furthermore, whoever sleeps or sits together with the guru in this manner [commits a fault]. (39)
He goes to a terrible hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras,
having rendered the words of his guru void and planted his own words instead. (40)
The mind of one who intends to overcome the Guru is cooked in the ocean of hell;
and those Kaulikas who consume the food of animals in manifold ways [are likewise doomed]. (41)
The Goddess becomes angry with them; therefore, one should never have sexual union with them.
One should recite the *lopāmudrā* mantra three hundred thousand times, or otherwise recite the *ajapā* mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with sacrificial food and clarified butter; then one will certainly become free from sin.
Gazed upon by the Guru, the disciple should rise and leave his seat.
One should not transgress whatever has been spoken by the Guru, whether it be true or false; nor should one engage in impetuous sexual intercourse or speak falsely within the Guru’s abode. (44)
He goes to a terrible hell, as declared by Śambhu;
a wise man should not sit upon a seat in the presence of a deity or his guru.
The lion-throne (siṃhāsana) should be given to the guru; the highest seat (uttamāsana) to the elders; the regional seat (deśyāsana) to the juniors; and an ordinary seat (samāsana) to others. || 46 ||
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
having taken fruits, flowers, and so forth, one should offer them according to one's ability. (47)
Thus, the mantra-practitioner who does not act accordingly shall become a brahmarākṣasa;
however, if the Guru is satisfied by the offering of an embrace even once, [he attains success]. 48.
Then what indeed would the practitioners who serve their guru not obtain?
By abandoning the guru, one goes to hell;
by abandoning the guru, death is certain; and by abandoning the mantra, there is poverty.
By abandoning the mantra of the guru, one shall go to the Raurava hell;
a disciple who abandons his guru will certainly be subject to penance.
By reciting the Śrīpādukā mantra one hundred thousand times, one is liberated from sin;
however, one should never associate with a disciple who abandons the mantra. (51)
Being pure, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, accompanied by fire offerings and libations;
furthermore, Brahmā, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Viśvāmitra, and others [have taught this].
Through service to their gurus, they attained perfection in the three worlds;
by the grace of the guru, Śiva became the all-knowing, all-pervading Lord.
If the Guru is satisfied even once, the practitioner shall indeed become Śiva himself.
Then what is there that practitioners who serve their Guru do not obtain? (54)
Therefore, one should practice service to the Guru with great effort;
one should always protect both this Guru and the mantra. 55.
One should never step over the bed or seat of a guru, nor his vehicle, sandals, or shoes; likewise, one should never step over his bath-water or his shadow.
A wise person should not spend time in vain through activities such as gambling;
rather, he should spend it in the worship of deities, the recitation of mantras (japa), sacrifices, hymns of praise, and the like. 57.
One should spend one's time incessantly by listening to the compassionate words, discourses, hymns, and scriptures of the Guru; one should never speak of the faults of others.
One should avoid passion, greed, intoxication, anger, malice, and the like;
one should not, even in thought, revile the family tradition, the guru, or the deity. (59)
If the practitioner desires success for himself, he should perform daily these four rites: worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-oblation. (60)
One must avoid union with the wives of others and the like,
as well as [union with] a maiden’s womb, playing with animals, [a woman] with disrobed garments, or one whose breasts are exposed.
One should not look upon the property of others, and one should avoid the wives of others. || 61 ||
One should not revile a learned brahmin who observes vows, nor should one find fault with the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Saṃhitās, the Purāṇas, the Āgama scriptures, or the Kalpas.
One should not have faith in the worship of another mantra nor perform the propitiation of another mantra;
having performed the invocation of one [deity], one should not practice the means of another.
From remembering another [deity], one incurs the suffering of a Yoginī’s curse;
premature death shall befall him, and once dead, he shall go to hell. || 64 ||
What more remains to be accomplished by others, since she provides everything:
the scriptures of the Kula vision, the Kula substances, and the Kaulikas themselves. (65)
[He saw] servants or instigators, reciters as well as spectators, instructors or liberators, and those who assist in the attainment of yoginī-siddhi.
One should not speak ill of women;
one should not revile, loathe, laugh at, or insult a woman—whether she be a maiden, a young girl, naked, or even mad. (67)
One should not speak unpleasantly or falsely to any member of a *kula-yogin* family;
nor should one say of a woman of the *kula* that she is "ugly" or "lowly. (68)
One should examine the devotion of the heroes and what they have done or left undone;
for whatever woman there may be in the world, she originates from her mother’s lineage. (69)
The Kulayoginīs become enraged by the transgression against women;
one should not strike them even with a flower, even for a hundred offenses committed by women.
A wise person should always avoid censuring noble women or heroes, stealing substances that constitute reality, and striking those who guard the Kula tradition. 71.
The entire world consists of women, and one should oneself likewise become so;
one should not harm any living beings, nor should one revile a woman with beautiful eyes.
One who is devoted to the worship of Śakti should not revile the right [path], the left [path], nor likewise the words of the gods; he should not revile the Siddhānta of Śakti.
One should not revile the words of the elders, nor should one revile a proponent of the Vedas; one should not revile those worthy of great respect, nor should one revile a devoted wife. (74)
One should not revile the celestial realms and so forth, nor should one revile those who abide by their commitments;
one should not revile meat excessively, for one should avoid reviling in all circumstances. (75)
One should not reproach a maiden who is intoxicated, of low birth, in her menses, with sagging breasts, deformed, with disheveled hair, or afflicted by lust. (76)
The woman is the embodiment of power;
the entire world consists of power, and she herself likewise becomes so.
For the Goddess, whose form is power, is established in the midst of creation. (77)
Creation has arisen from Śakti, and it dissolves back into Śakti once again;
therefore, Śakti is the primary principle and should be worshipped with diligent effort. (78)
One should eat together with a woman and offer oblations in the presence of the fire;
one should diligently and devotedly bring a woman dressed in reddish garments.
One should always perform the worship of Śakti so that she becomes pleased;
for when Śakti is pleased, there is happiness, but from neglecting her, there arises suffering. (80)
The Śākta practice consists of that which is to be chewed, that which is to be eaten, as well as that which is to be drunk, and likewise fragrance and flowers.
Having first offered [the food] according to one's capacity, as well as ornaments and so forth; || 81 ||
Thereafter, the practitioner who seeks success should make that [power] his own;
he should abandon pride, disgust, and shame regarding the Śakti, as well as the appearance of anger.
One should never strike even with a flower, much less with a weapon;
one should not feel pride in one's power, for Caṇḍikā is prone to wrath.
If one is frequently struck by astonishment, one will meet with destruction or the acquisition of death;
yet even if one dies, one goes to hell, whereas through worship, one attains prosperity.
One who has controlled the mind should contemplate as being the house, comfort, and everything else—the forms of young women—as well as the chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and consumed. (85)
Upon seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind, provided that such a sight of a noble family occurs through the power of fortune. (86)
At that very moment, one should perform mental worship there for them—whether they be young girls, those intoxicated by youth, or likewise elderly women who are beautiful. (87)

Having paid homage to one who is contemptible or extremely wicked, one should dismiss her; likewise, one should avoid striking them, censuring them, being deceitful toward them, or saying anything unpleasant. (88)
Under no circumstances should one act otherwise, for it creates an obstacle to success.
Women are goddesses; women are life-breaths; women alone are the ornament. (89)
One should always remain attached to one's wife;
otherwise, one might even fail to see one's own wife as fallen, naked, insane, or with exposed breasts.
On that day, one should not take pleasure with a woman, nor should one gaze upon her womb;
for she will become averse to sexual union and remain above his heart.
One must never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should especially honor them.
Having placed a large conch shell at the site of recitation, one should perform the japa while holding it aloft.
In the practice of *japa*, there is no restriction regarding time, purity, and so forth;

one may engage in sexual intercourse, touch, or especially gaze upon a woman—particularly one of noble birth and auspicious appearance—and consume meat, fish, curd, honey, or other edible substances according to one's preference. (93)
Having consumed food, a seat, or portions of a meal, one should perform the recitation of mantras while abstaining from further eating;
likewise after drinking liquor, eating meat, or approaching a woman in her menses. (94)
For one who recites the mantra of the goddess Caṇḍikā, there shall be suffering at every step.
(p. 227) The Greatness of the Kaulika.
They are Śākta within, Śaiva without, and are considered Vaiṣṇava in the assembly.
Wearing various disguises, the Kaulas wander upon the surface of the earth;
yet one who is devoted solely to Viṣṇu is devoid of the outward signs such as the worship of the Kula.
Whether walking, sleeping, wandering, or even stumbling, one who is devoted to Viṣṇu has his entire being and every movement permeated by the sentiment of Hari’s name.
Victory to you, O Viṣṇu, O Hara, O Brahmā! The Great Goddess is to be remembered by those of noble lineage, through various extensive meanings, both in the forest and in the home. 98.
Recitation at night is praised, as is wandering about at night and the worship of Śakti at night; how could one who does not perform these in any way whatsoever be a Kaulika practitioner? 99.
One should always dwell alone, like a deaf man, having transcended all attachment;
here there is no restriction of direction or time, nor any rule regarding posture and the like.

In the practice of a Śakti-mantra, there is no restriction regarding time for recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings; here, it is said that one may follow whatever rules accord with one's own inclination.
(228) Mental purity such as ritual bathing and so forth, mental recitation is the most excellent;
mental worship is divine, as are mental libations and other rites. (102)
Every moment is indeed auspicious; nowhere is there an inauspicious time.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilights and the dead of night. (103)
One who touches clothing, seats, places, houses, bodies, and so forth need not perform purification there; rather, one should maintain a mind free from conceptual construction.
In this [practice], there is no need for purification, nor is there any defect such as impurity;
the mantra-practitioner who contemplates in this way shall partake in the accomplishment of all desired aims. (105)
In his assembly, speech consisting of both prose and verse arises;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants lose their luster. (106)
Even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people?
[One should honor] this body, which consists of all the gods, this physical form which consists of all the gods. (107)
One should contemplate oneself as the form of the deity, non-dual;
for the self and the supreme self are the all-pervading, autonomous Lord of the universe. (108)
One should always contemplate oneself as being of the nature of Brahman;
even enemies will become friends, and kings will serve one directly. (109)
All proclaim the certain glory of the practitioners; even those who were ill-disposed now become well-disposed, and all the arrogant bow down. (110)
Obstacles and even the most formidable adversaries are overcome by the practitioner;
therefore, one should always worship the Goddess, whether unwashed or having already eaten. 111.
In a place that is very dark and impure, one should cause the offering (bali) to be given with the mantra;
whether one is afflicted by a severe illness, or pure, or even impure. || 112 ||
Whether it be at the improper time or the proper time, the qualified person is indeed always one who considers his purpose accomplished, with a mind that is perfectly contented. (113)
No unrighteousness exists at all, and some degree of righteousness may become great;
one should eat the food of a noble family and sleep with one of noble birth.
The noble-born should never engage in the practices of a family lineage that belongs to a beast;
for whatever conduct is prescribed in a particular mantra, such indeed is its dharma. (115)
One should offer to the deities food gathered by that hand, water gathered by that hand, and flowers gathered by that hand. (116)
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and meditated, the wise one should recite [the mantra] at night;
devoted to all accomplishments, he should recite the mantra at all times. || 117 ||
There is no fault in recitation at any time, nor in any place;
he who, devoted to recitation, performs it constantly shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
Of all sacrifices, the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) is praised as supreme;
by the mere practice of recitation at night, Caṇḍikā becomes the bestower of spiritual perfection (siddhi).
If the night has passed through the iḍā, one should mutter the mantra of Śakti;
if the life-force (jīva) has passed through the piṅgalā, one should always mutter the mantra of Puruṣa.
If, even after thousands of births, perfection is not attained, one nevertheless becomes successful through that [practice], whether by attaining heaven or indeed liberation itself. 121.
One must not entertain doubt in this regard, for the loss of accomplishment arises;
those bound souls, deluded by the scriptures, meet their dissolution in astonishment. (122)
In this case, one should possess a pure mind; then success (siddhi) shall be granted as liberation (apavarga).
Through these [means], success occurs at that very moment; there is no other wonder than this.
There is no atonement for one who has fallen from his family;
one who has fallen away from all proper conduct should practice the conduct of his family.
One who has fallen away from the conduct of his family shall go to the Raurava hell.
In the scriptures, a means of atonement is seen even for those who have committed great sins;
however, for one who has fallen from his lineage, no atonement is seen anywhere at all.
Calamity, misfortune, disease, poverty, strife, and fear;
even the wrath of the Yoginīs and stumbling at every step [shall cease]. (126)
One who follows the family tradition yet is dear to the Yoginīs, one who is falling away and ruined, devoid of luster and evil-minded;
one who is censured, hated by all, agitated, and abandoned by his companions. (127)
He wanders from country to country and his undertakings always suffer failure; even there, the Śākinīs who abide by the path of the Kula and protect the Kula [will encounter him]. 128.
In former times they were devoured; however, a boon was granted to them by me alone:
"Therefore, a hero who possesses proper conduct shall be dear to the Yoginīs. (129)
Through the conduct of the Kula, one attains divinity and union with the Yoginīs and Vīras; through the opposite of that, the Kaulika falls into the womb of an animal.

The attainment of mastery through command shall belong to him by virtue of his constant observance of conduct; [otherwise, it fails] due to the lack of purificatory rites and the transgression of the guru’s word. (131)
Furthermore, by abandoning right conduct, the Kaulika becomes fallen;
for him, worldly enjoyment leads to liberation, and sin becomes as good merit.
And through the pure disposition of the practitioner, saṃsāra itself becomes liberation;
one should always perform the great worship by means of the five elements. (133)
It must be performed with extreme secrecy and in every way well-ascertained;
thus, the illustrious one, devoted to right conduct, remains intent upon recitation and worship. (134)

The Protector (Pālaka) of the principles of the Kula dissolves into the Supreme Principle; he becomes an adept who is the locus of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā). || 135 ||
Expiation, falling from a cliff, renunciation, the observance of vows, bodily mortification, atheism, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and fasting—(p. 233)—[these are not means for liberation]. 136.
And one should avoid [these] with great effort if one desires success for oneself:
the five great sins, the killing of a hero, the drinking of intoxicants in vain, and the theft of a hero's property. (137)

Sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero (or a virtuous man), and fifthly, association with such persons—these are declared to be mortal sins (mahāpātaka); one should avoid them in every way. || 138 ||
One who worships the Siddhavidyā should not eat safflower, nālikā, or even the tamarind; having eaten these, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. || 139 ||
One who worships Tripurā should never eat a piece of sugarcane, should not say "Śivā Kālī," and should never cut down a Kadamba tree. 140.
If one should act out of negligence, one shall incur the curse of Sundarī;
likewise, he who does not maintain proper conduct while relying upon the Kula-dharma [shall suffer]. (141)
For that great sinner who always acts according to his own whims,
there is no atonement whatsoever in the Mahāraurava hell, which is densely crowded with torments.
He is said to be always a beast and shall incur the curse of the deity,
[for any act] whether secret or manifest, performed through knowledge or ignorance. (143)
If the performance of a prohibited act occurs anywhere,
the practitioner must perform the appropriate expiation in each such case.

Having properly understood the place, time, age, and wealth [of the offender], one should correctly determine the gravity or lightness of the sin resulting from the performance of a prohibited act, according to the prescribed rule.
The disciple should perform penance for his teacher for the purification of all sins; indeed, the disciple should also carry out that very penance prescribed for him. 146.
Alternatively, the chanting of the Guru’s name is remembered as the remedy for all sins, just as the impurity of gold is purified by fire. 147.
One should burn away the impurity of improper conduct with the fire of expiatory rites;
by chanting the name of the Guru one hundred thousand times, one is purified of all sins. 148.
Alternatively, by reciting one hundred thousand ajapās and three hundred thousand lopās,
the practitioner is always liberated from all sins.
The extraction of the Lopāmudrā mantra:
the sky (ha) joined with the void (kha), followed by Śakti (e) and the visarga, is the Ajapā mantra.
From that [arise] the power of space (viyacchakti), then desire (kāma), and the Supreme Goddess Earth (kṣauṇī). || 150 ||
Ākāśa, Bhṛgu, and Kāma; Śiva, Śakra, and Pārvatī; Candra, Anaṅga, and the goddess Dharā; Lopāmudrā is thus revealed. (151)
What is the use of saying more here? The secret is now being told:
for all those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, right conduct bestows a happy state.
Just as a king incurs the faults of his subjects and a husband the faults of his wife, so too does the teacher always incur the sins of his disciple; of this there is no doubt. (153)
The guru should explain the conduct three times to his disciple;
if the disciple does not accept it, then no sin accrues to the guru.

The Kula scripture must be protected from the uninitiated (paśus); however, one may set aside the discourse on Kula-dharma in the presence of the uninitiated. One must never do so, just as one would not recite the Vedas before a Śūdra. 155.

One should not speak of the sacred seats (pīṭha), fields (kṣetra), traditions (āgama), and lineages (āmnāya), nor of those who practice their vidyās and the Kaulikas, nor even of the substances of the Kula and so forth, in the presence of a bound soul (paśu). 156.
Just as one protects wealth, grain, clothing, and so forth from thieves, one should likewise protect the family dharma from [the consumption of] livestock. 157.
The deities favor those who maintain the well-guarded Kaula conduct; such a person attains whatever success they desire, whereas they destroy those who reveal [the teachings]. 158.

That Goddess who is Bhuvaneśvarī, uplifted from the worlds of the three realms, who stands at the forefront as the creator of the manifestation of knowledge, the deity who takes refuge in her own form and its colors—
she is eternal, complete, dwelling in the home of the householder, cherished by her beloved, and tender.
O practitioner! Worship her constantly with the five qualities, through austerity and through enjoyment. || 159 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 10 ||
The Eleventh Chapter:
The Description of Emotional States (Bhāva).
The threefold nature of emotional states according to the distinctions of "beasts" (paśu) and so forth.

Now I shall explain the state of being (bhāva) according to the Tantra; for the state of being is said to be threefold, following the sequence of the Divine (divya), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu). (1)
Through their respective distinctions, there is a threefold nature of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity.
The Guru is threefold, and likewise the Mantra and the Deity.
The primordial state is the greatest, most auspicious, and the bestower of all accomplishments.
The second is indeed the middling one, and the third is censured by the world;
[these results are attained] through extensive recitation, as well as through fire-offerings (homa) and bodily austerities.

Without the state of being (bhāva), neither mechanical devices nor mantras yield fruit; what is the use of hundreds of thousands of heroic accomplishments (vīrasādhana), or of drawing in hosts of noble and ignoble beings? (4)

What is the use of worshipping the *pīṭhas*, what is the use of feeding maidens and so forth, what is the use of giving gifts for the sake of affection within one's own family, and likewise for others? (5)
Of what avail is the state of having conquered the senses, and of what avail is the practice of family traditions, if one whose self is purified in being were not devoted to his lineage? (6)
Through devotion one attains liberation; through devotion, the increase of one's lineage;
through devotion, there shall be the growth of one's clan; and through devotion, the purification of the body. (7)
What is the use of elaborate nyāsa rituals, what is the use of extensive purifications of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), or what is the use of fruitless worship, if true devotion does not arise? (8)
By whom is knowledge honored, and by whom is it not produced?
The absence of fruit arises necessarily from the presence or absence [of its cause]. || 9 ||
The description of the divine state:
first, the divine state is explained according to the path of the Tantra.
Whichever deity resides in whichever [place], that [place] is filled with a mass of splendor. (10)

Having visualized the entire world as consisting of light, one should perform the conceptualization of the forms, either with mantras corresponding to each respective form or with their own specific mantras. || 11 ||
Having perceived himself as consisting of that [divinity], and likewise all states of being, one should meditate upon all of that within the woman with a disciplined mind. (12)
From eight years until the end of sixteen, she is called a "young woman" (yuvatī). If there is the manifestation of the inner state (*bhāva*) therein, that state is considered supreme. (13)
Drinking again and again from her feet up to her toes,
one's darkness of sin shall be shattered by the moonlight of the jewels in her toenails.
The hero should always possess a supple inner heart and remain free from agitation;
he should have well-rounded knees and the beautiful splendor of shanks, thighs, and hips.
With her navel, the line of body hair, her chest, and her full breasts;
with her neck, the region around her eyes, the tips of her hair, and her abundant smiles. (16)
With divine glances filled with the intoxication of honey-like sweetness,
his senses became tender and satisfied, and he took refuge in the state of the fourfold aims of life.
Then, during the worship of Kāmakalā, the practitioner with a steady mind should meditate upon Kāmakalā;
at the time of withdrawal, he should again [unify] his own [self] with the nectar-filled essences of her being.
One should contemplate the face in the form of a drop (bindu), below that the pair of breasts, and below that the "half of the supreme" (saparārdha) facing downwards. 19.
It is filled with the nectar of all knowledge, bestows the power of all speech, accomplishes all aims, and causes the delight of all. || 20 ||
He is the embodiment of all gods and the like, and is saluted by all the gods;
he is completely full of delight for all and the cause of the enchantment of all. (21)
It accomplishes all aims and brings about the subjugation of all;
thus, this meditation on the Kāmakalā should be well-guarded by the most excellent practitioners. (22)
The practitioner should always contemplate his own self in this form:
in the region of the genitals, at the base, he is the form of Śiva, with the luster of gold.
Situated at the navel, it has the luster of the solar disc and the brilliance of the rising sun;
in the heart, it has the form of a flame of fire, and above that, the radiance of the sun.
In the throat, it has the form of a lamp-flame; at the uvula, it resembles a bell made of lapis lazuli;
between the eyebrows, it has the luster of a jewel, shining like the orb of the moon.
The practitioner should contemplate the universal splendor within the eyes;
having held, touched, seen, or meditated upon the body of Kāmakalā.

Having contemplated that form of the creative power (kalā) within the Kulas and within the Akula, a collection of objective entities arises through reflective awareness (vimarśa) for a moment in a similar manner. (27)
Because one is born into a noble family, all that has been told is auspicious;
for the Goddess herself truly abides as the reality within the family. (28)
Therefore, she should be worshipped with great effort as a limb of that family scripture by one who possesses the family goddess and the primordial goddess, Niścalā. (29)
That person is blessed in the world who remains steadfast in that very state;
thus has been described the meditation on Kāmakalā, which bestows all perfections.
The wife of another should be known as superior, while one's own wife increases affection;
when she arrives, he should offer a welcome through his own playful charm by means of amorous dalliance. (31)
Having raised her from the bed and grasped her by the tips of her hands, he should then cause her— well-attired, capable of assuming any form at will, and seated on his left side— to lie down.
Having meditated there upon the Kāmakalā, whose form begins with the bindu and so forth,
one should then offer perfume and garlands and apply the kula-substances.
Having given and consumed betel-leaf accompanied by the causal [mantra],
the practitioner should inquire about the entire lineage narrative, both mundane and supramundane.
If one who knows the Kula scriptures— even if he is a perfected master (siddha)— engages in censure, fear, anger, or harsh speech toward her, he will certainly perish. (35)
Having abandoned faults and the like there through training, as if by a rain of oil, one should not indeed cultivate [the mind] with harsh speech; for if it is done so, it will be fruitless. || 36 ||
In the Kula scripture, the secret is indeed the root of Kula; from that, the world arises.
It is better to abandon one's Kula-mantra, and even better to abandon one's Kula-guru. (37)
One's own family should never be abandoned on account of a perceived fault;
for if, by the power of fortune, there should be an abundance of kinsmen within one's own family, [one remains there]. (38)
One should establish them in a uniform manner and avoid any inconsistency;
there should be separate locations, separate meditations, separate worship, and separate hymns of praise. (39)
One should not strive [to avoid this]—what is the use of such excessive talk?
This applies both to a family of heroic offspring and to a family of heroic wives. (40)
O Goddess of the gods, it remains forever; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By the force of their breath, even that very region is destroyed.
(243) Through joy, there shall be for the Goddess a bath in nectar; of this there is no doubt.
Born of the Kula, she resounds with the slapping of her arms in the great battle. (42)
For she protects the world by not indulging in faults; [she avoids] envy, hatred for her husband, harsh speech, quarreling, and the like. (43)
Furthermore, because of her association with the low-born, that goddess, the beloved of Hara, did not [grant her favor];
thus, having abandoned her family, she should strive for her own spiritual perfection.
Regarding the method for the ripening of the fruit:
what is this method for the ripening of the fruit said to be according to the path of Tantra?
The supreme Vīrapatnī is herself Maheśvarī. (45)
Her daughter is the eternal Raudrī, the primordial of the family sciences;
her daughter-in-law is Bhuvaneśānī, the awakener of all mantras. (46)
Whether by right means or by wrong means, if the wife of a hero is a Guru, the practitioner becomes an achiever of all goals through initiation alone. (47)
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune a wife of a hero is obtained, what on this earth could not be accomplished after bringing its fruit to maturity? 48.
The ritual for the ripening of the fruit is honored by all the gods;
it yields both seen and unseen results, [as do] the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras. (49)
They come for the sake of the ripening of the fruit; therefore, with special effort, their dismissal should be performed, along with protection according to the power of one's disposition.
One should make the family well-disciplined through the specific injunctions of various kalpas;
for there is no dharma greater than the dharma of devotion to one's husband in the three worlds. (51)
The husband is the constant bestower of life; the husband alone is the supreme goal;
the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman; the husband is the lord, greater than one's very life. || 52 ||
The Lord consists of all holy fords; the Master consists of all gods;
and the husband likewise consists of all goddesses—such is the Great Guru.
That woman who, having abandoned one who embodies all the gods, goes to another's domain,
will certainly be born as a sow, a donkey, a crow, or a jackal.
But as for me, O Queen, there is neither fear nor shame here, as if toward my own son; for whoever goes to your linga anywhere, assuming the form of a husband— || 55 ||
O Goddess, water consecrated with the root mantra should be sprinkled on her body;
if she is not outside at that time, then indeed her own husband [should do so].
Women of good family should be trained according to such instructions as these:
having arrived, she should sit by his side; looking at his face, she should remain steady. (57)
She should be skilled in discerning facial expressions and gestures, and she should be joyful at the sight of her husband;
she should not offer a reply to a non-answer, and she should speak only during auspicious activities.
Having performed the protection rite according to the prescribed method, the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the great worship of the Yoginīs and likewise of the Baṭukas. (59)
For the sake of destroying obstacles, [the rite] should be performed according to the family-day (kula-vāra), asterism (ṛkṣa), and conjunction (yoga).
At the root of their primary tree, one should [worship] the Root-Vidyā and Kālikā. (60)
In the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*), the practitioner should effect the descent of the *kula*;
for that which is the form in which this best of those who know the *kula* finds delight. (61)
Having assumed that form as his body, the practitioner, with a steady mind,
performs the deposition of the seed-syllable therein and effects the protection of the Kula.
Having understood the origin of the *kula* through signs, sentences, and words— whether it be born of the gods or born of men— according to the true *Kula-śāstra*, [one should proceed]. (63)
Having understood the classification of the families, the wise one [should perform the rite] beyond the fifth month,
or during the seventh or eighth month, in the midst of trees or by a lake.

Having placed his hand [upon it], he should recite eight thousand times the mantra known as Pādukā according to the method of withdrawal (saṃhārayoga); then it will indeed fall from the tree by itself.
"I worship the sandals"—this is declared to be the mantra of the sandals.
When this is performed, whatever fruit falls [as a result] is ordained by the gods. (66)
And that which belongs to its own master falls due to the coming and going of the reverse;
having recognized this as the fruit of the sign, one should then bring it and wash it.
Having offered fragrant substances and pungent substances, the supreme practitioner,
having consecrated them with the nectar of the dhenumudrā, should perform the fire-oblation unobserved.
Having performed it in this manner at night, one should then eat the remnants of the sacrifice;
as soon as that has been eaten, one shall indeed become long-lived on earth. (69)
The primary Madhumatī, which bestows enjoyment, is held in his hand;
for him, the eternal Madhumatī arises—of this there is no doubt. (70)
I shall now describe the fruit of Madhumatī; listen to me.
Speech as sweet as a stream of nectar issues from his mouth. (71)
The omniscient lord of all scriptures, the leader of his lineage, the illustrious one, enjoys abundant happiness until the end of the moon and the sun. (72)
And by celestial maidens and apsarases, as well as divine gandharvas and cāraṇas, who were endowed with various graceful charms and were highly skilled and proficient in the arts. || 73 ||
With abundant dancing and singing, with various means and elixirs such as the nectar of immortality and other delightful, divine enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain; || 74 ||
Having mounted this chariot held by the hands of celestial maidens, the Supreme Goddess arrives, full of eagerness, her heart longing for the practitioner. 75.
Where the god Kāmeśvara has attained the essence of his desire,
there indeed the celestial maidens constantly arrive by the thousands.
Having made the city suitable for the Indras, they dwell there together with the practitioners;
having reached that sacred seat (pīṭha), they enjoy abundant happiness.
Having remained on earth for a long time, one shall attain liberation at the end.
For practitioners who possess knowledge of the Kula, there is no fault in the falling of the fruit. (78)
For the sake of causing this fruit to fall, he creates obstacles at every step by attaining noble birth, everywhere acting out of his own self-concealment. (79)
Likewise, an obstacle was certainly created against the fruit atop the tree;
if, by the turn of fate, the loss of the fruit-bearing tree should ever occur. (80)
In this case, the practitioner would also be possessed of conceptual thought;
therefore, the Kula-worship does not take place until purification has occurred. (81)
Therefore, one's own kinsmen must be avoided with great effort;
for there is no one on this earth who is fit for the performance of this task.
If one performs [the rite] in a place situated at a great distance, devoid of names and letters, there may be an obstacle or the falling away of the fruit. (83)
There, the practitioners who serve the Kula are not afflicted by defects;
for although this [path] is primarily characterized by obstacles, it may sometimes be a means of attaining the fruit. (84)
(249) Everywhere, the accomplishment of the fruit must be performed by means of convention alone;
if it were performed by common folk once they have already attained their own fruit, [it would be useless]. 85.
The fruit arises from that very [practice], and by that sin one is certainly bound;
yet the supreme practitioner, possessing a divine nature, though mortal, becomes equal to Śakra.
This divine state, which brings supreme bliss, has been told to you. It must not be given to just anyone; it should be guarded with great effort from the spiritually blind. || 87 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the intermediate state of heroism (vīrabhāva):
having become one whose mind is free from the pairs of opposites, with the form of the digit of desire (kāmakalā) in the heart. (88)
Worship should be performed at night; one should always be endowed with the underlying purpose.
Taking one's own lineage along, one should personally assume the form of Bhairava. (89)
One should perform the extensive ritual placement (nyāsa) upon that body, which is the form of Bhairavī;
likewise, one should perform the entire placement consisting of the nine-yoni diagram.
In the midst of a couch of flowers, strewn with heaps of blossoms and filled with various fragrances, the Yantra is prepared with the Kula-substance.
Having written [the mantra], one should worship it if one has the capacity, preceded by the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭa).
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, [one should worship] whichever one of the previously mentioned pots [is appropriate]. (92)
Having established [the site] by means of the causal rite and having filled it according to the distinctions of the Brāhmaṇas and other castes,
one should first inscribe there the mantra originating from whichever specific lineage.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity there, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, displaying the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should contemplate that [mantra] as nectar (*amṛta*).
Upon seeing the vessel of the guest-offering (arghya), the hosts of Yoginīs indeed dance;
all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on their joy;
having divided the vessel of the water offering (arghya) into three parts, one part is given to the Guru.
Having given one [portion] as an offering to the family, and with another performing the libation to the gods,
he drank the full essence of the lineage, adorned with various ornaments.

Having become one whose nature is bliss, he should worship the Supreme Goddess, having first worshipped her respective mantra according to the procedure prescribed for each specific ritual manual (kalpa). 98.
Then, having performed the rite of dismissal (visarjana), he should subsequently unite [the offering] with his own lineage;
by drinking the nectar through the natural flow of devotion, the Goddess partakes of the ambrosia. 99.
(251) Through the tasting of the fluids of those respective families, the Goddess’s pleasure is produced;
by the mere grasping of that fruit, one ascends the peak of Mount Sumeru. 100.
Merely by the embrace of the creeper, his body becomes washed with nectar;
when the root-yoga has been performed there, he should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having taken the sacrificial substance, one should satisfy [the deity] with it;
and having performed the libation, one should follow [the deity] while circumambulating to the right.
Then, having prostrated according to the ritual prescribed for the Kalpa, one should thereafter satisfy [the deity] with this hymn of praise:
"This Vīra-kula is indeed beautiful and most enchanting. (103)
In whatever region the Hero resides, that family and its offspring likewise [prosper];
there is no fear of pestilence there, nor any fear of the king and the like.
There, auspiciousness always increases wealth and sons;
there, Lakṣmī and Vāṇī remain forever firmly established, without a doubt. (105)
On the Prabodhinī day, the mantra-flower must certainly be applied with effort from the root of Brahman; thus, no obstacle shall arise. (106)
p.
252) That union with another hero cannot be seized even by the gods;
it is not subverted by the Yoginīs, nor is it joined with sin. || 107 ||
If one goes to a cremation ground on any day,
or specifically on a Tuesday, the fruit of worship there shall be equal to that of seven days.
If one departs on the fourteenth day, one obtains the fruit of worshipping for an entire fortnight;
but if one does not depart and does not worship at that place, one is undoubtedly a mere beast. 109.
"O God, there is none superior to another"—intent on such thoughts, when the practitioner falls into agitation, the agitation of the Goddess arises. (110)
Therefore, the wise and excellent hero, through diligent effort, should be engaged in enjoyment;
for through enjoyment one attains liberation, and through enjoyment one achieves the Kula-sādhana.
Whatever one speaks, sleeps, does, or worships—the wise person should perform all that while meditating upon it as having the form of the Kula. 112.
Alone in a desolate region, in a cemetery, in a lonely forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank, he should dwell joyfully, free from attachment. (113)
The time for recitation by heroes is praised at all times;
it should be performed in every sacred seat and in every land—of this there is no doubt. (114)

And the rite of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) must be performed by heroic men; it may be performed even by divine beings, but not by those who are bound [by worldly ties] (paśu) or by commoners. || 115 ||
It is certain that even the work of a commoner is better than that of a beast;
for that eternal practice of mantra-sādhana which was previously proclaimed by the Goddess [is superior]. (116)
The hero of great power should prepare collyrium, pills, and so forth;
there is no difference between him and a divine hero, yet that which constitutes a difference is now described. || 117 ||
The distinction between the divine (divya) and the heroic (vīra) is stated:
the divine hero is generally peaceful, humble, sweet, and endowed with artistic grace and beauty, like a deity; whereas the heroic hero possesses a haughty mind. (118)
Whether adorned with supernatural powers or anointed with sandalwood paste,
whether concealing his outward form or manifest, he is a divine practitioner (divyasādhaka). || 119 ||

Whether his limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste or not, whether he is a Vaiṣṇava or a non-Vaiṣṇava, whether he is unrefined or refined— he who is constantly sprinkled [with water] is the Lord of the Family (Kuleśvara).
One should always remain joyful and content whether faced with insult or honor; one may be intent on reviling the deity or even intent upon its worship and other rites. (121)
Delighting in worship yet free from it, established in the Kula and Akula doctrine, and endowed with his own true nature, he should roam upon the earth like a god.
Just as there is no Vedic refinement for a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas, so too devotion does not flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu. (123)
Just as liberation without the knowledge of power (śakti) leads only to ridicule, so too there is no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra without a guru. 124.
Just as a woman deprived of her husband is excluded from all ritual duties, so too is a hero without his family, or my practitioner without the Goddess. (125)

One who belongs to the Kaula lineage is not [merely] an initiate; therefore, one should be intent upon the inner state (*bhāva*). For without the Kula, there is no [attainment] for the divine ones or likewise for the heroes. (126)
Mantra-siddhi shall not arise even in hundreds of millions of births for one whose family is undisciplined; how can such a person be a worshiper of me? (127)

Therefore, one should always act with effort so that [the disciple] becomes endowed with discipline; for in this scripture, there is no eligibility whatsoever for one who lacks the proper disposition within the lineage. 128.
By that, the practitioner whose being is purified becomes a Kaulika;
this Vīrakula is indeed more delightful even than the divine.
The Description of the State of the Animal (Paśubhāva): I shall now proclaim the third state, the state of the animal, which is censured by all.
