Having received the knowledge of the animal according to the prescribed rule, one should be intent upon that state. (130)
First, one should diligently practice purification for the sake of the goal from the very beginning;
one should not consume fish, nor should one even mentally recall women. (131)
One should have no greed for another's property, nor should there be any mental attachment to its enjoyment,
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded and most beautiful sacred field, one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual], and one should abandon crookedness from afar. (133)
The deity, of radiant white complexion, should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed.
There should be worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day, and one should perform the recitation (japa) at the three junctions of the day. (134)
At night, one should never touch the rosary or the yantra;
nor should one recite the mantra after eating; in all ritual acts, one should remain observant of silence.
On the occasion of a festival day, the best of practitioners should certainly not approach a woman;
rather, having personally brought flowers, incense, and water, he should perform worship.

One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it; furthermore, one should not approach even one's own wife with passion except during her fertile period. 137.
One who has faith in listening to the Purāṇas and is devoted to the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences should not eat at night, nor likewise should a wise man consume betel leaf.
Whatever has been commanded by the Guru, all that one should perform with diligence;
likewise, one should offer flowers of one's own birth as well as the causal substances.
Having touched this, one becomes pure after three nights by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One who is devoted to the Goddess should not accept dyed clothing. 140.
One should perform the rites beginning with the *kalpa* as taught in the *Viṣṇutantra*, and likewise carry out its practice;
however, one should not engage in talk concerning the stories of heroes, even if it is praised by heroes. (141)

One devoted to dharma should perform the daily śrāddha, offer mouthfuls of grass to cows, perform the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana), bathe at sacred fords (tīrtha), and visit the site of the sacred seat (pīṭha). 142.
The animal (paśu) is of two kinds, distinguished by whether it is initiated (dīkṣita) or uninitiated (adīkṣita).
Indeed, the animal is twofold: the uninitiated and likewise the initiated.
It is certain that the right to perform worship belongs only to the initiated. (143)
He who is a Guru never has authority anywhere else;
nor does the former [Guru] have authority regarding the arrival and departure from the place of worship and so forth. (144)
All those belonging to the former [tradition] should be excluded from one's own country by all followers of the Kaula path;
merely by seeing them first, one should perform the ritual vision of the Kula.
The sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils may somehow be endured;
however, the sight of one’s own past [actions] cannot be [endured] at all—this is the truth, the firmly established truth. (146)
(258) Although that [individual] soul is certainly and eternally identical with the Goddess due to its omnipresence,
nevertheless, doubt arises at every step regarding the nature of the Goddess. (147)
Better is the abandonment of one's family, better is the destruction of one's own kin;
better would it be to be reviled by one's own family, better still to be censured by one's own kin. (148)
Better is the ruin of one's own family, better is the destruction of one's own lineage;
better is the downfall of one's own family through body, mind, or speech. (149)
One should not form a prior attachment because it causes the destruction of the limbs of the Goddess;
in the Kula scripture, these two are certainly considered the gravest sins. 150.
There is great infamy within one's own family, and likewise in the case of another's union; from such association with cattle, even greater sin is produced. (151)
Due to conversation with a Goloka [cowherd] and speaking in Sanskrit with a commoner (paśu), the great mantras do not succeed; this is the truth, the truth, most certainly so. (152)
Killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, approaching a woman who should not be approached, theft, and association with such persons—these are the classes of mortal sins (mahāpātaka). || 153 ||
(259) Through initiation they perish, and others perish through recitation;
[so too do] the killing of a hero, drinking liquor in vain, and union with the wife of a hero. 154.
Omitting the meaning of even a single portion of this text from one's teacher, as well as knowing Vīravarāha and yet disparaging him or failing to praise him— 155.
Nor is the depositing of wealth with him called theft; yet association with such a beast must be avoided—namely, conversing with him, sharing a bed, or sitting together on the same seat. (156)
Eating together in one place and, beyond that, social association—this is declared to be the sin of association for a noble-souled person of high birth. (157)
For them, there is neither sin nor, at their passing, an accumulation of merit;
neither sacred fords, nor the Gaṅgā, nor Kāśī have power over them.
Merely by the recitation of this great vidyā, the four mortal sins are destroyed, and contact with such sinners never leads to one's own ruin. (159)
If, through ignorance, association with animals should occur by fate,
then one should exert effort for the sake of the vow for a period known as twelve years.
Staying near a woman of noble family, devoted to serving her family, eating the remnants of her food, and constantly uttering the name of her husband; (161)

At the conclusion of that, having worshipped her thoroughly and satisfied her with diligent efforts, one should become pure; then, by receiving the vidyā once again, one shall attain purification. || 162 ||
If one should become incapable of observing the vows, that best of practitioners should satisfy [the deity] with gold and give it to a family for the sake of destroying sins. (163)
Having incurred contact through knowledge [of the corpse], one is not purified by death;
and when dead, one assumes the womb of a crow, a vulture, or similar creatures in every respect. (164)
One who is joined with various afflictions falls into the hells;
one should not initiate such a person, nor should one even grant them a vision [of the deity]. 165.

In this matter, one should diligently avoid discourse concerning the scriptures of the goddesses; likewise, one should avoid, through action, mind, or speech, the worship of the scriptures of the bound souls (paśus) and the like. 166.
Those who commit great sins must be abandoned by practitioners of the Kula;
regarding prohibitions, the practitioner should always follow the Kula scriptures.
One should avoid all texts concerning animal sacrifice as one would another's wife;
they are like milk placed in a dog-skin, which should not be offered even to the twice-born. (168)
Likewise, the Kaulikas should not listen to the Dharma from the mouth of a beast;
nor should those Kaulikas who lack faith in these Kula-dharmas [do so]. (169)
The Kaulas and those who observe the vows of the Paśus, who mock both sides, do not turn away from their transgressions until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa. (170)
They remain in Raurava for as many years as there are hairs on their bodies, [only through] initiation, worship, burnt offerings, and likewise through being beheld by [the Guru's] gaze. || 171 ||
If anyone is defeated by a mere beast through the power of knowledge alone, the Goddess will certainly take everything from him after pronouncing a curse. 172.
Having received the knowledge of the sacrificial animal (paśu), if one becomes intent on worship, then, having gazed upon its face, one should look upon the face of the Kula. || 173 ||
Thus, if it is not so, a loss of knowledge occurs for one of noble birth;
whatever is taught by the Paśus is performed by the Kula practitioners. (174)
Whatever great vidyās there may be of Caṇḍikā, it is certain that each and every one of them always serves for the purpose of exorcism against those [obstacles]. (175)
By the falling of the gaze of a beast, the practitioner will certainly be destroyed;
even if, by chance, he obtains the vidyā from a beast through men born of noble families. (176)
Having requested forgiveness from the twice-born for the transgression, one should receive the vidyā once more:
"O Mother, whatever was done out of ignorance, without having reflected upon the Kulakaulika [tradition]," (p. 262).
"Forgive that sin, O Mother; remove it, O Goddess, and show mercy.
Having thus prayed with great effort, [he offered] jewels and an abundance of gold and other riches. (178)
Having worshipped the couple of the Kula lineage with diligence on the eighth day, one should observe it;
for one who has fallen from his practice, the eighth lunar day is the only [time] for this, and not otherwise.
That alone shall be the time for initiation; no other time is praised, even if there are many kinds of Kula practitioners who have fallen away from their vows.
There is no one equal to a *paśu* disciple; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
The conduct of the *kula* is kept secret from the *paśu*, for they consider that to be their supreme [duty]. (181)
Neither the discussion of this scripture nor the showing of this book should ever be done in front of an uninitiated person (paśu), even at the cost of one's life. || 182 ||

Having fashioned [an image] and beheld the face of the Sun, the Lord of the Clan (Kulanāyaka) should be remembered even in a lifeless piece of wood, a clod of earth, a pebble, or even a blade of grass. 183.
The Goddess is conceived everywhere, yet not in the mantra-body of the sacrificial animal; everything, whether pleasure or pain, is fashioned as presided over by consciousness. 184.
In that very state, because volition is absent, there is no such restriction;
therefore, everything belonging to the Goddess should be offered by those devoted to the worship of the Goddess. (185)
It must be protected in every way for the sake of the animal's welfare;
in that regard, two matters must never be disclosed under any circumstances. (186)
The bound soul (paśu) is established as being twofold: by its own nature (sabhāva) and by its state of dissolution (vibhāva).
It is "by its own nature" because it manifests through three births in the form of a bound soul. (187)
From the state of a hero, a god is indeed born;
from a god, a hero is born, and from a hero, a god is born. || 188 ||

In the divine and the heroic there is no doubt; this is called "equanimity. The determination of existence is inexpressible; for existence is a property of the mind—how indeed could it be verbal? || 189 ||
Therefore, existence should not be described; only a mere indication has been given.
Just as the sweetness of sugarcane or molasses is always known by the tongue. (190)
Therefore, existence is indeed conceptualized as non-existence by the mind, since that which is the one Great Existence alone assumes manifoldness. (191)
Through the disappearance of the distinctions of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), the distinction between entities will dissolve;
the Lord, who is a mass of solid bliss, assumes the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (192)
That very Self is the essence of all flavors; He is the Lord, the supreme and great.
He alone is indeed to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon.
Therefore, it should be directly realized by heroes through various scriptures; it should be heard from the words of the Vedas, and it should be reflected upon through means such as contemplation.
This very one, who is the self of all, will certainly become manifest when he is meditated upon through the logical arguments taught by the Guru. || 195 ||
In that body, however, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, is directly manifest;
and through manifold dispositions, even those dispositions are dissolved therein.

Just as the single taste [of water] assumes diversity through the process of being milked from a cow after various kinds of fodder have been consumed, so too does [the Self] assume multiplicity through the practice of [identifying with] the products, such as milk. || 197 ||
From grass, indeed, sap is produced, and from that comes a superior sap;
from that comes curd, from that the oblation, and from that also the emergence of essence.
That very [emptiness] is its cause, yet it is not called its effect;
and there, that which is always perceived is neither effect nor cause. (199)
In the very same way, this very self is born, will be born, and has been born within various forms of wombs; it is manifested through the diversity of its effects.
He is born, he is dead; he is bound, he is liberated;
he is the man, he is the woman, and he is also the neuter; he alone is indeed that which is bodiless (Anaṅga). || 201 ||
Just as it assumes diversity through union with various meditations,
that very Self alone is eternal, existing in the form of flavor.
That which is unmanifest is made manifest by nature (prakṛti) with certainty;
therefore, it is known through its connection with nature, and never by any other means. || 203 ||
Just as a jar is not perceived in the absence of its connection with "jar-ness," so too, even when being distinguished from others, it does not attain [the status of] difference. (204)

A person does not attain distinction in any way whatsoever without power (śakti)—neither through ritual applications, nor through knowledge, nor through sacred revelation, nor through the lineage of gurus. (205)
p. 266) A description of the knowledge of Brahman by its very nature:
"By its very nature Brahman is known; by its very nature it dissolves again."
The entire world is presided over by Prakṛti; indeed, the universe is desired by Prakṛti.
By its very nature, everything undergoes differentiation; by its very nature, everything dissolves.
There is no objective reality that is "nature," nor indeed is there a "person" (puruṣa), for the Supreme Lord alone exists.
The knowledge of the equal flavor of these two is the reality of things, the supreme state;
the union of both, however, is the reality of things as well-established. (208)
In this [state], that person—the wise one whose nature is consciousness—is known by himself;
he is eternally changeless, and the person is beyond the reach of the means of valid cognition.
The self-existent Self becomes manifest everywhere by itself;
there are many means for knowing the eternal Brahman. || 210 ||
Nevertheless, through its union with primordial nature (prakṛti), it quickly attains perceptibility,
just as seafarers take up their ship in a favorable region and clan.
Having crossed over various lands, one enters the ocean after a long time;
yet, having boarded a boat upon its shore, they return again in an instant. || 212 ||
If there is no difference in kind (*vaijātya*) in that case, how can each of those be a cause?
Therefore, it is through a continuous succession (*paramparā*) that they attain the status of being causes.
p.
267) Nor are those [other factors] the direct causes; rather, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the cause.
The female state should be known as *prakṛti*, while the male state is considered the *puruṣa*. || 214 ||

Let it be understood by the best of practitioners through the distinction between the cognition and the object of cognition, just as light is the manifestor in the case of the direct perception of a jar. (215)
Therefore, the eye and so forth are slightly more than that [non-conceptual cognition];
however, "pot-ness" is indeed the cause of differentiation for this [cognition]. (216)
Likewise, other things do not become manifestors with respect to an individual;
rather, this [manifestor] alone is the direct cause, and it is certainly the primordial nature (prakṛti). // 217 //
He in whose body the divine state and the heroic state are established shall attain the supreme direct realization in a single lifetime. || 218 ||
That very Self is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and wanders the earth for the sake of experience;
that very Self is celebrated as Bhairava, the son of the Goddess. || 219 ||
Worship should be performed by means of the divine (divya), the heroic (vīra), and the animal (paśu) [practitioners] according to their respective paths;
however, among the three states (bhāva), two states are well-established.
The two paths to liberation, which are the essence of the Kula and the most excellent of the Kula, should not be spoken of [to the uninitiated]. || 220 ||
If a practitioner does not worship with those substances that have been prescribed for a particular entity according to the sequence of the ten-day rite, he becomes fallen. || 221 ||
One should not teach the internal disposition there, nor should one prescribe worship there;
however, by receiving the mantra from a Kula lineage, purity of disposition arises. || 222 ||
Therefore, becoming intent on the true nature of reality, the wise person should worship the Goddess.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter:
The Method for Beads.
Now I shall describe the method for beads according to the way of the Tantras.
The procedure for recitation (japa) begins from the middle of the ring finger and proceeds in due order by moving clockwise.
One should recite [the mantra] over the ten joints up to the base of the index finger;
he who recites it at the tip or the middle of the index finger is indeed a commoner.
Four things perish for him: life, knowledge, fame, and wealth.
This is declared to be the Śaktimālā, which illuminates all mantras. (3)
(Alternatively:
the three joints of the ring finger, the three joints of the little finger, the three joints of the middle finger, and the joint at the base of the index finger. (4)
One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palms.
For if there is a separation of the fingers, the recitation leaks away through the gaps. (5)
Whatever is recited upon the tips of the fingers, whatever is recited while skipping the central bead (*meru*),
and whatever is recited at the joints of the beads— all that shall be fruitless. (6)
O Great Goddess, regarding the description of the different types of rosaries: for daily recitation, the hand-rosary (karamālā) bestows auspiciousness;
likewise, the bead-rosary (akṣamālā) and others are for the sake of attaining success in every way.
(Alternatively:
A rosary made of pearls bestows both sovereignty and liberation;
it eternally grants all perfections and brings all kings under one's control. || 8 ||
Just as one made of pearls, so too one fashioned from crystal;
a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows all perfections for the sake of liberation.
A garland of coral is considered best for subjugation and for bestowing fortune and knowledge;
likewise, a garland of rubies bestows the fruit of sovereignty.
A rosary of putrajīvaka beads bestows knowledge and prosperity;
through a rosary of lotus seeds, wealth and great riches are produced. (11)
A garland of red sandalwood bestows subjugation and good fortune;
a rosary of rudrākṣa beads brings forth one's heart's desires through recitation. (92)
A rosary made of lotus seeds destroys enemies; one made with knots of kuśa grass destroys sin;
and a rosary made of putrajīva fruit quickly bestows a son.
A golden rosary shall grant all desires; one made of coral yields abundant wealth; a crystal rosary bestows good fortune; and a rosary of rudrākṣa beads grants inexhaustible fulfillment of desires.

For the Śākta practitioners, a rosary made of crystal or red sandalwood is prescribed; one made of *putrajīva* seeds is ten times more effective, one of conch shells is a hundred times, and one of *rudrākṣa* is a thousand times. (15)
With coral and rubies, the merit becomes ten thousandfold;
with crystal it is said to be ten thousand, and with pearls it is declared to be a hundred thousand.
With lotus seeds, there shall be ten lakhs; with silver beads, it is said to be ten million (koṭi);
with gold, it shall be one hundred million; and with red sandalwood, it is infinite.
A garland made of *indrākṣa* seeds always bestows great accomplishment;
by means of garlands of red sandalwood, one certainly attains the state of Śiva. (18)
With a knot of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* beads, it shall yield infinite fruit;
with *guñjā* seeds, all perfections (*siddhi*) shall be attained; and with wood from the *vilva* tree, it bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). (19)
A rosary fashioned from conch shells bestows all prosperity;
such a rosary has been described in general terms, and now it is described in detail.
Regarding the description of the garland for a specific deity:
one should fashion the garland of the maiden with red sandalwood,
using ivory as the *kālikā* (central bead) and a king’s tooth as the *meru* (central peak).
A rosary of great conch shells is prescribed for the worship of Ugratārā;
likewise, it should be known that a rosary of *unmukhī* seeds bestows liberation. (22)
For Vaiṣṇavas, a rosary is considered to be made of lotus seeds or Tulasī;
for Gaṇeśa, it is made of elephant tusks, while for Śiva, it is said to be made of Rudrākṣa beads.
In the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāraka*), [the beads may be made] even from the teeth of donkeys or boars.
Regarding the number of seeds in a rosary (*mālā*), it should consist of one hundred and eight or fifty-four. (24)
A rosary composed of thirty-six beads is classified as superior, inferior, or middling; alternatively, a rosary with a number of beads equal to that of the Mātṛkās should be diligently prepared. (25)
In the case of general recitation, it should be performed twenty-seven times;
one seeking liberation should recite twenty-five times, and one seeking wealth should recite thirty times. (26)
For one seeking nourishment, twenty-seven [recitations] are prescribed; for malevolent rites, fifteen;
and for all accomplishments, one hundred and eight—thus have the wise declared.
All rites should be performed with fifty [beads]; there is no doubt in this matter.
The seed-beads should be well-rounded, beautiful, and strung like jujube seeds. (28)
Having given a sacrificial fee to the artisan and having taken the rosary, the best of practitioners should then perform the consecration according to the authority of the scriptures. (29)
Whatever man recites the mantra with unsteady garlands,
all that he shall find to be fruitless, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.
A thread made by a virtuous woman, whether of cotton or silk,
as well as a lotus-fiber thread or a hempen thread— (31).
One should string the rosary with a thread from a silkworm;
the thread, made of gold or other materials, should be tripled three times over.
White, red, and likewise black [are used] for pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), and malevolent rites (abhicāra);
through the red [color] one attains liberation, and with the white [colors], the accomplishment of yoga and so forth. 33.
With yellow [flowers], one's desire is fulfilled and fame is gained; with black [flowers], there is the occurrence of diseases and other evils.
For daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, white and red [flowers] are likewise auspicious and recommended.
One should likewise cast the seeds and the thread into the five products of the cow;
having washed them with the root mantra, one should then tie the thread.
With a mind focused on nothing else, one should personally have a garland woven by the teacher, the father-in-law, the son-in-law, or sons; it should never be made by anyone other than these.
A garland fashioned by a beloved woman is considered to bring swift success.
Taking each individual jewel, one should designate a *brahmagranthi* (Brahma-knot) for each. (p. 275) 37.
One should not perform [the rite] without a knot, for it is defiled by the touch of one who is unworthy;
this applies to the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Gaṇeśa, and Śrīkara [traditions] as well. (38)
Furthermore, upon touching the seed-syllable, the wise man should diligently perform the consecration;
for where there is no defect whatsoever, it remains eternally free from knots.
In the case of Kālikā and Tvaritā, however, there are six varieties beginning with Vajra;
for Totalā and Vanavāsinī, there are specifically those beginning with Vārāhī.
And for the goddess Caṇḍikā, it is prescribed that [the rosary] be without knots;
taking each individual bead, the practitioner, with a steady mind, [should proceed]. (41)
Then, while recollecting the Tāra-mantra in his heart, he should apply the Brahma-granthi;
he himself should mutter the mantra, while another should utter the Praṇava.
It should be made resembling a cow's tail or in the form of a serpent; then, having fashioned a single *meru* at the end of the garland, the best of practitioners [should proceed]. (43)
One should worship the Guru while meditating on him, and the Nyāsa-mantra on the right;
one should also [meditate upon] the Deity on the left, and through such meditation, one shall attain perfection. || 44 ||
One should know that Meru is the Guru, while the seed-mantra of the mantra is on the right.
Having thus prepared the rosary, one should perform its consecration. (45)
The analysis of the sequence for consecrating the rosary:
one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, both in direct and reverse order, interspersed [with the beads].
Having consecrated the rosary with the Śiva-mantra, one should cast it into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Peaceful, mounted upon the sound of Śakra, and adorned with Nāda and Bindu—this Śiva-mantra has been declared for the benefit of practitioners. (47)
One should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), reciting the root mantra;
[these consist of] ghee, milk, water, along with sugar and honey. (48)
This is known as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), each [of the first four] being one pala;
half a pala of cow dung and milk, and likewise one prastha of curd, all in equal measure.
Cow’s urine should be one *prastha* in measure, and clarified butter should be half of that;
having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should prepare the *pañcagavya*.
Immediately thereafter, one should bathe it with non-cold water;
one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and purify it with the Sadyojāta mantra.
The garland-removal mantra:
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta!
In existence, in non-existence, and in beginningless existence, take refuge in me; salutations to the one who arises from existence! || 52 ||
One should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, using the left hand as the presiding deity.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the Eldest; salutation to the Most Excellent; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Time;
salutation to the Maker of Time; salutation to Strength; salutation to the Maker of Strength; salutation to the Destroyer of Strength.
Salutations again and again to the subduer of all beings; salutations to the Transmental (Unmanā). || 54 ||
The wise one should fumigate it with excellent incense while reciting the Aghora mantra:

"Oṃ, to those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the terrible, to all of them everywhere, to all those who possess the form of Rudra, let there be salutation to you. (55)
One should smear it with fragrant sandalwood, saffron, and human [semen]. || 56 ||
Oṃ, may we know that Puruṣa; may we meditate upon Mahādeva;
may Rudra impel us toward that. || 57 ||
Then the steadfast one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times for each [deity], and thereafter,
he should likewise recite the Īśāna-mantra one hundred times over Mount Meru.
Oṃ. Īśāna, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the sovereign of Brahman, the supreme lord of Brahman—may Śiva be auspicious to me; Sadāśiva! || 59 ||
Then, following the ritual for the consecration of the life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the rosary, the wise practitioner should install the rosary upon a pedestal made of gold or other materials,
or he may place it upon lotus-shaped leaves of the *aśvattha* tree. (60)
Or, having established [the deity] upon a pedestal, one should worship one's own chosen deity,
together with its limbs and enclosures, using extensive ritual offerings.

Then, by means of the sequential application of each individual seed-syllable, the supreme practitioner should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) one hundred and eight times.
The mantra for the consecration of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the rosary is as follows:

[the syllable] *au* bearing the form of the nasal bindu, mounted upon the power of life-force (*prāṇaśakti*), followed by the *praṇava* (OM) and then "to the Lord of the Rosary" (*akṣamālādhipataye*). (63)
Having recited the root mantra ending with the heart-mantra, one should worship the rosary in due order;
then, one should perform a fire-offering (homa) according to one's ability with sesame seeds mixed with ghee.
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homakarma), one should perform double the recitation (japa).
Then [one should utter]: "Tāra" (Oṃ), "to the Lord of the Rosary," and then "Susiddha," and so forth.
p.
279) Furthermore, [recite] "O you who accomplish the two goals that fulfill the purpose of all mantras, grant success, svāhā! while reciting this over the rosary with the mantra. 66.
There, one should mutter the root mantra one thousand and eight times, or even one hundred and eight times; having muttered it, one should then offer the rosary.
Then he [the preceptor] should have the disciple recite it eight thousand times, or even one hundred and eight times; having performed the recitation, he should conceal the rosary.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his ability,
the practitioner should perform the consecration of the rosary himself in the absence of the guru.
The wise one should avoid showing the rosary; he may reveal himself to the Guru, but never the mantra.
He should not show his rosary or his ritual gestures even to the Guru.
Since spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas carry it off from one who is exposed, one should therefore protect it with great effort. (71)
In the Japanese tradition, having worshipped the rosary, one should keep it concealed;
one who is impure should not touch the rosary, nor should one fashion it in an unclean state. (72)
If the rosary falls from the hand, it should not be used for recitation by the wise for three days;
an expiation must be performed, and one should recite the mantra one thousand times. (73)
(Alternatively,) if it falls from the hand or makes a sound, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
When the thread has worn out, having spun a new thread, one should recite it one hundred times again.
If the garland should break, the practitioner, having performed an even more extensive worship,
should then perform worship of the gurus and the artisans.
Having performed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) as before, one should again perform the recitation (japa).
All such garlands are thus consecrated for every deity. (76)
Now I shall further describe another supreme garland consisting of the *kula*, namely the description of the worship of the rosary (*akṣamālā*),
using substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, as well as the *svayambhū* flower. (77)
One should worship the rosary with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), as well as with camphor, agallochum (aguru), musk (kastūrī), and deer-musk (mṛgamada). || 78 ||
Having prepared the rosary, one should perform the consecration according to the prescribed rules.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the garland that is the most excellent of all. (79)
p.

281) For one by whom mantras are accomplished through mere consciousness at that very moment, due to the distinction between the mantra and the practitioner, whether in direct or reverse order. || 80 ||
One should form a rosary composed of syllables, in which a syllable is separated by a mantra and a mantra is separated by a syllable; this kindles all mantras. (81)
One should never transgress the final syllable, which is like Mount Meru;
this is the supreme secret and must not be disclosed to just anyone.

By means of a garland of letters fashioned from the syllables of the Mātṛkā, joined with the Bindu and arranged both in direct and reverse order, together with the Kṣa and Meruka syllables and the eight groups of consonants.
Each mantra consisting of a pair of syllables, when recited, bestows swift accomplishment.
Having uttered the syllable together with the bindu (anusvāra), the wise practitioner should subsequently recite the mantra. (84)
Having visualized Mount Meru, one should perform the recitation and must not overstep it.
Now, in this context, I shall describe the consecration of the yantra. (85)
The procedure for the consecration of the mechanical image (*yantra*):
gold, silver, and copper are respectively the best, the middling, and the lowest [materials].
It is said that [the merit] is a hundred thousandfold when offered in copper, and it becomes ten millionfold when offered in silver.
In gold it yields infinite fruit, and likewise equally so in crystal;
[the weight may be] one tola, two tolas, three tolas, or five tolas. (87)
Having prepared a dose of one *tola*, four *tolas*, seven *tolas*, or a *pala*—
or whatever is pleasing to the practitioner— the excellent adept should place it upon the ritual seat.
Having caused a beautiful and very charming yantra to be drawn according to the prescribed rite, with excellent lines and a fine face, using the previously mentioned metallic substances; || 89 ||
Alternatively, having fashioned an image in the form of one's own deity,
one should then perform its consecration according to the authority of the scriptures.
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantras should form a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and then perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and so forth;
thereafter, he should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), purified with the Śiva-mantra.
There, the mantra-practitioner should cast the yantra, thoroughly permeated with the syllable Om (praṇava). Having extracted that wheel from there, he should place it upon a golden plate.
Having bathed [the deity] well with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water,
one should lift the water away with a cloth and place [the deity] upon a golden throne.
Having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), and then touching the diagram with kuśa grass, [one should recite]:
"We know the Praṇava for the King of Diagrams," and immediately thereafter— (94)
"Let us meditate upon the Great Machine; may that Machine inspire us.
Having thus recited the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times, he should then proceed. (95)
Having invoked the Goddess, one should worship her, preceded by the ritual placement of life (jīvanyāsa), with the sixteen types of offerings and various kinds of elixirs (rasāyana). || 96 ||
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess according to the procedure prescribed for her own ritual manual, with various kinds of fruits, substances, and an abundance of various unguents; 97.
Then, for the sake of attaining one's desired goal, one should perform a thousand recitations;
thereafter, having offered the bali-oblation, one should prostrate before the supreme maṇḍala.
The wise one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter;
thereafter, he should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor as well as to the artisan.
The consecration of a deity is the very act of establishing the deity; a wise person should perform it in this manner.
One should prescribe the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and so forth as taught in its own ritual manual (*kalpa*), and therein instruct upon the *gāyatrī*.
(284) I have already described the specific procedures for the consecration of a deity;
now I shall explain the supreme preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for mantras. 101.
The description of *puraścaraṇa*:
even one who is devoid of fortune or even a fool becomes immortal through its realization;
he shall accomplish all perfections and become a manifest Lord of Siddhas. (102)

At the outset, one should perform the preliminary service according to the rules and in accordance with the prescribed ritual; thereafter, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected becomes fit for its application, and not otherwise.
For a mantra that is perfected through *puraścaraṇa* is indeed the bestower of fruit;
what need is there for fire-offerings, what need for recitations, and what need for the elaborate ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*)? (104)
If there is no preliminary service for all mantras intended for subjugation, one is as incapable of performing any rites as a living being deprived of life. || 105 ||
Even a mantra that lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is proclaimed as such;
for the preliminary service of mantras is said to be their primary life-force.

Therefore, having first performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), the most excellent practitioner should then carry out the ritual application (prayoga) for the sake of attaining accomplishment (siddhi). || 107 ||

285) Explanation of the difference in results based on the difference in location: A place measuring one *krośa* is prescribed for a village, while by one's own choice it is considered appropriate for rivers and the like.
Beyond the city, at a distance of one *krośa*, or even two *krośas*.
One may traverse as much ground as is necessary for the purpose of procuring food and other such activities.
Recitation performed at home is said to be equal [in merit], while that performed by a river is recorded as being a hundredfold more effective.
In a sacred forest or a grove, it is said to be a thousandfold;
on a mountain, the merit is ten thousandfold; and in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī, it is a hundred thousandfold.
They say that ten million [times the merit] is obtained in a temple, and infinite [merit] is gained in the presence of Śiva;
or wherever it may be in any place, at a linga facing west.
Whether at Svayambhū, at Bāṇaliṅga, or at any other [liṅga] in its vicinity;
or at Prayāga, at the celestial river (Gaṅgā), or at Vārāṇasī or Varāhaka. || 112 ||
Whether on a mountain peak, in a cremation ground, in the depths of a forest, at a solitary linga, in an empty house, at a crossroads, or in the presence of Śiva. || 113 ||
One should perform the purascarana rite at these locations: on a solitary tree, on a mountain, at the foot of a banyan tree, or in a temple of Śiva, especially during the dead of night.
For the purpose of warding off obstacles, the ritual procedure for worship is as follows:
indeed, pieces of wood from a milk-exuding tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) should be consecrated ten times with the weapon-mantra.
The hero should then establish the ritual stakes (kīlakas) according to the sequence starting from the east.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa; likewise Vāyu, Kubera, Īśāna, and thereafter Brahmā and Ananta. (116)
Having worshipped each in their respective directions, one should afterwards present the bali offering;
the space between Īśāna and Śakra should always be known as "above" by the wise. (117)
It is described as being between Varuṇa and Asura and below;
when the field is thus pinned, the practitioner of mantra is not overcome by obstacles. (118)
There, the lord of heroes should duly worship Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇeśa,
preceded by the ritual at the location of the lamp according to the prescribed rule.
Then, on the previous day, the practitioner, having become pure and being of steady mind, should construct there a maṇḍala consisting of four gates. (120)
Having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should recite the Gāyatrī a thousand times;
this is first [prescribed] for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sins. (121)
One should properly satisfy the Brahmins with food, respectful treatment, and so forth, and having fully honored one's own guru with many garments and ornaments. (122)
One should begin the recitation afterwards, preceded by obtaining permission for it;
at the time of commencement, one must certainly worship the wife of another.
Having himself restrained his mind, he should honor the initiated woman with garments, flowers, and other offerings,
as well as milk-rice and flour-cakes endowed with various flavors. (124)
Milk, curd, as well as buttermilk, fresh butter with sugar, sugarcane products, sweetmeats, and various kinds of elixirs (rasāyana). || 125 ||
Various kinds of fruits, as well as various fragrant ointments—sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise saffron. || 126 ||
A seat, sandals, clothing, as well as ornaments and the like, incense, a lamp, silk, and likewise a supreme garland of flowers. (127)
The hero should bring together the five tattvas and the eight kulas in the empty house;
then, at the entrance, he should worship the deities of the gateway.
The wise one, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and Yoginī at the four gates in order starting from the east, [should proceed]. (129)
Thereafter, the practitioner should offer an oblation (bali) to them;
having caused the spirits to depart, he should then attend to the location of the lamp.
Adorned with various ornaments and seated upon the prepared throne,
he should perform the rites prescribed for his own ritual manual and then sprinkle [the vessel] immediately thereafter.
Then, with the water for the *arghya* offering, [he should purify] the ritual materials and himself;
thereafter, [he should visualize himself] adorned with various ornaments and purified by the *arghya* water. (132)
Having performed the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should lead the eight Śaktis to bliss;
this is the practice of the reverse contemplation (vilomāmarśa) through the differentiation of the forms of the eight maidens.
A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā who is an ornament to her family; a Veśyā, the daughter of a barber, a Rajakī, and likewise a Yoginī. || 134 ||
They are wise, praised among all classes, and bestowers of all perfections;
they have been given names according to the eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmāṇī. (135)

Having first offered a seat and repeatedly welcomed him, one should then offer water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (pānīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water again. || 136 ||
One should bathe [the image] with water scented with perfumes and flowers, and perform the grooming of the hair;
then, having fumigated the hair, one should offer a silken garment. || 137 ||
Then, having spread a pair of sandals upon a seat in another place and having placed her there seated, adorned with various ornaments; 138.
Having adorned [the deity] with ointments, one should offer perfumes and garlands;
then, one should meditate upon each respective power according to the prescribed sequence. || 139 ||
Meditation on the Eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmāṇī:
[One should meditate on her] mounted upon a swan, golden-hued, four-faced, and three-eyed.
In his lotus-like hands, he holds the *brahmakūrca*, a lotus, a staff, and a rosary.
The wise man should meditate upon Brahmāṇī, who possesses a beautiful form, is adorned with a crown of matted locks, and is endowed with the ornaments of a woman. (141)
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, white in complexion, and endowed with three eyes;
she holds a skull, a hand-drum, an arrow, a trident, and an axe that bestows fearlessness.
Holding [attributes] with her lotus-like hands, adorned with the jewel on the moon-crested [Śiva], three-eyed, resembling saffron in hue, Kaumārī, whose vehicle is the peacock. || 143 ||

She holds a spear, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is beautifully adorned, belongs to Viṣṇu, is mounted upon Garuḍa, is dark-complexioned, and is intoxicated with the wine of honey.
Holding a bell, a conch, a skull-cup, and a discus in her lotus-like hands,
she is clad in yellow garments and adorned with pearls and jewels.
She who rides upon a boar, smoke-colored, with a face like that of a boar,
holding a shield and a club, as well as a boon-bestowing sword and another supreme weapon. (146)
She held a lotus in her hand, was adorned with beautiful ornaments,
possessed the luster of sapphire, belonged to Indra, and was seated upon Airāvata.
She bears a moon-like face and holds a vajra, a conch, a bow, and arrows;
adorned with various ornaments, she is ever devoted to her worshippers. (148)
And [he saw] Cāmuṇḍā with a terrifying face, adorned with a garland of severed heads, laughing loudly, seated upon a corpse, and resplendent with jewels and pearls. || 149 ||
One should meditate upon her, who is fond of her devotees, possessing the luster of a dark blue cloud, and holding a skull, a shield, a trident, and a sword in her lotus-like hands.

One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī seated upon a lion-throne, radiant with a golden-yellow luster, adorned with jewels, and holding a citron fruit, the gesture of fearlessness, a garland, and a lotus.
Having meditated thus, the hero, by means of the mudrās beginning with Āvāhanī, should sequentially invoke each respective Śakti and worship them upon their heads. || 152 ||
Furthermore, having offered water for the feet and other offerings, the practitioner, with a steady mind,
[should place the vessel] then in a spot made of gold or other materials in the center of the circle of food. (153)
One should offer the chewed, the sucked, the licked, the drunk, the eaten, and the consumed;
if they are uninitiated, one should then offer the *māyā* right there.
Then, a person should recite the hymn beginning with the eight Śaktis, starting with Brahmāṇī, into their left ears:
"O Mother Goddess, obeisance to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman."
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra. || 155 ||
O Maheśī, O boon-granting Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 156 ||
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all obstacles, you who delight in the play of Kumāra!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra. || 157 ||
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O carrier of the son of Vinatā!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, you who lifted up the earth with your tusk!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 159 ||
O Goddess who assumes the form of Śakra, worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the accomplishment of the mantra. (160)
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads and smeared with blood, O destroyer of fear!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra.
O Mahālakṣmī, O you of great energy, O destroyer of agitation and torment!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra. || 162 ||
O Goddess, who consists of measure and the measurer, yet who is beyond both measure and measurer;
O Goddess, who are one yet manifold, whose form is the universe—salutations be to you! 163.
Whoever, being self-controlled, recites this hymn at the commencement of undertakings while looking upon wise men, for him no obstacle shall arise. (164)
O son, these have been described to you as the door-deities of one of noble lineage;
if they are not worshipped at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [the rite is flawed]. (165)
All the fruit of his worship is seized by yakṣas and rākṣasas;
however, if she is overcome with shame, he should feed her outside of that house.
Having stood, one should recite the hymn of praise until satisfaction arises; then, having sipped water (ācamana), one should offer mouth-fresheners such as betel leaf and the like. 167.
Then one should again offer a garland and fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with mud;
one should apply it individually at each end of the long [line] joined with the *bindu*. (168)
Then the hero should recite their respective names in the dative case, followed by the heart-mantra; these are the mantras that have been taught for them. (169)
Having recited [the mantra] in sequence according to one's capacity and then offered it, one should recite a hymn of praise;
then, having dismissed [the deity], paid homage, and requested a boon, one should become happy. || 170 ||
If no others come—neither one's own daughter, nor one's younger sister, nor an elder sister, nor a maternal aunt, nor one's mother, nor her co-wife—(then one may marry). 171.
Even if she is inferior in age or by birth, the supreme art (the consort) is to be honored with the essence of one's lineage by all who have abandoned their own egoism. 172.
In the absence of all [these], any one of them should be worshipped with effort—whether she be consecrated or unconsecrated, a mother, or even a barren woman. || 173 ||
p.
294) In the absence of the former, the latter is to be worshipped, since women possess a portion of the Goddess.
If there is but one person who knows the Kula scriptures, he is certainly worthy of worship therein. (174)
Everywhere indeed the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, are to be worshipped;
yet, if even a single young woman there is worshipped and looked upon [with devotion], [that act alone suffices]. 175.

All the supreme goddesses are indeed worshipped by the best of practitioners—at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, especially upon the completion of a hundred thousand recitations. || 176 ||
If one does not honor one's beloved wife, then one is besmeared by obstacles;
there is no fruit for what was previously earned—what need is there to speak of the next life? (177)
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, with every effort one should [perform this] which pacifies the anger and torment of the goddesses and destroys obstacles. (178)
In every way, one should worship the woman of the family with great effort;
having completed the worship of the Śakti, one should then proceed with the primary ritual. 179.
Then, one should worship the Goddess according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual;
thereafter, starting from early morning, one should perform recitation (japa) until midday. (180)
Neither deficient nor excessive, and not omitting even a single day, the practitioner should perform it once, twice, or thrice a day. (181)
One should perform ablutions with pure water and eat sacrificial food (haviṣya);
staying constantly in a single village, one should go and salute the guru.

One should always perform the salutation of the deities in this manner toward the directions other than [the one facing], whether rising in the morning for worship or again at the time of bathing. (183)
Whether refined or unrefined, or likewise born of low caste, she is to be honored by all castes when performing the worship of the family in noble lineages. (184)
One should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music, watching dancing, as well as oil massage, the application of perfumes and unguents, and the wearing of flowers. (185)
One should never touch women, Śūdras, or twice-born men who have not bathed;
one should abandon bathing with hot water and eating food that has not been offered. 186.
One should not engage in various types of wandering, nor should one roam here and there;
one must not commit violence against living beings, and especially not violence against animals. (187)
Except for the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna), one should avoid all violence toward the Goddess;
likewise, one should strictly avoid the invocation of other mantras and all forms of censure. || 188 ||

One should never recite [the mantra] while wearing a turban, a bodice, or being naked; nor with hair disheveled or uncovered, nor with hands lacking the purificatory thread (apavitrahasta), nor while impure, nor while talking idly. (189)
One should never recite [the mantra] while having one's hands uncovered, or even while having one's head covered; nor when the mind is distracted by anxiety, or when one is angry. (190)
Whether lying in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), walking, or even standing still,
one should not recite [the mantra] on a street, in an inauspicious place, or in a dwelling of darkness.
Upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes,
or upon sneezing, passing wind, or yawning, one should cease the recitation of prayers.
Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having properly performed the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma-ṣaḍaṅga),
one should recite the remainder [of the mantra], or otherwise gaze upon the sun.
One should never converse with a woman, a Śūdra, an animal, or likewise one who has fallen from the path of practice; one should observe the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). || 194 ||
And during the time of recitation, he should always carefully avoid his wife;
he should always sleep on a pure bed, remaining clean and wearing pure garments. 195.
Every day he should wash his bed and sleep alone without fear;
the wise man should not look upon any other scripture except the Vedas and Āgamas. (196)
Eating only at night, pure and consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should recite the vidyā during the day;
by day, the hero should always remain entirely celibate. 197.
The wise one should pass the day incessantly engaged in meditation upon the deity;
at night, however, he should worship the Goddess according to the sequence of the Kula tradition.

Having worshipped with the five tattvas, one should perform the recitation according to one's capacity; however, during the period of *puraścaraṇa*, if a vision of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) should occur, [one should continue]. (199)
At that time, the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā) there is not omitted even mentally. In this context, the worship of the seat is described according to the Tantric injunctions. (200)
(298) The names of the goddesses to be worshipped in the four seats (pīṭha)— in Devīkūṭa, O highly fortunate one, and likewise in Uḍḍīyāna— [are as follows]:
Yoganidrā is at Kāmarūpa, and Mahiṣāsuramardinī is there as well. || 201 ||
Kātyāyanī is in Kāmabhūmi; she is Kāmākhyā, the bestower of desires;
she is Pūrṇeśī in Jālandhara; and she is Caṇḍikā on Mount Pūrṇa.
In Kāmarūpa, however, in the region of Vehāra, Dikkaravāsinī is to be worshipped;
or else, if by good fortune one has the sight of Kāmarūpa itself. (203)
Then, the worship of the goddesses Bhaga and the others is performed there according to the procedure to be described,
having ascertained their respective names.
Having meditated again upon the Lord of the Family, the hero, with his own mind fixed on the Imperishable (Acyuta),
should complete the worship preceded by that recollection.

At the time of worship, one's own wife, even if born of a low caste, should be worshipped with effort according to the prescribed rite; however, one should avoid the two-fold [impurity] in that regard. || 206 ||
Regarding the concealment of the mantra according to family custom:
just as Viṣṇu’s city is to be kept secret, or as Śambhu the Lord, or even the lotus-born Brahmā, or those twice-born ones headed by Vyāsa. || 207 ||
Indra and the other guardians of the world, all the gandharvas and kinnaras, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others—the secret ones, the cāraṇas, and the bards—(p. 299). || 208 ||
Just as that which arises from the scriptures was spoken by them and kept secret and protected,
so too must the Kula practice, which is very difficult to obtain, be guarded by a follower of Śiva.
The difference in the number of recitations according to the different ages:
"By this procedure, the practitioner of mantra should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
For those [mantras] for which the number of recitations and burnt offerings has not been stated by the wise," (210)
Eight thousand is the number prescribed for their recitation and fire-offerings;
and in whatever mantra a specific number is ordained for the recitation, that same number applies.
In all those cases, the number of mantras increases according to the sequence of the ages:
whatever number is stated for the Kṛta age in the Kalpa-texts, it becomes double in the Tretā age. (212)
In the Dvāpara age, it is said to be threefold, and in the Kali age, the count is fourfold;
for neither the divine nor the heroic [paths] requires the exertion of serving the ages.
In this regard, there is an increase in the number of sacrificial animals according to the sequence of the ages;
their worship indeed takes place at the three times of day, but never at night.
The procedure according to the path of Tantra has been taught in all the scriptures as being fourfold for Tārā, except when using a rosary of conch-shell beads. (215)
Having done thus, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should mutter [the mantra] four hundred thousand times;
or, taking a necklace of human bones, one should mutter it one hundred thousand times.
For those who lack meditative cultivation, who are petty and of base minds, the recitation of four times [the required number] is prescribed for success; otherwise, it will not come to pass.

The ritual procedure for Unmukhī Kālikā is a perfected lore (*siddhavidyā*) such that there is no need for the exertion of service through the [successive] ages; especially in the Kali age, Tārā, Kālī, and likewise Unmukhī [are effective]. (218)
For these [goddesses], the prescribed rule for serving the pair (yuga) never exists;
now, the specific distinction regarding Unmukhī and Kālikā is being told.
During the day, one should recite the mantra according to one's own count while observing celibacy;
at night, however, [the count is increased] by means of meat, wine, fish, ritual gestures (mudrās), and those arising from sexual union. || 220 ||
Having thus worshipped the Great Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
he should then, while naked himself, engage in dalliance with a naked woman, even if it involves the hardship of passion.
The practitioner should diligently recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi.
For all those of twice-born status, however, the procedure here is said to be twofold. (222)
Likewise, for Śūdras, it is declared that [the mantra] entered during the night yields great fruit.
Then, having completed the number of recitations prescribed for their respective rites,
they should then perform a fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter in the fire, amounting to one-tenth of that [number].
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 12 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter: The Ritual of Homa.
Now I shall describe the ritual of homa according to the tantras.
First, one who is expert in the knowledge of architecture should examine the ground.
One should carefully clear away splinters and other debris from the site for the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or otherwise one should dig a man-deep hole,
measuring either nine cubits or seven cubits.
Or it may be five cubits in measure, provided with four corners,
free from cracks, possessing four gates, and adorned with divine vision.
The practitioner, for the sake of attaining success, should first prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is encircled by a divine garland and wound around with thread.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are of various forms: square, triangular, semi-circular, equilateral, circular, hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal; these are their names.
(1) Regarding the measurement of the square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*):
one should mark out an area measuring one cubit (*hasta*) as before.
This sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square on all sides; such a shape brings auspiciousness.
Those who know the tantras understand a cubit (hasta) to be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) long,
measured by the middle joint of the right hand of the artisan.
The measurement finger (mānāṅgula) is declared by the length of the middle finger;
it is said that the mānāṅgula is fashioned from eight barley grains.
(2) The wise one should divide the square sacrificial field into five parts;
he should place one part in front, measuring half of a half of the corner.
The knower of mantras should rotate another pair of threads according to that same measurement; then he should lay them down so that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a womb (yoni).
(3) A wise person should divide a square sacrificial area intended for a half-moon-shaped pit (*ardhacandrakuṇḍa*) into ten parts.
The knower of mantras should discard each successive portion, both below and above.
One should drop the bowstring at the front and then rotate it according to that measurement;
this beautiful pit will take the form of a half-moon. || 12 ||
(4) Having divided the field into four parts, one should place one part on each of the two sides; then, using that same measurement, one should mark [the center] in front again. 13.
The wise one should draw two lines; this is declared to be a triangular pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In a field divided into eighteen parts, the wise one should place one part outside for a circular pit.
By that measurement, one should rotate [the cord] to form the unsurpassed circular *kuṇḍa*.
One should divide the area of the hexagonal *kuṇḍa* into eight parts on both sides of the central line. (6) 15.
The best knower of the tantras should place a single share by this measurement from the center and should fashion four fish-marks on both sides.
Then one should provide six sūtras; the hexagonal pit is the most excellent.
(p. 305) [7] The lotus pit.
The field, having been made square, should be divided into eighteen parts.
Having set aside one part outside, one should rotate it to form a circle;
one should then fashion three circles for the pericarp and the other parts on the exterior.
This lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa) has been described as enchanting to the eye.
(8) As for the eight-cornered pit (aṣṭāsrakuṇḍa), one should divide the previously mentioned field into twenty-four parts. || 19 ||
Having set aside one part on the outside, one should fashion a square;
[this is done] by measuring half of half the corner of the inner square.
One should mark the corners of the outer square and,
according to the rule, drop eight lines toward each direction.
This pit is indeed described by those learned in the tantras as being octagonal;
the measurement of its excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit itself.
The characteristics and measurements of the girdles (mekhalā), as well as the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and the girdles themselves, are as follows:
leaving a space of two finger-breadths from the edge of the pit and so forth, the auspicious girdles should be constructed. (23)

The three girdles of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be known, in order, as being one, two, and one-and-a-half finger-breadths in height and width, respectively, when measured by the span of a closed fist. || 24 ||
For a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one aratni, those [fingers] consist of two or three aṅgulas;
the measure of an aratni should be known by the wise as eighteen aṅgulas.
Half a cubit is proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths;
in a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit, the characteristic of the rim consists of four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
The inner edge of the girdles (mekhalās) should be one finger-breadth all around from the rim;
a wise man should increase that proportionally for a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit.
In a two-cubit pit, those [lines] should be known as eight, four, and three finger-breadths;
in pits of four cubits, they are eight, six, and four finger-breadths.
In a pit measuring ten, eight, or six cubits, they should be ten, eight, or six [cubits] respectively;
in a pit measuring eight cubits, they should be twelve, eight, and eight finger-breadths.
In a sacrificial pit measuring ten cubits, the wise should know that the girdles are to be ten, twelve, and ten fingers in width and height respectively on all sides.
p.
307) Regarding the characteristic of the womb:
first, the womb of these [vessels] is above, like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.
The yoni of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one fist, one aratni,
and one hasta is said to possess a length, width, and height of six, four, and two aṅgulas respectively.
The characteristic and measurement of the stalk: from the west side of the womb, the stalk has a width of four finger-breadths;
its base and tip are desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth in measure respectively.
The stalk between the two girdles is for the purpose of establishing the surrounding rim;
starting from the base, the stalk should have a perforation in its center at the level of the womb.
The best knower of the tantras should not place the yoni in the corners of the fire-pits (kuṇḍa);
the yoni is prescribed for pits measuring one fist, one cubit, or one hand.
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the length of the yoni by one finger-breadth for each successive pit;
likewise, one should also increase the tip of the yoni by a sequence of two barley-corns at each step.
One should fashion the fire-pits with a navel measuring one cubit, and within that, the interior navel should be fashioned like a lotus.
Alternatively, its measurement is declared to be in accordance with each respective fire-pit (kuṇḍa). || 36 ||
In the case of sacrificial pits measuring one muṣṭi, one aratni, or one hasta, the navel should be four or three finger-breadths in height and width;
in other pits, one should increase these dimensions accordingly.
The one of noble intellect should mark the navel at a distance of two *yava*s from the [central] line;
one should avoid placing the *yoni* in the *kuṇḍa* of the *yoni*, and the *nābhi* in the *kuṇḍa* of the lotus.
Having divided the navel-region into three parts, one should fashion the pericarp in the middle;
with two outer portions, one should arrange eight petals.
A pit measuring only a fist is prescribed for fifty oblations;
for one hundred oblations, it should be the measure of an aratni, and for a thousand oblations, the measure of a hasta.
One should fashion a hand-sized sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the measurement of the diagonal cord;
likewise, it should be made by the practitioner even for those measuring four cubits and more.
For ten thousand [steps], two cubits are prescribed; for a hundred thousand, four cubits are declared;
for ten million, six cubits; and for a crore, eight cubits is traditionally taught.
Alternatively,
a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit is prescribed for a single hundred thousand [recitations].
One should increase it by hand up to ten lakhs.
A sacrificial pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a *koṭi-homa*.
Regarding the description of the fruits of the sacrificial pits: the square pit is declared to grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 44 ||
The Yoni-shaped pit bestows sons; the half-moon shape bestows auspiciousness;
the triangular shape causes the destruction of enemies; and the circular shape is for rites of pacification (śāntika).
For the rites of cutting (cheda) and killing (māraṇa), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is hexagonal and resembles a lotus;
for bestowing rain and pacifying disease, the pit is said to be octagonal.
Alternatively, the womb-shaped pit (*yonikuṇḍa*) bestows eloquence; the lotus-shaped one brings about attraction;
the circular one bestows prosperity; and the half-moon shape removes fear. (47)
Indeed, a circular triangular pit (kuṇḍa) bestows the siddhi of the Khecarī;
a square one bestows peace, prosperity, nourishment, and supernatural powers. || 48 ||
The hexagon is the cause of all prosperity, the increaser of wealth and good fortune; it is the source of all success and the bestower of human prowess.
Likewise, the eight-sided [mandala] should be known as bestowing the desired fruit; indeed, all qualities and all undertakings reside in the four-sided one. (50)
For Brahmins it should be square; for kings, it is desired to be circular;
for Vaiśyas, it has the appearance of a half-moon; and for Śūdras, it is said to be triangular.
One should know that the square is the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for all [rites], according to the consensus of some Tantrikas; it is the supreme body of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The difference in results arises from the difference in the shape of the pit (kuṇḍa).
The head is said to be in the east; the two arms are in the south and north; the belly is called the pit; and the feet are in the west. 53.

One should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or by making one that is one cubit in size and very beautiful with sand. 54.

Having constructed one of these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), which is square on all sides and measures one finger-breadth in height, one should then prepare the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk and sruva).

The wise one should fashion the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) for the sacrifice according to the method to be described hereafter, using wood from any one of the following: the *śrīphala*, the *śiṃśapā*, or a milky-sap tree (*kṣīraśākhin*). (56)
Having taken [the measurement], one should divide it by thirty-six to the extent of a cubit;
with twenty parts there shall be the staff (daṇḍa), and with those eight parts there shall be the altar (vedī).
The neck is measured by one part, and the face is measured by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the pedestal (vedī). || 58 ||
The opening at the mouth should be made equal in width to the throat,
measuring one finger-breadth of the little finger, to allow for the passage of clarified butter.
Having determined the proportions for the arrangement, it should be constructed in the middle of the altar; the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made with one part,
and outside of that, one should fashion a moat (avaṭa) all around with one part.
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and half a part [in depth];
one part all around should be fashioned as petals.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be around the mouth and the altar (vedī), measuring half a part on all sides;
the drum (gaṇḍī) at the base and tip of the staff (daṇḍa) should measure three and four finger-breadths respectively.
The pair of *gaṇḍīs* (bosses) shall consist of two parts; this is declared to be the circumference of the staff.
The back portion of the altar (*vedi*) should be shaped like a tortoise and consist of six parts. (63)
One should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a boar;
this is declared to be the characteristic of the back of the mouth of the *sruk* ladle.
One may fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
its handle is declared to be measured by twenty-two parts.
Its circumference is four parts, and its head, which holds the clarified butter, is one *karṣa*.
One should bury it in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint with two parts [of its length] visible.
At the base and tip of the staff, there should be a *gaṇḍī* adorned with a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*).
Having left six finger-breadths from the base, and likewise twelve from the tip, [the ornament should be placed].
The mantra-practitioner should hold the *sruva* ladle and must not show its base;
thus has the rule for the *sruva* been declared according to the prescriptions of the tantra. (67)
The best of practitioners should perform eighteen consecrations (saṃskāra) for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or rather, the ritual preparations;
for eighteen are the consecrations of sacrificial pits prescribed by the Tantras. (68)
Having performed the inspection with the root mantra, one should then perform the sprinkling with the weapon mantra;
with that same [mantra], the striking with *darbha* grass is prescribed, and the sprinkling with the armor mantra is likewise considered necessary. (69)
The digging and lifting [of earth] are performed with the Astra-mantra; filling is done with the Hana-mantra;
leveling is performed with the Astra-mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be done with the Varma-mantra.
The pounding is performed with the *hetimantra*, while the cleansing is done with the *kavaca* mantra;
immediately thereafter follows the anointing and the fashioning of the artistic form.
Thereafter, one should perform the tripling of the thread, as well as worship with the Heart mantra;
then, one should perform the "vajrification" with the Śara mantra, using auspicious Kuśa grass and the Heart mantra.

One should construct a four-way crossroads with a protective covering and perform the cutting of the sacrificial posts; one should consecrate the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) during the sacrifice with these aforementioned purificatory rites.
Now, the description of another method of consecration:
Alternatively, one should consecrate those [lines] with the four [mantras], beginning with Vīkṣaṇa.
One should draw three lines each—eastward, northward, and westward—with the Hṛdaya-mantra. (74)
The gods Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara are traditionally assigned to the eastward-pointing lines;
Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu are assigned to the northward-pointing lines. (75)
Then, one should draw within the sacrificial pit a six-cornered yoni, an eight-petalled mandala, a circle,
and a square enclosure.
Having performed the sprinkling with the syllable *Tāra* (Om), one should worship the deities of the seat (*pīṭha*),
and then Kālavahni and Rudra within the mandala.

Then the wise one, having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the tortoise, the earth, the island of jewels (ratnadvīpaka), and the jeweled mansion, should thereafter worship the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
In the middle of the golden altar, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, one should place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in their proper order. (79)
One should worship these [deities] starting from the east, then in the center, then again in the center,
and thereafter worship the bulb of supreme bliss (paramānandakanda) and, beyond that, the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla).
Then [he should meditate on] the lotus of the meaning of all reality, with the *prakṛti*s as its petals,
the *vikāra*s as its filaments, and the *mātṛkā*s as its pericarp.
The orb of the sun, the orb of the moon, and the orb of fire;
as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas, and the self among the inner selves. (82)

Having worshipped the Supreme Self, and thereafter the Self consisting of knowledge, one should [worship] those [deities] whose seeds are the initial letters of their names and so forth, ending in the dative case and accompanied by the word "namaḥ. (83)
One should worship these [deities] beginning with the Praṇava in the circular [mandala], as well as Bhuvaneśvarī;
one should worship Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśa, whose nature is Yoga. (84)
Having said "Salutation to the Pīṭha," one should worship in the pericarp.
Regarding the meditation on Vāgīśvarī:
[one should meditate on] Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus. (85)
One should worship her, joined with Vāgīśvara, with ritual offerings;
having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should likewise utter Vāgīśvarī joined with the syllable *ṅe*. (86)
This great mantra of Vāgīśvarī is proclaimed to end with "namaḥ";
then, one should bring forth the fire by means of the mantra of the Lord of Yogins.
Having placed [the substance] produced from sun-crystals and the like, or that which comes from the house of a Vedic scholar,
into a copper vessel and wrapped it in a packet, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters.

In the south-western direction, the practitioner should purify that [image] according to the rule by means of the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) and the weapon-mantra (PHAṬ), using the four rites beginning with inspection (VĪKṢAṆA). || 89 ||
Then, while recollecting the unification of the earthly element with the fires of *audarya* (digestive heat) and *vaideha* (fire),
one should join the consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire within the sacrificial fire.

The practitioner, having consecrated it with the *tāra* mantra, rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, protected it subsequently with the *astra* mantra, and veiled it with the *kavaca* mantra. (91)
Having circumambulated it three times while it is being honored, the preceptor then performs a circumambulation around the sacrificial pit, preceded by the recitation of the *tāra-mantra*.
With his knees touching the ground, he should cast the fire facing himself into the womb of the Goddess, perceiving it as the seed of Śiva.
Afterwards, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and so forth to the God and the Goddess;
then, having shown the Jvālinī mudrā, one should kindle [the fire] with this mantra.
Regarding the recitation of the fire-mantra:
having uttered "cit piṅgala hana daha paca" twice, this mantra is proclaimed as "sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā. (95)
I bow to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in every direction. 96.
The practitioner of mantra should duly attend upon the fire with this verse from Manu,
and should then place the tongues of the fire-eater within his own body.

In the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, [the letters] from *sa* to *ya*, joined with fire (*ra*), the moon (*i*), and the lord of speech (*a*), and accompanied by the bindu, are to be placed everywhere. (98)
The preceptors have declared seven mantras for the tongues of fire;
those tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinctions of qualities in ritual acts.
The tongues of fire are described according to the divisions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*:
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and another is considered to be Suprabhā.
And those [mantras] consisting of sattva, which exceed the Bahurūpa, are used in sacrificial rites. || 100 ||
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā; after Lohitā come Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā. || 101 ||
The tongues of fire prescribed for rites performed for specific desires are:
Viśvamūrtti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, and Manojavā. (102)
Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī are said to belong to Tamas;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
The tongues of those of auspicious seed—immortals, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, and piśācas—would be equal in luster to their own respective names. (104)
The Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities of the seven tongues of fire;
one should then project the limb-mantras of Agni upon the body according to the method previously described.
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa,
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara— thus they are proclaimed. (106)
