The six-limbed mantras have been declared, joined with their respective seed-syllables (jātis).
The preceptor should then project the eight forms of Jātavedas upon his own body.

One should place [the mudrās] on the head, the shoulder, the side, the hip-joint, the hip, and the side of the garment, following the direction of circumambulation; they are described in their respective order as follows. 108.
Vahni, Saṃjñā, Jātavedas, Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, Aśvodaraja, and another called Vaiśvānara— these are his names. || 109 ||
Kaumāratejas would be Viśvamukha, who is remembered as Devamukha;
beginning with the word *tārāgnaye* and ending with *namaḥ*, these are the forms of Fire (Vahni). || 110 ||
Having prepared a seat, one should contemplate the form of that fire.
The meditation on Vahni is desired as one who holds a spear, a svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness with his four long arms, and who has the luster of the hibiscus flower.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, and wearing a crown of matted locks.
Then, one should sprinkle pure water upon the girdle,
and spread darbha grass— without the tips or roots— around the girdle.
The knower of mantras should place the boundary-sticks (paridhi) in the various directions, excluding the east;
having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, those eight forms beginning with Brahmā are to be honored. || 114 ||
Meditating upon the fire, one should worship it in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, [bring him] here. (115)
"O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites at the end of the word [lohitākṣa];
ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), this is declared to be the mantra beloved by the Purifier (Agni). || 116 ||
Then one should worship the tongues of the fire in the center and in all six corners;
subsequently, one should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) upon the filaments according to the prescribed method.
On the petals, one should worship the forms bearing the Śakti and the Svastika;
on the tips of the petals, the Mothers are to be worshipped along with Aṣitāṅga and the other Bhairavas.
Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the various directions according to their described characteristics;
thereafter, taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands, one should hold them facing downwards.
Having taken darbha grass, the preceptor should heat it three times in the fire;
he should purify its tip, middle, and root in their proper order. (120)
Having taken them with the left hand, the mantra-practitioner should sprinkle them with the right;
having heated them again, he should cast the darbha grasses into the fire.
One should place those two on a bed of kuśa grass to the right of oneself;

then, having performed the six purificatory rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa), one should take the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī) and sprinkle it with the water of the arghya offering.
Having poured the clarified butter (ājya) into that [fire], one should consecrate it with the rites of inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth;
then, having removed the embers toward the northwest, one should place them back into the fire while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
This is designated as *tāpana* (the heating rite) by the teachers who are knowers of the tantras;
having cast a pair of blazing *darbha* blades into clarified butter, one should then throw them into the fire.
This is the purification with the heart-mantra of the Guru;
having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with a pair of blazing *darbha* blades while reciting the armor-mantra (*savarmāṇa*), [one should offer] clarified butter (*ājya*). (125)
One should cast the darbha grass into the fire; this is declared to be the "illumination" (abhidyotana).
Having displayed the blazing darbha blades in the clarified butter with the Astra-mantra, the Guru [proceeds]. 126.

One should cast those [embers] into the *jātavedas* fire; this is declared to be the "illumination. Having taken the embers with clarified butter and having united them with the fire, one should touch water. || 127 ||

Holding two *darbha* blades, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with the thumb and the ring finger, one should purify the clarified butter with the *astra-mantra*; this is the purification (*utpavana*).
In the same manner, one should perform the immersion of one's own face with ghee using the heart-mantra and two blades of kuśa grass; thus, the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are proclaimed.
Having placed a pair of darbha blades, one span long and knotted, within the clarified butter,
he should divide it into two parts and contemplate them as the two wings, white and black.
Having meditated upon the *iḍā* channel on the left side and the *piṅgalā* on the right, and the *suṣumṇā* in the middle, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.
Taking clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle, the wise one, with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, should offer it into the right eye of the fire, saying: "Svāhā to Agni! (132)
p.
322) Having likewise taken [the offering] from the left, one should offer it into the fire-eye on the left with the heart-mantra, saying: "Svāhā to Soma! (133).

Having taken a portion of the clarified butter from the southern part with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the *hṛn-mantra*, one should offer it into the mouth of the fire, saying: "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (134)

Thus, the wise one should cause the portions of clarified butter to fall, and then offer oblations in sequence; in this manner, he should perform the opening of the eyes and the face of the fire. 135.
The best of practitioners should again offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the *sāvitrī* and the *vyāhṛtis* for the purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*;
he should then offer oblations three times with the fire-mantra (*agnimantra*). || 136 ||
One should perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), in their proper sequence,
offering eight oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with the Praṇava individually for each.
The rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and then the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana);
immediately following these, there should be the birth-rite (jātakarma) and likewise the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa). || 138 ||

Next, the going forth [from the house] is prescribed, followed by the first feeding of solid food; then the tonsure and the initiation [upanayana], and further, the Mahānāmnī and the Mahāvrata rites. (139)

Likewise, the Upanayana, followed by the Godāna, marriage, and death [rites] should be performed; among auspicious rites, those ceremonies ending with marriage are to be done during the periods of cruel [planets]. (140)
(323) Those who know the Vedic scriptures declare that [the fire] ends with death;
therefore, one should worship his parents and unite them within oneself. 141.
Having taken five fuel-sticks drenched in clarified butter, one should offer them into the fire according to the prescribed rule,
using the mantras of the tongues, limbs, and forms of the Fire-god in their proper sequence.
The one most skilled in mantras should offer one oblation for each [deity],
having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon and poured it four times into the *sruc* ladle, covering it with that [spoon].
Standing before the fire with a disciplined mind,
the preceptor should offer oblations into the fire with the *sruva* ladle, using the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, for the sake of success.
One should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara.
The extraction of the mantra of the Lord of Obstacles is as follows:
first the Tāra (Om), then Ramā (Śrīṃ), then Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by Klīṃ and Glauṃ. (145)
Having uttered "gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada ante sarvapadaṃ janaṃ me vaśamānaya," followed thereafter by the wife of Vahni (svāhā), [one should worship]. 146.
The king of mantras of Vighnarāja, which is very difficult to obtain, has been told;
this is considered the common mouth of fire for all the gods. (147)
Then, having unified [the deity] and worshipped the seat of the deity within the fire, [one should proceed].
One should worship that deity, who bestows desired boons, in the form of fire.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into its mouth twenty-five times with clarified butter using the root mantra; this indeed is the unification with the fire.
Contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity together with one's own self,
one should perform the joining of the channels and offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.

This junction of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) has been taught by those who know the scriptures; one should perform the oblation for the primary limbs and the enclosures (āvṛtis) in their proper sequence. 151.
The best of instructors, acting as a mantra-practitioner, should properly offer oblations one by one with clarified butter,
using sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets, according to a tenth part of the number of recitations.
A wise person should always know the mudrās in hand-homas:
Śūkarī is characterized by the contraction of the fingers, and Haṃsī is formed by releasing the little finger. 153.

With the little finger and the index finger extended, it is called the "Deer" (mṛgī) mudrā; it is taught to be of three types, used respectively for malevolent rites (abhicāra), nourishment (puṣṭi), and pacification (śānti), and so forth.
(325) When an offering is made with empty hands, there is no fruit;
whatever gift is given or offered into the sacrificial fire with empty hands [is fruitless].
The donor receives no fruit of merit, and the officiating priest shall go to hell. || 155 ||

Knowing this, one who understands the distinctions should perform the oblation with diligence, using clarified butter and honey; indeed, sugar, clarified butter, and honey constitute the "triple honey" (madhutraya).

Or else, with the substances previously mentioned, the practitioner, with a restrained mind, should perform the fire-oblation in the consecrated fire using the materials prescribed by his own ritual manual. (157)

One should perform the fire oblation according to the prescribed rite with a tenth part of the number of recitations; however, when no specific sacrificial substance is mentioned, sesame seeds and clarified butter are said to be the oblation.
The distinction between Chinnā and Kālikā is now being expounded:
during the day, one should perform ten percent of the recitation joined with the three sweets (madhuratraya). (159)
Having performed the oblations and completed the count, one should then carry out the ritual for the night;
in the yoni-shaped sacrificial pit, one should offer abundant ghee along with meat and fish.
326) Description of Rituals for Desired Ends: Now I shall explain the procedure for rites with specific desires, which bestows success in all Śākta practices.
Through oblations of *mallikā*, *jāti*, and *punnāga* flowers, the arising of good fortune shall occur. || 161 ||
By offering oblations of fruits produced from the bilva tree or its leaves, one attains kingship; by offering lotuses, one obtains prosperity.
With blue lotuses, a man may bring the entire world under his control, and likewise with flowers [he gains] prosperity;
[he achieves this] with bandhūka flowers, vakula flowers, those arising from the japa plant, and those produced from the kiṃśuka tree.
For the purpose of subjugation, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with honey for success;
by offering oblations of salt mixed with honey, he attracts a beautiful woman.
Through the oblation of fuel-sticks of *vañjula* wood, one brings forth rain before long;
an oblation with pieces of *amṛtā* soaked in milk destroys fever. (165)
Through *dūrvā* grass one obtains longevity; through *kadamba* flowers one attains power over others (*vaśya*); and by means of a *homa* of *rājī* and salt, one slays enemies without delay. (166)
With honeyed ghee, one who is destitute shall obtain wealth;
it is declared that every substance for the oblation should be endowed with the three sweets (trimadhuropa).
By performing a fire-oblation with flowers produced from the *nandyāvarta* plant, a man becomes eloquent;
by offering oblations with *bilva* blossoms, he shall obtain his desired prosperity. (168)
By performing oblations with *palāśa* flowers, a man becomes radiant;
likewise by using sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, and other such substances. (169)
For the purpose of subjugation, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations; he shall bring the entire world under his control.
By performing oblations with the root of *nirguṇḍī*, a person is released from fetters. (170)
A fire sacrifice performed with salt mixed with neem oil brings about the destruction of enemies;
one may paralyze adversaries by offering salt mixed with turmeric powder.
By offering ripe, succulent fruits and fragrant flowers, the practitioner who performs the oblation correctly attains everything he desires. (172)
By an oblation of *mālatī* flowers, one becomes eloquent and a swift poet; by an oblation of speech, one may bring under one's influence men and even kings. (173)
Having offered lotuses, one shall conquer enemies; with dūrvā grass, one shall obtain peace.
With palāśa flowers, one shall attain nourishment, wealth, grain, and prosperity. (174)
By offering the flesh of a hare mixed with honey,
one obtains gold, wealth, knowledge, and excellent women. (175)
When a homa is performed with the feathers of a crow, it produces enmity among men;
by homas of black pepper, the enemy certainly meets his death. (176)

When the fire has been properly consecrated, one should perform a hundred thousand oblations with excellent fuel-sticks made from the *vaṭa* tree; this destroys the entire multitude of calamities. 177.
Or, by offering oblations with *apāmārga* wood, or with wild sesame seeds, or with rice, the wise man shall become possessed of abundant grain within a year. (178)
Through an oblation of *dūrvā* grass one becomes long-lived, and through honey, this occurs within a year;
with *āragvadha* flowers there shall be prosperity, and with clarified butter one obtains wealth. (179)
By offering cow’s milk, one shall obtain the increase of cattle; there is no doubt in this.
A wise person should always perform the optional oblation ten thousand times.
Having fashioned a hundred leaves adorned with creeper-flowers, the wise and excellent practitioner should consecrate them repeatedly according to the prescribed rite.
Then one should indeed offer those oblations into the consecrated fire according to the prescribed rite;
by that, the merit of worshipping for ten thousand ages is produced.
By this sequential yoga, whatever practitioner should practice upon the earth,
for him nothing whatsoever remains difficult to attain within the three worlds. (183)
He becomes a hero and eloquent, and shall attain all accomplishments;
one should offer oblations with clarified butter, buttermilk, meat, and blood.
With red flowers mixed with clarified butter and especially with blood,
as well as with meat and other such offerings, the wise one should perform oblations in the cremation ground.
For the sake of attaining all perfections, one should especially offer oblations of meat, blood, sesame seeds, hair, nails, cooked rice, milk-rice, and clarified butter.
By performing it in this manner, one obtains supreme accomplishment in all things;
whatever desire one may long for, that one certainly attains. (187)
Having become a human like a god, he enjoys abundant happiness;
the wise man should offer oblations into the sacrificial pit of the womb within the properly prepared fire. 188.
With oblation, with cooked food, with meat, and with blood, and especially with red sandalwood and black flowers. || 189 ||
Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations in a cremation ground with pure curd-rice;
by his command, he shall become a lord of wealth like Kubera and a husband of Śacī like Indra.
By means of this power, having become like the wind, one may move upon the earth like a god.
Then, having meditated, one should perform the fire-oblation with curd, prepared rice, and grains. (191)
For the sake of attaining all fruits through the single method of a thousand-fold [repetition],
one who desires knowledge should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with sugar.
Indeed, the fourteen sciences become instantly capable of destroying all impurities when [applied] with the cloth of a menstruating woman, together with honey and clarified butter. (193)
Indeed, by performing ten thousand recitations according to the prescribed rite with the flesh of a cat, along with ghee and honey, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained.
By means of hair belonging to a *cāṇḍāla*, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) will certainly be attained;
likewise, by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *bandhūka* flowers that are red in color, [the same result] is certain. (195)
The unfortunate woman shall attain good fortune and all perfections; of this there is no doubt.
The one most skilled in mantras should offer oblations of *rambhā* flowers and *śālamatsya* fish. (196)
Having attained all perfections, one shall obtain liberation at the end;
one should offer a thousand oblations of bilva leaves together with unbroken grains of rice.
One obtains charming speech, especially on the Great Eighth Day (Mahāṣṭamī).
Knowing this, one should perform [the rite]; now the measurement of the materials is stated.
Regarding the measure of the substances for the *homa* and so forth:
one *karṣa* is the measure for ghee in the *homa*, while milk is recorded as being the measure of a *śukti*.
And there should be five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in that same quantity, as well as honey in equal measure.
Milk-rice is known to be like a mouthful of food; curd is measured by a handful (prasṛti);
parched grain (lāja) is to be understood as a mere fistful, and likewise, flattened rice (pṛthuka) is measured by two finger-breadths (śukti). 200.
There should be half a pala of jaggery, and sugar in the same amount;
likewise, fish and meat are to be known [as equal], and blood in the measure of a śukti.

Half a mouthful should be the measure for the sacrificial porridge (caru), and it is traditionally held that this extends up to the size of a joint of sugarcane; one should likewise prepare the leaves, flowers, and cakes, each measuring one unit.
They know that plantains and oranges should each be offered as a single unit;
a citron should be divided into four pieces, and a jackfruit into ten. (203)
The coconut is of eight kinds, and the wood-apple is of three kinds; the wood-apple should be known to be of three kinds, and the cucumber is of three kinds. (204)
Other fruits should be unbroken; the fuel-sticks should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of *dūrvā* grass are prescribed, and the *guḍūcī* stalks should be four finger-breadths long. (205)
The rice, mung beans, black gram, and barley should be measured by a handful;
the husked rice should be half of that, or otherwise measured by a handful. 206.
Wheat, red rice, and sesame seeds are each measured by a handful (muṣṭi);
mustard seeds are also measured by a handful, and salt is measured by a śukti.
Twenty marīcas and one *pura* the size of a jujube fruit; asafoetida should be known as equal to that, and ox-gall should be equal to that. (208)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron—each the size of a tamarind seed—are prescribed by the teachers. (209)
The preceptor should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during the oblations of kindled fuel,
as lying down during the oblations of clarified butter, and as seated during all other matters.
In all ritual acts, the wise one should offer oblations into the fire within its mouth;
the blazing crest of the fire’s mouth must be understood by the best of practitioners. (211)
The declaration of auspicious and inauspicious results based on the distinctions of the fire's color and other qualities:
"The auspicious and inauspicious should likewise be known from the distinctions of the fire's color and other qualities.
[A fire] resembling gold, vermilion, the rising sun, saffron, or honey... (212)
The color of Suvarṇaretas is proclaimed to be beautiful; the sound of fire, resembling the resonance of a kettledrum, a water-laden cloud, or a lordly elephant, brings auspiciousness.
Resembling the *nāga*, campaka, *punnāga*, *pāṭala*, and *ayuthikā* flowers;
resembling the *padma*, *indīvara*, *kahlāra*, clarified butter, and guggulu resin. (214)
A pleasant fragrance is said by those who know the tantras to belong to the purifier (fire);
the flames of the fire are auspicious when they are free from flickering and possess a brilliant luster.
These are auspicious for practitioners, but otherwise they would bring about undesirable results.
Smoke that is as white as a kunda flower or the moon is declared to be fire that brings good fortune. (216)
Smoke that is black in color will certainly destroy the practitioner; smoke white in color quickly burns the kingdom, while that resembling the sound of a crow [is likewise inauspicious]. (217)
A sound from fire resembling a harsh voice brings about the destruction of all; a foul odor from the fire that consumes oblations will bring suffering to the sacrificer. (218)
A crest with broken curls brings death and the loss of wealth;
smoke resembling the wing of a parrot or having a luster like that of a pigeon [is likewise inauspicious]. (219)
It causes the swift decline of horses and cattle;
when such faults occur, the practitioner must perform an expiation. || 220 ||
Regarding the determination of expiation:
one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra;
having offered according to the prescribed number for one's own [status], one should perform the remainder of the rite.
Having offered the full oblation with the sacrificial ladle using the root mantra,
the preceptor should dismiss the deity, together with the limbs and the surrounding retinue, into the water-pot.
Having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, and having offered one oblation each for the tongue and other parts of the fire, he should sprinkle water upon himself.
Having prepared the fire and arranged one's own enclosing sticks and the strewn grass,
one should burn them in an occasional or optional oblation, but not in a regular (daily) rite.
335) The procedure for the optional libation (tarpaṇa) has been declared; the rule for the fire-oblation (homa) has been explained, and now the rule for the libation is also being told.
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform a propitiatory libation (tarpaṇa) by one-tenth of the number of oblations offered in the fire sacrifice.
The best of practitioners should perform [the ritual] everywhere with water from a sacred ford, milk, clarified butter, or even liquor, or else with scented water. || 226 ||
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), one should visualize the seat (pīṭha) of the deity within the water;
or else, having first prepared the yantra in the vessel for the offering or elsewhere, thereafter [one should proceed].
Then, having worshipped the Goddess together with her retinue of attendants,
one should first satisfy the Guru and the others in the yantra according to the proper sequence.
Having offered a single handful of water with each [hand] and having thus gratified the host of rays,
one should then gratify the mouth of the deity according to the prescribed rite with the previously mentioned substances.
One should also perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of the oblation (homa).
In this context, the libation for specific desires (kāmyatarpaṇa) is also described in detail.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner, having satiated his chosen deity and the Great Goddess according to the prescribed number, should perform the optional libation (kāmyatarpaṇa).
And one should satisfy [the deities] with milks and likewise with streams of blood, with marrow, and with their respective own hair. (232)
By washing away the family taint of the abducted maiden,
and indeed with the blood of rams, buffaloes, and human beings, (233)
One should satisfy the Supreme Deity with the blood of a rat and a cat;
by this mere act of satisfaction, one shall become a master of supernatural powers (siddhi) in person. || 234 ||
A succession of poetic compositions, like a stream of grape juice, arises from him;
becoming equal to Bṛhaspati, he rejoices on earth like a goddess.
For him there are neither sins nor merits; he shall certainly be liberated while living.
With the liquid resin of black aloe-wood, he may bring this entire world under his control.
By means of water mixed with sandalwood, a man obtains good fortune;
and by means of waters mixed with saffron, he may paralyze the entire world.
With water mixed with white sugar, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati;
with water scented with camphor, one may even subdue the asuras.
By means of ten thousand drops of water mixed with *rocanā*, one is liberated from all evil planetary influences;
this propitiatory rite (*tarpaṇa*), which bestows auspiciousness, has been declared in all the scriptures. (239)
The ritual procedure for Unmukhī and Kālikā:
the practitioner of the *rātrikalpa* of Unmukhī and Kālikā.
The wise man should satisfy them with wines and fish-meat alike. || 240 ||
Then, when the full number has been reached according to the measure prescribed for his own ritual manual,
he should establish [the deity] within the lotus of his own heart along with the hosts of his retinue.
Thereafter, the excellent practitioner should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the deity with scented water, using one-tenth of the amount used for the libation (tarpaṇa). || 242 ||
Having taken scented water with the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kumbha),
one should then recite the root mantra for such-and-such a deity.
"I shall consecrate [him]; after that, the heart-mantra immediately follows. Having uttered this and visualized him upon one's own head together with the mantra, (244)
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess together with her limbs and the deities of her enclosures;
thereafter, one should quickly sprinkle water in the proper sequence and subsequently drench the Gaṇas.
Having performed the consecration according to his own number, he should thereafter feed Brahmins accompanied by their respective mantras, regarding them with the thought that they are deities. (246)

Having worshipped according to the rules and having fed [the deities] with substances dear to each respective deity, the practitioner [should perform the rite] ten times the number of oblations made during the consecration. (247)
One who practices the daytime rite for the Chinnākālikā [mantra], and one who practices the Chinnā [mantra] for the daytime rite,
should with a spirit of devotion feed those ten parts [of the mantra] with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna). || 248 ||
One should observe the ritual for the night with Brahmins who are experts in the respective Mantras;
one should cause them to be served meat, fish, and hard foods to chew.
Regarding the description of feeding the Brahmins and so forth:
by feeding the Brahmins with the perception that they are deities, the practitioner shall become one whose mantra is perfected; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (250)
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, consecration, and feeding of Brahmins—this five-limbed rite is declared for the sake of perfect accomplishment. (251)
(Alternatively:
Recitation, fire-oblation, libation, consecration, and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite; offering water to the Sun, drinking water, prostration, and worship. || 252 ||
The feeding of Brahmins constitutes this tenfold preliminary service; a wise person should perform the fire-oblation and other rites with a tenth part of each respective ritual action.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite and the offering (*arghya*) to the Sun according to the previously prescribed rule,
one should perform the drinking of water using a tenth part of the water used for the Sun’s offering. (254)
Having meditated upon oneself as the form of the deity with a disciplined mind, one should take water in the right hand and, at the end of the root mantra, [address] the specific deity: || 255 ||
After [offering] "pāyayāmi namaḥ," one should then drink that [liquid] from one's own mouths;
having completed that same number [of repetitions], one should then [worship] one's own deity at the end of the root mantra.
One should offer salutation with the words "I bow" ten times for every sip of water;
thereafter, one should perform worship according to the prescribed ritual injunctions. || 257 ||
One should provide a meal for Brahmins as a tenth part of the number of prostrations;
for by the mere propitiation of Brahmins, that which was deficient becomes complete. (258)
Alternatively, on that day, one should perform [the rites] according to a tenth part of the respective recitation;
this procedure for the castes, beginning with the twice-born, is declared to be auspicious. (259)
For those incapable of performing the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, twice the number of recitations (japa) is prescribed;
for the other castes, thrice that number and so forth is prescribed. || 260 ||
If, in any part of the ritual procedure for the group of ten, there should be a deficiency, one must perform those very same ten rites; one must not allow the "ten-fold void" to occur.
Then, one should worship the guru with devotion using various offerings;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru for the purification of the mantras. || 262 ||
One should cause it to be given to the guru, the son of the guru, or the guru’s wife;
in their absence, the practitioner should give it to one of noble birth or to a member of a spiritual lineage.
And having given [the offerings], the best of practitioners should conclude the great worship;
through the performance of the specific rites according to each respective ritual manual (kalpa), the accomplishment of the mantra arises. || 264 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 13 ||
The Fourteenth Chapter:
The Description of Puraścaraṇa;
or, Puraścaraṇa is desired in another manner as well.
The practice of *puraścaryā* in a cremation ground is said to be difficult to find on this earth. || 1 ||

The supreme practitioner is indeed authorized for the practice in the cremation ground among all practitioners of mantras—whether in the Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, or other mantra traditions—and especially so in the Śākta tradition; he should accomplish it there. || 2 ||
Regarding the procedure for the practice at the cremation ground:
on a Tuesday, when the night has passed into its watch, and on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights, the practitioner [should perform it]. (3)
One should especially accomplish one's welfare by means of this during the dark fortnight;
on a funeral pyre that has not been washed, the wise practitioner, free from fear, should perform the rite. (4)

The food offering (naivedya) shall consist of meat with spices, jaggery, goat meat, wine, flour-cakes, milk-porridge, and various fruits, prepared according to the procedure prescribed in its own ritual manual.

Having brought flowers and other offerings, the practitioner himself, free from fear, accompanied by friends who hold weapons in their hands and are endowed with similar virtues, [should proceed]. (6)
If the practitioner is afraid, there should be practitioners in the four directions;
if not, he alone is proclaimed to be Bhairava himself. (7)
Adorned with garments, ornaments, decorations, and the like, facing the east,
he should sit steady and pure on the western side of the funeral pyre.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial grounds with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra (astra),
while meditating on the dust of the Guru’s feet, stepping forward with the left foot first.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and likewise the Mātṛkās according to the prescribed rule, one should recite this with palms joined in reverence.
The mantra for self-protection:
And whatever gods, terrifying rākṣasas, piśācas, yakṣas, siddhas, and hosts of gandharvas and apsarases are stationed here— || 11 ||
May the yoginīs, the mothers, all the bhūtas, and the women who traverse the sky be the bestowers of siddhi here, and likewise my protectors. (12)
Having prostrated thus, one should cast three handfuls of flowers into the midst of the funeral pyre;
thereafter, [one should worship] the Lord of the Cremation Ground, Bhairava Kālabhairava.
The knower of mantras should diligently worship Mahākāla in the four directions beginning with the east using water for the feet and other offerings, and thereafter present the bali offering.
The offering of the bali consists of the Praṇava, the Kūrca-bīja, and thereafter the Lord of the Cremation Ground.
At the end of this, one should say twice: "Obeisance to you who accept this offering of food mixed with meat. || 15 ||

"Make [the deity] accept the two [offerings], then perform the warding off of obstacles; grant me success at the end—thus, one should offer the bali-oblation at the conclusion with the word 'svāhā'. (16)
One may likewise perform the ritual dismissal with milk or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
before doing so, the wise practitioner should recite the seed-syllable of Māyā from the Bhairava-bhayānaka [tantra].
Having offered the bali as before, one should bring the bali to the south;
at the end of the *kūrca* mantra and at the end of the word *kāla*, the word *bhairava* follows thereafter. (18)
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Lord of the Cremation Ground in the east and west;
and at the end of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should offer it to Mahākāla in the north as before.
Then, having offered three supreme oblations in the midst of the funeral pyre, [he should address her as]:
"O Kālarātri! O Mahākālī! O Kālikā of terrible sound! (20)
"Accept this offering, O Mother; grant me supreme accomplishment.
Having given the offering to Kālakā, one should cause it to be given to Bhūtanātha.
At the end of *hūṃ* and at the end of *bhūtanātha*, [one should say] "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (*śmaśānādhipa*).
With this mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should cause the supreme *bali* offering to be given. (22)
Then one should say "Kūrcaṃ sarvagaṇanāthādhipataye," and at the very top of the cremation ground, one should offer the bali oblation as before.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with "Tārā" and likewise with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should sprinkle the bones [with that water] and then place the mantra upon that seat.
Having written this supreme wheel on either birch bark or a banyan leaf,
and having written his own mantra as well, he should place it upon the seat.
Regarding the recitation of the mantra for the subduing of heroes (vīrārdana) for the purpose of warding off obstacles:

having spread out a seat and sat upon it in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), the wise practitioner should subsequently extract the two *kūrca* seeds followed by a pair of *māyā* syllables. (26)
Having said, "O Kālikā, O Vajradaṃṣṭrā, O Pracaṇḍā, O Caṇḍanāyikā, rend the Dānavas," he then uttered the pair [of mantras] beginning with "han. (27)
Then, after "mahāvighnaṃ chedaya dvitayaṃ," followed by "svāhā," the mantra for the subduing of heroes (vīrārdana) is considered to end with the armor (varma) and weapon (astra) syllables. || 28 ||
One should cast a clod of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions;
in their midst, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles. (29)
If, due to the power of negligence, the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear,
[he should prepare] a wick made from the roots of *arka*, *indusita*, and *vāṭyāla*. (30)
Having placed a lamp in a pit,
the practitioner should worship the weapon-mantra there and then protect the lamp.
When that great lamp is overcome by obstacles,
one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites according to the procedure prescribed for one's own specific ritual manual.
Regarding the description of the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa):

having performed either the sixfold deposition or the deposition of the Tāraka, one should then worship. And the sixfold deposition becomes manifold through the various divisions of the Vidyās. || 33 ||
The *tāraka* (the saving mantra) is declared in all scriptures according to the path of Tantra. One should place the *mātṛkā* within the locus of the *mātṛkā*, encapsulated by the *tāra*.
The Savior (Tāraka) is proclaimed as the Tāra encased within the Mātṛkās;
and having worshipped his own Goddess according to the rules, the excellent practitioner—
Becoming intent on mantra and meditation, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
According to the specific number of syllables in the mantra, such is the count for the recitation: if it consists of a single syllable, one should then recite it one thousand times.
For a mantra of two syllables, it is eight thousand; for one of three syllables, it is fifty thousand;
beyond that, O Gajāntaka, the knower of mantras [should recite] one thousand.
Or, having begun at night, one should perform [the rite] until sunrise;
however, one should offer the *bali* at the beginning of the recitation (*japa*), and also offer the *bali* afterwards. || 38 ||
Whether at the end of the recitation or during the recitation, if the words "Give!
Give! are spoken, then one should also offer a sacrifice (bali) consisting of either a buffalo or a goat.
I shall now describe the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidānavidhāna) for the sake of attaining success.
[The victim should be] youthful, handsome, dark-complexioned, and free from defects such as wounds and the like. (40)
Having oneself first turned toward the east, one should bring the bali offering facing north and then sprinkle it on one's left.
With water for the guest-offering (arghyodaka) and this mantra beginning with Tārā, the Lord of Heroes [should worship] Narmadā, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, and Sarasvatī. (42)
O Maheśānī, bring here the presence of the Kāverī, the Candrabhāgā, the Sindhu, the Bhairava, and the oceans at this birthless bathing place. 43.
Oṃ! To the destroyer of the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), who resides on Mount Hemakūṭa;
to the one who is both transcendent and immanent, the supreme abider (parameṣṭhin), and to the embodied form of the syllable Hūṃ. || 44 ||
Then, having performed the ritual sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa), one should worship the bali offering;
likewise, one should worship Brahmā at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and the Earth upon the head. (45)
Likewise, having worshipped Ākāśa in the ears, Sarvatomukha in the neck, the luminaries in the eyes, and Viṣṇu in the mouth; || 46 ||
One should worship Candra on the forehead, Śakra on the right cheek, Vahni on the left cheek, and Samavartin on the neck. (47)
One should place Nairṛti at the tip of the hair, Pracetas between the eyebrows, Śvasana at the base of the nose, and Dhaneśvara on the shoulder. 48.
Having worshipped the Lord of Serpent-Kings in one's heart, one should recite this;
otherwise, [the body] becomes filled with sin and joined with impurities such as excrement, urine, and fat. (49)
Neither a deity ever accepts that offering, nor does it accept the offerings of others, such as buffaloes and the like, even when they are worshipped. (50)
The body becomes impure, yet the jackal indeed takes up the blood;
she should adorn it with garlands of blood and especially with vermilion (sindūra).
The mantra for the worship of the animal: Having gazed upon it, the wise one should recite the form of his own deity:
"O goat, you have arrived through my good fortune in the form of strength. (52)
I bow down, therefore, to Him who possesses all forms and who takes the form of Bali,
the destroyer of the donor's calamities through the gift that pleases Caṇḍikā.
Obeisance be to you, O Bala, who are the sacrificial offering to Cāmuṇḍā;
for the sake of sacrifice, offerings were created by Svayambhū himself. (54)
Therefore, I cause you to be slain today; thus, in a sacrifice, killing is not considered killing.
Then [arose] Vāgbhavā, Māyā, and immediately after that, Kamalā. (55)
Having uttered this, one should scatter three handfuls of flowers upon the head of Bala;
then, having thoroughly contemplated him with the thought that he is Śiva, one should worship him with the mantra for the severance of the fettered soul (paśu). || 56 ||
Then, having taken up that sword, the wise man should worship it and recite [the mantra] to Kṛṣṇa, who holds the Pināka bow in his hand and whose form is like the Night of Doom (Kālarātri).
Fierce, with red face and eyes, adorned with red garlands and unguents, wearing red garments, holding a noose in his hand, and accompanied by his family. || 58 ||
Meditating thus upon him drinking blood and devouring a mass of raw flesh, one should worship him thoroughly and pay homage with great effort. (59)
O Sword, you who are like a venomous serpent, with a sharp edge and difficult to approach;
you who contain glory within and bring victory—O Dharmapāla, homage be to you! 60.
Then, having formed the *puṭāñjali* gesture, the wise man should recite this mantra:
"O tongue, you are the goddess Caṇḍikā, the adornment of the world of the gods. (61)
Then, having uttered the pair of *māyās*, one should say "Kālikakāli";
at the end of the word "Vajreśvari," there is "Lauhadaṇḍa" joined with the suffix *ṅī*.
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should worship the limbs with "namas.
[The mantra consists of] the poison-syllable (viṣa), the pair of māyās (hrīṃ hrīṃ), the pair of kālis (klīṃ klīṃ), followed by the word vikaṭa.
Then, at the fangs, *spheṃ* twice; then *phetkāriṇi*, and *khādaya* twice;
then *chedaya* twice, and *māraya* all the wicked ones. (64)
Then, with the sword [of wisdom], one should sever the pair "a-ja," the pair "khi-la," the pair "ci-ki," and the pair "pi-bat," followed by the pair "sphroṃ. (65)
Having recited the two *kili*s, the pair of *kāli*s, and thereafter the heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*),
the best of practitioners should raise the sword consecrated with this mantra.
Having first given [the offering] while facing east, and then having cut the *bali* facing north with the mantra "Āṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ," thereafter—
Having prepared blood mixed with water, rock salt, sugar, and honey,
and provided with fragrant flowers, one should offer it while reciting the mantra.
The extraction of the nourishment mantra (āpyāyana-mantra) is as follows:
[one should utter] the Praṇava, Vāgbhava, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and the word Kauśikī; then, after that, "with blood," and thereafter "may you be nourished" (āpyāyatām). 69.
Having offered blood, the hero should present the head along with a lamp;
he should not look about in the directions, nor should he seek the company of his kinsmen.
Of water and other such obstacles, of serpents, elephants, and fanged beasts, as well as of birds, insects, and piśācas— or whatever else resides in the mind— (71).
Having contemplated all that as being like a dream, one should avoid fear in every situation;
and having completed the practice, one should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru.
Then one should cast the materials of worship into water or into a pit;
for one who has properly mastered a single mantra, there is nothing anywhere that cannot be accomplished.
What need is there to speak of a man who possesses many mantras? He is Śiva himself.
At the end of one's own lineage, the *puraścaraṇa* must be performed at night, and not otherwise.
It directly bestows all accomplishments, is saluted by all the gods, removes all sins, and destroys all diseases. || 75 ||
There is nothing else that bestows accomplishment, being devoid of the heroic practice (vīrasādhana);
[only one who is] of great strength, great intelligence, great courage, and pure [attains it]. || 76 ||
For those who are exceedingly pure, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare of all beings, I shall proclaim this supreme *vīrasādhana*. (77)
There is nothing superior to this *vīrasādhana* for bestowing accomplishment swiftly.
All success is indeed attained within a day and night during the Kali Yuga. || 78 ||
In the Dvāpara age, that is accomplished in a month; in the Tretā age, however, in a year;
but in the Kṛta age, in ten years—this is the truth, there is no doubt regarding success.
One should clothe [the deity] with a waist-band and a lower garment using the root mantra;
furthermore, one should apply sandalwood paste and other substances to the exterior with the root mantra. (80)
Having bound the turban with the root mantra and applied a half-tilaka mark with vermilion,
one should bow to the chosen deity and the guru during the middle watch of the night.
And that [practice] should be performed by the practitioners together with the family-mantras (kulamantra), provided the heroic practitioner is unperturbed and has consumed his food. 82.

There, having partaken of the divine offering and the sacrificial animal, one should perform the practice; on the previously mentioned day, the hero, endowed with various services, should perform the *śava-sādhana* (the practice using a corpse). 83.
Rice mixed with fish and meat, molasses, goat meat, flour-cakes,
milk-rice, liquor, and likewise an offering of black-gram rice.
Sesame, kuśa grass, and mustard seeds; likewise, a lamp and excellent incense; cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, khadira wood, and fresh ginger. (85)
Betel, a silk thread, a piece of elephant hide, and a woolen blanket;
a cup, and a sacrificial post of the measure of one's own span. || 86 ||
Having taken the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as prescribed in its own ritual manual, as well as the materials for worship,
[one should offer] those pierced by a staff, pierced by a trident, pierced by a sword, or those revived by water.

One who has been pierced by a thunderbolt, bitten by a snake, or is an outcast (caṇḍāla) or possessed by a powerful spirit; one who is young, handsome, brave, fallen in battle, or radiant—[these are the types of persons for whom this rite is performed]. || 88 ||
A wise man should not personally strike one who is fleeing or one who stands facing him in battle; he should avoid using [magical] mantras against such persons.
One who dies by his own will, one who has been dead for two years, an elderly person, a woman, or likewise a twice-born man;
one who dies while not ill, a leper, or one who has been dead for more than seven nights—[these are those whose bodies may be touched]. || 90 ||
Having completely abandoned one who is deficient in limbs and having taken up another from among those previously mentioned, he should bring him to the place of worship with the root mantra. || 91 ||
In an empty house, on a riverbank, on a mountain, or likewise in a secluded place;
at the foot of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, or in a forest clearing near such a place. (92)
Having taken recourse to the place of the lamp, one should draw the Vīrārdana on the ground;
where the ground is marked by the Vīrārdana, neither illusion nor delusion exists. (93)
One should perform all the previously mentioned rites, such as the worship of the Guru (gurupūjā) and so forth;
with the mantra beginning "ye cātra," one should scatter a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) upon the ground.
The mantras beginning with the Aghora-weapon [mantra]:
one should indeed perform protection with the Aghora-weapon or with the Sudarśana;
then again the pair *māyāsphura*, and again the pair *prasphura*. (95)
Then, in that state which is the ultimate nature of reality, exceedingly terrible and most fierce, there is a pair of *caṭa* syllables; and at the end of that, again, a pair of *pracaṭa*.
The mantra of Aghora consists of two *kaha*s, two *vama*s, then two *daha*s, followed by two *ghātaya*s, ending with *varma* and *phaṭ*. (97)

Having extracted the *hālāhala* [seed-syllable], which has the nature of the thousand-spoked [discus], this great mantra of Sudarśana is proclaimed, ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras. || 98 ||
Then, one should worship [the object] sprinkled with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) preceded by the Praṇava. [The mantra is:
"Oṃ, [with] the Kūrca [bīja], obeisance to the dead body, Phaṭ. (99)
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate while making physical contact [with the ground], saying:
"O Kuleśvara, supreme bliss of Śiva, you who are exceedingly great joy! (100)
O Śaṅkara, who has the form of Ānandabhairava and sits upon the lap of the Goddess; I am a hero, I take refuge in you; remain present for the worship of the Goddess. 101.
After bowing down with this mantra, one should then perform the purification of the corpse:
"Oṃ, the seed-syllable of sound, obeisance to the deceased body. (102)
Having uttered this and washed the excellent corpse with scented water, if it should become stained with blood, the Kula practitioner shall consume it. (103)
The excellent practitioner should fumigate it with fine incense and smear it with fragrant sandalwood; having placed the ritual offerings to his right, he should proceed.
According to the specific qualification [of the recipient], one should worship there with wine;
having taken it there, everything should be given away, and one must not touch it at all.
Then, having established protection in the directions while recollecting the Vīrārdana mantra,
the hero next takes his seat upon a soft cushion, assuming the vīrāsana posture.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, one should duly apply the network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*).
Then, having established self-protection with the *aghora* mantra, one should remain composed. (107)
"Oṃ durge durge rakṣaṇi svāhā"—with this mantra, the hero should scatter mustard seeds in all directions. (108)
Oṃ! You are sesame, whose deity is Soma; you are the cause of satisfaction for all.
You are the bestower of heaven upon the ancestors and the protector of mortals like me. 109.
"Bringer of peace amidst the obstacles caused by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas"—having thus cast sesame seeds there, he should take one-fourth from the corpse and so forth. (110)
Having thus performed the protection, he should lead the corpse before himself;
having spread out a bed of kuśa grass, he should place the corpse there. (111)
Having placed the hero’s betel-leaf, together with cardamom and other ingredients, into his mouth, he should then turn the corpse face downwards.
Having placed that [object] upon it, one should smear it with sandalwood paste;
then, having visualized a square area extending from the base of the arms to the waist.
In the center is a lotus with four doors and endowed with eight petals;
there, one should place a skin rug spread over a woolen blanket.
One should also offer the bali-oblation to the lords of the cremation grounds as before,
and one should cast ten pieces of wood in the ten directions, beginning with the east.
Having cast [the materials] there, one should worship the ten deities beginning with Indra;
then, having written the word "viṣa" in the place of Indra, [one addresses] the Lord of the Gods.
Accept this offering, O pair; cause the pair to accept it.
Having warded off obstacles, bestow success—*ṭha* twice. (117)
With this mantra, one should first offer a bali-oblation consisting of meat;
having performed the respective naming and other rites, one should present the bali as before. (118)
One should also offer a bali together with liquor to the spirits presiding over the corpse, and one should likewise assign it to the sixty-four Yoginīs and the Ḍākinīs. (119)
Then, at the doorway, the hero should station an assistant practitioner who is endowed with equal qualities, learned in mantras, and has conquered his senses.
Having seated one who knows the ritual of consecration and is skilled in the divine hero [mantras],
and having offered a seat, at the end of his own mantra and finally after the supreme [mantra]— || 121 ||
Then, with this mantra "phaṭ," one should perform the invocation;
having placed kuśa grass under the soles of the feet and grasping the hair of the corpse.
Having firmly tied his topknot and accomplished his firm resolve,
he should there worship the Goddess extensively with manifold ritual offerings.
Having risen and stood before the corpse, one who is devoted to faith should recite:
"Oṃ, O Lord of Gods, be submissive to me; thereafter, [grant] my heroic state. (124)
"O illustrious one, you who have taken refuge in those who seek shelter, grant me success!
Having thus addressed him with this mantra, the practitioner, with palms joined in reverence, [should pray]. (125)
Oṃ! O Bhīma, O you who cause the fear of the fearful to cease, O you with auspicious eyes, O compassionate one!
Protect me, O Lord of the gods of gods, O sovereign over the lords of corpses! 126.
Thus, one should draw a triangular wheel upon the sole of his foot;
then the corpse will be unable to rise and shall become motionless.
Alternatively, the best of practitioners, while recollecting the root mantra,
should then bind the two feet of the corpse with a silk thread.
Having seated him again, one should draw his arms out to the sides,
spread kusha grass upon his hands, and have him place his feet thereon.
Having joined the lips together, with a steady mind and steady senses, one should always meditate on the Goddess in the heart and perform the recitation while observing silence. (130)
If nothing at all is obtained until midnight,
one should scatter mustard seeds with that same *arghya* water while reciting the *Jayadurgā-mantra*.
Having cast up the sesame seeds as before and then gone seven steps, one should worship the Goddess there as well and recite the supreme mantra. || 132 ||
O Goddess, a man should recite the mantra fearlessly, or he shall attain accomplishment (siddhi), according to the previously mentioned sequence and method for the rosary. 133.
"There is no fear from a moving seat; once fear has arisen, one should speak thus:
'O Goddess of gods, whatever you request—be it an elephant or anything else—it shall be given. (134)
"Furthermore, on another day I shall give [it]; tell me your own name.
Having been addressed thus in Sanskrit, he, being fearless, should repeat [the mantra] once more. (135)
If he speaks sweetly again, then one should speak sweetly in return;
then, having caused him to swear an oath, the man should request his boon. (136)
If he does not act truthfully and does not grant the boon, then the wise man should again recite with a one-pointed mind, as before. (137)
For even a god does not move there without a human form;
therefore, one must diligently discern whether it is a human or one born from a divine womb.
A mother, or a maternal aunt, or likewise a maternal uncle's wife, having arrived, creates an obstacle by concealing her form through illusion. (139)
Arise, my child; everything that needed to be done for you has been accomplished, there is no doubt.
The time of dawn has arrived, and your father is calling out from the house.
(359) Generally, people are free from envy and kings are wielders of the rod of punishment; by whom has this ever been seen? Therefore, it will turn out to be unfavorable. (141)
With such various statements as these, one should not abandon the recitation (japa);
for the hosts of ancestors who dwell in distant lands have passed away there. (142)
Then relatives arrive there, assuming divine forms; and taking with them his wife, sons, servants, and others, he is led away by his enemies.
All the sons, brothers, younger siblings, and servants wept for the touch of their own beloved’s body, her garments, ornaments, and so forth. (144)
Once seized, one is led away by the foot-soldier guards; therefore, one should abandon fear of them.
On whichever day there is apprehension, that very day it will manifest. (145)
If one is not shaken by that, then what is there not to be gained?
[There is] the Goddess assuming the form of a woman, and the Man assuming the form of a brahmin. 146.
If a woman, whether virtuous or not, should grant a boon, one shall obtain that boon for three nights upon the utterance of the words, "Take a boon. (147)
Then, what on this earth could not be accomplished by that lord of heroes, who was himself sinless and refined by birth in a noble lineage? (148)
The supreme goddess Asaṃskṛtā is beyond doubt for one joined with sin;
she speaks another [form of] refined speech (saṃskṛta), whether face-to-face or not. || 149 ||
She herself is the Goddess, of this there is no doubt; he himself is the Lord Bhairava.
Otherwise, he would indeed possess a body fashioned by Māyā. (150)
She should not choose a groom there, nor should she say anything at all; if she speaks such a refined narrative or expresses herself clearly in this manner, [she is considered pure]. (151)
If one does not [attain it] spontaneously, then by the words of a Kaulika, the untroubled boon should be accepted;
or else, some intense light, whether white or blue-red.
Either a word is produced correctly, or even the nectar of immortality is obtained;
having reflected upon this, it should be accepted—thus has the direction been proclaimed. (153)
But men who are unrefined in intellect have many kinds of duties toward the gods;
one must necessarily fear them, for there is no trust whatsoever to be placed in them.
The Bhairavas and the Baṭukas, devoted to the Kula scriptures, assumed crooked forms through their attachment to this scripture. 155.
Having become a son, he may steal one's knowledge; having become a woman, she may delude one.
Therefore, one should exert effort in investigation regarding that [knowledge], whether it be from oneself or from another. 156.
When the truth has been realized, one should abandon the recitation of mantras and so forth;
having known that the fruit has been attained, one should then release the *juṭikā* (the topknot). || 157 ||
Then, having given away horses, men, elephants, and boars made of flour as requested by them, one should subsequently observe a fast.
On the following day, having performed the daily rites, one should then drink the *pañcagavya*;
there, one should feed twenty-five Brāhmaṇas.
Or five by five less, up to ten in sequence;
having bathed there and eaten, one should dwell in that most excellent place. (160)
If there were no food to be eaten by the Brahmins, then [the king] would fall into poverty;
if he were to become impoverished because of that, then the God would become enraged. (161)
One should observe [the vow] for three nights, six nights, or nine nights;
if one should indeed approach a bed [with a woman], then one should predict disease. (162)
Upon hearing song, one becomes deaf; from seeing a dance, one loses one's sight;
and if one speaks during the day, then one shall fall into muteness. (163)
Indeed, the deity remains within the body until the end of the fifteenth day;
one must never, under any circumstances, utter disparagement against cows or Brahmins. (164)
Being pure, he should touch gods, cows, Brahmins, and others every day;
at dawn, after completing his daily obligatory rites, he should drink water infused with bilva leaves.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṅgā on the sixteenth day,
he performed the libation of water to the gods for more than three hundred [deities].
"Without bathing and libations, there can be no propitiation of the deity";
by this injunction, the practitioner attains success. (167)
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures here, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari;
whether with or without its constituent parts, it is likewise either fruitless or fruitful.
Having performed this very sādhana, one becomes most dear to Śakti. In the absence of a corpse, the vīrasādhana should indeed be performed in a cremation ground.
An alternative method for describing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is now stated for the sake of men attaining results quickly:
one should dig a pit at a crossroads in the four directions, reaching down to the heart of a man. (170)
The wise one should indeed kindle the lamp of life at the *brahmarandhra*;
likewise, one should dig a single [pit] in the center, where there shall be a seat of earth. (171)
One should perform the consecration there according to the sequence of the path previously described;
one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) to Mahākāla and the other deities as before.
Having performed the worship as prescribed in the ritual manual, one should recite the mantra with a disciplined mind;
even if naked, one should recite the mantra dedicated to all the deities ten thousand times.
And at the conclusion of the recitation, having offered the bali-oblation and a sacrificial fee according to one's means,
the wise man shall attain all perfections and be honored by all the gods.
Having set out on the journey as before in the attire of a hero, the excellent practitioner, together with other practitioners, [should bring] various ritual materials for the worship. (175)
In the previously mentioned place, the hero should likewise bring forth a corpse,
[shaped] as a square measuring one cubit in size, using the mantra of the armor-weapon (varmāstra).
Having drawn the maṇḍala there, he should place the corpse within it;
thereafter, [he should worship] the pair of Lords and the pair immediately following them. 177.
"Perform my task, svāhā! To the weapon, phaṭ!"—having said this, the practitioner should then envelop both himself and the corpse. || 178 ||
One should draw three lines and thereafter present the offering;
one should also give instructions to the Ḍākinīs, Hākinīs, and Śākinīs. (179)
Having offered [the oblation] combined with meat, honey, and sesame seeds according to the sequence of east and west, one should indeed give it to Vāmadeva and cause it to be given to Raktadanta.
For the sake of splendor, one should offer three oblations of ghee mixed with honey and sugar;
on the south, one should direct [the offering] to Rudrakāla Vajranābha.
One should cause to be offered rice-cakes with ghee and barley flour;
and having given these to Agni in the form of a bali-offering in the northern direction, [one should proceed]. 182.
Having offered an oblation of jaggery-rice and milk-porridge,
the practitioner should then worship the Goddess according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual.
Having established the corpse with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) using oil and turmeric,
the practitioner should then perform an anointing and bathe it.
Having swept that place with a cloth, one should worship the seat of the great preta;
then, having performed the installation of the living soul (jīvanyāsa), one should worship it with water for the feet and other offerings. || 185 ||
Having tied a tuft with the root mantra, one should draw a lotus as before;
having offered the seat as before, the practitioner should utter the root mantra. (186)
Standing in the form of a horse-rider, the wise man should mutter the mantra;
by reciting it with an undistracted mind, success is produced. || 187 ||
If the practitioner is afraid there, he should remember the pair of the Guru’s feet;
by the grace of the Guru’s feet, the assailants will not harm him. (188)
Having thus stabilized the mind, one should recite the mantra with undistracted intellect;
if at any time the deity indeed appears on the left, [one should proceed].
One should indeed engage in conversation with her, but one should not utter pleasant words;
the best of practitioners should address her with the sound "hūṃ" while remaining on his right side.
Having gone to the south, she too should say, "Give!
Give! Even so, one may offer the bali with the mind alone if one is physically unable.
Having obtained his own desired object, the hero should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor; then, having cast the corpse and other remains into the water, he may go home at his ease.
Having carried the corpse to the foot of a banyan tree and worshipped the Goddess there, the best of practitioners should bathe, perform ablutions, and recite the mantra ten thousand times. (193)
One shall become a hero, the lord of all accomplishments; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having diligently placed a corpse upon one's own lap at the root of a *bilva* tree, [one attains this]. (194)
Having gazed with the Nṛsiṃha-mudrā, the wise one should recite the Mātṛkā;
having recited it there a thousand times, he shall indeed become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 195 ||
Placing his hands between his knees, with his chin and lips closely joined,
and his hands touching the ground, he trembled again and again. (196)
One should open the mouth wide and lick with the tongue;
this shall be the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having recited [the mantra] a thousand times there, one indeed becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
[One should use] saffron, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, and thick sandalwood. (198)
Having prepared camphor, padmaka wood, keśara, and yellow sandalwood together in one place, a person should then prepare each of them individually. (199)

The practitioner should [employ] the seed-syllable of each individual substance, as well as that of the combined substances, joined with lightning and fire (ra), the end of the eye (i), and the moon-drop (bindu). 200.
The knower of mantras should recite the root mantra eight thousand times;
by merely applying its tilaka, one shall bring even a king under one's control.
O Hero, one should personally draw blood from the tip of the tongue into the sky;
having formed a pill with that very [blood], one should worship Kālī therein. || 202 ||
O Cāmuṇḍā of terrible roar, you who are blue, with a blue banner, a flickering tongue, and a skull-bowl; seize the blood at the tip of your tongue! (203)
"Accept the offering, grant a boon; O Kālī, Kālī, fierce and terrible one, [bestow] blood in the stainless sky! Then [follow] the weapon-mantra (astra), then the armor-mantra (kavaca). (204)
It is proclaimed as Kālikā out of a desire for the welfare of heroes;
the pair of kūrcas is declared to be the supreme mantra of Nīlā. (205)
Then *viyat*, *bhṛgu*, and *amā*; then *bala*, *indra*, and *ravi*; then *rati* joined with a fragment of the moon (*candrakhaṇḍa*); and after that, the word *nīla*. (206)
With "patāke huṃ phaṭ" at the end, this is considered the mantra of the eastern peak;
this great vidyā, difficult even for the gods to obtain, has thus been described. || 207 ||
Victory to the illustrious Goddess Dharaṇī at the site of the excellent blue banner;
therefore, this blue banner should be joined with the practice of Nīla.
One should contemplate the seeds of Śrī, Śakti, and Smara at the end of that, followed by "Hūm. Then, one should extract the long Bhṛgu (Sa) joined with the emission (Ha), which is the armor-mantra.
After "Ugracaṇḍe," one should place the word "pada" followed by the pair of words "mām ante rakṣa. Then, after the word "śatru" (enemy), one should utter the word "bhakṣa" (devour).

At the end of *hrīṃ klīṃ saḥ*, [one should place] the seeds of Śrī, Śakti, and Smara; then, having addressed him with "grant me sovereignty," one should utter Bhṛgu accompanied by the creative emission (*sarga*). (211)
Then one should utter the syllable *klīṃ*, followed by *kāma* (*klīṃ*), *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), and finally *ramā* (*śrīṃ*).
This mantra, beginning with the fixed syllable (*dhruva*), is said to consist of forty-one syllables.
Ugracaṇḍā, the great vidyā, is celebrated as Lolajihvā;
that vidyā who is Mahātārā is celebrated as Karālā. (213)
The extraction of the mantra of Mahātārā:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), then "Tāre" and again "Tāre," followed by "Namaḥ Svāhā"—this ten-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed. (214)
And Mahātārā, the bestower of all accomplishments, has been described;
she should be addressed with these very words, a thousand times, using the root mantra alone. (215)
Having applied a tilaka on his forehead, the practitioner himself, free from fear,
stands before [the deity] on the conjunction of the Mahā-aṣṭamī and Navamī.
One should cast the corpses of goats, buffaloes, and rams in the four directions, as well as headless trunks and heaps of skulls, adorned with lamps and other offerings. (217)
Having spread a headless trunk in the middle, he there assumed the form of a Gandharva, his mouth filled with betel and his eyes anointed with collyrium. || 218 ||
Having performed [the ritual] and recited the *tāra* mantra, one becomes a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvara*).
Then, at a previously mentioned location, and especially at a crossroads (219).
Whether it be a corpse more than two years old, or up to five years, or even one that is young, or a fetus from the seventh or eighth month; || 220 ||
Having brought a Cāṇḍāla who is subdued [and thus] bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment,
one should first establish him and then perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa).
Having written the mantra of the preta, and having likewise worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should provide a seat and perform protection for oneself.
Through the means of a corpse, all accomplishments are attained; thereafter, one should perform the ritual nourishment of the deity in the mouth of the corpse according to the rules.
Then, by reciting all the mantras, one becomes a master of all accomplishments. || 223 ||
Uttering the mantra beginning with the syllable *tāraṃ* (om) and ending with *namas*, this is the mantra for placing the corpse;
thereafter follows the mantra for the corpse-seat.
The mantra is said to end with *bhuvaneśī* at its beginning and *phaṭ* at its end.
Taking a water-pot girdle (*karaka-kañcī*) and adorned with a garland of severed heads (*muṇḍa-mālā*), [he should proceed]. || 225 ||

Having made a forehead mark with that very [substance] and adorned himself with those respective ashes, one becomes the master of all accomplishments by reciting [the mantra] even once in a cremation ground. || 226 ||
Having brought a fish, the hero among yogins (vīrendra) should cast it into a cemetery for the ancestors;
by reciting [the mantra] there even once, union with the deity occurs. (227)
There, having bowed to Mahādeva and Mahādevī, the practitioner, by applying that ash-mark (bhasmatilaka), shall himself become Vīreśvara. || 228 ||
At night, in the marketplace of the dead, [there dwells] Unmattānandabhairava,
naked, pure, adorned with ashes, and with disheveled hair.
Bearing a skull and holding a sword in his hand, the wise practitioner should recite the Mātṛkā;
then, by reciting it a hundred times, great siddhi arises for him. (230)
Having brought there a ḍākinī, a yoginī, or even some other woman of the earth, and having worshipped her with a thousand times the [oblation] for Gajāntaka, || 231 ||
Having performed the recitation, the best of practitioners shall become a lord of all siddhis. For the practice with a primary corpse, great corpses are recommended.
In the practice of Nīla, small creatures that are devoid of life are recommended for practitioners as they bestow all accomplishments upon everyone. (233)
Having abandoned the *brāhmaṇa-gomaya* (cow-dung of a Brahmin), one should accomplish the *vīrasādhana*.
Thus has the auspicious *nīlakrama* been described. 234.
It must not be taught to anyone, for it is the cause of the accomplishment of mantra.
On a Tuesday or a Saturday, one who is composed should [procure] a human skull. (235)

Having mixed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and smeared it with sandalwood and other substances, one should deposit it in the ground within a forest, measuring half a cubit in depth.
If on that day, during the night, a person were to recite the mantra alone a thousand times, he would become a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa). || 237 ||
Having brought the corpse and buried it right there at its door,
one should [recite] one hundred and eight [times] every day from that day until that same day.
He shall become the lord of all accomplishments; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Alternatively, a man may dwell in a solitary forest, using a bed of bones as his seat. (239)
Having recited [the mantra] during the day from sunrise until sunset, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis);
likewise on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights. || 240 ||
Beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise, by reciting [the mantra] during that interval, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments. || 241 ||
Regarding the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) during an eclipse of the moon or sun:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, being pure and having previously fasted, one should stand in water reaching up to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean. (242)
Alternatively, having bathed in pure water and being composed in a clean place,
one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind until liberation from the morsel of food. (243)
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence using a tenth part [of the total].
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a grand worship and feed the Brahmins.
Then, having worshipped the Guru who has attained mastery over the mantra, one should satisfy him;
for no other time is praised as superior to the moment of a solar eclipse. (245)
In that regard, whatever action is performed during the autumn season, especially from the fourth to the ninth lunar day, shall yield infinite fruit.
Having worshipped with devotion, he should then recite the mantra one thousand times at night alone, in a secluded place that is a mere abode of darkness. (247)
One should be devoted to fasting from the eighth day until the ninth;
such a person shall become a lord of all accomplishments—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (248)

At the junction of time on the eighth lunar day, the practitioner of mantra, having entered a bower of one hundred and eight creepers, should worship them with effort according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed worship according to the ritual procedure prescribed for his own kalpa,
the practitioner should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with a mind focused solely on desire.
And by taking a torch with the root of their leaves and placing it at the ear,
great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) shall be attained immediately through the sight and worship of the creeper. (251)
Having drawn the eight families and the yantra itself upon a creeper-cottage (latāgāra),
and having worshipped them there and performed the consecration, he should present it to her.
Having recited the mantra a few times and led [the deity] away, being intent on the meditation of the deity,
one should dismiss it, pay obeisance, and then, well-restrained, recite it oneself.
Having offered an oblation to the goddesses with joy, there is no doubt that one attains success in mantra;
or else, having brought the Guru, one should worship him as a deity.
Having gratified the preceptor with garments, ornaments, gold, and other gifts, as well as his son, his daughter, and especially his wife; || 255 ||

Having performed worship and recited the mantra, one shall become a master of supernatural powers (siddhi) oneself; and having meditated upon and fully worshipped the lotus feet of the Guru within the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra), [one attains the same]. || 256 ||
By reciting [the mantra] with the thought that it is a deity alone, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi);
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to the extent of one's wealth.
By the mere permission of the Guru, even a corrupt mantra is perfected.
However, in this scripture, neither a human nor even a god has the authority to transgress against the Guru. (258)
If the practice of these [mantras] is performed while they are devoid of mantra and without the mouth of the Guru, the loss of accomplishment occurs. || 259 ||
One should not reveal this tantra and its mantras even to one's own sons;
otherwise, one will certainly go to the abode of the King of the Dead (Yama). || 260 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter: A Description of the Worship of the Kumārīs.
Now I shall explain the worship of the Kumārīs according to the ritual injunctions of the Tantras.
For rituals such as the fire-oblation are indeed fruitless without the worship of the maiden. || 1 ||
Devoid of that [initiation], rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) are fruitless and do not yield complete results, just as a body devoid of life;
so too is the worship of a deity or of the Guru. (2)
In the same way, there should be honor for a maiden of noble birth;
indeed, one should bestow upon the maiden whatever she desires according to one's ability. || 3 ||
For thus, what is impossible becomes possible; indeed, in the absence of giving, there is a loss of fruit.
A flower given to a young maiden is considered equal to Mount Meru.
Furthermore, whatever else has been given—whether it be food, edibles, and so forth—even if it is small in quantity or deficient in mantra, it shall become possessed of great merit. || 5 ||
The fruit of worshipping a maiden:
from the worship of a maiden and also from feeding a maiden, [one obtains great merit].
Merely by venerating a young girl, one becomes like a young girl.
The abiding of all deities within the body of the maiden makes her the Goddess Kumārikā; Śiva, too, is Kumārikā.
Kumārī is the manifest Yoginī; Kumārī is all the deities.
By the mere worship of her, the worship of the three worlds is accomplished.
The Great Goddess Sukumārī is established in a threefold form. || 8 ||
There is the higher (parā), the lower (aparā), and the third, the both-higher-and-lower (parāparā);
that time in which nothing exists—not gods, asuras, nor great serpents.
Then, as the three worlds were being dissolved, the Kumārikā was born;
she is the primordial power of creation, manifest there in a threefold manner.
She has become the sesame seed, the form of creation within the ocean of existence;
she is the embodiment of Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ, that one Kumārikā who is to be worshipped. 11.
Having unified [the deities] as three, and again as seven, eight, or nine,
O Goddess of gods, one should worship according to the rule in the eternal sequence.
One should worship either one hundred and eight or even a single maiden;
when worshipped they accept [the offering], but if treated with contempt they depart. (13)
Through the worship of the maiden, all the gods are satisfied, as are the asuras, the nāgas, and even those who are malevolent planets;
likewise the bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas, and rākṣasas. || 14 ||
All the deities are cruel, as are Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Bhairava; likewise, all things beginning with the earth, including the entire cosmic egg with its moving and unmoving beings. || 15 ||
