Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—they are all pleased, and indeed all are pleased with him who worships a maiden. || 16 ||
By worshipping the Kumārīs, one obtains the fruit of ten million offerings;
when worshipped, they destroy obstacles as well as most formidable enemies. (17)
All diseases and all portents flee away without a doubt;
the planetary spirits, yakṣas, ghosts, vetālas, and serpents go to their destruction.
Asuras, guhyakas, pretas, yoginīs, and secret ḍākinīs;
great terrors, famines, and thousands of portents [shall arise]. (19)
Bad dreams, untimely death, and whatever other calamities may arise—
none of these prevail over him simply by virtue of worshipping the Kumārī.

The supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as the subterranean realm (*pātāla*), the magic pill (*guṭikā*), and the collyrium (*añjana*)— this quartet, along with the divine *vetāla*, shall be attained through the worship of the Virgin (*kumārikā*). (21)
I shall describe the characteristics of the maiden, their defining marks, and the method of worship according to the path of the Tantra;
[this applies] from after the second year until she reaches her eighth year.
A maiden should be understood as such until [the age of] sixteen, for she bestows the fruits of mantra and tantra; or rather, until the flower has appeared. || 23 ||
To them, one should offer flowers and fruit, or fragrant sandalwood and milk-rice;
as well as food offerings dear to children, prepared according to one's lack of resources.
The best of practitioners should satisfy them with pleasant conversation.
According to the difference in age, there is a difference in the names of the maidens: a one-year-old girl is Sandhyā, and a two-year-old is Sarasvatī. (25)
At three years she is Tridhāmūrti, and at four years she is Kālikā;
at five years she is Subhagā, and at six years she becomes Umā.
Mālinī is manifest with seven [letters], Kubjikā with eight years,
Kālasaṅkarṣā with nine, and Aparājitā with ten.
In the eleventh year, however, she is Rudrāṇī; in the twelfth, Bhairavī;
in the thirteenth, Mahālakṣmī; and in the twenty-second, Pīṭhanāyikā.
The Kṣatrajñā is considered to consist of fifteen [syllables], while the Vācikā is held to be sixteen;
thus they should be worshipped in sequence until no flower remains. (29)

379) Regarding the declaration of auspicious days: one should perform worship from the first lunar day (pratipadā) until the new moon (darśānta), according to the variations in the increase [of the lunar fortnight].
On all the great festival days (mahāparvan), and especially on the Pavitraka day.
On the Mahānavamī day, the lord of heroes should worship the maidens;
he who is devoted should worship Piṅgalā with sixteen [maidens].
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion, one shall obtain all prosperity;
one should worship the Kula-vidyā, the singular Bālakabhairavī.
The narration of the mantra for the worship of the Kumārī:
Thus, one should worship the body of Consciousness through union with the Praṇava (Oṃ). [The mantra is:
Vāṇī (Aiṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and then the two Kūrca-s (Hūṃ Hūṃ). || 33 ||
And these are to be known as the Praṇavas for the worship of the Virgin (Kumārī):
[the syllable] enriched with the eleventh vowel (au), joined with Bhṛgu (b), the Bindu (m), and the Indu (i). || 34 ||
The seed of consciousness is said to bestow prosperity upon practitioners.
Thus, it is [manifested] in two ways, three ways, sevenfold, and again ninefold. (35)
One should worship regularly and invariably according to the prescribed rule. Water should be offered with the Vāgbhava [syllable], and water for washing the feet with Māyā [syllable]. (36)
One should offer the arghya with the syllable *lakṣmī*, sandalwood paste with the *kūrca* seed-syllable,
flowers with the *śakti* seed-syllable, and one should cause incense to be offered with the sixth [seed-syllable].
Through Vāgbhava there is security for the city; through Māyā, the eightfold qualities;
through the seed-syllable Śrīṃ, the attainment of prosperity; and through the seed-syllable Hrīṃ, the destruction of enemies. (38)
By means of the Bhairava seed-syllable, one attains the state of a sword;
first, however, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites according to one's own tradition.
The special deposition on the body of the maiden:
thereafter, the supreme special deposition (viśeṣanyāsa) upon the body of the maiden;
the mantras for this special deposition.
Aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ klauṃ hsauḥ, obeisance to the heart of Kulakumārikā. || 40 ||
Aiṃ haiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klāṃ eṃ svāhā, svāhā to the head! Aiṃ klīṃ saiṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock! || 41 ||
Aiṃ, to the armor of Kulavāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī, Huṃ!
Klīṃ, to the weapon, Phaṭ!
Aiṃ, salutation to the eastern face, Siddhi Jayā. || 42 ||
Aiṃ, salutation to Jayā, the northern face.
Aiṃ Klīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Kubjikā, the western face.
Kraṃ, salutation to Kālikā, the southern face. || 43 ||
One should perform the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa) and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the body of a virgin girl;
or else, one may worship a single maiden one hundred and eight times.
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion, one should offer her everything: water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), incense again, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth. (45)
Becoming filled with youthful exuberance, with his own mind fixed on Acyuta,
he should gaze upon the adorned young girl and meditate upon his chosen deity.
Thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity, such as one hundred and eight times;
one should perform three circumambulations, and it will be auspicious at the beginning and in the middle.
Then, having paid homage to her with the thought that she is a deity, one should dismiss her;
afterwards, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given consisting of silver, gold, and pearls.
The fruit of worshipping a maiden:
By worshipping a maiden alone, one obtains the fruit of worshipping ten million [goddesses].
In the worship of a maiden, one should not even consider her caste. (49)
They are endowed with all noble lineages and do not arise from low birth; nor do they originate from various defects, for they are possessed of both virtues and beauty. (50)
In every way, those [goddesses] are to be worshipped by the noble-born as bestowers of auspiciousness;
to the extent that one acts for their pleasure, one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 51 ||
When great danger has arisen, one should worship the Virgin Goddess;
at that very moment one attains liberation—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 52 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—they are all satisfied, and indeed all are satisfied, by him who worships a maiden. (53)
If one marries off a maiden oneself, sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa are destroyed;
likewise, the killing of a cow, the killing of a woman, and indeed all sin are utterly annihilated.
Mothers, fathers, and brothers from all sides—indeed, all those who are such—one should perform the gift of a daughter to them. (55)
For them, there shall be the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, good fortune, and all prosperity;
they shall dwell eternally in the world of Rudra as the three-eyed Lord Hari.
One shall obtain the fruit of sixty thousand horse-sacrifices;
this is declared to be the Kumārī-kalpa, or one may perform any other [rite]. (57)
Having brought the Baṭuka-pūjana,
the Sandhyā, and the nine maidens, and having worshipped them according to the rules as before, the Hero should bring the nine boys.
The determination of the auspicious time:
[One should worship] Baṭuka, five years old, and Gaṇeśvara, nine years old, with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and ornaments, according to the extent of one's available wealth. (59)

Having worshipped with the understanding that they are deities, one should satisfy them with ritual materials, free from stinginess regarding wealth, for the sake of accomplishing the fruit of one's own purpose. (60)
Having performed the worship for the nine nights in successive order, increasing by one each day,
one should dedicate that worship of the nine nights to Mahādevī.
Having offered betel-leaf and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should dismiss those young maidens;
thus is the worship of the nine maidens performed every year.
Indeed, that virtuous soul who performs this shall attain the favor of the deity;
having obtained his heart's desire, he shall dwell in your presence. (63)
(384) Śakti-worship,
or else beautiful young women who have attained the bloom of youth.
The knower of mantras should worship according to the rules with devotion during the nine nights.
Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, Mahotsukā, Karālikā, Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Durgā, Vaṭuka, and Gaṇeśvara. (65)
One should satisfy them with offerings and other articles as before;
if they are satisfied and endowed with mature exultation, then [the rite is successful]. (66)
The practitioner, having reached a sacred ford (tīrtha), should dwell in the presence of Śiva;
thus, one who observes the vow of an ascetic (yativrata) should worship the Goddess every year.
Whether every six months, every three months, or month by month,
the wise person should worship three, five, or seven [images] with the thought that they are deities.
He shall become the beloved of Śiva and Śivā, his self enriched with all sovereign powers;
or else, the worship of the divine couple is described by another method.
The procedure for the worship of couples is highly recommended during the transition into Libra or Aries, as well as at all other solar transits;
[the couples being] Gaurī and Śiva, Ramā and Viṣṇu, or Vāṇī and the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā).
Śacī and Indra, Rohiṇī and Candra, Svāhā and Agni, Prabhā and Ravi, Bhadrakālī and Vīrabhadra, and also Bhairavī and Bhairava. (71)
Having brought them together with effort, one should worship them according to the previous method,
using their respective names preceded by the three *tārās* and ending with *namaḥ*, in accordance with the prescribed rite.

Having worshipped the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), the seed-syllable of Power (Śaktibīja), the seed-syllable of Śrī, and the threefold Tāraka with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should satisfy them with the principles (tattvas) and so forth. (73)
One should also form couples endowed with mature joy;
when this is done, there is no doubt that the deities of the couples will be pleased. (74)
The gods favor him and grant his heart’s desire, he who performs the worship of the couple with devotion every year. (75)
Endowed with all sovereign powers, he shall dwell in the worlds of Śiva;
on a Friday, he should diligently worship a beloved woman who has reached the prime of youth.

should worship the Supreme Goddess in her chamber of passion.
Having become unshakable oneself, one obtains the *svayambhūkusuma* (the flower of the self-arisen).
For when Śakti is devoid of Śiva, she indeed rains [down] at the very beginning. (42)
That indeed is the supreme flower, known as the Svayambhū-flower;
by the mere attainment of that substance, what on earth cannot be accomplished? (43)
The substance of the Svayambhū-flower is exceedingly difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
she who is in her season by her own will is Śakti, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī herself.
The practitioner must carefully preserve its flower;
he should worship the Śakti with garments, ornaments, and flowers. || 45 ||
When the flower appears at the proper time for one who has been initiated, that indeed shall be the *kulapuṣpa* (clan-flower), which bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 46 ||

I have previously described the [mercury] born from a pit (kuṇḍodbhava) and that born from a cow (golottha). Now, another variety of the pit-born mercury, which bestows accomplishment (siddhi), is being stated. || 47 ||

Having brought forth the auspicious power as previously described according to what is appropriate, and having performed the rites prescribed for his own ritual manual, the practitioner, with a conquered mind, [proceeds]. (48)
Then, having offered food to be chewed and food to be sucked, as well as garments, ornaments, and so forth,
one should worship her temple of love with pure unbroken grains of rice.
One whose mind is itself unshakable should meditate with the nature of desire; by means of pure mantra and medicine alone, one should churn the abode of passion. (50)
For even while she is being churned, the supreme reality arises;
one should diligently grasp that auspicious substance born from the *kuṇḍa*.
These four substances are the cause for the accomplishment of mantras;
among these substances, however, the *svayambhū* flower is the greatest. (52)
In some places it is obtained from the king of the gandharvas, or perhaps not;
having obtained that supreme substance, it is combined with lac juice.
Having prepared a pill from musk and saffron well-mixed with sandalwood— or even with red sandalwood— one should keep it well-concealed.

Having purified the king of mantras according to the sequence previously described and having written it down, the practitioner should worship it with devotion on whichever lunar day he has reached. (55)
Those mantras and vidyās that have been declared to be corrupted by defects such as being "asleep" (supta) and so forth,
become awakened through their application until she returns once more.
When the second [lunar day] had passed, Kalāvatī became visible;
by the sequence of the lunar days, that goddess bestows fruit on the full moon (paurṇamāsī). (57)
There, by the mere performance of the practice— especially during the dark fortnight—
the [deity] who has waned reaches fullness as soon as that lunar day arrives.
Then one should perform the application of the sciences and the mantras and so forth, in such a way that she is never again like that when awakened. (59)
Regarding the description of the fruit of worship:
whoever performs worship daily with *svayambhū* flowers, [he is honored by] the yoginīs, the great nāgas, and those who are rākṣasas and dānavas. (60)
Indeed, kings and all women will always become submissive;
by means of this unbroken formulation, one shall obtain the accomplishment of the Madhumatī.
One may obtain accomplishment through each [deity] individually with flowers and other offerings according to the prescribed rule.
Now I shall describe the supreme worship for desired ends (kāmyapūjana) of the Śākta practitioners.
Regarding the description of worship for specific desires:
one should worship the Goddess, together with all her rays, using red lotuses at night according to the Kula tradition on a yantra drawn according to the prescribed rules.
Within just one month, all the millions of great sins committed by heroes throughout previous births will certainly go to destruction. (64)
Fortune will certainly remain firmly under his control in his house.
One should worship the King of Wheels with *japā* flowers for the duration of one month. (65)
By means of family tradition, at night, with mantra, and through a spirit of devotion, one [destroys] even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in previous births. 66.
One shall destroy [all obstacles] here, of this there is no doubt; the man becomes wealthy.
One should worship Śivā as before with young leaves of the ketakī tree. (67)
One shall destroy even the multitude of minor sins (upapātaka) within a single month;
incomparable good fortune arises for him—of this there is no doubt. (68)
O Supreme Goddess, by worshipping for just one month with delightful hundred-petaled lotuses as before, one shall destroy all sins. (69)
One should worship Śivā with Campaka flowers, as delightful as jasmine, as previously described;
within just one month, she surely destroys the sins committed in previous births. (70)
Or, by the grace of the Blessed Lady, the practitioner of mantra may obtain good fortune;
he should worship the Great Goddess with white lotuses with a spirit of devotion. (71)
As before, one shall destroy all sins, even those committed over thirty lifetimes; by merely a month [of practice], liberation stands within his grasp. (72)
By worshipping the Goddess for just one month with Bandhūka flowers,
the three worlds shall come under his control and all his sins shall be destroyed. (73)
One should worship the Supreme Goddess for exactly one month, as before, with bilva leaves together with aquatic flowers; of this there is no doubt. (74)
He too shall always be prosperous and a remover of all sins, [by worshipping] with mallikā, mālatī, jātī, kunda, and śatapatraka flowers. || 75 ||
One should worship for the duration of a single month with white lotuses and blossoms;
by means of this very sequence of family tradition, one purifies the sins born of a hundred lifetimes. (76)
It destroys the sins generated by the killing of a Brahmin and other such acts; of this there is no doubt.
Liberation is truly in his hand, and he is equal to the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) on earth. 77.
Having worshipped [the deity] for one month according to the previous sequence, with flowers such as the agasti, bāla, bandhūka, java, and red utpala, with a mind focused on diligent effort; 78.
The practitioner of mantra shall bind even the great sinners; he will become visibly possessed of desire.
[He should worship] the Goddess with campaka, pāṭala, bakula, and nāgakeśara flowers. (79)
One should worship with white water-lilies and *sindhuvāra* flowers in the same sequence as before;
his circle of good fortune (*saubhāgyamaṇḍala*) is certain within just one month. (80)
Even one who is burdened with great sins, if he should worship the Goddess with sprouts of *śamī* and *dūrvā*, or with the tender leaves of the *aśvattha* or the *arka* tree, [is purified]. (81)
In one month, it certainly destroys the impurity accumulated over seven lifetimes.
Now, therefore, the means for achieving success in all branches of knowledge is being written. 82.

The practitioner, firm-minded and pure, together with the eight families beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, [should perform this] at a crossroads, or by a river, or at the root of a banyan tree, or at a trident-shaped site. (83)
On the ground of the hungry ghosts, at the root of a bilva tree, in a marketplace, or in a royal palace,
one should write the extensive mantra with vermilion, having it targeted against the person to be subdued.
Then, having worshipped the Kula according to the rules with the Kula-essence (rasa),
and having offered libations, one should remain within that [state] and recite [the mantra] at night with diligence.
Then, indeed, accomplishments arise by means of one hundred thousand [recitations];
furthermore, at night, in a meritorious house, in a garden, or in a temple of the gods. (86)
Having brought the lady of noble birth, one should initiate her with the root mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the agitation of the *kula* in the manner previously described. (87)
The Ritual for Jewel Worship:
I shall now describe in detail the ritual for jewel worship.
The Hero should fashion flowers out of rubies.
p.
413) They should perform the worship of the King of Mandalas as before, with various fragrant flowers smeared with powdered camphor. (89)
Within twenty-one nights, twenty rulers of the earth shall indeed become one's servants, and it shall destroy even great diseases.
The practitioner becomes as radiant as the sun; of this there is no doubt.
The practitioners [should offer] golden flowers adorned with pearls and gems. (91)
They should perform worship with various jewels as before;
within twenty-one nights, the princess will come under one's control.
A hero endowed with artistic grace and beauty is born fortunate upon the earth;
one should worship him with many golden flowers fashioned from coral. (93)
As before, one should worship the Supreme Sovereign according to the sequence of the Kula practice, with various flowers; within seven days, this will be firmly accomplished.
All cruel ones shall become subject to him, and he shall destroy the hosts of his enemies;
likewise, he should worship with golden flowers set within emeralds. 95.
For twenty-one nights, one should worship with various flowers in succession according to the rules;
for him, Bhairavī will unfailingly become a granter of boons.
One should worship the wheel with flowers made of great rubies and joined with gold; by doing so for three weeks, [the result] is certain. (97)
All those Suras shall be under his control, and he shall become equal to Bṛhaspati;
[this is achieved] with flowers fashioned of gold, devoid of diamond filaments. (98)
Within twenty-one nights he shall delude this world;
gods and demons alike will come under his control—of this there is no doubt. (99)
One should worship the discus with sapphire-blue flowers and golden blossoms;
likewise, for twenty-one nights, one may worship it with blue lotuses.
Enemies meet their destruction and the remaining ones indeed become submissive;
the wise one should worship with flowers fashioned from go-meda or with golden flowers. 101.
With *kiṃśuka* and *kunda* flowers, as before, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
within seven days, enemies will be brought under control, and their destruction will ensue. (102)
After three weeks, one destroys the accumulation of great sins;
thereafter, one is worshipped with fresh flowers made of gold and jewels.
Then, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices is certainly attained;
for carnivorous beasts indeed become submissive to him—of this there is no doubt. (104)
A wise person should worship the supreme maṇḍala with flowers fashioned from lapis lazuli, or with campaka and other blossoms; thus, he may paralyze the three worlds in an instant. (105)
By worshipping the Supreme Goddess with flowers that have become *nirmālya* (remnants of an offering) twenty-one times, one becomes a destroyer of great sins.
If one should worship Śivā with golden flowers composed of various jewels, then the gods, sages, serpents, rākṣasas, and others [will be pleased]. (107)
All indeed become submissive within three weeks; of this there is no doubt.
It destroys the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. (108)
One should worship for one month with flowers made of gold;
then, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices is always attained. (109)
If gold, jewels, and flowers are not available, then listen:
the worship must be performed by diligent practitioners using their own flowers as previously described.
Whatever flower is to be offered wherever by the high-souled one,
that very thing should be given in that very place, whatever is to be given with the desire for happiness.
One should worship the Mistress of the Wheel with the very nature of ornaments;
by means of the flowers of the vulva alone, one may thoroughly paralyze the three worlds. (112)
Within just a month, one may destroy even the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes; one shall delude everyone throughout the earth encircled by the oceans. 113.
Now I shall explain the practice for the seed-syllable of Tripurā. The practitioner, firm-minded, wearing white garments and adorned with white perfumes and other such things, [should proceed]. (114)
Adorned with white ornaments, wearing white garlands, and pure, he should be a celibate student riding a white bull and occupying a white seat. || 115 ||
One should worship with white flowers and likewise with white food offerings (naivedya),
such as flour cakes, milk-rice (pāyasa), milk, and various kinds of food.
The lord of heroes, having made his formal resolve, should accomplish the syllable of Vāgbhava using sugar, sweetmeats, and various fruits.
The wise practitioner, while recollecting Vāgīśī, should mutter the Vidyā known as Vāgbhava, which is the practice of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable;
she is white-kneed and adorned with bright flowers and ornaments. (118)
Wearing garments of extreme whiteness and adorned with ornaments of vajras and pearls, her hand is radiant, holding a rosary made of pearls. (119)
Having thus meditated upon Vāgīśī as holding a book, a boon-granting gesture, and bestowing fearlessness, the most excellent practitioner should worship her. (120)
One should meditate upon her as consisting of light, raining down a shower of nectar from the base [of the spine] up to the aperture of Brahmā;
from that, she should be visualized at the tip of the tongue in the form of nectar.
Having meditated, one should recite the mantra the number of times prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
thereafter, even one whose heart is lost, who is vulgar, foolish, or a great sinner [is purified]. 122.
One who is deceitful yet unable to speak even a single clear syllable;
one who is dull, foolish, of extremely poor intellect, whose wisdom has departed, and whose mind is ruined. (123)
He too becomes eloquent, like another Vācaspati,
a conqueror of the pride of the assembly of true scholars, with unimpeded splendor.
He was one who understood the essence of the seven types of reasoning, the meaning of words and sentences, and the ornaments of sound;
he was preceded by [a mastery of] the meters and ornaments that expand the youthful energy [of poetry]. 125.

Through the composition of verses, he becomes a creator of great epics (mahākāvya), one who has reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the established doctrines of Vedānta. || 126 ||
He was a knower of the essence of astronomy, history, and other fields, as well as of Mīmāṃsā and the Smṛtis;
he was a master of the Purāṇas, the Rasas, the Vādās, and many mantras of the Gāruḍa tradition. (127)
He was a knower of the true meaning of the Pātālaśāstra, the Vijñānabhūta-tantra, and other treatises;
he was highly skilled in various arts such as painting and diverse crafts. || 128 ||
He was a knower of the sounds of all languages, an expert in the art of all scripts, a master of various sciences and the Vedāṅgas, and renowned throughout the world. (129)

He becomes a knower of all speech and an omniscient one born upon the earth. Now, the practitioner intent on the art of desire should perform the practice of the seed-syllable of desire in a red chamber.
Adorned with red ornaments, anointed with red perfumes,
and properly clothed in red garments, he stands in the center as the very essence of the Kāmakalā.
One should worship with various red flowers, with food offerings resembling red in color, and with various presents, oblations, saffron, and other such items.
She whose nature is a vibrating radiance extending from the root-center to the aperture of Brahma,
adorned with ornaments possessing the splendor of the Bandhūka flower.
Having reflected thus, the heroic lord, the excellent practitioner, should worship the Supreme Goddess after having recited the Kāmarāja mantra the prescribed number of times.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess; she can delude the three worlds in an instant.
Kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods all come under her control.
Like Kandarpa himself, that lord of heroes was a taker of the pride of women;
and a woman thought of in his mind would come under his control like a servant. (136)
Whether it be a woman, a goddess, or even an asura-woman; a vidyādhara-woman, a kinnara-woman, or a yakṣa-woman, or even a nāga-maiden—whosoever comes within the range of his vision, (137) p. 419)
The daughter of a most fierce king was a perfected maiden (*siddhakanyā*), her mind scorched by the fire of the blazing god of love, difficult to behold. (138)
With moistened eyes and trembling corners, bewildered and overwhelmed by passion, she offers him her entire being and becomes subject to his will. (139)
Resembling the moon reflected in moving water and reddened by the rays of the rising sun, when meditated upon, it agitates [the mind] within the womb of women at that very instant. (140)

That very [goddess], possessing the luster of the color of vermilion, when meditated upon in the heart, likewise effects total delusion, intoxication, subjugation, and the drawing of the mind. || 141 ||
Or else, when applied to the crown of the head and raining down drops of blood through the practice of concentration (*dhāraṇā*),
it brings the entire world under one's control. (142)
Regarding the description of the practice for deluding the three worlds:
one should then swiftly attract even Rambhā and Tilottamā. Having meditated upon a woman of red complexion, [one should then act] by means of her splendor. (143)
One should visualize the Vidyā upon her head as raining down a stream of nectar;
meditating thus, one shall enchant a woman whose mind is inflamed by passion. 144.
In a mere instant, the lord of heroes can bring the three worlds under his control;
through meditation on this Kāmakalā, he becomes like another Pañcakāma.
Then, having sequentially joined Śrīṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, and Hūṃ with Saṃsu, one should fashion the yantra; therein, Kāma shall be situated within Manmatha.
Then, having formed the Kandarpa-sampuṭa and placed it within the interior of the corners,
the excellent practitioner should perform all this known as the Makaradhvaja.
One should direct [the mantra] toward the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) to delude this world;
this practice, named "Deluder of the Three Worlds," has thus been demonstrated. || 148 ||
421) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice for accomplishing the seed-syllable of Śakti; [this is] the practice for accomplishing the seed-syllable of Śakti.
One should contemplate the supreme [deity] within the body, extending from creation to dissolution.
She was raining down streams of flowing nectar, destroying all poison, shining with a golden luster, and possessing a radiance like a flash of lightning. || 150 ||

She holds a skull-cup filled with the shimmering crescent moon, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bears the gesture of primordial wisdom—she who is the very embodiment of nectar. || 151 ||

Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should recite the seed-syllable with golden-colored offerings; reciting it the previously specified number of times, he shall destroy various obstacles. (152)
By remembering her, the Hero attained the state of having a blue throat;
as a minister equal to Vainateya, he destroys the burden of poison. 153.
Nāgas become paralyzed at that very moment by the mere sight [of it];
it destroys bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas—of this there is no doubt. (154)
It shall destroy all quartan fevers and epileptic seizures, as well as evil diseases, malevolent grahas, and the hosts of ḍākinīs who take various forms. (155)
He appears like the Three-Eyed One [Śiva] surrounded by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and vetālas;
or rather, he is seen by one who contemplates this vidyā as complete. (156)
Situated in the center of the navel-circle, the heart-lotus, and the face-circle, she is as clear as a ruby for the practitioner through meditation. (157)
The eightfold sovereignty over that [realm] will swiftly come forth for him;
by remembering her name, the practitioner of mantras shall become beloved by the yoginīs. (158)
The circle of mothers resides within his body; by means of that, he shall become happy along with them.
Having meditated upon the mantra, he will undoubtedly possess sons, wealth, and wisdom. || 159 ||
Having drawn the king of wheels, one should worship it completely;
the Great Goddess then bestows the supreme siddhi of the Khecarīs. (160)
Sixty-four million yoginīs of great splendor, having reached this wheel, abide there; of this there is no doubt. (161)
By the recitation of the complete Vidyā, all beings certainly become subject to one's will;
one may agitate those who dwell in heaven, the earthly realm, and the depths of the netherworld. 162.
By the grace of Mahāvidyā, the lords of heroes indeed cause [all things] to tremble;
through Vāgbhava one attains lordship over speech, and through Kāma one becomes equal to Kāmadeva. (163)
(423) One should offer everything to Śiva by means of the seed-syllable of Power (śakti-bīja) within the three peaks;
indeed, all perfection arises from the recitation of the three peaks. || 164 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 16 ||
The seventeenth chapter:
The Ritual of the Crest-Mantra (Mantraśikhāvidhāna).
Now I shall describe the crest-mantra of all mantras, which bestows spiritual accomplishments.
By the mere knowledge of which, the Vidyā quickly becomes propitious. || 1 ||
The power that resides in the root-aperture (mūlarandhra) in the form of a serpent, and the whirling vortex therein, is called the apāna by the wise. || 2 ||
Following the prescribed method for wild rice, she coos constantly while remaining ever-aroused;
she goes even to the aperture of Brahmā and enters her own abode.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind therein precisely through the sequence of going and returning;
by that, the crest-ornament of mantra is born, which illuminates all mantras.
Just as nothing at all appears in a house filled with darkness,
so too mantras devoid of their crest-syllables (śikhā) never attain accomplishment.
The instruction on the topknot (śikhā) must be guarded by the practitioner at all times;
without this, one does not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
That fourfold creation which is born from a certain womb is dissolved again into that same womb, beginning with the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) and ending with Śiva.
This indeed is the supreme Yonimudrā; its binding has been proclaimed.
By the mere binding of it, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish. (8)
But he who recites [the mantra] in one way and performs it in another way, that mantra shall not succeed; this is the truth, the truth, again and again. (9)
Those mantras that are severed, obstructed, pinned down, or paralyzed;
those that are burnt, terrified, deficient, defiled, or disregarded—[these are overcome by this]. || 10 ||
Those who were divided, possessed by delusion, cursed, and fainted;
those who were old, children, as well as those who were exhausted, mature, and proud of their youth. || 11 ||
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, who are devoid of vigor and abandoned by living beings, are deprived of their portions and cut into pieces a hundredfold. || 12 ||
When employed by the practitioner according to this procedure, all of them, when directed, swiftly become bestowers of both supernatural power (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa). || 13 ||
Whatever auspicious form of syllable is uttered by the mantra-practitioner, each of those is accomplished without effort through the binding of the *yonimudrā*. (14)
Having initiated him according to the rule and consecrated him a thousandfold,
he shall then become an authorized practitioner (*sādhaka*) in this tantra, O best of practitioners. (15)
Even if one were to commit thousands of killings of Brahmins or destroy the three worlds, one is not tainted by sin through the binding of the *yonimudrā*. (16)
He is not defiled by the faults of the sins or merits he has committed;
even after having perpetually committed thousands of innumerable sins. (17)
By the mere utterance [of the mantra] and through the binding of the *yonimudrā*, even corrupt mantras are mastered; how much more so, then, other mantras? (18)
Mantras that abide in their proper place grant boons, and those abiding in meditation bestow fruits;
yet even those well-perfected mantras become enemies when they are deprived of both their place and meditation. 19.
I shall describe specifically that place by which [these states] are accomplished:
the manifest (sakala), the unmanifest (niṣkala), the subtle (sūkṣma), and likewise the manifest-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala).

Śiva has declared that the sixfold locus is differentiated by parts (kalā) yet transcends parts; know that which is "with parts" (sakala) resides in the station of Brahmabandha, and that which is above it is "without parts" (niṣkala).
The mind is named the subtle, residing in the heart, both with parts and without parts; it is situated in the *bindu*, undivided from the creative powers (*kalā*), and beyond those powers above that.
(427) That very power of sound (nāda-śakti), proclaimed by Śiva as possessing the limbs of the kalās,
has entered into these locations; thus the mantras are celebrated as being "situated in their places" (sthānastha).
Having visualized the deity within the heart, the recitation of the mantra arises;
or rather, those mantras should be understood by the practitioner as being established in meditation. (24)
Even a malevolent mantra is mastered if it is encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable Om), provided that firm devotion toward it arises constantly in whoever practices it. (25)
His mantra shall become perfected merely through the recitation as prescribed.
Now, therefore, the cause of success for all vidyās is being written down. (26)

Together with the eight families beginning with the Brāhma family, the practitioner—steadfast in mind and pure—at a crossroads, or by a river, or at the foot of a banyan tree, or at a trident-shaped site; || 27 ||
On a cremation ground, at the root of a bilva tree, in a marketplace, or in a royal palace,
one should draw a large yantra with vermilion, inscribed with the name of the person to be accomplished.
There, having worshipped the Kula according to the rules with the essence of the Kula,
and having offered libations, one should perform the recitation (japa) of that which resides within it, practicing at night.
Then, by means of a hundred thousand [recitations], they indeed bestow accomplishment,
whether at night, in a meritorious house, in a garden, or in a temple of the gods. (30)
Having brought the queen of noble birth, one should initiate her with the root mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the agitation of the *kula* in the manner previously described. (31)
If success is not achieved even when this has been performed, one should practice the root mantra.
Kāmarūpa is the supreme seat among all seats, yielding great fruit. (32)
Whatever worship is performed here even once by the practitioner,
Śivā shall dwell in his body, leaving behind all other sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Beyond that, the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is said to be a hundred times superior,
where the Primordial Goddess Mardinī dwells together with ten million attendants.
That sacred seat (pīṭha) is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness;
from it arise the goddesses, the gods, and the sages born of his being.
All [the deities] manifest here; therefore, the Great Kula is concealed.
That seat (pīṭha) is indeed twofold: concealed and manifest, always [present] for the bound soul (paśu).
It is manifest, hidden, of great merit, and indeed difficult for a practitioner to attain;
yet, O Lord of Gods, it is manifest everywhere and is obtained by those who are beautiful within the Kula. (37)
Even in that case, accomplishment is certainly achieved by means of the *lakṣa* [recitation];
or else, the great method of practice (*sādhana*) is described in another way. (38)
Having brought the Goddess, one should assign her to his body, ending with the pervasive placement (vyāpaka),
and having worshipped her according to the rule with the sixteen services (upacāras). || 39 ||
First, the best of practitioners, having written the mantra as prescribed on the summit of Devīkūṭa, should worship it according to the Kula path.
In the first [circle], one should worship the goddess of the seat with perfumes and flowers;
then, the highly fortunate root goddess together with her attendants.
Having performed one hundred thousand recitations there, one should then enter Uḍḍīyāna;
having worshipped Yoganidrā at that sacred seat (pīṭha), one should then perform the sacrifice.
There, with a concentrated mind, one should mutter the mantra of one's own chosen deity one hundred thousand times;
then, having gone to Kāmarūpa, one should worship Kātyāyanī there.
Having worshipped the Goddess, one should then recite the mantra with a concentrated mind for one hundred thousand times;
then, having gone to Jālandhara, one should first worship Pūrṇeśī.
There too, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind,
he should then go to Pūrṇagiri and worship Caṇḍī with a concentrated mind.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind;
first, one should worship Kāmākhyā upon a seat marked by a drop of vermilion.
Then, at the conclusion, one should worship Mahādevī, the dweller of the Dikkaras.
Having thus recited the mantra of the Mistress of the Pīṭha (Pīṭheśvarī), one should worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā). || 47 ||

Having recited seven hundred thousand times at night with a concentrated mind upon the seven seats, he should then, after completing the count, question the Great Goddess, the most excellent of the Kulas.
"I am indeed your chosen deity; choose an excellent boon.
Then, having prostrated before the Goddess of Devas, he should choose an excellent boon.
If that goddess does not act as previously described,
he should remain unperturbed and devoted to the service of the traditional conduct of his lineage.
Alternatively, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī in all the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
then she herself, who is dear to the best of the Kulas, becomes pleased. 51.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one becomes a master of all accomplishments;
thereafter, having meditated, one should first perform the placement (nyāsa) known as the "interior of the Mātṛkās."
Having performed the placement according to the previously stated rule, one should likewise place the Mātṛkā,
from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, by means of their sequential arrangement.
Furthermore, having performed the five-limbed [prostration], one should practice the fivefold pervasion from the head down to the feet, and then from there back up to the head. (54)
Then, having performed [the ritual] with the root mantra, the practitioner should meditate;
he should contemplate Kālī, who is intent upon the great passion for battle with the mighty Daityas.
In the right [hands] are the discus, the sword, the arrow, and likewise the trident;
in the left [hands] are the conch, the shield, the bow, and the raised index finger.
She was holding a sharp arrow and seated upon a buffalo;
the goddess wore yellow garments and possessed a pair of full, elevated breasts. (57)

Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who is enriched by the splendor of her matted locks and crown and who bestows happiness upon the realm of the ancestors, one should worship her with mental offerings.
One should worship with devotion according to the prescribed rite within the lotus of one's own heart; then, having meditated upon "I am He," one should place a flower upon the head.
Having performed the rites beginning with the placement of the jar and ending with the worship of the pedestal as before, the hero should then worship Sadāśiva.
And having meditated upon the Supreme Deity according to the previously mentioned rite, one should invoke her into the center of the yantra, as envisioned by means of the root mantra.
One should perform the rites of invocation and so forth just as before;
having worshipped Mahādevī, one should then worship [the others] immediately thereafter.
Thereafter, one should worship to the left of the Goddess the previously mentioned family of the Guru;
having recited the Śākta mantra, one should then worship the Gurus and others, as well as Nārada. (63)
On the eight-petaled [lotus], one should worship the goddess beginning with Durgā, preceded by the long vowels.
Durgā is to be known as the first, and Varavarṇinī as the second. (64)
Āryā is the third, and the fourth is Kanakaprabhā;
Kṛttikā is declared the fifth, and the sixth is Abhayapradā.
Having recited the mantras of Kālī and Surāgiṇī according to the sequence previously described,
one should worship the weapons on the tips of the petals in order, using the letters beginning with 'ya'.

Thereafter, one should recite the mantras of the Brahmā-group and so forth, then the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside of that, and then their weapons outside of those; having recited these, one should offer libations according to the prescribed rule.
Then the best of practitioners should worship the Goddess as before;
having offered libations to the Great Goddess, he should perform the recitation of the mantra.

Therefore, I shall now declare the secret convention of the Mother Mahiṣamardinī, for the perfect accomplishment of the Kula practice and for the successful attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (69)
The syllables *bhāntaṃ*, *viyat*, *sanayanaṃ*, *śvetaḥ*, *mardinī*, and the pair *ṭha*—
this is declared to be the eight-syllabled Vidyā known as Mahiṣamardinī.
The eternal one, who is the primordial cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction, must not be taught to anyone; yet, when taught, she brings about spiritual accomplishment. (71)
For one who is exceedingly devoted and pure, she is indeed sought;
then the eightfold group should be bestowed, for his practice becomes fruitful.

The wise practitioner should recite the vidyā beginning with the Praṇava, or he may recite it beginning with Māyā; or likewise, he should then recite it beginning with the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja), or beginning with the Kavaca.
At all times and in all places, the wise one should recite that mantra beginning with *kāma*.
However, for the purification of speech, one should recite that Goddess beginning with *vāgbhava*.
The common science of breath (prāṇavidyā) is Hṛllekhā, the Siddhakhecarī;
the goddess situated before this bestows divine powers and success upon the gods. 74.
Especially in the Kali Yuga, she is the bestower of great siddhis;
she is the liberator from the bonds of Māyā for the gurus and the lords of the Kula. (76)
Therefore, this nine-syllable mantra should be constantly protected with effort.
One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform a fire oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number.
The practitioner should understand that the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of eight hundred thousand recitations;
having performed the recitation according to his capacity and completed it, he should then recite the hymn of praise.
Praise to the Slayer of Mahiṣa: Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World, Primordial One of the Triple City, embodiment of the Three Deities!
O Goddess who grants boons to your devotees, O Slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations be unto you. (79)

O dark-complexioned one with a formidable countenance, salutations to you, O beautiful goddess of the gods, for the destruction of disease and obstacles and for the prosperity of the family traditions. 80.
I bow to you, whose face is gracious with devotion for the Kula, who are the beloved of Śaṅkara’s very life-breath, and whose mouth is filled with blood and flesh. 81.
Having thus praised Śeṣa with this hymn, one should perform the remaining rites as before;
then, having performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), one should carry out the practical application (prayoga).
This great lore (mahāvidyā) should not be given to just anyone;
it may be obtained by those of the highest lineage through the power of their fortune, as the tutelary deity of their family. 83.
When initiated by women of noble lineage, she alone bestows accomplishment; it is not otherwise.
435) Now, the practice of the female messenger (*dūtī*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite of generating the messenger (dūtī).

Whether one is a devotee of Śakti, Viṣṇu, Śiva, or a worshiper of another deity, because of this [practice] one shall quickly attain perfection; it cannot be otherwise even in ten million births. (85)
One who desires the accomplishment of the mantra should perform the union with a female messenger (dūtī);
what need is there for the procedures of recitation and ritual placement, or for the elaborations of meditation, worship, and so forth? (86)
As long as the messenger (dūtī) is not worshipped, how can there be accomplishment?
Having assumed the form of a Gandharva, the practitioner should worship her in the womb. (87)
Having become happy in this world and the next, one shall become a son of a goddess on earth.
In the three triangles reside the three gods: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. || 88 ||
One should always worship Caṇḍikā, the family deity, in the center of the *yoni*;
there, one should worship the Vidyā, the sustainer of the world, with the nectars of the *kula* according to the *kulakrama*.
That man shall become the best of practitioners and equal to Śiva;
wherever worship, recitation, or libation is performed there— || 90 ||
The fruit of that for the performer is indeed infinite; of this there is no doubt, since by entering the womb of a young woman, all perfections (siddhis) shall be attained.
Therefore, the supreme practitioner, adorned with all ornaments and decorated with red garments, should worship in the womb of women. (92)
Out of supreme bliss, at night one should perform worship by means of the five principles;
the excellent practitioner should carry out the ritual assignments (nyāsa) and other rites as prescribed in his own specific manual.
The top of the elephant tusk, fashioned from gold, silver, or other materials,
should be installed in the *arghya* vessel along with water consecrated by the *hetu* mantra.
One should also place a *hūnikā* made of pure linen cloth here;
and one should worship flowers, one above the other, in the midst of the ritual tasks. || 95 ||
First, one should worship the frog, then Rudra conjoined with Kālāgni, as well as Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Ananta, and Varāha. (96)
Having worshipped the earth, as well as the bulbous root, the stalk, the eight petals,
and the filaments, one should then perform worship upon the pericarp.
The practitioner, for the sake of attaining accomplishment, should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in sequence, honoring them as if they were unprecedented. 98.
Having worshipped, in due order, the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Wisdom-Self, one should then likewise pay homage to those who have the form of the Guru. || 99 ||
One who is perfected in the practice of non-duality, devoted to the guru, firm in her vows, intent upon righteous conduct, and endowed with sattvic devotion. (100)
One should fashion [an image] free from malice and deceit, affectionate toward devotees, and endowed with qualities such as cleverness, magnanimity, courtesy, and compassion. || 101 ||
One who is endowed with beauty and youth, possessed of virtue and good fortune, in whom confidence has been inspired by the mind, or who has come to a rendezvous. (102)
Or else, she who had arrived at that very moment, tormented by the fire of passion, smeared with red cloth and adorned with red perfumes; || 103 ||
One should employ a slender woman who possesses fragrant red flowers, who is adorned with all ornaments, and who has been perfumed with excellent incense for the purpose of acting as a messenger.
One who should worship such a [deity] upon a couch of flowers, having performed the network of ritual placements (nyāsa) on his body as prescribed in his own ritual manual; 105.
With a steady mind, one should worship with the sixteen types of offerings;
and having recited the mantra, one should offer fragrant flowers into the center of the sacrificial fire.
One should worship the Mistress of the Kula on a fine couch strewn with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances. (107)
Having always worshipped with devotion, with a steady mind and steady senses,
[one should worship] Baṭuka, Gaṇapa, Durgā, and likewise Kṣetrapāla. (108)
For the sake of attaining success, the practitioner of mantra should worship [the deities] in order starting from the east;
he should worship Kāmeśī at the apex of the triangle and [the other two goddesses] in its center.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the presiding lord of the Kula, as well as Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, and likewise Vāsanta and Madana within the triangle; 110.
Thereafter, one should worship the breasts; then, upon her face, one should worship Kalādhara, [extending] from the right foot up to the head, and likewise from the left head down to the foot.
The best of practitioners should worship the digits (kalās) of Kāma and Soma:
namely Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dūtī, and the charming Kānti. 112.
Vimalā, Modinī, Ghorā, Madanonmādinī, as well as Mohinī, Dīpanī, Śoṣaṇī, and Śaṅkarī. (113)
And Rañjanī, and likewise Kramā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Priyadarśanā;
joined with the sixteen vowels, one should worship these as the arts of love (kāmakalās). || 114 ||
Pūṣā, Ramā, Sumanā, Rati, Prīti, as well as Dhṛti, Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and likewise Aṃśumālinī. || 115 ||
Aṅgirā, Pāvanī, Chāyā, Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā,
Tuṣṭā, and Amṛtā— these are the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon. (116)
Indeed, she should be worshipped with her own [mantric] vowels for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
one should worship Bhagamālinī in her house of passion (madanāgāra).
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable, followed by the word *bhaga*, and then *bhuge*, *bhagini*, *athodari*,
at the end of *bhaga*, and *bhagamāle*, *bhagāvahe*.

O you who are in the secret place of the vulva, O you whose womb is the vulva, O you who cause the vulva to fall [upon others], O you who bring all vulvas under control, O you whose form is the vulva; beyond that [is the mantra]. 119.
One should write all [the syllables] in their true form upon the eternally moist edge of the vulva;
then, one should likewise write "bhagāni me hyānaya ante varade" (O Giver of Boons, bring my vulvas here at the end). 120.

*rete surete atha bhaga klinne klinnadrave tataḥ | kledaya drāvayā'moghe bhagavicce tataḥ param || 121 ||* O you who are in the secret place, O you who are in the most secret place, O Bhaga! O you who are moist, O you whose essence is moisture! Make [her] moist, cause [her] to flow, O Amoghe! O Bhagavicce! [Thus,] thereafter.
At the end of the words *kṣubhaḥ kṣobhaya*, one should then utter the word *sarva*.
One should say *sattvān bhageśvari*, followed by the Vāgbhava syllable (*aiṃ*) and *blūṃ jam* at the beginning. (122)
Bheṃ blūṃ moṃ blūṃ, at the end of which one should utter "heṃ heṃ klinne," and then one should recite:
"Bring all female organs (bhagas) under my control. || 123 ||
One should extract the mantra by uttering "badhū" followed by "hrbleṃ," then "bhuvaneśī," and then "bhagamālini," "bhagamālā," and "nityā," each joined with the suffix "ṅe. (124)
Having worshipped the Great Vidyā Bhagamālā,
the practitioner should then worship the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) in the center, which consists of universal bliss. || 125 ||
One should worship one's own vidyā through the union of the east and west;
therein, there is no invocation (āvāhana), nor likewise the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa).
Having performed the worship according to the rules upon one's own *liṅga*, [one should then recite] the *Tāra* (Oṃ), Bhuvaneśvarī, and the three syllables of Tripurā. (127)
"Salutation to Śiva"—this ten-syllable vidyā has been proclaimed.
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should worship Śiva upon his own liṅga. (128)
One should worship with the names Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Īśāna;
and thereafter, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
Having fully worshipped Śāntyatītā, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure;
having uttered the entire vidyā, one should perform worship within that triangle.
Having offered flowers, incense, and so forth, with his own mind free from conceptual construction, he should form the Sarvasaṅkṣobhaṇī mudrā and move the yoni. || 131 ||

Having placed the two middle fingers in the center and pressed them down by the little fingers and thumbs, one should form the index fingers like staffs with the ring fingers positioned above the middle fingers. (132)
This, however, is considered the supreme mudrā that agitates all;
or else, the mantra-practitioner may cause agitation by means of the mudrā known as the "elephant trunk. (133)
Placing the right hand face downwards with the thumb held straight,
one should extend all the fingers so that they take the form of an elephant’s trunk.

The elephant-trunk gesture (gajahastā) is declared to be the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which bestows spiritual accomplishments; one should utter the garland of bhagas while reciting the seed-syllable of Drāviṇī.
When these two are joined in an unshaken state, the Great Bindu is produced;
it is composed of *rajas*, it is *rajas* itself, and it is consciousness—of this there is no doubt. (136)
Prakṛti is the supreme sovereign, and Puruṣa is said to be the seed;
the union of Śiva and Śakti is indeed Yoga, without a doubt. (137)
The sound "śītkāra" is the form of the mantra, while speech becomes praise;
the embrace is musk, and the kiss is camphor. (138)

Biting with the nails and teeth and so forth, worship with flower garlands and the like, playful dalliance and such, incense and lamps, the pressing of the breasts—these constitute the worship of Śiva. (139)
Know that sexual union is the act of satiation; the emission of semen is the discharge. Having purified oneself with the substance of the Kula, one becomes composed of Śiva and Śakti. (140)
One should offer the nectar of vigor, which is the supreme Brahman, into the lotus-mouth of Rāhu,
within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the three qualities, the supreme abode of the illustrious Bindu.
One who, through the distinction between superior and inferior, is of noble lineage yet honored by all, becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed if he is fickle and intent on reviling others. (142)
Then, having completed the primary rite and taken up an excellent substance,
one should satisfy the Great Goddess and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Śakti.
One should satisfy Śakti with fine garments, ornaments, and other such gifts;
thus, the threefold great worship of Tripurā has been described. (144)
Therefore, one who possesses great wisdom should always remain free from conceptual construction; then, with extensive hymns of praise, one should purify all things. 145 ||
In the sacrifice of the body through non-conceptuality, no fault is found;
how then could there be the killing of a horse in sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha? (146)
(443) All edible things constitute the sacrificial offering:
fruit, milk, clarified butter, honey, *maireya* wine, and sugarcane juice.
That which is made from flour, that which is made from grain, and likewise that which is fashioned on a wheel. || 147 ||
The wise declare that whatever intoxicant arises from the *sahakāra* tree, in its various material forms, must be avoided because it cuts away one's spiritual qualities (*dharma*). 148.
When purified by knowledge, that [rite] destroys even great sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and the theft of gold. (149)
Through worship alone, that knower of mantras becomes free from conceptual construction;
the excellent practitioner should always investigate everything with sound reasoning. (150)
In this world, the gods drink milk and do not eat the blood of cows;
they do not eat fish, O dear one—how then can that [milk] belong to a widow? 151.
Know that just as water is drunk when it is tainted by contact with other things, so too among objects; bring a vessel filled with water for the aquatic creature. 152.
For that water, kept for seven days, remains endowed with life;
there is nothing whatsoever that is not meat, including all such things as milk and the like. (153)
Just as fire always and eternally resides within the śamī tree, so too should discernment be known by diligent practitioners to exist within all living beings. 154.
Just as fire is manifested through the friction of wood and other materials,
and that very wood is consumed by it, so too is the world, which consists of Brahman, [consumed]. (155)
This knowledge is declared to be free from both sin and merit;
it belongs to one engaged in sacrifice and not to anyone else, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
One should avoid everything impure, all base and intoxicating things, and gold and such;
purity arises from the thorough knowledge of dharma and adharma and from purification. 157.
One who knows mantras should investigate feces, urine, the menses of women, as well as nails and bones in their entirety; it is nothing but delusion—of this there is no doubt. (158)
The menstrual blood of a woman is a supreme substance; by it the body is produced. How can there be defilement therein, by which the supreme state is attained? (159)
That which is the seed of the person is called the *bindu*;
the *bindu* is the supreme substance, and this body is of the nature of Śiva. (160)
(445) By means of the Śiva-principle, there is no defilement by bones and so forth in the Vaindava [state].
From that [arise] earth, water, then air, ether, and the moon and sun. (161)
By these [elements], however, the gross body—which originates from semen and blood—is produced;
from the father, three arise: marrow, bone, and sinew. (162)
From the mother, three things are produced: skin, flesh, and blood;
this body is declared by the supreme sages to consist of six sheaths.
The principle that "the purity of the root is the purity of all" applies here:
if the body were pure, then there would be no defect in it. (164)
In every respect, there is certainly no fault in the seminal fluids; therefore, by whom can that which is the pure cause of the body be defiled? (165)
Everything on the path of knowledge is free from conceptual construction and thus beyond reproach;
however, if one should possess conceptual construction, that person becomes a partaker of sin. (166)
Know that food consists of Brahman, for from it all beings arise;
since it is composed of various living souls, by whom can its excrement be defiled? (167)
For various kinds of deities are constantly present within the water;
by what, then, has the urine produced from that water been defiled? (168)
(446) The consumption of cow urine and the eating of cow dung by Brahmins is nothing but a delusion regarding the impurity of excrement and urine; of this there is no doubt. (169)
Everything may indeed be pure, yet one's latent impression (vāsanā) may be contemptible;
therefore, the wise practitioner, purified by reasoning, should investigate this. || 170 ||
From the perspective of ultimate reality, the distinction between the worshipper and the worshipped is false; this entire world has arisen from that which is rooted in illusion.
Furthermore, the distinction between the worshipper and the worshipped is indeed false from the perspective of ultimate reality. (171)
Therefore, with every effort, one should purify [the mind] by means of the path of knowledge;
the practitioner, through sound reasoning, should know that everything is composed of Brahman. 172.
Having concluded the primary rite, one should then take up the most excellent substance;
having gratified the Great Goddess, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
The great threefold worship of Tripurā has been declared;
now I shall describe the supreme ritual for the union with the messenger (dūtī) for all Śākta practitioners. 174.
Having performed the ritual for the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjāvidhi) for the assembly of the female deities as before, the supreme practitioner,
having established the Śakti there, should worship her as well as previously. || 175 ||
Having worshipped the Goddess as described with a spirit of devotion,
one should then, with a concentrated mind, worship the five Kāmas within her. (176)
Māyā, Kāma, and likewise Pūrva, Blūṃ, and Strī in due order; then the seed-syllable of Kāma, Kandarpa, and Manmatha. (177)
And likewise [one should worship] Makaraketana and Manobhava, joined with the syllable *ṅe* and preceded by *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, in due order with perfumes and flowers. (178)
Having performed the worship, one should thereafter offer reverence in the four directions to Vaṭuka, Bhairava, Durgā, and Kṣetrapālaka. (179)
Having drawn a triangular yantra upon its top, the practitioner should worship Bālā herself in the center, seated upon a great corpse-throne. || 180 ||
One should meditate on Gaṇeśa at the crown of the head, the Lord of the Kula (Kulādhyakṣa) at the tips of the hair,
Durgā on the forehead, Lakṣmī on the eyebrows, and Sarasvatī on the tongue.
One should worship Madana dwelling upon the two breasts;
in the mouth, the Moon of Nectar (sudhānidhi); and on the back, the seed-syllable *glūṃ* as previously mentioned.
Resorting to the right side from the head down to the feet, the digits of Kāma (kāmakalā) are to be worshipped in all parts of that Nāyikā’s body. 183.
In that [mandala], there is the worship of the sixteen digits of desire (kāmakalā):
faith, joy, contentment, and likewise fortitude, immediately following that.
Prosperity, Beauty, Charming, Pure, and likewise Joyful. || 184 ||
Moghā, Manobhavakarī, Pramadā, Mohinī, as well as Dīpanī, Śoṣaṇī, and again Vaśaṅkarī. (185)
And likewise, the *rañjanī* [syllables] are the digits of desire, resplendent with their respective vowels.
Then follows the worship of the sixteen digits of the moon; thereafter, the lunar digits are to be worshipped from the head down to the feet. 186.
Pūṣā, Vaśā, Sumanā, Rati, Prīti, Dhṛti, as well as Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and Bahumāyā after her. (187)
Madirā, Śaśinī, Chāyā, as well as Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā, Tuṣṭi, and Amṛtā—these digits of the moon (candrakalās) are to be worshipped. || 188 ||
One should worship in the temple of Madana, adorned with red sandalwood;
having first recited the Bhagamālā mantra, one should perform the worship immediately thereafter.
Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśī, and Kamalā; then Vāgbhava again; then Jaṃ Blūṃ; and thereafter one should utter "Klinne Sarvāṇi. (190)
After that, "bhagāni," then "vaśamānaya," followed by "strīṃ sphrīṃ kledinī" as the seed-syllable, and then "klīṃ klīṃ. (191)
"Salutation to Bhagamālinī, Svāhā!"—thus one should worship her situated in the center of the wheel.
Having worshipped the wheel, one should then worship one's own goddess. || 192 ||
Having worshipped according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as with incense, lamps, and various food offerings, the practitioner of the lineage (kulasādhaka) [should proceed]. || 193 ||
Having performed the salutation, he himself should remove that remnant;
immediately thereafter, he should worship his own Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (194)
Having uttered the root mantra, [one should say] the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśvarī, and the word "namaḥ"; thereafter, one should then say "śivāya. (195)
One should worship that [deity], as well as Puruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmeśvara;
and immediately thereafter, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vidyā.
Then, having recited the complete Vidyā, one should worship Śānti, Śāntyatītā, and the enclosure of the six limbs within the triangle. || 197 ||
Avadhūteśvarī, Kubjā, Kāmākhyā, and Samayā; likewise Vajreśvarī, Kālikā, and Dikkaravāsinī. (198)
There the practitioner should worship Mahācaṇḍeśvarī Tārā;
then, having obtained her permission and having consumed excellent betel, [he should proceed]. (199)
Having deposited one's own *śiva* there with the mudrā called *gajahasta*, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, free from agitation. (200)

With a mind steady and unshakable, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer that recitation to the Goddess immediately thereafter. (201)
One should worship her while she is agitated by the pleasures born of the mind; one may dwell there for a very long time.
Then, having taken the flowing liquid of the moon from that [place], one should satisfy Śivā.
Having offered praise and performed circumambulation, one should then dismiss [the deity].
Having performed the rite of dismissal, one should then satisfy the Śakti.
Having given the sacrificial fee according to rule, as well as food, drink, and other offerings;
by merely performing the sacrifice in this manner, there is no doubt that the mantra will be perfected.
The Sacrifice of the Messenger through Another Method: Now I shall proclaim another unsurpassed sacrifice of the messenger (dūtīyāga).
Having reached the day [of the rite], one should [worship] the Goddess in the vulva according to the prescribed rule. (205)
Having performed worship, one should likewise recite the mantra twenty thousand times;
for such a person, the Great Vidyā Lakṣmī shall become difficult to attain on earth.
Having reached the eighth lunar day of both fortnights,
one should duly invite the Yoni and worship the Yoginī right there.
Thereafter, having worshipped the Goddess of gods, the practitioner, with one-pointed mind, should recite the root mantra six thousand times throughout the day and night. (208)
Having attained the great knowledge, one becomes the son of the Goddess on earth.
Now, therefore, I shall explain another excellent method regarding the performance of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). 209.
One should worship the Goddess, the remover of all suffering, in the vulva;
having addressed the vulva with the words beginning with "bhaga," one should then [worship] the Bhagavatī in the vulva.
From that, one indeed attains the accomplishment of the mantra by reciting it one hundred thousand times;
by two hundred thousand, one becomes a great orator; and by three hundred thousand, a great poet. || 211 ||
By means of one hundred thousand repetitions of the Veda, one becomes a master who has reached the further shore of the Veda;
and by a measure of five hundred thousand, one attains perfection of speech.
By one hundred thousand recitations, he shall attain the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā);
by seven hundred thousand, the man becomes a lord of heroes (vīrendra) and is liberated while living.
Beyond this, I know nothing; he is Śiva himself, without a doubt.
Having duly obtained power, the practitioner of steady mind [attains this]. 214.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, he should then place the root-mantra upon the yoni;
having kept a vigil at night, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with his senses subdued. || 215 ||
Having touched the *yoni*, one should recite the mantra alone for one hundred thousand times with devotion;
the perfection of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) is thereby attained—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (216)
All success is in his hand; this is the truth, the absolute truth, most firmly established.
Or else, it occurs during the equinoxes, as well as at the end of the months and the fortnights.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
or in a cremation ground, or according to one's ability, in the presence of the Guru or Śiva.
Having carefully brought a creeper, one should draw the wheel upon the womb according to the ritual rules,
using saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
The practitioner, with a steady mind, should inscribe the mantra upon it, invoke the Supreme Goddess, and worship her according to the rules with devotion. (220)
One should recite the mantra day and night at the region of the womb of women, one hundred thousand times or more; thereafter, one should perform ten homas for each [recitation]. || 221 ||
Having performed the worship according to the rules with extensive offerings as one's means permit, and having subsequently satisfied the guru, the accomplishment of the mantra arises. || 222 ||
He shall become a great orator, wealthy, and a favorite of the king;
prosperity shall always abide in his home, and eloquence shall certainly reside in his mouth. (223)
On earth, such a hero becomes equal to Śakra and is liberated while living.
453) [Now follows] another method for the production of the messenger (dūtī).
Alternatively, there is another excellent way to employ a female messenger (dūtī). || 224 ||
There, one should establish that female messenger (dūtī) and worship her according to the prescribed rite,
having given her garments and ornaments as is appropriate.
Having fumigated a red cloth, one should make it into a messenger (dūtī) endowed with auspicious marks;
having drawn a lotus on the ground, one should write [the mantra] within a hexagon.
Upon that [liṅga], he should place a woman adorned with ornaments in a secluded spot;
then, he should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and various extensive offerings.
Having conceived her as being in the form of a goddess, one should worship her according to the prescribed rite;
one should then place the mantras of the five arrows upon her limbs in their proper sequence.
One should duly perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the very sequence prescribed in one's own Kalpa;
having initiated [the disciple], one should then worship him with the thought that he is the Goddess herself, using her root mantra.
Or one should worship the Goddess in the vulva, because Śivā consists of the vulva;
likewise, one should worship Kāmeśvarī in the vulva and Vajreśvarī in the navel. || 230 ||
One should worship the Supreme Deity in the heart, the face, and the middle of the breasts;
having always kept the *yoni* unsullied (*akṣata*), one should then recite the supreme Vidyā. (231)
Having performed ten thousand recitations, one becomes a master of all siddhis;
having brought a Śakti according to the rule, one should worship her in the yoni-maṇḍala.
Having worshipped his own goddess, together with her weapons and retinue—
namely Bhaginī, Bhagajihvā, Bhagāsyā, and Bhagamālinī.
She whose teeth are the Bhaga, whose eyes are the Bhaga, whose complexion is the Bhaga, and whose skin is the Bhaga;
she who has breasts like the Bhaga, whose limbs are the Bhaga, who dwells in the Bhaga, and who glides through the Bhaga.
Having worshipped the Goddess Bhagavatī in her private parts with a garland of *bhaga* syllables, [one should employ] the *vāgbhava*, the *kāmabīja*, and the *kamalābīja*. (235)
Having thus offered the three seed-syllables followed by the dative case endings and ending with "namaḥ," and having performed worship, one should thereafter recite the root mantra. (236)
Having performed ten thousand recitations, he becomes intent upon all accomplishments;
he is a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, all-pervading, all-knowing, and a lord.
Now the greatness of the *dūtīyāga* (the ritual of the messenger) is being told in detail. (p.
By taking recourse to the womb of women, all perfections are attained; of this there is no doubt. || 238 ||
This worship of the Mother is secreted in all the tantras;
having performed the ritual of worship in this manner, one shall become endowed with all accomplishments. || 239 ||
He obtains pure speech and becomes the foremost among poets;
having attained incomparable sovereignty, he shall bring the three worlds under his control. || 240 ||
The practitioner is constantly honored by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Devas, Kinnaras, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and human beings. (241)
He is beloved by all, yet extremely difficult even for yoginīs to attain;
in the end, he rejoices with the Goddess herself, resembling the Destroyer of Smara.
Having diligently worshipped the creepers with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and other offerings,
one shall be liberated from all sins and rejoice upon the earth for ten thousand kalpas.
If one gratifies a beloved woman with garments, ornaments, and garlands, he attains incomparable prosperity and shall go to the abode of Pārvatī. (244)
He who feeds a young woman with fish, meat, curd, honey, flour-cakes, milk-rice, and other such foods, shall become a lord of the earth. (245)
He who would please Sundarī through body, mind, or speech shall become the most excellent of practitioners and dear to the Mothers. (246)
If one should see a young girl who is naked in a secluded place,
then at that very moment, one should worship the Goddess, meditating upon her according to the prescribed rite.
And having become beloved by all, he shall be eloquent and a unique poet; this, however, is the secret hidden on earth among all the tantras of all beings.
Having learned everything from the mouth of the Guru, a man becomes equal to Śiva;
indeed, the practitioner who knows the mantra should always be free from conceptual construction.
Having understood the optional and occasional rites, one should worship Caṇḍikā;
herein, the authority belongs only to the initiated, and never to anyone else.
Regarding the various means for the accomplishment of mantras through the script of the elements (bhūtalipi), such as the methods of liquefaction and so forth:
now, in all cases, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times.
Through the conjunction with the three nectars (amṛta), even a wicked mantra becomes effective. || 251 ||
Having encapsulated the mantra with the three nectars— the *bhūtalipi*, *hṛllekhā*, and the triad of *modinī*— he who worships it will, before long, [attain success]. (252)
By reciting it one hundred times in both forward and reverse order, his mantra becomes perfected.
The five short vowels, the conjunct consonants, the void (vyoma), the earth (īra), fire (agni), and Jalandhara [are its components]. (253)

The last, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [of each group] are, in sequence, the five syllables of the classes; together with the letter *va* and the white moon (*śveta-indu*), they form [the seed-syllables]. (254)

This is declared to be the Bhūtalipi, consisting of forty-two syllables; for if a mantra is not perfected through preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and other such practices, it will certainly not succeed.
In that regard, seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed:
melting, awakening, subjugation, afflicting, nourishing, drying up, [and piercing]. || 256 ||
One should perform the cremation [of the mantra] in sequence until the end; then one will certainly become a perfected one (siddha).
One should cause the mantra to be strung together with the very seed-syllable of Varuṇa.
Having drawn the mantra and the yantra with yellow orpiment, camphor, and saffron,
one should write the mantra composed of the names of uśīra and rocanā.
One should place that written [mantra] in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water;
through worship, recitation, and adoration, the mantra, once melted, bestows accomplishment.
If, even after being melted, he is not perfected, one should cause him to undergo awakening;
having encapsulated his name within the Sārasvata seed-syllable, one should recite it. (260)
If success is not achieved even when this has been performed, then one should subsequently subjugate [the target] by means of red sandalwood,
kuṣṭha, turmeric, madana, and realgar.
Having written these mantras upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf, it should be worn around the neck; otherwise, success will not be attained and it will cause him affliction.
One should recite the verses in an alternating sequence of low and high pitch;
likewise, one should meditate upon the deity in that same form of alternating aspects.
Having first written the mantra with milk and then stepped upon it with one's foot,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) day after day with that very same mantra.
