If, overcome by shame, the practitioner becomes distressed, he should then nourish [the mantra];
he should join the three seed-syllables of the Bālā [mantra] at its beginning and end. (265)
Having written the vidyā with cow’s milk and honey, one should hold it in the hand;
nourished by this, it shall become perfected, otherwise one should perform the rite of drying.
One should compose the mantra by interlacing it with two seed-syllables of wind (*vāyu*).
This *vidyā*, written with the ashes of a corpse, should be worn around the neck. (267)
If, even after being dried, it is not perfected, it should be burnt by means of the fire-seed (agnibīja);
that is, each individual syllable of the mantra [should be burnt] with the fire-seed.
In the rite of cremation, one should join [the mantra] from beginning to end, from bottom to top;
having written the mantra with the oil of the Brahma-tree (Butea monosperma), one should wear it.
By wearing it around the neck, the mantra then becomes perfected;
thus one should perform the supreme preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in this sequence.
The Means for Attaining Mantra-Siddhi Without Preliminary Rites and the Like:
Now I shall further explain another cause for the attainment of mantra-siddhi, by which mantra-siddhi may be achieved even without preliminary rites and the like. (271)
The seed-syllable of Ugrāprabhā is this unprecedented pair: Śiva (H), the white-rayed one (S), enriched by the fifth and the final vowels (Ū and AU), which,
when meditated upon for even a moment within the orb of the sun, [destroys all sins].
He destroys bad karma and becomes a king among speakers. || 272 ||
He triumphs over hosts of enemies; in debate, he humbles the kings of speakers; he is a thief of the hearts of beautiful women and possesses long life;
and he composes fine poetry unseen even by the sovereign poets.
Even the state of Madhumati is to be abandoned, how much more so the collection of supernatural powers? || 273 ||
Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra and all the letters of the Vedas into the womb of a noble young woman, [one should avoid those] corrupted by the defects of sleep and so forth.

Having understood the paths both within and outside the teacher's household, knowing the ritual procedures, and being more proficient through the refinement of his mind, he, with a tranquil heart, shall accomplish [his goal]. (274)
O Mother, on the immeasurable and excellent ground that follows the path of the noble ones, may those people who satisfy you with the waters of sacred fords,
with flowers as red as blood, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments— [may they attain their goal].
Having assumed the guise of a young woman, he is meditated upon with the thought that it is indeed he. || 275 ||

Having worshipped you— who are born of a most pure lineage— in the *yonicakra*, he who is devoid of shame and pity serves you with all your renowned retinues preceded by the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*).
Having himself assumed a physical form, he causes agitation among the yoginīs. || 276 ||
O celestial tree, the lord of the gods, the sovereign of the immortals, having fallen due to a curse, touches the central branch while his circle of limbs is like that of a beast.
The Lord of the Family, having joined those two together,
should join that which is to be sought within the enclosure of Manu on the outside.
O Mother, may he who is skilled in your arts, who can assume any form at will,
whose mind is free from evil thought, and who has dispelled the dense darkness of fear and dispute, depict you with threefold edges— like the moon, the source of nectar.
[He is] praised by the vast masses of dust from the soles of [your] feet. || 278 ||
O God, that wise one, the lord of the practice for liberation, having thoroughly understood his own body as consisting of those [elements] worthy of worship, attends upon them;
having extracted the seed and power of those who have shaken off the intoxication of passion.
Thereafter, [he should place] the hard seed-syllable and the world-supporting goddess within that. || 279 ||
If one recites [this mantra], having attained absorption within me, he shall immediately attain the state of the city of the gods (Svarga) and be honored by the hosts of Siddhas.
It is perfectly perfected when joined with Śiva, Bhṛgu, Madapṛthvī, and Śakti, and it has been brought forth from the respective glories of Hari, Hara, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā). || 280 ||
He is known as the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), the agitator of passionate women, the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Fortune (*śrīpati*), and the sovereign of all.
Having joined the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) below the hard [syllable] of Bhṛgu (BHA), and having placed KṢOBHINĪ at its tip, one effects the destruction of the world's fear. || 281 ||
If Vīrasiṃha, who causes agitation within the lineage of noble young women through the state of passion, is recited or even once meditated upon—
having applied the seed-syllable of power (Śakti-bīja) below the pedestal of the intoxication of love— [the goal is attained].
Kubera, who takes the form of Smara, Hara, and Hari, is capable of assuming any form at will. || 282 ||
By the forceful sprinkling of water from the droplets of the lotus-eyes of the deer-eyed women of the enemy clans, the heat of my internal sins was shattered; thus,
the root of greed— the root of Śiva’s and Bhṛgu’s pride— was uprooted along with its very foundation.
If one honors the root of the castes, which is to be sought among the teachers. || 283 ||
Even one who is a lord of treasures, a protector, or a master of speech—if he possesses a mean mind—then this is merely the primary form of sovereignty over the earth.
The nose, free from obstruction and agitation, is to be abandoned in this manner;
above that is the deer-mark; these two constitute the pair of Bhavānī.
He who is uniquely skilled in the foremost gift among all the boons for humanity,
the king of mantras that causes agitation through the dharma of the flower-arrowed god (Kāmadeva),
[worships] the independent Vādirāja, whose head is stainless with dharma.
The seed-syllable of Bhavānī is joined with your *samanaya*. || 285 ||
Even Maheśa is not able to describe both types of celestial chariots; what then can the Lotus-born Brahmā say here with his thousands of births?
He who recites this king of mantras here by means of his own merits [attains them].
She worships her mother with devotion arising from the lotus-feet of you [the Lord]. || 286 ||
Indeed, at no time and for no reason whatsoever does his priceless body ever abandon another man— even one such as me—
whether that instruction was received from the mouth of a guru, from a child, or even from a beast.
Why has even that which was written by one's own intellect suddenly disappeared? || 287 ||
Beyond the city of the enemy of Smara (Śiva), at the shore of the sovereign city of liberation,
he is dissolved in the supreme state through the enjoyments of all auspicious fortune.
In the division of the anus-pura, one should likewise place the seed-syllable of the color black (kālikā), joined with the directions and the color white (dantavarṇa). || 288 ||

If one recites the entire mantra— which is adorned with two eyes, joined with the letter *nā* at the head, followed by the fierce fang (*vikaṭadaṃṣṭrā*), and combined with the seed-syllable— it is the secret, more secret than the secret.
What is there in these three worlds that can be obtained with difficulty? || 289 ||
If one contemplates all that was previously recited in sequence as being within the middle, and that which is beyond speech as the very nature of that middle,
then he alone becomes the solitary one who is the essence of consciousness and bliss.
And in the midst of the forest land, a man [saw] me out of curiosity. || 290 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 17 ||
The Eighteenth Chapter: An Exposition on the Characteristics of Attainment.
Now I shall describe the signs of attainment as they occur for the practitioner.
One might suddenly perceive the fragrance of incense or of flowers.
Or perhaps one always receives kind words even from women;
or the practitioner may, in a dream, mount a bull, an elephant, or a horse. (2)
He too shall become one whose mantras are perfected; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Or, in a dream at night, he may experience union with throngs of women.
Strolling upon the peaks of mountains such as Gaja and others, beholding the king, and likewise seeing the queens and witnessing dance and song. (4)
Likewise, he who in dreams ascends a palace, a bed, or a beautiful mansion, or even a chariot or a boat; || 5 ||
For him there shall be perfect success, and he too shall become Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
[He should avoid] a banner, an image, a king, and likewise blood. (6)
Smeared with blood upon one's own body, likewise smeared with wine;
looking upon wine, or meat, or a woman of lovely smiles.
If a practitioner is surrounded by women in a dream, he will attain the accomplishment of the mantra; this is indeed the truth, there is no doubt. (8)
Whether one eats the flesh of a cow or the flesh of another animal, or should ever obtain it, eat it, or even touch it; (9)
There may be a vision of goddesses, celestial women, and gandharva maidens, as well as the lotus-faces and breasts of women with trembling hips. (10)
The fruit of these, moreover, is supreme and weightier than the greatest;
it consists of their grace, affection, parental tenderness, and a pleasing countenance. (11)
The signs of accomplishment are to be recognized on earth by the sign of accomplishment, if the mind does not waver;
and if, by the power of fortune, the vision of the lineage arises. (12)
Old age shall not befall him, and all perfections (siddhis) will remain in his hand;
likewise, there shall be the eating and the sight of the unseasonable panasa fruit.
Sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, as well as looking upon one's teacher [in such a manner], eating the food of others, and especially the consumption of blood. || 14 ||
Having partaken even of divine food, the practitioner becomes perfected;
he beholds the practitioner in the form of a substance, or the deity itself. (15)
Whether it be a sword or a shield, nectar or a manuscript, a substance of accomplishment, a corpse, or even clothing, ornaments, and so forth— (16)
If the practitioner obtains a red garland or red flowers in a dream, he will truly become a Siddha;
of this there is no doubt, it is certain. (17)
He sees either an elephant or a horse, as well as a Śiva-liṅga;
likewise, he goes to sacred seats (pīṭhas) and other such places, and there beholds the deities.
A garden or a grove, the sight of a Brahmin or an ascetic, as well as a child, a mendicant, or one who is greedy for fruits and the like—[these are auspicious sights]. (19)
Trust in beasts, birds, fruits, and the like is a pleasant sight;
when a task has been resolved upon in the mind, the sound of conch shells and such is a festival.
The sound of flutes and lutes, song, various sights, conversation with strangers, and likewise the discovery of lost property; || 21 ||
The sudden establishment of one's existence, the praise of a person whose origin is unknown, great honor for a lowly man, and the praising of a virtuous deed—[these are the signs of a fool]. 22.
Lack of knowledge regarding the unseen scriptures, being radiant, being beloved by the people, obtaining a mantra, and likewise seeing the daughter of one's gurus in a dream. (23)
The most intense vision of the consorts and the practitioners,
as well as Asugandhi, Sugandhi, Śraddhā, and Puṣpodbhava.

"Even in a dream, one who performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite should understand this during the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* ritual; having thus realized it, the lord of heroes (*vīrendra*) should carry out the practice. (25)
468) Now I shall describe the censurable marks, which are blameworthy and cause the failure of the vidyā.
In a dream, there was a black-clad warrior; by him, a blow and a meeting occurred. || 26 ||
Sexual union with the wives of others, destruction, as well as death;
disturbances in the kingdom, fire, wind, and the sight of creatures that cause slaughter. (27)
The teacher’s attainment of reproach, the provocation of diseases for living beings, faith in the worship of other mantras, and the disparagement of the worship of one’s own deity. (28)
In that place, which is not a family of those who have attained their goals, one should perform the recitation for the sake of attaining one's goal;
thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetreśa, and likewise the Yoginīs.
One should worship at the time of night and always offer a bali-oblation to Kumāra, Baṭuka, Bhadra, Lakṣmī, and the very beautiful Nāyaka.

Having worshipped one’s own power (svaśakti), the Lord of the Five Fields (pañcakṣetreśa), and the Yoginī together with the yogins according to the prescribed rule, one should afterwards present the sacrificial offering (bali).
Then the mantra will certainly become perfected without obstacle;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme ritual application for specific desires (kāmyaprayoga). || 32 ||
Regarding the description of the performance for desired results:
having observed the state of *rajas* (passion) and having worshipped one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) at its source during the deep of night, one should recite the mantra for three days.
The supreme practitioner obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand sacred seats (lakṣapīṭha),
as well as the siddhis of the Vetāla, the sandals, and likewise the sword.
The man who, free from agitation, beholds the blossoming house of the Kula and recites the mantra, obtains collyrium and the *tilaka*. (35)
With a steady mind, the practitioner who performs it for the measure of ten thousand times in complete secrecy shall indeed become a treasury of knowledge.
Whether refined (saṃskṛta) or vernacular (prākṛta), worldly or Vedic—all these come under the control of the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
Alternatively, having eaten on the ground with disheveled hair and being well-restrained, a wise man who recites [the mantra] ten thousand times shall obtain this very same fruit. (38)
The practitioner who, beholding another woman naked, recites the mantra ten thousand times,
shall immediately become the beloved of the Vidyā herself.
By the mere sight of him, the disputants are rendered tongue-tied;
his speech, consisting of both prose and verse, flows forth in the assembly. (40)
Through familiarity with his speech, even the eloquent become rendered mute;
all the wise, filled with joy, bow down before him by his very name. (41)
Or else, by consuming the sacrificial oblation, the fruit shall arise according to the previous sequence;
or again, for one desiring wealth or longing for great sovereignty. (42)
A man who desires to become equal to Bṛhaspati,
knowing the reality (tattva), should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times after having summoned his lineage.
He who indeed performs sexual intercourse shall obtain all fruits;
or else, having placed [the image] upon his hand, he who is firm-minded and pure in heart [shall do so]. (44)
He too attains the state of a poet and goes to immortality,
if he constantly beholds a thousand fertile women on earth.
Then the proponent, having well-established his doctrine, should descend to the surface of the earth;
having meditated upon the Goddess in the Mahācīna-krama, he should worship the Goddess. || 46 ||
One should worship with a flower produced from that tree with a spirit of devotion;
he shall become the family deity, residing in the family tree, and pure.
Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the prescribed rite within the root-lotus of the Brahma-tree,
one should satisfy the assembly of Mothers with the essence of that stream of nectar. (48)
Having seen a lotus, as well as a bilva fruit, a wagtail, a peacock, a chowrie, the solar disc, a sesame flower, and a lake; 49.
Having observed the threefold [signs] and having recited [the mantra] hundreds of times with a pure disposition,
one perceives a serene countenance, pleasant speech, beautiful eyes, and a gracious smile.
The practitioner of steady mind obtains, respectively, fine attire, good fortune, fragrance, association with virtuous people, and happiness itself. (51)
Even the fruit obtained from the Great Cīna method, which is encircled by the great Cīna trees and creepers—
even with a sixteenth part of that fruit, those corpses cannot equal it.
Entering a bower of creepers yields fruit exceeding that of the corpse-seat;
one should recite mantras within those bowers for liberation from great sins. (53)
One who desires wealth should recite the vidyā during union with another's wife;
in the absence of a woman, the best of practitioners should discharge his own semen.
One should recite the mantra undisturbed for the sake of attaining the perfections of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha;
thus, according to the Chinese tradition, Tārā bestows swift results. (55)
Tripurā bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation precisely through the sequence of the Guru’s words;
Kālikā grants the fruit [of practice] precisely through the Mahācīna-krama. (56)
The seventy-seven varieties of Śrīvidyā that have been proclaimed on earth— among them, equality should be understood in the practice of secret sādhana.
The forty varieties of Bhairavī known on earth—among them, their equality should be understood in the practice of the secret sādhana. (58)
Whatever vidyās are Mahācaṇḍās, for them this very procedure is prescribed;
indeed, Chinnamastā bestows accomplishment (siddhi) through the Mahācīna-krama alone. 59.
Whatever Caṇḍikā vidyās there may be, their procedure is recorded as being thus:
as is Kālī, so is Tārā; as is Bālā, so is Unmukhī.
As is Kālī, so is Durgā; as is Durgā, so is Jaṭā.
As is that Bālā Tripurā, so is Tripurabhairavī.
Sundarī is to be known in that same way, and Mardinī is likewise another; whatever other Mahāvidyās there may be, they certainly exist in that same manner. 62.
Through practice, one should bring the mantra and the yantra, which exist separately, to a state of unity.
One should not show this yantra and this mantra even to one's own sons. (63)
Otherwise, one will certainly go to the abode of the King of the Pretas.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme means for accomplishing desired objects. 64.
Having joined the Mātṛkā in forward and reverse order at the end of the root mantra,
one should then address it twenty-five times.
At dawn itself, the wise practitioner should contemplate water as being composed of the *mātṛkās*.
By drinking that water, the mantra-practitioner will quickly become eloquent and a poet. (66)
Within three months there is no doubt; within six months one becomes a lord of speech.
Such a man shall become a performer of desired rites, a great orator, and one who retains whatever he has heard.
From the eighth [repetition], the hero becomes a master of all mantras, honored by the universe, and attains omniscience; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (68)
Within two years, one attains the eight siddhis, and within three years, one becomes Śiva.
One should visualize the root mantra on the tongue in the form of a lamp-flame.
Having visualized the deity as white in color, the practitioner who recites the mantra shall obtain the fruit as previously described after three months. (70)
According to each specific variety [of practice], one shall obtain the corresponding fruit.
Indeed, it should be recited at dawn exactly one thousand and eight times.
Alternatively, I shall describe another method according to the path of the Tantra:
having performed everything beginning with the offering of the bali-oblation as previously described, the wise practitioner [should proceed]. (72)
Having gone to a cremation ground with disheveled hair and naked, one should recite ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (73)
Having worshipped the Goddess in the cremation ground with a thousand essences of the Mahācīna tree and its creepers, the best of practitioners [should worship] the son of a Brahmin.
Then he attains sovereignty, provided he has not fled,
having offered thousands of bilva leaves smeared with the blood from his own limbs.
Having worshipped the Goddess in the cremation ground, one attains equality with Vāgīśa;
the hero, lying on the cremation ground, seated upon a corpse, remains pure.
By reciting the mantra repeatedly, all accomplishments (siddhis) shall then arise;
one becomes a poet, eloquent, wealthy, skillful, beloved by all women, and happy. (77)
The practitioner of Caṇḍikā himself is born [as her equal]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, he may destroy petty rogues, thieves, and malevolent spirits. (78)
Standing in water reaching up to the navel and meditating on the Goddess situated within the sun,
the practitioner who recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times attains prosperity.
By worshipping the Goddess here in a cremation ground with a thousand flowers of the *arka* tree smeared with lac, one attains all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). || 80 ||
One shall become wealthy, powerful, eloquent, and beloved by all women;
one shall be happy—of this there is no doubt—just as Mahākāla has spoken. 81.
One should worship that [deity] with the mantra *śāgaṇeṣiṣmayentraṃ kage lpa mapra bha*;
her limbs are smeared with red sandalwood and she is adorned with red flowers. (82)
Having worshipped her there with jasmine flowers, especially with *javāpuṣpa* blossoms, one should recite the mantra there, O Gaṇeśaliṅga-prabha. (83)
Having worshipped the Goddess there with flowers produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, as well as with the *svayambhū* flower, whoever indeed meditates upon the Deity [shall attain success]. (84)
Having gone there, one may attain accomplishment, or else one shall go without fear;
having worshipped according to the ritual on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days. (85)
After offering the *arghya*, one should then offer the *javā* flower,
*varvara*, sandalwood, the *arka* flower, as well as the white *aparājitā*.
Having offered the *arghya* especially while meditating on the Goddess as situated within the sun,
one should perform the recitation (*jāpya*) one hundred and eight times for each year of one's life. (87)

The practitioner of mantra who is devoted to the morning bath shall attain the perfection of command; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. He should daily recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
By reciting [the mantra], wealth, grain, and other riches will quickly be attained for him;
by this ritual procedure, the practitioner of mantras shall conquer the planets, minor spirits, and enemies. (89)

Now it is said: having performed the ritual of striking with the foot according to the procedure of the Tantra as prescribed in his own Kalpa, the practitioner, whose senses are conquered, [proceeds]. (90)
Endowed with all the ritual substances and intent upon meditation on the deity, whether during a dispute, at the time of recitation, or in any practice of the Kula, (one should act thus). 91.
There, first having drawn a wheel saturated with vermilion powder,
one should worship the supreme Goddess, whose nature is the foot, at night while staying in the house.
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, he should then address her thus:
"Come, O Mother, O Sustainer of the World, you who move amidst the multitude of wandering beings. (93)
"O Lord of the World, tell me [the truth] regarding this night consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Having thus invited him seven times while remaining well-restrained, [he spoke]. (94)
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion and offered the supreme bali-oblation, the practitioner, with a steady mind, should then gaze upon the King of Wheels (cakrarāja). 95.
Having observed the impact of the footstep, one should discern its auspicious or inauspicious nature;
if the sign faces the practitioner, it is favorable for both, even if they are situated on the same side. (96)
The omen on the left as well as on the right is certainly auspicious;
if it is reversed, it will most certainly yield a contrary result. (97)
An auspicious line in the middle of the foot bestows good fortune through its favorable conjunction;
however, the opposite result is certainly obtained from the reverse. 98.
The short [mantra] is said to yield a short fruit, while the long one bestows a long fruit.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the Pādukā-mantra in brief. (99)
"Today I worship the sandal, which is adorned from beginning to end," he should say, "since it is the great power (mahāśakti) among all beings that resides at the tips of the feet. (100)
Therefore, those two feet should be worshipped everywhere by one who desires prosperity;
for the Goddess, who is without beginning or end, exists in the form of the sandals and other such objects.
Residing in the womb of women, this great vidyā, which bestows all accomplishments, is independent; it must never be disclosed.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, the Goddess is the embodiment of withdrawal;
by means of the sequence of emanation, the Mistress of Gods is the promoter of the Great Emanation. (103)
By way of the sequence of maintenance, that Goddess is the one who sets in motion the principle of maintenance;
she is the embodiment of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and she is the embodiment of Mahādeva.
In the first [case], there is the attainment of the Madhumatī through the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama);
at the end, there is attainment by means of the field (kṣetra), and in the remainder, there are the Gandharva births.
In this assembly, the supreme art bestows great liberation;
the sandal is the supreme vidyā, endowed with seven syllables.
Without this, the Great Vidyā does not bestow any fruit at all;
this Great Vidyā has been declared, and it must always be guarded with great effort. 107.
Out of affection for the world, this which is now spoken is indeed very difficult to obtain:
this tantra, its mantras, and likewise its supreme application. (108)
One should not show it even to a son who is exceedingly devoted and has given one his life;
otherwise, one will certainly go to the abode of the King of the Dead. 109.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. 98.
The Nineteenth Chapter:
The Procedure for the Six Acts.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the six acts.
Then follow pacification, subjugation, immobilization, as well as inciting enmity and eradication.
The sixfold ritual of slaying and their characteristics are now described.
Regarding the characteristics of the six rites beginning with pacification (*śānti*): the removal of diseases, malevolent spells, planetary influences, and so forth, is declared to be *śānti*. (2)
The subjugation of all people is declared to be "vaśya," while the obstruction of the activity of all is declared to be "stambhana. (3)
That which generates hatred among those who are affectionate is considered mutual enmity.
Having understood the proper time for the attainment of true knowledge and other factors, one should accomplish the ritual acts.
One should offer the *bali* at a crossroads using the previously mentioned *bali-mantra*,
specifically at night at the beginning of the ritual practice, for the sake of attaining success through Śivā.

481) Having understood the determination of the mantras, yantras, and times for those respective rites, as well as the directions, time, deities, and so forth— for the rite of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*), the sky (*vyoma*) is proclaimed [as the deity].
Vāyu is remembered for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), while Agni is further considered for the rite of killing (māraṇa).
The sky is clear, the wind is black, fire is red, water is transparent, and the earth is yellow;
this is declared to be the form of the five elements.
The orb of the sky is marked with six dots;
that of the wind is triangular and endowed with a svastika; and that of fire is joined with a crescent moon.
The wise know that the mandalas are a lotus for water, a square with a vajra for earth, and they have the appearance of their respective elements.
They say that the colors are colored by their own [qualities] and are also enveloped by their respective names.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are known as the qualities of the elements (bhūta-guṇa). || 10 ||
A wise person should observe the arising of the elements for both sides: there, a sharp-minded one perceives the arising of earth when the breath touches the staff of the nose;
the arising of water when it touches above; and the arising of fire when it has gone upward.
The wind touches transversely, while the path of the wind is touched all around. || 11 ||

The rising of earth is praised for subjugation and immobilization; the rising of water is auspicious for propitiatory rites, nourishment, and other such virtuous acts; furthermore, the rising of fire is excellent for immediate results. (p. 482)

For the performance of killing and rending an enemy, as well as expulsion and suffocation, the impelling force belongs to Air; for pacification and the neutralization of poison, it belongs to Space. || 12 ||
On the day of the rising of each respective element, properly conjoined with its corresponding mandala,
one should prepare the yantra using yellow pigment (rocanā), red chalk (guṇḍikā), and turmeric (haridrā).
Then, by means of house-soot, funeral pyre embers, and poisons,
he [struck] the moon, water, earth, sky, wind, and fire in succession.
The letters shall be the seed-syllables of the mantra for the six rites in their proper order:
for subjugation and the others, the pen should be made of dūrvā grass; for attraction, it should be made of a peacock's tail feather.
[The rites of] inciting hatred, expulsion, and even killing with a crow’s wing;
the description of the deities of the six acts: Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī, in due order. || 16 ||
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship them at the beginning of each rite.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the determination of the proper times for the six rites. (17)
The determination of the time for the six rites:
the fifth, second, fourth, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with Mercury, Jupiter, or the Sun, are highly esteemed for rites of pacification (śāntika).
The sixth, the fourth, and the thirteenth lunar days joined with Jupiter and the Moon are auspicious for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika); likewise, the eighth and the ninth [are also recommended].
The tenth and the eleventh lunar days, as well as the days of Sunday and Friday;
for the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa), the new moon day, the ninth, and likewise the first lunar day.
The full moon day joined with Saturn is for the rite of inciting hatred;
likewise, the fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight when they fall on a Saturday [are used for that purpose]. (21)
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), the lunar day is auspicious, especially at dusk;
specifically, the fourteenth, the eighth, and the new moon of the dark fortnight are likewise so.

The fifth and tenth lunar days, when joined with the day of Mandara (Sunday) or the Sun, are recommended for rites of killing; likewise, they are auspicious when joined with the day of Mercury or the Moon.

The full moon day (paurṇamāsī) should be known as the lunar date for the rite of immobilization (stambhana). One should perform auspicious rites when there is the rising of a benefic planet and during an auspicious planetary period.
(484) Ferocious rites and the act of killing are performed under the asterism Riktārka and during the Mṛtyu-yoga.
The directions are considered to belong to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. || 25 ||
Starting from sunrise, ten ghaṭikās in succession constitute the seasons, beginning with spring; thus they occur day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while spring is for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).

The cool season (śiśira) is known for immobilization (stambhana), summer (grīṣma) is said to be for inciting enmity (vidveṣa); the rainy season (prāvṛṣ) is known for expulsion (uccāṭana), and autumn (śarad) for the rite of killing (māraṇa).
Regarding the determination of the seats and other requirements for the six rites:

for the rite of pacification (śāntika), the skin of a cow or a sheep is used; for subjugation (vaśya) and paralyzing (stambhana), the skin of a tiger or even a rhinoceros is recommended; and for causing enmity (dveṣaka), the skin of an elephant is prescribed. (29)
For the purpose of eradication, or likewise for the killing of a bear or a ram, or even upon the hide of a buffalo or a horse, the most excellent practitioner should perform the rite. (30)
The wise declare that the postures known as Padma, Svastika, Vikaṭa, Kukkuṭa, Vajra, and Bhadraka are the [six] āsanas. (31)
The lord of heroes, having placed both soles of his feet upon his thighs, should bind his two thumbs with his hands in reverse order. (32)
This is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is honored by all;
through the performance of worship and recitation (japa), one should practice the holding of the big toe.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting upright and comfortably, that is called the Svastika posture.
Having placed the two ankles at the sides of one's own navel on the feet, this is called the Svastika; or else, one may place the other hand upon the left [thigh]. (35)

Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the hands placed between the knees and thighs and resting them on the ground, one is established in the "hairs" (romastha), which is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
having firmly bound the two sides of the feet with the hands, one remains perfectly motionless. (37)
This is the Bhadrāsana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons.
Having placed the feet successively upon the thighs, with the toes facing inward toward the knees. (38)
One should assume the hands in the manner described as the unsurpassed Vajrāsana;
then, according to the ritual procedures of one's own specific tradition, one should perform the worship and other rites. 39.
The procedure for the mudrās consists of six mudrās to be known in sequence as those called the lotus, the noose, and the mace;
as well as the pestle, the thunderbolt, the sword, and others, for rites such as pacification and so forth. (40)

Having brought the two hands together facing each other, with the fingers slightly bent and raised, and having joined the thumbs at the base of the palms—this is the Padma-mudrā (Lotus Gesture). || 41 ||
Having joined the tips of the index fingers of both the left and right fists with the tips of the thumbs, one should then cast them toward the tips of the index fingers.
This mudrā, called Pāśa, has been proclaimed by the learned:
having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced. (43)
Furthermore, when the two middle fingers are joined together and extended,
this is declared by the learned and proclaimed as the *gadāmudrā*.
Having formed a fist with both hands, placing the right hand over the left— this is the mace-mudrā (*muṣalamudrā*), which destroys all obstacles. (45)
Having encircled the two ring fingers and bent the two index fingers,
one should [hold] the little finger and the middle finger with the thumb in successive order.
This is declared by the wise and proclaimed as the Vajramudrā;
having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers, they are united with the thumbs.
When the remaining fingers are extended and touched together, it is the sword-seal (khaḍgamudrā).
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored are proclaimed [as its varieties]. (48)
The colors of the deities of the six rites have been declared in their proper order;
whatever be the color of the deity in a given rite, that same color should be used for the offering.
And likewise, the "flower" (puṣpa) should be known for the successful accomplishment of practitioners;
one should perform the acts of killing interspersed with the mantra according to the ritual rule. (50)
The applications within the six rites are:
*grathana* (stringing), *vidarbha* (interlacing), *sampuṭa* (enclosing), and likewise *rodhana* (obstructing).
Yoga and pallava—these are the arrangements for the six ritual acts.
Having interspersed the letters of the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) with the weapons of the yoga-mantras according to the rule,
one should know that this is "grathana" (interlacing), which is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika).

One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between two syllables of the mantra; this very process is known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation. (53)
The *sampuṭa* (encasement) is known as the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra at both the beginning and the end;
this is said by those who know mantras to be recommended for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*). || 54 ||
Rodhana, yoga, and pallava— among these, the mantra at the beginning, end, and middle of the name is considered rodhana;
however, for the performance of incantation to cause enmity (vidveṣa), the excellent nyāsa is recommended.
The name should be at the end of the mantra; this is considered the *yoga* for eradication (*uccāṭana*).
The mantra should be at the end of the name; this is remembered as the *pallava* for killing (*māraṇa*). (56)
489) Regarding the procedure for the rosary among the six rites: it should be prepared with beads made of either pearls or crystal.
Or, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, one should recite it with a mixture [of syllables] during rites of pacification (śāntikarman). || 57 ||
One should perform the recitation for the rites of subjugation and enrichment with coral and red gems;
for the rite of attraction, one should recite with gems corresponding in number to the limbs of the mantra.

Having prepared a rosary from horse teeth strung on hair and thread belonging to the person against whom one seeks to act, one should perform recitation for the purpose of inciting enmity or causing expulsion.
One who desires the destruction of an enemy should fashion a rosary from the teeth of a donkey that has died in battle and perform the recitation [of mantras] with it. 60.
The general rosaries have been described; the specific types were indicated previously.
Having placed the rosary upon the middle part of the ring finger, the practitioner—
In rites of pacification (śāntika), immobilization (stambha), and subjugation (vaśya), one should move [the hand] with the thumb at the front;
for incantations of causing enmity (vidveṣa) and eradication (uccāṭana), one should recite while joining the index finger and the thumb.
For the rite of killing, the recitation is said to be performed by joining the little finger with the thumb;
or one may perform it with the *mātṛkā* [alphabet] according to the injunctions of the specific tantra. (63)
In all ritual applications, one should perform two thousand recitations.
Alternatively, another method for the great *sādhana* is now described. (64)
Regarding the procedure for attraction:
having written the seed-syllable with saffron on a great Chinese tree,
and having inscribed the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) beside it, one should strike it with divine glances.
Afflicted by desire, she goes to that place where her worshipper is;
there, with substances such as yellow orpiment (gorocanā) and the like, she should draw her own moon.
In the midst of that, [one should contemplate] an exceedingly beautiful, charming, and auspicious image, blazing,
accompanied by the name, and interlaced with the seed-syllable of Kāma.
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess from a distance of a thousand yojanas;
that power, never seen before and difficult to attain, quickly approaches.
Then the princess, beautiful in all her limbs, free from fear and shame, auspicious and devoted to the mantra, approaches the practitioner in the proper manner. (69)
When the practitioner, having entered the center of the wheel,
contemplates himself as being ruddy and possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, (70)
The best of practitioners should also contemplate the object of attainment as having become reddened;
by this sequential yoga, he becomes youthful and possesses the form of Kāmadeva. (71)
He is the most fortunate of all the fortunate, the subjugator of all the worlds;
he is characterized by all red offerings, his form established through the mudrās.
Whoever worships the Cakra while interweaving the name of another person will truly become like a servant to that person—whether he be a lord of wealth or even a master of speech. (73)
Having placed the name of whichever woman within the center of the wheel—
whether she be invisible, or even if she be present, or even if she wears the yoga-mudrā— (she shall be brought under control).
By force, he quickly brings forth a yakṣiṇī,
a princess, a nāginī, an apsaras, a gandharvī, or even a celestial maiden.
The wives of their enemies [beheld] a Vidyādharī of divine form, the daughter of a sage, tormented by the heat arising from passion, with her hips and beautiful breasts quivering. (76)

The practitioner, with a steady mind, [should meditate] upon her whose inner heart is pierced by the arrows of desire and whose eyes are restless, through meditation on the great art of passion (mahākāmakalā). || 77 ||
It would agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of Pātāla.
One part of gorocanā and one part of saffron—78.
Then, one should rub two equal portions with sandalwood;
by applying a tilaka from one of them, one brings the three worlds under control. (79)
Having consecrated [the object] one hundred and eight times with the mantra, one shall bring it under control—
whether it be a king, a city, a village, or whatever else is mentioned.
All that will certainly come under the practitioner's control;
having mixed together the flowers from the female organ with the flowers from the male organ, the practitioner [should proceed]. (81)
By offering three handfuls of joined palms, one shall bring the king under control.
Regarding the application of the doll:
the practitioner should draw it on the ground with yellow pigment (rocanā) at a secret location.
Having drawn a beautiful and charming image of Sundarī, richly adorned with elegant ornaments and arrayed in all her finery, (83)
On the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the womb of women,
one should place the name of that woman interlaced within the *Aṅkuśa* Great Vidyā.
The goad (aṅkuśa) is proclaimed as being mounted on fire (the letter *ra*), joined with the upper and lower (*u* and *m*), and pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. || 85 ||
One should inscribe the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) at all the joints of the body;
it consists of the final vowel [AU] situated upon the earth [L], and is endowed with the dot of delight (the nasal bindu). || 86 ||
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), which bestows all accomplishments, has been described;
one should contemplate it, shining like a blue pomegranate flower, within the joints of the body. (87)
Then, having become oriented toward that hope and himself taking the form of the Goddess,
he should bind the *kṣobhiṇī* mudrā and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (88)
Having brought her into the abode of Madana, which consists of nine moving suns,
she was then intensely tormented by the arrows of Kama, her every limb being more affected than even that.
One should thus attract a woman who is single-mindedly devoted, who reels with love, and who is languid with passion, even if she be hundreds of leagues away.
Having obtained a goad in the northeast and having drawn the yantra there,
one should begin on the eighth night and complete it on the fourteenth.
Since a mortal, having filled his mouth with betel, with hair loosened and senses conquered, should himself recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; (92)
With eyes rolling from wine, united with another’s wife, naked as the directions yet adorned by fragrances, sandalwood, and flowers—such was he who was the ornament of his lineage. (93)
If the heroic practitioner worships the yantra by means of her name, she, afflicted by desire, comes to that place where the deity and the worshipper are. 94.
494) Now, the description of another practice: if, at the time of night, one's own family [is situated] upon a couch;
Seated on his left side, adorned with red garments. || 95 ||
Enveloped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, it was exceedingly beautiful; richly adorned with every elegant ornament, its eyes were wide and trembling.

Having written the mantra on the forehead, interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished, [one should visualize it] upon the pair of breasts, which resemble the broad frontal globes of an elephant that has conquered its enemies. (97)
Placing his arm upon her shoulder, while she artfully supported the mountain of her breasts, he—
his mouth filled with betel— directed his intent toward that noble family.
Having performed the recitation of the *kulākula*, one brings [the target] under control at that very moment;
and by means of the name written upon the yantra, one leads that person there at that very moment.
She was situated beyond a distance of a hundred yojanas, dwelling between rivers and mountains,
and guarded by fetters and other means across thousands of other islands.
Her waist was agitated by her breasts, her eyes were like trembling blue lotuses, and her shimmering orb of hips was revealed by her rounded buttocks. (101)
Her heart drawn by the practitioner,
she creeps into the interior of a cavity within the hollow of a door-panel fastened with iron.
If the practitioner of the Kaula path attains such success in attraction, he becomes like a deity moving about, seated within the heart of the practitioner. 103.
Having obtained an offering from a family by some pretext,
whether he be Vīravara, a divine being, or the most excellent of practitioners, at night— (104)
Having taken up his own lineage and the specific station of that lineage,
he should draw the goddess Mālinī, radiant in her deep red garments.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished, interlaced with one's own mantra, in the middle of one's own left thigh using a gem, [one should place it] in its center.
The excellent practitioner, himself in the form of Kāmakalā, having invoked the Great Goddess there—united with the Kāmarāja mantra—and having meditated upon the God, [should proceed]. (107)
Having performed worship, one should then recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
she by whose name it is offered will surely come under one's control.
For when this ritual application is performed, the deities indeed become powerful;
so too do the yoginīs and the apsarases—what need is there to mention others, such as the servants of Yama? (109)
If people perceive him as either a celestial being himself or a hero-siddha, then he will fall from his status. (110)
Therefore, it must be guarded with effort and never revealed;
for if one were to think, "He knows the practice of attraction through this [method]," [the secret would be lost]. (111)
If the practitioner, with a steady mind, [practices] the Svapnavatī-vidyā, then at that moment a certain loss occurs for him in the blink of an eye. 112.
Whether by night or by day, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
having recited it, no obstacle whatsoever shall ever arise on his path. (113)
A hero should perform the practice of the Kula in great secrecy;
he should always act without attachment, especially when performing the extraction of the Kula.
When one watch of the night has passed, the wise man, for the purpose of entering a family home,
[should go] into the midst of water, on a difficult path, or to a grove or a cremation ground.
Whether in an empty house, at the foot of a bilva tree, or in a place devoid of people,
he who goes forth after having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times will certainly succeed.
Furthermore, no obstacle shall arise for him in his practice in any way whatsoever;
or else, having recited [the mantra] eight thousand times in all his undertakings, he shall succeed.
If the steadfast one always proceeds in this way, then no obstacle arises;
nor does an obstacle occur there, nor here, nor anywhere else during the intervals of the recitation.
His journey will succeed and no obstacle shall arise for him;
or else, having written the entire *mātṛkā* on the exterior of the wheel, [he should proceed]. (119)
Having inscribed the name of the person to be accomplished upon a birch-bark leaf, a gold leaf, a silver leaf, or a copper leaf, one should wear it on the left arm.
He is invulnerable to all creatures, especially to tigers and the like;
or else, he should employ his own name joined with the Mātṛkās and adorned with the Cakra. (121)
By means of camphor, saffron, and other such substances, one shall attain freedom from old age and immortality;
or likewise by this same procedure using yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and sandalwood (candana). || 122 ||
Furthermore, whatever is present there, whether stationary or moving, even the entire sphere of water, is pervaded by that which is known by the name [of the deity]. 123.
That great hero, having transcended [all obstacles], will undoubtedly bring [all things] under his control by means of the seed-syllable Kāmarāja, which is the essence of the Great Kāmakalā.
Having placed each [syllable] with one intervening space, one should write the syllables of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended;
one should likewise write the *bali* offering and encircle it with the letters of the *mātṛkā*. 125.
Having placed it within gold, one should wear it on the left arm, or on the crest-lock, or on a garment, or anywhere upon the body. || 126 ||
For she makes the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, her slaves;
she utterly deludes kings, horses, and wicked elephants. 127.
[It destroys] thieves and bandits, as well as those who perform sorcery with mantras, the *cakras* and *vajras*, the *vetāla*, and likewise the irrepressible *rākṣasa*. (128)
The Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas are held in check by her in the form of the Wheel;
whatever is done by that hero, all of that he shall bring under his control like a servant. (129)
Then, one should contemplate the earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, extending to the four oceans, as having entered into the midst of that [fire] and as blazing. 130.
Through the practice of meditation for six months, one becomes like the god of love;
by his very glance he attracts the world, and by his very glance he brings it under his control.
With a glance she agitates a woman; with a glance alone she removes poison.
With a glance she attracts Vāgīśa, and with a glance [she captivates] the All-Seeing One. 132.
By the sight of these four kinds of women, one may destroy irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
This worship of the wheel, mixed with vermilion, should be performed at night. (133)
When one worships the Goddess in this manner—both in the center and in the cardinal and intermediate directions—one performs a great attraction even of women situated at a distance. (134)
Then, having written the entire threefold world according to the sequence of the guardians of the directions upon birch bark with yellow pigment, agallochum, and saffron; 135.
In the midst of that, having inscribed the name of a city, a country, a mandala, or even a district, if one should cause it to be buried in the ground; (136)
O highly fortunate lady, this supreme wheel, which causes agitation before [the enemy], should be held in the left hand, or at the throat, or at the base of the arm. (137)
One should wear it on the topknot, or on a garment, or wherever else one pleases;
it should be smeared with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), and combined with lac (lākṣā) and red resin (laktaka).
Then, having combined the juice of the *dhūstūra* plant mixed with the milk of the *arka* plant, together with the liquid of musk, one should mix them into a single substance. (139)

Having drawn this wheel with the name of whomever the excellent practitioner [uses], for that person, [the effects of] tigers, elephants, disease, enemies, serpents, poison, and so forth [are neutralized]. (140)
There is no fear anywhere from thieves, malevolent planets, water, enemies, śākinīs, or ḍākinīs; nor is there even the supreme fear of black magic (abhicāra). 141.
One should constantly propitiate the Goddess; she will destroy untimely death.
Indeed, no one at all is capable of harming even a single hair of such a person.
Alternatively, one should likewise [draw] the Goddess situated in the center, within the interior of the triangle,
joined with the name below, and anointed with yellow pigment and saffron. (143)
And by causing [the deity] to be installed for seven days, one becomes a servant like a slave;
[one should offer] betel, incense, water, leaves, flowers, fruit, and curd. (144)
Milk, clarified butter, ivory, cloth, camphor, musk, saffron, cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg; || 145 ||
Whether it be fruit, an object, or anything else whatsoever, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and gives it to anyone at all, [that person becomes successful]. 146.
He truly becomes submissive; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Indeed, all women become submissive and become like female servants. (147)
This method of forceful extraction has been explained; it shall not be otherwise.
Having drawn [the diagram] with yellow pigment, one should wear it facing the direction of Indra (the east).
Even one who has become possessed of all limbs becomes mute at that very moment by [this] name;
even one with a thousand faces certainly becomes mute. (149)
Having combined it even with the juice of *mahānīla*, as before, and having burnt it in the fire while facing south, one kills [the enemy] without delay. (150)

Having made [an image] marked with the names [of the enemies] using buffalo and horse dung mixed with cow urine, and having placed it inside a shallow earthen bowl, [the enemy] will be hated by all living beings. (151)
One should draw [the figure] with yellow pigment (rocanā) and the wing of a crow;
it should be properly wrapped in blue cloth and bound with a blue thread. || 152 ||
Hanging in that space, it becomes a supreme expulsion;
[this is achieved] with milk, lac, yellow pigment (rocanā), and the juice of mahānīla.
Having written it, one should carry the wheel; it will bring all castes under one's control.
By this very procedure, one should cast it into the midst of water.

Having attained incomparable good fortune through bathing, drinking, and eating, there is no doubt that one will become like a celestial woman, with a complexion as fair as the earth situated in the midst of this [water]. 155.
If one should worship one's own wheel, having drawn it in yellow pigment while constantly meditating upon the garland of flames, one will always cause agitation within seven days. (156)
Facing the eastern direction, one should paralyze all disputants;
one should draw the wheel with vermilion and worship it while facing the north.
Whatever is here, the world is always subject to the servant;
having drawn a wheel with red ochre, one should worship it while facing westward. (158)
He shall always be one who brings all women under his control and causes them to be deluded,
whenever he worships the Cakra while constantly facing the south. (159)
For whomsoever [this is done], a great loss will constantly arise for that person.
Having become the mouth of fire, the wise man should worship the Cakra at night. (160)
This wheel, when smeared with gorocanā and placed in the midst of milk, brings about paralysis, enmity, disease, the eradication of enemies, and subjugation. 161.
Thrown into the midst of cow urine, it causes the eradication of enemies;
the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) situated in oil is the supreme means for inciting hatred.
The practitioner should perform ten thousand recitations of that which stands in the midst of blazing fire and destroys all enemies during ritual applications.
Having prepared a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the proper injunctions of the scriptures,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) therein upon the consecrated bearer of oblations (havyavāhana).
Having washed it with cow’s milk and purified the salt, the wise mantra-practitioner should offer the powdered substance as an oblation; within seven days, he shall bring people under his control.
One should again offer oblations with rock salt sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter;
by this, one shall bring under control all the gods, Gandharvas, and even the Suparṇas. (166)

A pure prastha of salt, divided separately into five parts, [should be offered] under the name of whichever person; by this very act, that person shall be brought under control, without a doubt. (167)
Taking pure salt mixed with honey, one should offer it as an oblation;
by giving fifty oblations of water, one brings the desired object under control.
I shall now specifically describe the ritual procedure for the worship of Dakṣiṇakālikā and the particularities of the *dakṣiṇā*.
At the end [of the mantra], there are the two *kūrca* and *lajjā* syllables, as well as the first seed-syllable. (169)
Having performed the yoga, one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times to bring [the object] under control.
One should meditate on Kālikā, who has a serpent as her sacred thread and bears the crescent moon upon her head. (170)
The practitioner, having addressed her one hundred and eight times with the previously mentioned substance, [should worship] her who is endowed with a mass of matted hair and resides near Mahākāla.
Having made a tilaka with that very [substance], one shall bring this world under control;
or, having consecrated it a hundred times with a tilaka of gorocanā.
The best of practitioners brings the king under his control in an instant;
there is one seed-syllable at the beginning and likewise one at the end. (173)

The knower of mantras, having joined the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya) with "dakṣiṇe kālike ca," and having uttered the mantra ending in svāhā, there shall be a great summoning (ākarṣaṇa). || 174 ||
Having meditated upon her with red fingers and hands, likewise holding a single trident, and seated at the forefront of Mahākāla, one should perform the rite of attraction.

The knower of mantras draws toward himself that which is stationary, that which moves, and even that which dwells in the depths of the netherworld; what need is there to mention other women on earth? (176)
And one should bring the remainder under one's control; now the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) is described:
[one should visualize] a woman with tawny eyes and black complexion, holding a knife and a skull-cup.
Having meditated thus, one should expel the enemies and perform the recitation as before; at the end, having added two *ṭha*s, one should recite the supreme mantra. (178)

The practitioner, for the purpose of slaying enemies, should meditate upon Kapilā, who is two-armed, holding a flaying knife in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left, standing yet slightly stooped.
The specific results according to the meditative states (*dhyāna*) have been stated; now the general results of Kālī will be described.
Piṅgākṣī causes expulsion, and Kekarā causes flight.
When released, she drives away; when trembling, she terrifies;
when agitated, she causes commotion; and when bent low, she strikes down. || 181 ||
Whether terrified she contracts [the mind], or awakened she awakens it;
whatever state a person meditates upon, there he should also bring it to mind. (182)
In all these cases, the mark of mere intention (bhāva) is to be applied;
one should perform all rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) and so forth at the conclusion of sexual union. 183.
By means of wood from the *dhūstūra* tree and with the feathers of an owl and a crow, the knower of mantras shall destroy his enemies through oblations in the funeral fire (*citāgni*). || 184 ||
For the purpose of exorcising enemies, the knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in a fire made of funeral pyre wood,
according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed the oblation with the feathers of an owl and a crow, one should prescribe [the rite] according to the procedure for inciting enmity, so that they are filled with mutual strife. (186)
By means of an oblation of owl feathers, the miscarriage of a woman’s fetus shall occur;
one should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rite with a measure of one thousand.
Having taken charcoal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday night,
one should wrap it in a black cloth and bind it with red threads.
Having consecrated that [substance] one hundred times with mantras, one should cast it into the enemy's dwelling;
within seven days, his certain expulsion will occur. || 189 ||
Having prepared a bolus smeared with the juice of the great *cīna* tree,
whoever it is in whose name this is offered shall meet death before long.
One should write the mantra upon human bone using turmeric mixed with alkali; having recited it one thousand times at night on a Sunday.
In whosever house it is thrown, death shall come to him within three months;
in a field, there will be loss of crops, and in a horse, a loss of speed.

(507) There is loss of wealth in the treasury, but its depletion occurs in the middle of the village; in the names of those who are hateful and those who cause hatred, there will be great mutual enmity between them. (193)
Regarding the description of the ritual application of the doll:
one should recite the mantra starting from the third day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day.
One should fashion five auspicious and well-proportioned dolls, complete with their primary and secondary limbs.
One [image] should be made from the wood of the tree to be worshipped; another likewise from flour;
another may be made from clay from the hand of a potter; and another likewise from honey. || 195 ||
One should sprinkle salt produced from the five [elements], which has been ground and purified with milk,
and likewise sprinkle it in sequence with milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Then, with water properly mixed with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey,
one should fashion a gentle effigy, beautiful in all its limbs.
Having infused life into the effigy, one should thereafter perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon that pure effigy made of wood, which is clothed in red garments. 198.
One should offer into the sacrificial pit an image made of flour with its face turned downwards, beneath the seat;
likewise, one should place an earthen image at the region of one's own feet.
One should suspend an image made of beeswax from the sky above the sacrificial pit;
thereafter, while touching an image fashioned from salt, one should recite the mantra.

Having taken up fire and kindled it according to the rule with the wood of the *nakṣatra* of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should recite one's own mantra one thousand and eight times. (201)
Having worshipped the deity mentioned in the mantra upon a silver leaf in that [place],
the wise man, having offered arghya with lines of kuśa grass, white mustard, and dūrvā grass, should prostrate himself.
With these mantras, one whose mind is disciplined should [pray] at the beginning and end of the ritual practice:
"O Tvarānandana, O Śatrughna, O Havyavāhana, [come] in the night! (203)
O Jātavedas, Great God, with the luster of molten gold, be satisfied along with me by this oblation offered with mantras. 204.
O Lord of Svāhā, consumer of all, salt, burn the enemy, O slayer of foes!
Oṃ! O Durgā, you who cause the perversion of all things, the entire world is seized and joined with you. 205.
O Great Goddess, salutations to you; O bestower of boons, be a granter of boons to me!
O Great Goddess, composed of darkness, O you of excellent vows, [belonging] to Mahādeva! 206.
O Kriyā, having offered the Puruṣa as a sacrifice, bring him under my control and give him to me!
Oṃ Durgā, Durgā, you are Durgā, the one who is agitated by the obstruction of difficulties! 207.
O Goddess who bears the conch and the discus, O terrifier of wicked enemies, homage to you! Burn my enemy and bring him under my control, O Caṇḍikā!
O Śākambharī, Great Goddess, O sinless one, be my refuge!
O Bhadrakālī, bestower of auspicious success and freedom from the fear of worldly existence! || 209 ||
Slay my rivals, slay them! Burn them, torment them, dry them up!
Having drawn out and cut away their vital breaths with the powers of the sword, Rudra, and the others, bring them here! 210.

O Great Goddess Mahākālī, O Mother who dwells in the place of protection! Having withdrawn the object of the rite and dissolved it, the most excellent practitioner [should dissolve] the effigy. || 211 ||
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer oblations into the kindled fire;
first the right foot, and immediately after that, the hand. (212)
This is declared to be Śivadūtī; after that follows the left hand.
From the middle upwards, the fifth should be [the thumb], and the sixth is said to be half a part.
The seventh part shall be on the left side; such is the sequence of parts remembered.
Or, in ritual applications, there may be a division of seven by seven according to the rule.
Having thus performed the oblation, one should worship the fire and then prostrate like a staff;
the patron should gratify his own preceptor with wealth and grain.
By means of this mantra, the practitioner shall bring under his control both asuras and devas;
how much more so human beings and kings, who are instantly deluded by it? (216)
For the rite of killing, the lord of practitioners should, according to the prescribed rule, place the four previously mentioned effigies as before.
One should prepare another [mixture] according to the procedure to be described:
with the excrement of boars and pigeons, sesame trees, and asafoetida.
With fingernails, hair, and likewise with the dust from the left foot, all ground together with the milk of the *snuhī* plant and combined with the previously mentioned salt. || 219 ||
Having properly fashioned the effigies, the wise practitioner should perform the rite of infusing life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā);
he should then carry out the recitation of mantras, worship, and other rites according to the path previously described. (220)
Then, during the first part of the night when the fire has been kindled,
one should worship Durgā or Bhadrakālī according to the prescribed ritual.
The practitioner, with a steady mind, should mount upon his left foot and hold a sharp weapon in his right hand.
Having repeatedly severed [the bonds], the practitioner of mantra, abstaining from food and with senses conquered,
should offer oblations starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
By this very procedure, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation;
by its application for fourteen days, he shall cause the death of his enemy. 224.
In the case of a cruel disease, an evil planet, or a serpent, one should recite the mantra while touching [the afflicted part] with the index finger;
by remembering the Goddess who bears the trident and the gods, one shall conquer [the affliction] in that very instant.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), encircled by the [mantra] as prescribed, and place it within the heart of an image made of clay from a potter's site. || 226 ||
Having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for it and having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings,
one should kindle the fire and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
By merely completing the prescribed number of recitations, one brings the desired object under control;
thereafter, the knower of mantras, having performed worship, [should act] with pungent oil.
Having performed ten thousand recitations and prepared the *arghya* offering with pungent oil, one should again pour it over those [mantras];
having touched them, one should recite them ten thousand times once more.
One should pierce the enemy army so that in an instant they flee in the ten directions;
when their consciousness is lost, they shall become intent on flight. || 230 ||
Having recited the mantra over a *kuḍava* measure of perfected *guñjā* seeds,
one should secretly cast them into the midst of the enemy army at the onset of night.
Afflicted by great fevers, plagues, and passions, the leader of the army would,
through mutual conflict, fall into a state devoid of all activity.

For the purpose of paralyzing a stone pillar, the practitioner, using substances produced from one hand of a beautiful woman mixed with the dust from the feet of the person to be targeted, shall cause his enemies to be eradicated through the performance of a fire sacrifice (homa).
Having fashioned an exceedingly beautiful wooden image,
one should cut it limb by limb before [the victim], after it has been consecrated and its life-force established within it.

Combined with the fat of a crow and an owl, one thousand and eight [oblations] should be offered into the sacrificial fire in a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. (235) p. 512)
By performing oblations [with these], the enemy's house is destroyed within three days;
by the homa of *unmatta* wood, enemies become intoxicated in an instant.
One should offer as an oblation at night in the wilderness the wing of an owl and a crow joined with the blood of a dog; then the enemy shall become the guest of Death.
The minister, having consecrated an image of the enemy with the breath [of life] established within it,
and having sprinkled water over its limbs which are smeared with poison, should cast it into the water.
One afflicted by fever will quickly be brought to comfort by sprinkling with milk. [Now follows] the description of another method of application:
she is terrifying, holding the three-pronged index finger (tarjanītriśikha) with both arms. 239.
Having meditated on [the deity] as red within the orb of the sun, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
thus, one shall kill enemies along with their kinsmen without dispute.

Having meditated upon her, holding a sword, a shield, and a spear, wrathful, seated upon a lion within a solar disc, the practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra as before; thus he shall destroy his enemies. (241)
Holding a bow and arrows, she was formidable, seated upon a lion, and resembled a blazing fire;
she was discharging volleys of arrows and brandishing her threatening forefinger.
Having meditated thus, one should recite one's own mantra ten thousand times in the midst of water;
one will certainly and swiftly cause the enemy and the hostile army to vanish. || 243 ||
Then, having taken a funeral ball (piṇḍa) for a deceased spirit, one should have a small ball (golaka) made;
having marked it with the name of the person to be subjugated, one fashions an effigy resembling the enemy.
Having placed the living being right there, one should then cast it into the funeral fire;
by performing ten thousand recitations, death shall occur after three nights.
Having fashioned an effigy as before and having recited the mantra according to the previous method,
a great flame shall arise from it by means of a heated copper needle.
Having placed [the mantra] at the secret door, the enemy's death occurs within seven days;
having cast the enemy into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī, the most excellent practitioner [achieves this]. (247)
Therefore, having cast [the object] into the midst of the fire of time, one should perform the burning;
then, having meditated [upon it] at dawn, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
By practicing this for three weeks, the enemy goes to the abode of Yama,
provided it has been written on birch bark, gold leaf, or a neem leaf. (249)
Having performed worship, one should then burn [the effigy] in the fire; that is the destruction of enemies.
Having written the enemy's vidyā on a pure leaf made of fire-wood, [one should proceed]. (250)

Having manifested the mantra within the *puṭa*, having written it upon a cloth, and having performed the *vidarbha* expansion, if one recites it for a thousand births, the *vidyā* will indeed not yield its fruit. (251)

In the absence of a leaf, one should place the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*) inside a vessel made of red sandalwood belonging to a worthy family; having encased it, one should burn it with one's gaze while contemplating it.
If one offers oblations with the left hand, the rite becomes defective; of this there is no doubt.
Having enclosed the mantra within lotus petals, it should be consecrated with the *dīpana* mantras. (253)
One should cast it into water from the midst of clay; in that way, awakening will occur.
The seed-syllables of Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā are proclaimed as the illuminator. (254)
Having written "mṛta" (dead) upon an earthen vessel and having enclosed it with clay from a sacred ford, one should cast it into water; this is declared as the "punarnava" (renewal) mantra. || 255 ||
Just as the newly risen moon consumes that mantra, one should likewise cause that mantra to be burnt by means of the axle-tree (akṣavṛkṣa), even while employing the five weapons. 256.
Having placed a conch, a sword, a discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the Kaumodakī mace respectively into the five products of the cow, one should touch them and recite the mantra.
One should dig five pits in the cardinal directions according to the sequence previously mentioned;
and when the pits are filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the practitioner [should proceed]. || 258 ||
Having performed worship according to the prescribed ritual, one should reside in the center of those lower settlements, preceded by the five sounds. || 259 ||
Having filled [the area] with sand, the mantra-practitioner should surround it on all sides with earth;
there, he should scatter offerings for them in the proper sequence.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
and one should satisfy the poor, the wretched, and others with food and other gifts.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to one's means,
wherever this protection has been prescribed, whether in a country or even in a city.

In the village, the home, and likewise in the field, prosperity always increases; yet there may arise defects such as fire-omens and the like, accompanied by spirits, ghosts, and other such beings. (263)
May the calamities caused by malevolent magic—such as sorcery, enemies, thieves, and the like—not look toward that direction out of fear, being threatened by the command of the deity. (264)
And because this excellent treatise on the procedure for the six rites has been taught, it must be guarded with great effort; otherwise, one shall go to hell. (265)
One should worship Kālī in the heart with effort; their meditation is now described.
One should meditate upon Kālī according to the Kālikā-dhyāna: she whose face is formidable, who has sharp fangs and terrifying eyes. (266)
Wearing a girdle of shimmering emeralds, naked, seated in the vīrāsana posture, and standing upon Mahākāla. || 267 ||
Her cheeks were covered with the roots of the Vedas, her jaws were fierce and devouring,
she was smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads, and her breasts were full.
She causes the entire earth to tremble with the clashing of her drums, which are intoxicated by wine;
she holds a sword in her left hand and severed heads in her right hand.

She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possesses a terrifying face and a flickering tongue, is accompanied by birds and winged creatures, and is adorned with the crescent moon. || 270 ||
It was frequented by auspicious jackals with terrifying howls, arisen at the time of universal dissolution,
and filled with fierce laughter, violent roars, and formidable, violent outbursts.
Having taken up human skeletons, those intent on shouts of victory [honored her] who is always served by the entire multitude of perfected beings (siddhas).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. 19.
The Twentieth Chapter: An Analysis of the Lukī-Vidyā.
Now, the Lukī-Vidyā shall be explained here in brief.
On a Saturday, at midnight, a man who has gone to a crossroads— || 1 ||
Clad in the directions (naked) with hair disheveled, together with the five "M" syllables,
he should worship his own deity according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual.
The practitioner should offer an oblation of black-gram porridge prepared with well-cooked fish;
having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times and offered praise, he should proceed.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, he quickly becomes invisible.
Now I shall describe the accomplishment of the Vetāla; indeed, the Vetāla-siddhi is the most excellent of all excellences.
On a Tuesday at midnight, the best of practitioners, accompanied by his kula and his wife, should go to a cremation ground and take wood produced from a bilva tree.
Having dug [the ground], one should indeed recite the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī one hundred thousand times over a wooden post;
then, O Hero, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) one thousand times right there in the cemetery of the ancestors.
Having extracted a piece of wood and fashioned from that very material a staff marked with a sandalwood slipper,
one should then cast it into a cremation ground on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight dedicated to Durgā.
Having placed a corpse upon it and worshipped his own goddess,
the hero, seated upon the corpse-throne, should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Then one should offer the *mātṛbali* and subsequently address the wooden post:
"Sphreṃ Sphreṃ! O illustrious staff, beloved of the heart of the Yoginīs! (9)
"O Lord, you are held in my hand; carry out my command.
Having thus addressed the Vetāla, wherever he was worshipped, [he remained there].
Then, having quickly left that place, she returned once more to the cobbler, saying:
"Go, go, O illustrious one; O lady of excellent complexion, take these two sandals."
By the mere touch of my feet, he travels a hundred yojanas;
having thus addressed the sandals, one should then place them under the soles of the feet.
