Wherever his desire lies, there he may go at his pleasure. Now I shall describe the attainment of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi) for the benefit of practitioners. 13.
Having taken eight metals and fashioned [a vessel] measuring fifty finger-breadths,
one should write the root mantra there and recite that mantra.
Having first recited the previous mantra according to the previously stated number,
one should thereafter perform a thousand oblations into the great corpse.
Having dug [a pit] and tied [the corpse] to the tip of a living tree, one should cause it to dry;
then, on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight at midnight, being composed, [one should place it] in the midst of a funeral pyre. || 16 ||
Then, having addressed them with affection, one should offer oblations in the cremation ground (pitṛvana) using bilva leaves combined with the three sweets.
From the feet up to the top of the head, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should offer the bali-offering;
at the end of the bali, she is the goddess Mahāmāyā, the slayer of Mahiṣa.
With her face full of excellence, her hands excellent, and her countenance smiling, she approaches;
with a cry like that of a vulture, she raises and brandishes a sword.
O Ghoradaṃṣṭrā, O Mahākālī, you whose form is the sword! Kāṃ Īṃ Ūṃ! O Auspicious One, bring about expansion even from the enemy side! 20.
Thus having addressed him,
the man for whose sake he casts [the offering] is cut again and again, and even though he has gone away, he is drawn back once more.
The Explanation of the Attainment of the Phetkāriṇīs:
I shall describe the great attainment in the *Phetkāriṇī* according to the path of the Tantra:
the Kula-fish, the Kula-substance, the Kula-liquor, and the Lord of Kula. (22)
Having brought [the substance] to the place of the family and diligently offered it to the Goddess,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the worship according to the rules. (23)
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times while standing upon the ground,
a hole is produced there in the earth by a mere puffing of breath.
Or, even if the one to be accomplished resides a hundred yojanas away, he who glides along the surface of the earth goes to that very place. (25)
In this way, even through a narrow opening or a window, the practitioner—
a man who remains unimpaired— passes by contracting his body.
The Narration of the Accomplishment of Khecarī:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the great accomplishment known as Khecarī.
One should write the letters from 'ya' to 'kṣa' in four sections using vermilion powder.
Having encircled one's own cakra with the letters of the Mātṛkā in the center,
one should worship it at night according to the sequence of the Kula tradition.
At that very moment, the best of practitioners certainly becomes a sky-walker (khecarī).
Thus, through the practice for six months, the practitioner becomes a perfected one (siddha). || 29 ||
Then, the six-limbed deities possess rays that are white like crystal, dark blue, black, and reddish-brown, originating from the syllable Oṃ.
The principal female forms hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 30 ||
The six-limbed [mantra] should be applied to the limbs of the deity; this constitutes the rite of sakalīkaraṇa (the making of the whole).
Having formed the añjali gesture as in the case of the arghya offering, the rite of paramīkaraṇa (the supreme transformation) occurs. || 31 ||
O Goddess, for the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), the appropriate mudrā should be employed:
the heart [mudrā] is formed with the middle and ring fingers, and the head [mudrā] is said to be formed with the index fingers.
The *śikhā* is said to be formed by the middle and index fingers with the thumb;
the *kavaca* is declared to consist of all ten fingers, and the *netra* is described as being formed by three fingers.
O Śivā, having recited the mantra with the two fingers previously mentioned, one should then perform three claps;
by means of those very claps, one should bind the directions on all sides.
Then Śiva spoke the Kālikā-kalpa: "In times of distress, in royal palaces, in prisons, or in bondage..."
By remembering her, the goddess Kālikā liberates one from all bonds.
Mahākālī is the essence of consciousness; Maheśvarī is the form of Viṣṇu;
Brahmāṇī is served by gods and Gandharvas; she is the consort of Śiva. (36)
This supreme [power], consisting of the Māyā of Śiva, gives birth to Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
she, who is worshipped by the gods, becomes manifest to the practitioner in an instant through meditation. (37)
O beloved, the power of the goddess Kālikā cannot be described even by one with a hundred crores of mouths, let alone by five; how much less, O beloved? (38)
Our mother, the Goddess, through devotion entered her own body;
first she was Mātā, and likewise Guptā, and is called Māgurī. (39)
She is the helper of my sovereignty, the bestower of success upon me alone;
having attained lordship over me, she is my illustrious mother. (40)
"Without her, O Mother of the World, the universe cannot even stir.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara fainted from delusion and then regained consciousness. (41)
From the body of Śiva, Bhairava was born in a terrible form;
once born, he took refuge at the lotus feet of the Goddess, O Śaṅkara.
Embracing Pārvatī with that form, his body is so described;
through the yoga of meditation alone, one may attain all perfections. (43)
Having worshipped and recited the mantra of Tridaśatāriṇī one hundred thousand times,
the Goddess— who is the source of all ritual applications and who is gracious and affectionate toward her devotees— [becomes manifest].
Worshipped with a thousand arka flowers, she grants boons;
having recited this [mantra] a thousand times at twilight on a Sunday... (45)
One who possesses wealth shall become a lord of sensual enjoyments and beloved by all people;
if one recites it a thousand times, one shall obtain vast poetic talent.
One who honors his lawful wife at night on a Tuesday, even when she is adorned with a hundred red flowers, attains great sovereignty. (47)
Having worshipped [the deity] smeared with red sandalwood paste even with a hundred *brahmapuṣpa* flowers on a Tuesday at midnight, one receives honor from kings. (48)

On the thirteenth lunar day falling on a Sunday, one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should worship [the deity] in the field of Dharma with thousands of lotus flowers.
If one recites it a thousand times, one shall obtain abundant poetic skill;
at the time of night, it bestows sons and provides companionship with the Lord of the Earth’s consort.
Restraining his mind, he should recite [the mantra] upon his own bed at night;
he shall soon obtain long life and a son who brings him under his control. 51.
If one applies a tilaka made from a prastha measure of yellow pigment (rocanā),
consecrated with this mantra one hundred and eight times, [one shall attain success]. (52)
For even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people?
Those who take pleasure in the wives of others, or those who mutter prayers facing the west, [meet with such a fate].
By reciting the Kālikā mantra a thousand times, one indeed becomes wealthy;
by reciting it five hundred times at a crossroads while having disheveled hair and being naked, [the same result is attained].
Even for one who recites it eight times, Kālikā becomes pleased;
having obtained immovable wealth, such a person attains happiness on this earth. (55)
Having perfumed his mouth with camphor during union with his own wife,
he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at night while meditating upon Kālikā.
When well-pleased, Kālikā grants a vision in a dream;
[the practitioner] should always eat fish and meat at night, facing the western direction.
Whoever recites this one hundred and eight times at midnight—truly, truly, again truly—he shall be beloved by the Four-faced One (Brahmā). || 58 ||
One should recite [the mantra] every day for eight days in a forest of Arka trees while seated upon a tiger skin; thus one shall obtain a maiden endowed with virtuous conduct and qualities. (59)
He who recites [the mantra] for three days at night at the root of an Arka tree, with a measure of five hundred repetitions, shall become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). || 60 ||
If one recites it a thousand times at night during an auspicious hour at a crossroads,
the sick person will certainly be freed from a great disease.
A person facing westward, joined with the union of the bhaga and liṅga, performs the renunciation of poverty by means of recitation upon the head. (62)

Having washed the female and male organs upon approaching one's own wife, one should place that water in copper vessels and perform a libation (tarpaṇa) with the root mantra, O Goddess of Gods; thus one obtains great prosperity. (63)
The ritual procedure for the application of the *Saptaśatī*:

for the first chapter, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), Mahākālī is the deity (*devatā*), Nandā is the power (*śakti*), Raktadantikā is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and Fire is the principle (*tattva*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) for the propitiation of Mahākālī.

For the *Madhyama-carita*: Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Mahālakṣmī is the deity (*devatā*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śākambharī is the power (*śaktiḥ*), Durgā is the seed-syllable (*bījaṃ*), and Sūrya is the principle (*tattvaṃ*); its application (*viniyogaḥ*) is in recitation for the sake of pleasing Mahālakṣmī. For the *Uttama-carita*: Rudra is the seer, Sarasvatī is the deity, Uṣṇih is the meter, Bhīmā is the power, Bhrāmarī is the seed-syllable, and Vāyu is the principle; its application is in recitation for the sake of pleasing Sarasvatī.
[She who is] ten-faced, ten-armed, ten-footed, and has the luster of collyrium.
She shone with her vast array of thirty eyes.
With the luster of quivering fangs of noble lineage, she was of terrifying form and fearsome;
she bore a sword, arrows, a mace, a trident, a conch, a discus, and a *bhuśuṇḍi* weapon.
She who held a club, a bow, and a head dripping with blood—
she is that auspicious Śivā, the embodiment of Tamas, [who appeared] in the battle between Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
She has a white face, blue arms, and very white circles of breasts;
her waist is red, her body is red, and her calves, thighs, and knees are blue.
Adorned with variegated ointments, lovely, and endowed with every auspicious fortune, she is to be worshipped as having eighteen arms, yet possessing a thousand arms in battle. (68)
The weapons will be described here, starting from the lower right hand in sequence:
the rosary, the club, the arrow, the sword, the thunderbolt, and the mace. (69)
A discus, a trident, an axe, a conch, a shield, a noose, a spear, a staff, a shield, a lasso, a drinking vessel, and a water-pot. || 70 ||
The Supreme Goddess, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, whose arms are adorned with these weapons, should be remembered at the time of reciting hymns and on other occasions. 71.
Thus, this royal form is considered to consist of all the gods;
by meditating thus constantly, a man shall obtain his own desired object. (72)
She who was born from the body of Gaurī, who is the sole refuge of the quality of purity (sattva),
is declared to be Sarasvatī herself, the destroyer of the demon Śumbha.
And she, possessing eight arms, held a shaft, a club, a trident,
a discus, a conch, a bell, a plow, a bow, and another supreme weapon.
She is to be meditated upon at the time of praise and so forth, and during the slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Now follows the extraction of the mantra from the Vārāhī-tantra:
Then the Tāra, then Vāṇī, then Lajjā, and after that the wife of Fire (Svāhā); then again the Tāra and Vārāhī—this is declared to be the Caṇḍī mantra. (75)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. || 20 ||
The Twenty-First Chapter: A Description of the Stage of the Avadhūta.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the Avadhūta; listen!
Among the four stages of life, the stage of the Avadhūta is the greatest.
Liberation arises for him solely through the practice of the Kula-yoga;
however, if that should not be the case, then listen as I tell you what follows.
And when the state of gnosis has been perfected, one should request one's own Kaulika [consort];
by her command, having worshipped her within the Kula, one shall become liberated.
Then, one should practice yoga within the aperture of the Kuṇḍalinī power,
free from dualities, devoid of egoism, with purified channels and conquered senses.
Seated on a soft seat, intent on the restraint of the six [senses], the yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), should diligently practice yoga. || 5 ||
The Lord of Heroes, having placed both soles of his feet upon his thighs,
should bind the two big toes with his hands in a reversed order. (6)
This is the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is honored by all. Regarding the description of the mūlādhāra-cakra:
it is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the genitals.
One finger-breadth in the middle of that is declared to be the center of the body;
in this body there exists the *kanda*, which is devoid of merit and demerit.
Just as a spider moves within the midst of its web of threads,
so does this vital breath (prāṇa) move below within this root-cakra of the individual soul (jīva).
The individual soul (jīva), mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), is always present within all bodies;
from there, seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) have arisen.
On the outer sides of the spinal column are the auspicious channels consisting of the moon and the sun;
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated on the left and the right respectively.
From the middle of the bulb, the Suṣumnā is well-established between the two;
situated in the middle of the spine, it extends up to the crown of the head.
But when it has become straight, it is called the "Vajra," blazing and supporting the universe;
always hidden on the path to liberation, it is situated at the top of the penis. (13)
Within that [channel] is the channel called Citrā, beloved by yogis;
it is the goddess resplendent with five colors, dwelling within the five elements. (14)
The Goddess, joined with the five deities and illuminating the five principles (pañcatattva),
having filled [the space], she is diverse and exists in the form of a knot.
By her alone everything is strung together, from the root up to the five lotuses;
in the center of that is the Brahma-nāḍī, having the form of a lotus fiber.
In the center of that is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the mouth of Hara, which is Sadāśiva;
between the anus and the penis is the knot (granthi), the supreme junction of the Suṣumnā. || 17 ||
And in the foundation, at the location of the anus, there is a four-petalled lotus, golden-hued, beautiful, with the letters from *va* to *sa*, shining like gold. || 18 ||
A lotus in the form of a bud, joined with the earth-lotus plant;
then [the goddess] resembling the rising sun, holding a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff. (19)
One should meditate upon Ḍākinī, who has three eyes, possesses fierce fangs, is white as milk, and stands holding a sword and a vessel of liquor in her left hands. (20)
The vulva known as Kāmā, beloved by yogins, is situated within the pericarp;
indeed, the god of love named Apāna resides in the triangular base (ādhāra).
In its center is the Svayambhū-liṅga, facing westward;
it resembles the bandhūka flower and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
And [he is] wandering within the womb, cool like the moon;
above that is the Kuṇḍalinī power, coiled eightfold in shape.
Consisting of the eight constituent elements (prakṛtis), she extends transversely downward from the navel;
the goddess stands with her face turned downward and her tail pointing upward, being exceedingly beautiful.
That which begins with the letter 'a' and ends with the letter 'kṣa' is called Kuṇḍalinī;
she has the form of a flash of lightning and resembles a fiber of a lotus stalk.
The all-pervading Self, whose form resembles a sleeping serpent, throbs [within];
it stands eternally covering the opening of the gate of Brahman with its mouth. (26)
By whichever path one must go to the stainless Gate of Brahmā, the breath has entered through the mouth; that is then the mouth [of the path] leading to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (27)
Encircling the self-manifested linga (svayambhūliṅga) on the head like a crest-jewel,
there is no other path, nor a second way, to the Supreme within the body.
In the mūlādhāra is the pīṭha of Kāmarūpa, which is extremely difficult to attain;
there are lotuses with downward-facing petals, beginning from the base (mūla) and so forth in due order.
The fruit of meditating upon that is the Mūlādhāra-cakra.
Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis is the root of the kanda,
four finger-breadths in extent, like the egg of a bird.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon a square and a triangle measuring one finger-breadth;
having thus meditated, the lord of heroes, with steady mind and steady senses, [should proceed].
One should contract the base of the rectum and place the chin upon the heart;
having restrained the nine gates and filled the belly with air.
Then, by means of the seed-syllable of sound (śabdabīja), one should cause that goddess to be firmly whirled;
having pierced her mouth with the wind, one should cause it to become an upward-facing mouth.
Just as one might open a firm door with a key,
so too does the intensely radiant crest-lock of the one whose form is blazing with joy go forth in full splendor. (34)
Then, having pierced the root-cakra, one should split open the gate of Brahmā;
having pierced upward through the linga, one reaches the other lotus (puṣkara).
Through constant yoga of meditation upon the *mūlādhāra*,
there arise, in sequence, paralysis, agitation, leaping like a frog, the abandonment of the earth, and the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
These six qualities arise in human beings. || 36 ||
An excellence of luster in the body,
clarity of voice, brilliance of the digestive fire,
and lightness of the limbs of one's own senses.
Vivacity, health, and freedom from dejection. || 37 ||
The wheel of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhānacakra) is the fruit of that meditation;
it consists of six lotuses beginning with the root, auspicious and resembling buds. The great lotus of self-consecration has six petals and is located at the base of the linga. 38.
Resembling the *bandhūka* flower, it is always filled with water and adorned with the letters from *ba* to *la*,
shimmering with the color of vermilion. (39)
Holding a trident, a vajra, a lotus, and a hand-drum with her lotus-like hands, Rākiṇī is dark-complexioned and endowed with the three eyes.
There, the practitioner should meditate upon her as the sole mistress of the blood-element;
having meditated with a steady mind, he should effect the consecration.
In this world, that mortal who, having cast aside his own mind and the vast web of various unlearned scriptures, has shaken off old age and disease, truly knows.
He lives for a very long time, free from the fear of death. || 42 ||
The constant impurity of the human body brings about the supreme purity of men here,
even in a body as delicate as an autumn lotus petal.
The cool-rayed moon, firmly obstructed, has reached a state of density. || 43 ||
The fruit of that meditation is the maṇipūra-cakra;
above that, the best of practitioners should contemplate with his left and right [hands] a pure triangle situated in the center of a lotus, shining like lightning. (44)
In the center of that, one should meditate upon the god Brahmā, who has a swan for his vehicle,
is red in color, possesses four faces, and has three eyes. (45)
One should visualize a *kūrca* and a lotus, as well as a rosary and a water-pot; and one should always contemplate the syllable *oṃ*, the essence of Brahmā, situated below the navel. (46)
At the navel is a blue lotus called Maṇipūra,
ten-cornered and adorned with the letters from Ḍa to Pha, flashing like a mass of lightning.
There, having clearly visualized Lākinī, who is joined with fire and resides in the flesh-element,
one should then mentally divide that [element] immediately thereafter.
In this place, for one who has fixed their soul upon it, there shall be the attainment of supreme power in the underworld (pātāla-siddhi),

as well as the accomplishment of the peerless sword (khaḍga) and whatever else is desired on earth; [one gains] beauty, the power to leave the ground, and the ability to enter the cities of others, free from old age.
And there is the alleviation of the disease of all suffering, or else the deception of Time itself. || 49 ||
The result of that meditation is the unstruck wheel (*anāhatacakra*);
one should meditate upon the unstruck [sound] in the heart as twelve-petaled and tawny-hued, adorned with the consonants from *ka* to *ṭha*, which possess the brilliance of molten gold. (50)
There, one should visualize Kākinī, residing in the fat, with a yellowish luster and an intoxicated form,
holding in her lotus-like hands the gestures of fearlessness, a *ḍamaru* drum, a trident, and a noose. (51)
One should perceive oneself right there as having a beautiful form, adorned with various ornaments, and like the flame of a lamp, the size of a thumb.
There, one should contemplate the god Nārāyaṇa, the stainless one, resembling pure crystal, adorned by Vāṇī and Lakṣmī. (53)
Mounted upon Vainateya, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, clad in yellow garments, peaceful, and adorned with a forest garland. (54)
One should contemplate the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Pūrṇaśaila in that very place; thereafter, the practitioner of steady mind should cause it to be pierced. 55.
In this place, where their minds are constantly absorbed, the yogis remain stationed in celestial chariots; there, divine women endowed with wondrous forms and beauty cause them agitation.
Yet they possess incomparable knowledge regarding the three periods of time, while the agitation of the city is heard—
There shall be vision from afar, the power of moving through the air, and meeting with yoginīs. || 56 ||
The wheel of purity is the fruit of that meditation;
it is pure, sixteen-spoked, smoke-colored, and located in the region of the throat.
At its end is the white seed-syllable of space (Vyoma), seated upon a golden elephant.
One should contemplate the Śākinī as being within a lotus together with the sky, which is completely adorned with vowels resembling the color of the young morning sun.
She has the form of a skeleton, four arms, five faces, and three eyes;
she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā). || 59 ||
[He saw] a fanged goddess of fierce form, always intoxicated with the passion of honey, and the Lord Ardhanārīśvara, adorned with various jewels. (60)

Having thus meditated upon the auspicious King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), who has the moon as his crest, three eyes, and hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the best of practitioners should pierce it.
In this place, a man whose mind is fully absorbed becomes a seer of the three times, freed from disease;
having conquered old age, his hair becomes as black as collyrium.
He lives for a long time on earth, free from death. || 62 ||
In this state, if a yogi who has restrained his breath and fixed his mind constantly upon this place should become angry, he can shake the entire three worlds;
yet neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Hari-Hara, nor even the sun—
Nor even Gaṇeśa is able to quell this power of his.
The wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), which is the fruit of that meditation,
is two-petaled and adorned by the two auspicious syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
The wheel above the two eyebrows, possessing the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes, is Manonmanī.
One should contemplate every letter joined with the *bindu* within all the lotuses; [one should also contemplate] the other *liṅga*, situated in the center of the womb, as fresh and reddish-orange.
Jālandhara is the great pīṭha; one should contemplate Hākinī there—Hākinī who resides in the bindu and whose nature consists of semen, fat, and marrow. 66.
She holds a rosary, a hand-drum, a skull-cup, and likewise a book;
she bears a bow and a mudrā, is white in complexion, and is endowed with three eyes.
In the center of the lotus is the inner self, whose form is light and who is indeed the cause;
he is the radiance of the syllable Om, resembling the lamp at the end of an aeon, and consists of the entire universe.
Resembling the rising sun, it is the ever-present, imperishable bindu;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the most beautiful lotus at the gateway of agitation (saṅkṣobhaṇa). 69.
For one devoted to the yoga of meditation, there arises recollection of actions performed in previous births;
and therein, in the abode of the *bindu*, there is the capacity for seeing and hearing from a great distance. (70)
Here, with his own mental activity focused upon it, he engages in a dialogue with the image;
he even goes before others and—oh, what a marvel!—rises again from the dead.

Having performed here in this place the mudrā without support (nirālambā), which has been learned solely from the mouth of his own guru, the excellent practitioner, with a steady and sharpened intellect,
through constant practice perceives the entire expanse beyond the abode of the immortals.
He [is] the soft row [of hair] on Viṣṇu, and also the lord of the stars.
At the end of the division, there is a group of six lotuses clearly facing upwards; this indeed comes to pass for the practitioner, of this there is no doubt. (73)
Above that, within the half-moon, is the supreme solar disc;
above that, in the form of the bindu of the letter *ma*, is the lunar disc.
Indeed, with their minds they perceive the Nāda above the Bindu, resembling pure crystal; at the end of the Nāda, they behold the Bull-bannered Lord.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with matted hair and the moon,
clad in a tiger skin, he is situated in their midst, facing downward, together with his Śakti. (76)
For in this place, he is surrounded [by attendants], with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
possessing a gracious countenance, peaceful, and wearing a serpent as his sacred thread.
With the eye of wisdom, they behold Mahādeva above the Nāda;
they see nothing else there, for within that very place dwells the bull-bannered Lord.
Having withdrawn the mind from the three cities, where the vital breath is dissolved—
having fixed the mind established there, they know that meditation to be the Lord.
Having meditated thus, the best of practitioners should then effect a separation;
he who maintains the stalk of Śaṅkhinī, which is established as devoid of pervasive [duality], should proceed.
Resembling an ocean of nectar and extending for a hundred yojanas, it stands in the midst of a sandalwood grove; within that [grove] is a sacrificial altar.
In the center of that, one should meditate upon a crystal lotus facing west,
constantly dripping nectar into the body of the Goddess within the lotus.
(p. 543) Description of the thousand-petaled lotus:
the thousand-petaled lotus is below the visarga.
The moon rests within his mouth like a three-peaked mountain deprived of its deer, its interior filled with a mass of reddened filaments and shimmering networks of rays.
Within that is the extremely subtle Brahmarandhra,
which serves as the support for the channel known as Suṣumṇā;
this very state is divine and most secret.
It is inaccessible even to the gods and must be well-guarded with great effort. || 84 ||

This is the supreme station of the Kula known as Kailāsa, whose nature is the Bindu; there resides Maheśa, the god of gods, who is the swan that destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence within the weapon [of the heart]. He is the primordial god of all beings, whose inner essence flows with a continuous stream of aesthetic delight.
Releasing a stream of nectar, he bestows desired fruits upon yogins and is attainable through yoga. || 85 ||
By the mere knowledge of this state, there shall be no further rebirth for men in this saṃsāra,
through the yoga of continuous placement upon the aggregate of elements.
And there shall be complete power to create and to destroy. || 86 ||
Having fixed one's mind here upon Kailāsa, the supreme abode of swans;
The yogi, freed from disease, having cast down mental anguish and physical affliction, lives for a long time, liberated from death. || 87 ||
In this place dwells that sixteenth digit of the moon, which is free from the states of waning and waxing, eternally risen, and facing downwards; it possesses a luster like that of the morning sun,
and is equal to a single one-hundredth part of a hair-tip split into a hundred strands.
Because of its subtlety, it is like a continuous stream of nectar flowing without interruption. || 88 ||
Beyond this stands the Blessed Lady, the sovereign of the presiding deities of the elements; she is the digit known as Nirvāṇa, curved like a half-moon, situated within the sixteenth [digit].
She is that which is equal to a single part of a hair-tip split a thousandfold.
Because of her subtlety, she who is the mother of the three worlds is like the radiance of twelve suns.
The supreme power of Nirvāṇa, situated above the collection of parts known as Nirvāṇa,
possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns; she is profoundly deep, like the tip of the finest hair,
equal to a ten-millionth part thereof, the mother of all, eternally manifest, and stainless.
It is the supportless, vast stream flowing from the ground of the state of eternal bliss. 90.
Beyond this [power], further beyond the supreme, is the eternal, immeasurable, stainless, perpetually manifest, and actionless state of Śiva, which is the ground of the power of liberation.

Regarding that, some wise ones desire it as "the station of Viṣṇu," some as "the station of Brahman," some as "the station of the Haṃsa," and others as "the stainless station" or "the supportless. (91)

Having repeatedly projected his power from the abode of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] along with his own self into these locations ending with the Command (ājñā), and having meditated upon them in sequence,
he leads it up to the end of Sound (nāda), situated within the interior of the Great Lotus of the Kula dwelling in the sky.
One should meditate upon the primordial Śakti, whose form is consciousness, for the attainment of one's desired fruit.

Having directly drunk the divine flood of nectar— which resembles lac-dye and belongs to the swans dwelling in the great lotus-abodes situated in the sky— one should enter once more into the center of the Kula.
In each and every wheel, one should in due order satisfy those deities with the spreading essences of nectar.
One should satisfy all those beginning with Hākinī, who reside at the lotus-like feet, as well as that Kuṇḍalinī.
Kuṇḍalī, coiled in the shape of a serpent, resides there;
she enters the abode of Suṣumnā through both Iḍā and Piṅgalā. || 94 ||
Through union with Bhairava, one should bring forth the power (śakti) that consists of the bliss of nectar;
one should then slowly inhale the vital breath (vāyu) by way of the lunar path. (95)
One should perform the retention of breath (kumbhaka) according to one's capacity and exhale through the solar path;
one should inhale the air through the solar path and exhale through the lunar path. (96)
It is empty, like the moon in a reflection, subtler than the subtlest, supreme, pervading all, consisting of darkness yet the light of the true abode in the world,
the highest; it is composed of light, omnipresent, and free from all distinctions such as the seen, the unseen, destruction, and difference.
Having meditated upon that state, the best of practitioners have driven away even Death himself. || 97 ||
For one who practices in this way, day after day, it is certain that they are liberated from the ocean of existence through the sufferings of old age, death, and the like. (98)
Regarding the description of the fruit of binding the *yonimudrā*:
That fourfold creation which is born from this womb, and wherein it dissolves again, beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva—[that is this womb]. (99)
This indeed is the supreme *yonimudrā*; its binding has been proclaimed.
By the mere binding of it, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish. (100)
He who recites [the mantra] in one way but performs it in another way is not a recipient of its fruit; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (101)
Those mantras which have had their bonds severed, those that are pinned down, paralyzed, burnt, terrified, deficient, defiled, or disregarded—[all these are overcome]. (102)
Those who were pierced, those possessed by delusion, those asleep, and those in a swoon;
likewise the elderly, children, the mature, and those arrogant in their youth. (103)
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, devoid of vigor and abandoned by their essence,
are deprived of their portions and cut into a hundred pieces.
When employed by the practitioner according to this procedure, they all quickly become effective, bestowing both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa). || 105 ||
Whatever form of syllable the mantra-practitioner utters, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that very thing is accomplished without doubt through the binding of the *yonimudrā*.
Having initiated him according to the prescribed rite and having consecrated him a thousandfold, he then becomes an authorized practitioner, the best among aspirants, in this Tantra. || 107 ||
Even if one were to commit thousands of killings of Brahmins or destroy the three worlds, one is not tainted by sin through the binding of the *yonimudrā*. 108.
Therefore, those who desire merit must practice constantly;
through effortless application, perfection arises, and through practice, one shall attain liberation. 109.
Through practice one attains direct realization; yoga proceeds from practice.
The accomplishment of mantras comes from practice, and the mastery of the vital winds comes from practice. (110)
Through practice, one may thus deceive time and become a conqueror of death;
he who understands this distinction attains the supreme state. || 111 ||
Then, day by day, this living soul goes out eightfold [the size of] a finger-measure of the sun; and due to fasting, it becomes half of that.
If the vital breath flows threefold at the time of sexual union, twofold outside of eating,
and threefold thereafter, it is the movement of the deity.
Then the vital breath (prāṇa) abandons the body;
having brought it to a state of equilibrium with the body, or even if it is deficient, the most excellent practitioner [should proceed]. || 114 ||
Having restrained the downward breath at the opening of the Kuṇḍalinī’s mouth,
the wise practitioner should then join the individual soul (jīva) together with the Kuṇḍalinī.
Having performed the coming and going [of the breath], one becomes accomplished; there is no other way.
Whatever is drunk or eaten, all that is [consumed] at the mouth of Kuṇḍalī.
Having offered [the oblation], one attains accomplishment and is no longer bound by bondage.
549) The Explanation of the Conduct of the Avadhūta.
Alms should be sought, but not for one's own sake, nor from a woman who is a kuṇḍalī by nature. || 117 ||
"O Mother, give me alms; I am a *kuṇḍalin*, and I shall satisfy myself while dwelling in the hermitage of the *avadhūtas*, intent upon the bliss of Bhairava. (118)
I am Bhairava; there is no other, nor is there anything else superior to me anywhere.
All tantras, mantras, and modes of worship have originated within me, and not otherwise.
"I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava; I am intoxicated, the leader of the Kula.
Wearing red garlands and garments, one should always be endowed with the [proper] cause. (120)
Thus, while going for alms, the monk should be intent upon Bhairavānanda, appearing in whatever guise and remaining unobserved by anyone. (121)
Wherever he may dwell, in whatever stage of life, the lord of the family-yogis always remains like one who is intoxicated, mute, or an idiot, amidst the rarefied crowd of people.
Sometimes refined, sometimes fallen, and sometimes like a spirit or a *piśāca*,
the yogi, assuming various guises, should wander upon the surface of the earth. (123)
Just as wind touches everything, just as space is all-pervading,
and just as fire consumes all things, so too is the yogi always pure.
Likewise, food and other things from the house of a barbarian (mleccha) are pure when they have come into the hand of a yogi;
he is neither diminished by sin nor bound by rebirth.
Just as one endowed with the power of mantras is not bitten by snakes while playing with them,
so too the yogi devoted to knowledge is not harmed while playing with the serpents of the senses.
They worship the Great Goddess merely by attracting the limbs of the *kula*, offering whatever may be available there—be it perfume, flowers, betel, or food offerings. (127)
Having mentally cast that out with the water of the lineage from the exterior,
the Lord of the Kula, in the form of the Goddess, unites it within his own self alone.
There is no worship, nor its name, no final goal, and no vows or the like;
I am full, I am Bhairava, I am eternal bliss, and I am imperishable. (129)
I am of the nature of the stainless, I am indeed the changeless Lord;
I am devoted to all scriptures and the master of the meaning of all mantras.
A land more excellent than ours has never been born, nor will it ever be born;
having become one whose very form is bliss, you bring delight to all. (131)
Neither a yogi nor an enjoyer, neither a self nor one who desires, neither a hero nor a steadfast man, nor even a lord of practitioners—
he is a man of discernment, ever full of bliss upon this earth.
The second Maheśa is the one who, having been born after a long time, was shaken off. || 132 ||
In his ears are earrings, on his neck a garland of skulls, in his hand a drinking vessel, and in his mouth, alas, wine;
he has abandoned all ritual action and has cast away all worldly duty into dissolution.
The second Maheśa is the dispassionate Avadhūta. || 133 ||
To the left is a woman skilled in dalliance; to the right is a drinking vessel placed in the center containing the warm flesh of a pig seasoned with black pepper.
The lute upon the shoulder of the true gurus is charming and auspicious; the Kaula Dharma is an extremely profound elaboration, inaccessible even to yogis. (134)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Jñānānanda. 21.
